# PEG-LEG GREG — BOOK II

**Manuscript-only NotebookLM source. Chapters 83–180.**

---

CHAPTER EIGHTY-THREE

I had one day to prepare for a date. This was too much time. If Lyssa had said, Come now, I would have gone. Crutches. Blue shirt. Hair doing whatever it wanted. Done. Instead I had a full day in which to become stupid.

I discovered this after breakfast when I found myself standing in front of the little mirror downstairs and turning my head left, then right, as if a different angle might improve the beard. It did not.

The beard had reached a length where it was no longer technically stubble and had therefore acquired responsibility. I had trimmed it myself three days ago. This had been a mistake. Not a large mistake. No bleeding. No missing patch. Just enough unevenness that I could see it every time I looked directly at my own face.

The keeper came through carrying a bucket. She stopped. I stopped looking at myself. She looked at the mirror, then at me.

“No.”

“I said nothing.”

“You were thinking loudly.”

“That is not possible.”

“It is when you stare at your beard like it owes you money.”

I touched the left side. She sighed.

“Go pay somebody.”

“I can fix it.”

“You already did.”

Rude. Correct. I checked the dressing before deciding anything. Dry. No heat I could detect. No spreading redness. Swelling low after sleep. Right shoulder mildly stiff. Hands tender but intact. A haircut was medically unnecessary.

Good.

I went.

*

The barber was three streets farther than I remembered. Or the street was longer on crutches. Probably that. I could have hired a cart for three streets. I did not. This was not courage. The weather was cool, the paving mostly even, and I wanted to move.

So I moved. Slowly. Carrow had discovered several new ways to be in my way since I acquired crutches. Handcarts stopped at corners. Dogs slept exactly where a crutch tip wanted to land. People walking three abreast developed a profound philosophical commitment to remaining three abreast until the last possible moment.

Most moved. One man did not see me until he nearly clipped my right crutch with a basket. He apologized. I said fine. It was fine. Nothing happened. Useful category. The barber had one chair with arms and one without. I chose without because the arms interfered with crutches, then realized I had to get back out of it afterward.

Fine. He tucked cloth around my neck and asked, “Short?”

“Less stupid.”

He looked at my beard in the mirror.

“Hair or beard?”

“Yes.”

That earned a grunt.

Good.

I had spent years letting healers cut into me, artificers attach things to equipment I was wearing, armorers adjust straps while I stood inside metal, and one memorable field surgeon remove part of an arrow while explaining that the rest was staying until morning.

Apparently scissors behind my ear were where trust became difficult. I watched his hands in the mirror. He noticed.

“Hold still.”

“I am.”

“Your eyes aren't.”

“My eyes are not attached to the hair.”

“Lucky hair.”

I liked him immediately and therefore did not ask his name. This was progress in one very narrow field.

He trimmed the sides, took enough weight off the top that my hair stopped trying to become weather, and fixed the beard without making it look intentional. This was important. I did not want to look like a man who had spent an hour preparing to look like he had not prepared.

I had spent perhaps twenty minutes. Different. When he finished, I looked nineteen. That remained alarming sometimes. Not because I forgot. Because the face had stopped being the most impossible part of my life months ago. Then I would catch it unexpectedly and remember that the man doing calculations behind those eyes had once complained about waking with a bad back.

The young face looked pleased with the haircut. So did I.

“Good,” I said.

The barber held out his hand. Right. Money. Ordinary systems remained undefeated. I paid him.

*

On the way back, Sevren nearly walked past me. He had a courier bag across his chest, mud dried to both boots, and the expression of a man who had slept somewhere that charged money for the privilege of regretting it.

Then he stopped.

“Greg?”

“No.”

He looked at my hair.

“Oh.”

“Fuck you.”

“That is dramatically better.”

“I regret recognizing you.”

He grinned and shifted the courier bag higher. Sevren had been gone long enough that I had not noticed he was gone until he was standing in front of me again. This was either a failure of friendship or evidence that he had his own life.

I chose the second one.

“Route?” I asked.

“North road, then west. Two contracts, one box nobody would tell me was glass until after I put it under a sack of buckles.”

“Was it glass?”

“Yes.”

“Did it survive?”

“Yes.”

“Then excellent packing.”

“Accidental excellent packing.”

“Still excellent.”

He looked at me again.

“Why do you look respectable?”

“I always look respectable.”

“No.”

“Date.”

The word came out before I considered whether I wanted to say it. Fine. Sevren's grin changed.

“With Lyssa?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

That was all. No interrogation. I found this suspicious.

“You're not going to ask anything?”

“I was gone three days. I have six deliveries left, Octavia says I smell like horse, and the west road inn charged me for a blanket with a hole large enough to qualify as architecture.”

“Where was the hole?”

“In the blanket.”

“I mean position.”

He stared at me.

“No.”

Fair. He stepped around me, then stopped again.

“Night market?”

“Yes.”

“Crowded.”

“I know.”

“I know you know.”

He pointed at my crutches.

“West entrance is flatter.”

“I know.”

“Good.”

He left. I watched him go for perhaps three seconds. Then four.

His route bag bounced against his hip. Mud from roads I had not seen in this life flaked off his boots onto Carrow paving. In three days he had left the city, slept badly somewhere else, carried other people's contracts through places that did not know I existed, and returned because there were six more deliveries.

The world had always done that. I had simply been busy. Then my right hand started aching around the crutch grip. The world could continue without requiring symbolism. I went home.

*

I did nothing professionally useful for the rest of the morning. This was harder than expected. A Guild runner did not come. Vale did not send work. Edrin did not send anything.

Holl did not send anything. Arlo and Vessa continued the apparently difficult discipline of not requesting my presence. I considered going upstairs. No. One stair trip would cost something. I had what I needed downstairs. Blue shirt. Better trousers. Water. Food. Crutches. Pride.

Mostly. The keeper found me at the table with my notebook open. She looked at the blank page.

“What are you working on?”

“Nothing.”

“You wrote a heading.”

I looked down.

NIGHT MARKET.

Below it I had written:

TRANSPORT.
SEATING.
FOOD.
CROWD.
RETURN.

Fuck.

I closed the notebook. The keeper laughed so hard she had to put down the bowl she was carrying.

“This is logistics.”

“For romance?”

“No.”

“What is it for?”

“Not falling over.”

“Very romantic.”

“I hate this building.”

“You pay on time.”

Terrible woman. I opened the notebook after she left. Then I crossed out the whole list.

Not because the questions were wrong. They were good questions. Transport mattered. Seating mattered. Crowd density mattered. I knew the west entrance was flatter. I knew I would probably hire a cart home. I knew both crutches needed planting before somebody kissed me while standing, which remained among the stranger medical instructions I had received.

Enough.

I did not need to determine the optimal sequence of food stalls. I wrote one line instead.

WEST ENTRANCE. CART HOME IF NEEDED.

Then I closed the notebook. That lasted eleven minutes. I opened it again to check the time. There was no time written. Excellent.

I took a nap.

*

I woke hungry.

Nineteen.

Good.

The wound was still quiet. Some swelling from the morning walk. Not much. Hands better after rest. Shoulder better. I changed into the blue shirt. The shirt was no longer new. This bothered me for half a second.

Then I realized that was better. It was clothing now. I ate bread before leaving because arriving at a market hungry enough to make financial decisions based on smell seemed unwise. Then I arrived at the market and immediately made financial decisions based on smell.

Of course.

*

The west entrance was flatter. Sevren had been correct about something I already knew, which gave him no credit. The night market had swallowed three streets and part of the riverside square. Lanterns hung from ropes between buildings. Oil lamps burned under awnings. Steam rose from pots. Smoke drifted low enough that every third breath tasted like somebody else's dinner.

Carrow smelled like hot fat, river water, wet stone, onions, horse, spice, cheap perfume, and people who had worked all day and decided they deserved something afterward. Good smell. Crowd moved around carts and stalls in uneven channels. My route through it was slower than everyone else's and therefore more interesting to everyone else than I wanted.

Not much. A few glances. Most people had food. Food won. I had hired a cart to the entrance because I wanted my shoulders later. The driver left. I stood with both crutches planted and tried not to look like I was waiting too early.

I was early. Seven minutes. Possibly nine. I refused to check. Then Lyssa came through the crowd carrying a little folded cloth bag at her hip.

Gray trousers. Dark shirt. Hair tied back badly enough that several strands had escaped before she reached me. She saw me. Stopped. Looked at my head.

“No.”

I stared.

“You too?”

She laughed.

“You got your hair cut.”

“Yes.”

“For the date?”

“No.”

“Greg.”

“Yes.”

Her smile changed just enough to make the barber worth whatever I had paid him. Good investment. No. Not investment. Haircut.

“Looks good,” she said.

“Thank you.”

I had prepared several possible responses to that exact event without admitting I had prepared them. Thank you was not one of them. It worked. Interesting. Lyssa looked past me into the market.

“Food?”

“Yes.”

That worked too. We went.

*

The first stall sold skewers of meat glazed with something sweet and hot enough to make my nose run. I bought two. Lyssa bought fried dough from the next stall and tore one piece in half without asking whether I wanted it.

I took it. We did not discuss payment strategy. Excellent. Walking with food remained mechanically stupid because both my hands were occupied by crutches. I stood beside the stall and ate.

Lyssa ate beside me. No problem. Then we moved again.

The market was not designed for me. It was not designed against me either. It had benches in some places because people liked sitting. Low walls existed because walls existed. Stall owners left gaps because goods had to move. A woman carrying a tray needed the same clear path I did, except she could turn sideways more easily.

I started noticing routes. Then stopped myself. Not because routes were bad. Because Lyssa was telling me about a customer who had asked Rima to make sleeves tighter, then complained that the sleeves were tighter.

“Could be measurement error,” I said.

“No.”

“Fabric stretch?”

“No.”

“Different shirt underneath?”

“No.”

“You sound very certain.”

“She said, ‘I wanted them tighter, not tight.’”

I considered this.

“That is a real distinction.”

Lyssa stopped walking.

“Do not defend her.”

“I am not defending her. I am saying language has failed both parties.”

“Rima's language did not fail.”

“What did she say?”

“Take it off.”

I laughed hard enough that my left hip tried to shift into a stance requiring a foot that did not exist. The movement was small. Familiar now. I planted both crutches harder and waited. Nothing hurt. Lyssa saw the correction.

She did not ask if I was all right.

Good.

She said, “Still funny.”

“Yes.”

We kept going.

*

A man with three cups and a painted pebble was taking money from people. Not stealing. Probably. The cups moved quickly over a low board while he talked constantly. The game was simple. Pebble under cup. Cups moved. Pick cup. Win twice what you put down.

Simple games are dangerous because people confuse simple rules with simple systems. I stopped. Lyssa kept walking three steps before noticing.

“No.”

“What?”

“No.”

“I haven't done anything.”

“You have the face.”

“What face?”

“The one you make when you're about to spend ten minutes proving you understand something nobody asked you to understand.”

“That is not a face.”

“It is absolutely a face.”

The cup man called, “One copper finds the stone.” I looked at Lyssa. She looked at me.

“One,” I said.

“You're going to lose.”

“Probably not.”

“Good.”

That was the wrong response. I paid. The pebble started under the center cup. His hands were good. Not magical. Not impossibly fast. Practiced.

He spoke while moving.

“Center begins honest. Left likes trouble. Right has a wife and three children and cannot afford trouble.”

People laughed. I tracked center to right, right to center, center to left. Left. He stopped. I pointed left.

He lifted it. Empty. The crowd made the delighted noise people make when somebody else loses a small amount of money. I frowned. He lifted center.

Pebble. Interesting.

“Again?” he asked.

“Yes,” I said.

Lyssa made a sound.

“One,” I told her.

“That was one.”

“One more.”

“You said one.”

“I have updated.”

“Of course you have.”

I paid again. This time I watched his wrists instead of cups. Wrong. Not wrong exactly. Incomplete. His hands moved. His voice moved the crowd. A woman beside me laughed and leaned into my line of sight for half a second. The cup man had created that laugh deliberately.

I realized this immediately after the pebble was somewhere else. I chose right. Empty. Lyssa laughed. The cup man bowed to me.

“Very generous.”

“Again?” he asked.

“No,” I said.

He looked almost disappointed. Good professional. We moved away. Lyssa said, “You lost two copper to cups.”

“Yes.”

“You look happy.”

“I learned something.”

“There it is.”

“No.”

I looked back. The cup man already had another group. Same cups. Same pebble. Different jokes. I had tracked the object. He had been tracking people. That was useful.

I nearly said it. Then I decided I did not need to turn two lost copper into tuition.

“I enjoyed it,” I said instead.

Lyssa looked at me. Then smiled.

“That's worse.”

“Why?”

“Now you'll do it again.”

Possibly.

*

We sat after that. Not because I had reached a limit. Because I was getting close enough to one that sitting was smarter. There was a low stone edge around a dry planter near the square. We found space between two old women sharing roasted nuts and a boy asleep against his father's side.

I put the crutches against my right knee where I could control them and stretched the right leg carefully. Residual limb throbbed once. Then again. Expected. Lyssa handed me the rest of the fried dough.

“You bought this.”

“I know.”

“You're giving it away.”

“I know.”

“Economically dangerous.”

She kicked my intact boot lightly. I ate the dough. Across the square, two musicians were arguing while tuning. One had a bowed instrument. The other kept tightening a drumhead and testing it with one finger. Neither cared about us.

Good.

A pair of Guild workers in ordinary clothes crossed the square carrying beer. A merchant I had seen once at South Canal stood in line for something fried. Three children chased each other around a post until an adult caught one by the collar. Somebody behind us was explaining, incorrectly and with great confidence, how river tolls were calculated.

I almost turned around. No. Date. Lyssa followed my eyes anyway.

“You know them?”

“No.”

“Then stop listening.”

“They're wrong.”

“They'll survive.”

“Maybe.”

She laughed. The musicians stopped arguing and started playing. They were good. Not extraordinary. Good enough that the square changed shape around them. People did not stop entirely. They slowed. Conversations angled. A few children came closer. One vendor started clapping with the beat while still serving food.

I watched the crowd more than the musicians for perhaps half a song. Then Lyssa leaned her shoulder against mine. I stopped doing that too. We listened. This was not difficult.

Which was suspicious. After a while Lyssa said, “What did you do today?”

“Haircut.”

“I noticed.”

“Walked.”

“Heroic.”

“Napped.”

She turned her head.

“Nothing else?”

“No work.”

“No Guild?”

“No.”

“Vale?”

“No.”

“Magic?”

“No.”

That answer landed differently. Not badly. Just heavier. Lyssa knew enough not to ask why. I had told her Hessa had not cleared me. Or perhaps she had heard it through ordinary Carrow channels, which meant everybody knew everything except the parts they invented.

She said, “Did you hate it?”

“The nap?”

“The nothing.”

I considered lying. Not because the truth was dangerous. Habit.

“A little,” I said.

She nodded. Then the drum changed rhythm and the conversation ended because it did.

Good.

*

Later, Lyssa asked, “What next?” The market still had at least twenty directions. Food stalls. Cheap jewelry. Carved toys. Old books. A man selling knives too expensive for the table they were on. A woman demonstrating a folding lantern. Musicians. Dice. River fish. Sweet things. People.

I started sorting. Food again? We had eaten. Walking cost. Crowd increased toward center. Could sit through music longer.

Could find quieter edge. Could ask Lyssa what she wanted, which was sensible because she had asked me. No. She had asked me. I looked around once.

A stall near the far edge had small clay animals lined up in rows. Bad animals. Deliberately bad or incompetently bad, unclear. One horse had six legs. A duck looked threatening. A dog had no neck.

“That,” I said.

Lyssa followed my finger.

“The ugly animals?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“I want to know what happened to the horse.”

She grinned. We went. The answer was nothing. The horse simply had six legs. I bought it.

One copper. Lyssa stared.

“What are you going to do with that?”

“I don't know.”

“You bought it.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“I like it.”

She looked at the horse.

“You like that?”

“It has too many legs.”

“That is the opposite of your current problem.”

I looked at her. She froze. Then I laughed. She covered her face.

“Oh, fuck.”

“That was terrible.”

“I know.”

“No, genuinely excellent.”

“Greg.”

“Six legs.”

“Stop.”

I laughed harder. This time I was already sitting on the edge of the stall platform because the vendor had provided a stool for customers examining the lower shelf. Excellent infrastructure. Lyssa was red in the face.

“I didn't mean it.”

“I know.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

“Fuck.”

“Yes.”

She started laughing too. The vendor watched us with the expression of somebody who had sold a bad clay horse and wanted no further involvement. Reasonable. I tucked the horse into Lyssa's cloth bag because I could not carry it while using two crutches.

She looked at me.

“You bought a thing and now I carry it.”

“Temporary logistics.”

“Ah.”

“I will take it back when we sit.”

“You're very independent.”

“Fuck you.”

She smiled.

Good.

*

We stayed longer than I had planned. This was because I had stopped planning. Mostly. We ate something sweet that stuck to my teeth. Lyssa won a copper from me guessing which hand held a button. I accused her of cheating. She admitted nothing. We listened to half another song. We argued about whether the six-legged horse was intended to be running.

“It has six legs because three positions are shown,” I said.

“Then why does it have one body?”

“Movement representation.”

“It has six actual hooves.”

“Stylized.”

“It has two tails.”

I examined it. It had two tails.

“Advanced movement representation.”

“It's a bad horse.”

“Coward.”

By the time the throbbing in my residual limb became difficult to ignore, I had been ignoring it for perhaps ten minutes. Not ideal. Not catastrophic. I told Lyssa.

“Need to go?” she asked.

“Yes.”

The word arrived cleanly. No not yet. No five more minutes. Yes. She nodded.

We walked toward the west entrance. At the edge of the crowd, she handed me the clay horse. I stared at it.

“I cannot carry this.”

“I know.”

“You just removed transport infrastructure.”

“I know.”

I tucked it awkwardly inside the front of my blue shirt. One of the horse's legs poked against my ribs. Lyssa laughed so hard she had to stop walking.

“This is humiliating.”

“Yes.”

“Good date?”

I looked at her.

“Yes.”

“Good.”

We reached the cart stand. I hired one. My cost. Lyssa stood beside the cart while I got in. Crutches first. Right foot. Hands. Turn. Sit. Residual limb protected. Not elegant. Functional. She did not help.

Good.

Once I was settled, she leaned in and kissed me. Short. Then again, longer. Sitting remained technically superior. I did not say it.

Growth. Probably. No. Silence. She pulled back.

“I had fun.”

“Me too.”

“Even losing money?”

“Yes.”

“Horse?”

I pressed a hand against my shirt where six clay legs were trying to escape.

“Yes.”

She smiled.

“Good night, Greg.”

“Good night.”

The cart started moving. I did not ask when we were doing it again. This bothered me after half a street. Then I realized she had not asked either. Fine.

We had gone on one date. It had been good. That was enough information for tonight.

*

The keeper was awake when I got home. Of course. She looked at my hair. Then blue shirt. Then the clay horse when I pulled it out.

She stared.

“What is that?”

“Horse.”

“No.”

“Approximately horse.”

“Why does it have six legs?”

“Movement representation.”

She looked at me for a long time.

“How was the date?”

“Good.”

She nodded once. Then she took the horse from me and set it on the downstairs table. It looked terrible there. Perfect. I checked the dressing.

Still dry. More swelling than before the market. Expected. Residual limb sore. Right shoulder tired. Hands tender. No new damage I could identify. I drank water and lay down. The six-legged horse faced me from the table. I had spent money on a haircut, food, two losing rounds with cups, and a bad clay animal.

I had earned nothing. Solved nothing. Improved no system. The day had not been wasted. That thought arrived too neatly.

Suspicious. I turned onto my back. Phantom left foot felt like it was hanging off the edge of the cot. Actual leg ended well before the edge. Normal impossible.

Tomorrow existed.

No work scheduled. No training scheduled. No date scheduled. I could decide then. The horse had six legs.

Show-off.

CHAPTER EIGHTY-FOUR

The horse had fallen over during the night.

This was not surprising. It had six legs and none of them appeared to agree about the ground.

I found it on its side beside the downstairs table while eating breakfast. One tail had caught against the wall. The other pointed accusingly toward the door.

I set it upright.

It fell over again.

The keeper watched from the stove.

“Movement representation,” she said.

“Shut up.”

My residual limb was more swollen than yesterday morning and less swollen than last night. Acceptable. Dressing dry. No heat. Right shoulder sore in the familiar band between neck and arm. Hands tender enough that the first grip on the crutches made me notice them and not tender enough to change anything.

Date cost.

Worth it.

I was deciding whether that counted as an observation or an accounting category when somebody knocked twice and came in before the keeper answered.

Sevren.

He had changed clothes. Same courier bag. Less mud. This seemed unfair.

“You busy?” he asked.

“No.”

The answer came out quickly enough that I distrusted it.

Sevren looked at the notebook beside my bowl.

“You sure?”

I put a hand over it.

“Yes.”

“Good. Come with me.”

“No.”

He blinked.

I blinked.

Interesting.

“What?” he asked.

“You gave no information.”

“I was going to.”

“Then do that first.”

He pulled out the chair opposite me and sat without asking the keeper. She put another bowl on the table anyway. He accepted this as his due, which explained why she liked him.

“North gate,” he said. “Small delivery. Cart out, cart back. I have a seat I don't need and you looked at my boots yesterday like you wanted to interrogate the road.”

“I did not.”

“You watched me leave.”

“Four seconds.”

“That is romantic for you.”

“Lyssa would object.”

“Good. You learned something.”

I ignored that.

“How far?”

“Not far.”

“That is not a distance.”

“About an hour out with the cart.”

“Destination?”

“Roadside dye works past the north toll. Not a town. Barely a collection of buildings. I deliver a sealed packet, get a signed receipt, ride back with the same carter after he unloads two barrels.”

“What barrels?”

“I don't care.”

“You should if you're riding with them.”

“No, you should if you're riding with them. I am a courier.”

Fair.

“Why do you have a spare seat?”

“Carter's brother isn't coming.”

“Why?”

“Greg.”

“Relevant to whether the seat is structurally available.”

“He has a fever.”

“Then I don't want the seat.”

Sevren stared.

I stared back.

Then he understood.

“Oh. No. He hasn't been in the cart today. He's home. The carter told me at the yard.”

“Good.”

The keeper slid bread toward Sevren.

“You taking him somewhere?” she asked.

“North road,” Sevren said.

She looked at me.

I disliked this because she knew too much about the staircase and not enough about roads, which did not prevent the look from containing an opinion.

“Cart,” Sevren said.

“Seat?” the keeper asked.

“Yes,” Sevren said.

“Back today?” she asked.

“Yes.”

She looked at me again.

I said, “I am nineteen.”

“Unfortunately.”

Sevren ate bread.

I should ask Nerin.

No. Maybe. An hour sitting in a cart was not medically identical to an hour sitting at Vale. Road vibration. Getting in and out. North gate paving. Unknown seating. Unknown place to rest. Return dependent on carter. If I went and the limb swelled badly, I would still be an hour from Carrow.

Good questions.

Not infinite questions.

“When do you leave?” I asked.

“Half an hour.”

Of course.

I looked at the crutches. Then the horse. Then Sevren.

“Can the cart turn around without me?”

“Yes.”

“Can I stay seated while you deliver?”

“Yes.”

“Is there somewhere dry at the destination?”

“Warehouse awning. Office too, probably.”

“Probably?”

“I've never been there.”

That mattered less than I wanted it to.

I stood.

The keeper said, “You haven't finished breakfast.”

I sat.

Fine.

I finished breakfast.

*

The north gate was farther than the barber and easier because I did not walk there.

Sevren had arranged a hired cart from a freight yard two streets over. Not for me. For the barrels and whatever return load the carter expected. My seat was a plank across the front with a thin folded sack pretending to be padding.

The carter looked at my crutches, then at the seat, then at me.

“You need help up?” the carter asked.

“No.”

I considered the height.

“Yes. Not lifting. Hold the crutches.”

He did.

Good.

Right foot on the iron step. Both hands on the cart edge. Push. Turn. Sit. The missing left foot attempted to participate in the turn and contributed nothing. My hip twitched. I stopped before the movement became larger.

Sevren had already climbed up on the other side.

He said nothing.

Also good.

The carter handed me the crutches. I laid them along the side with the tips forward and kept one hand through both cuffs so a rut could not throw them into the street.

Then the cart moved.

I had been in carts since the amputation. Hired rides through Carrow. Infirmary. Guild. Vale. Home. This was different only because the gate was ahead.

Which was stupid.

A gate was wood, iron, stone, guards, traffic, and paperwork. Carrow did not become a different world because we passed under an arch.

Still.

The north gate approached.

Two freight wagons waited in one lane. A drover argued with a guard over three goats and a fee I could not hear. A woman with a basket walked through the pedestrian side without stopping. The city wall looked less impressive from inside because buildings had grown against it and people used the base for shade.

Our carter held up a stamped chit. The guard glanced at the barrels, counted us, and waved us through.

That was it.

Carrow ended.

Not dramatically.

The paving continued for another hundred yards before becoming packed road. Houses thinned. Workshops spread farther apart. A cooper's yard. Two sheds with hides stretched under roofs. A field behind a low stone wall.

Then there was space between things.

I had known there was space between things.

I had memories of roads longer than this kingdom. I had crossed mountain passes in weather that killed pack animals. I had slept in ditches, camps, inns, barracks, wagons, one abandoned shrine, and once inside a grain bin because the alternative had been being stabbed.

Those were not this road.

This road had wet ruts from yesterday's rain and white flowers in the ditch. The cart wheel hit a stone. My whole body moved upward half an inch.

My residual limb objected.

Ah.

Road.

I shifted my weight.

Sevren noticed.

“Bad?”

“Not yet.”

“Useful distinction.”

“Yes.”

He leaned back against the cart side and closed his eyes.

“You're not watching the road?” I asked.

“I've seen it.”

“You're a courier.”

“Exactly.”

I looked at the road for him.

Fields. Ditches. A low orchard. Two boys carrying a ladder between them. A woman driving a narrow cart toward Carrow with baskets covered in cloth. A mile marker with the top corner broken off. Three riders passed us going south, one with a Guild badge on his shoulder and none interested in me.

Good.

The world outside Carrow was disappointingly occupied.

I had expected this.

I still found it satisfying.

*

The first problem was the plank.

The second was that the first problem had been obvious.

A plank seat on a city cart for twenty minutes was a plank seat. A plank seat for an hour over ruts became a technical argument conducted through the right side of my ass.

I moved the folded sack.

Worse.

Moved it back.

Better.

Sevren opened one eye.

“Comfortable?”

“No.”

“Good cart.”

“This is a good cart?”

“Wheels are still attached.”

My standards had drifted.

The residual limb did not like repeated vertical jolts. Not pain exactly at first. Pressure and swelling, then a hot pulse after a deeper rut. I braced with my right foot and immediately discovered that bracing every rut would exhaust the right thigh before we arrived.

So I stopped trying to defeat the road.

This was irritating.

I held the cart edge loosely instead. Let my trunk move. Protected the limb without locking the rest of me around it. Better.

Not comfortable.

Better.

Sevren said, eyes still closed, “You look less stupid.”

“You weren't looking.”

“I checked.”

“Why didn't you tell me?”

“Tell you what?”

“To stop bracing.”

“I don't know anything about your leg.”

“You know carts.”

“Yes.”

“And you knew I looked stupid.”

“Yes.”

“That was actionable information.”

He opened both eyes.

“You want me to say something every time you look stupid?”

I considered the scope.

“No.”

“Good.”

He closed his eyes again.

I hated him.

Friendship.

*

We stopped once before the dye works because the carter needed to piss.

I did too.

This created logistics.

The road had a ditch, a hedge, and no conveniently placed private room. Before the injury I would have stepped down, walked twenty yards, solved the problem, returned.

Now getting down meant getting back up. Ground beside the cart was damp and uneven. Hedge gap narrow. Crutches would sink if I planted them in the soft shoulder.

I looked at the road ahead. Then behind.

Sevren hopped down.

“You staying?”

“No.”

He waited.

I disliked waiting people.

“Find me hard ground.”

He looked around, pointed ten yards back toward the mile marker.

“Stone pull-off.”

Good.

The carter moved the cart ten yards after he returned, because apparently civilization could be constructed from requests. The pull-off was crushed stone. I got down with the carter holding the crutches again. No lifting. Right foot. Hands. Turn. Crutches.

The privy problem remained a hedge problem.

I solved it without writing anything down.

Progress.

When I came back, Sevren was sitting on the broken mile marker eating an apple.

“Where did you get that?”

He pointed at the orchard.

“You stole it?”

“No.”

“You crossed a wall?”

“There was a basket by the gate. One copper.”

“You bought one apple for one copper?”

“Three apples.”

“Where are the other two?”

He tossed me one.

I caught it against my chest with one hand and nearly dropped a crutch.

“Fuck.”

“Good catch.”

“Bad throw.”

“You caught it.”

I put the apple in my teeth long enough to get back to the cart.

Undignified.

Efficient.

The apple was excellent.

*

The dye works announced itself by smell before buildings.

Sharp mineral bite. Wet wool. Wood smoke. Something sour enough that my nose tried to reject it.

Then the road curved and the place appeared below us beside a narrow stream.

Not a town.

Sevren had been accurate.

Four long sheds. One stone office. Drying frames in a field. Cloth hanging in strips under roofed racks, reds and browns and one violent yellow that seemed personally offended by nature. Workers moved between vats and sheds carrying poles, baskets, ledgers, buckets.

Nobody stopped because we arrived.

The carter drove to a loading shed.

Sevren jumped down with the sealed packet.

“You coming?”

I looked at the step. Then the yard. Packed gravel. Mostly level. Office perhaps sixty yards away.

“Do you need me?”

“No.”

“Then no.”

He nodded and left.

That felt strange for approximately three seconds.

Then I sat in the cart and watched people who did not need me.

A worker rolled one of our barrels down a ramp with another man controlling a rope from above. They argued about whether the barrel had been overfilled. A woman came out of the nearest shed with both forearms stained red to the elbow and shouted for somebody named only by profanity. A boy swept wet grit away from a drain. Two older men examined cloth in sunlight and disagreed about color with the seriousness of surgeons.

I understood perhaps ten percent of what mattered.

Excellent.

The barrel came off the cart.

Nobody asked me to inspect it.

Also excellent.

I ate the apple.

A few minutes later, the woman with red arms walked past, glanced at my crutches, glanced at the cart, and said, “Waiting on courier?”

“Yes.”

She nodded and kept walking.

No pity. No curiosity. No invitation into dye chemistry.

Perfect professional interaction.

I almost laughed.

Sevren returned with a folded receipt tucked into his bag.

“Done.”

“That was fast.”

“Yes.”

“What was in the packet?”

“Documents.”

“What documents?”

“I don't know.”

“You carried them an hour.”

“Yes.”

“And didn't ask?”

“No.”

I looked at him.

He looked at me.

There was a whole profession in that answer.

I wanted to ask what he was responsible for if the documents were wrong. Whether he verified seals. What happened if the recipient refused. Whether he knew contents when hazardous. How liability worked. How routes were priced. Whether distance or urgency mattered more. Whether he could decline a destination. Whether couriers were expected to recognize political names. Whether he had ever carried something he later wished he had not.

Good questions.

Some of them.

“Did they sign?” I asked.

He tapped the bag.

“Yes.”

Enough for now.

The carter still had loading to do.

One barrel off. Two bundles of wrapped cloth on. Then another smaller crate. We waited under the warehouse awning because the cart bed was being rearranged.

There was a bench.

I loved the dye works.

I sat.

Residual limb throbbing. Swelling more noticeable. Shoulder fine because I had barely used the crutches. Right thigh tired from bracing before I learned not to. Hands better than a walking day.

Tradeoffs.

Sevren leaned against a post.

“So?”

“So what?”

“You wanted road.”

“I did not say that.”

“You stared at my boots.”

“That remains weak evidence.”

“Do you hate it?”

I looked past him.

The stream moved behind the sheds. Cloth lifted in the wind. A wagon on the road above us passed without turning in. Somewhere inside the long building, somebody dropped something metal and swore.

“No,” I said.

Sevren nodded as if I had confirmed the weather.

That was all.

Good.

*

The ride back hurt more.

Not dramatically.

Cumulative systems were rude that way.

I knew how to sit now, which helped. The road had not improved. By the time the north wall appeared in the distance, the residual limb felt too full and my lower back had joined the complaint because apparently it feared exclusion.

I could still think.

Unfortunately.

The city looked different from outside.

Not profoundly. Walls. Roofs. Smoke. Towers I had seen from streets but not arranged like this. The north gate was a dark cut in stone with wagons feeding toward it from both directions.

Carrow looked finite.

That was the difference.

Inside, it occupied everything because I moved through pieces of it. Streets connected to streets. Jobs connected to people. Guild to lodging to Vale to green door to infirmary to market.

From the road, it had an edge.

Beyond the edge was more road.

I knew this.

Old Greg knew this with thousands of miles of evidence.

Nineteen-year-old Greg had just spent one hour proving it again.

Different evidence.

The guard waved us through.

Carrow swallowed the cart.

*

Sevren got off two streets before my lodging because he had another delivery.

Of course.

“You're not coming back?” I asked.

“No.”

“I thought same cart.”

“You have same cart. I have work.”

Right.

He slung the courier bag across his chest.

“Tomorrow?” he asked.

“For what?”

“Nothing. I'm asking whether you'll be alive.”

“Probably.”

“Good.”

He jumped down.

I said, “Sevren.”

He looked back.

“Thanks.”

“For the terrible seat?”

“Yes.”

He grinned.

Then he left.

No promise. No new route. No invitation to become a courier. He had six deliveries yesterday and apparently more today. His life did not pause because I had discovered roads.

Good.

The carter took me to the lodging for another copper because the freight yard was farther than I wanted to crutch after the ride.

I paid without calculating whether I could have saved it.

Mostly.

*

The keeper saw me enter and said, “You look terrible.”

“Road.”

“That a place?”

“Yes.”

She pointed at the cot.

I obeyed before she could become pleased about it.

Crutches down. Blue shirt off because I was sweating. Dressing check.

Dry.

Swollen more than morning. No heat. No spreading redness. No drainage. Sore. Not alarming by the standards I had been given.

I elevated the limb.

The six-legged horse watched from the table.

Show-off.

I drank water.

There were things I could write down.

Cart seat bad over distance.

Bracing every rut worse.

Crushed stone better than road shoulder for crutches.

Need predictable return transport.

An hour out was not the same as an hour seated in a room.

All useful.

I opened the notebook.

Then stopped.

The first thing I wrote was not any of those.

NORTH ROAD: WHITE FLOWERS IN DITCH.

I looked at it.

Stupid.

Accurate.

Below it I wrote:

DYE WORKS YELLOW IS OFFENSIVE.

Also accurate.

Then, because I was not completely irresponsible, I added:

CART VIBRATION COSTS MORE THAN EXPECTED.

There.

Balance.

I closed the notebook.

Tomorrow I would probably hurt.

Tomorrow I might have work.

Holl might send data. Edrin might send nothing. Alden might appear with a bad idea. Lyssa existed whether or not we had another date scheduled. Hessa still had not cleared magic. Vale still owned part of my future in copper-sized pieces.

Carrow was still here.

So was the road.

Neither had asked me to choose.

Good.


CHAPTER EIGHTY-FIVE

My leg objected to the north road before breakfast.

Not dramatically. Dramatic would have been easier to classify.

The residual limb was swollen enough that the dressing felt tighter, sore along the lower margin, and warm only in the ordinary sense that the rest of me was also warm. No new redness. No drainage. No smell. No fever. I checked twice because the first check had produced an answer I disliked rather than an answer I distrusted.

Still dry.

Good.

My right thigh hurt in places I had not assigned responsibility to yesterday. Lower back too. Hands were better than after a long crutch day. Shoulders were better. Apparently travel redistributed suffering instead of eliminating it.

Useful.

I wrote that down beneath DYE WORKS YELLOW IS OFFENSIVE.

The keeper put porridge in front of me and looked at the notebook.

“You writing about your holiday?”

“It was four hours.”

“Long holiday.”

“I delivered nothing.”

“You ate an apple.”

“That was not labor.”

“You watched other people labor.”

“Educational.”

She snorted.

I had planned to spend the morning downstairs. Planned was generous. I had decided not to go anywhere until the swelling reduced and then had immediately begun constructing exceptions.

Guild if requested.

Infirmary if necessary.

Food if unavailable here.

Alden if he arrived with blood.

Lyssa if she arrived without blood.

Fire.

Structural collapse.

Unusually interesting noise.

The last category made the entire system suspect.

Somebody knocked.

The keeper looked at me.

I looked at the door.

“Interesting noise,” she said.

“Shut up.”

Holl came in carrying a wooden box under one arm and three folded sheets in the other hand.

He stopped when he saw me at the table.

“Good. Sitting.”

“I do that now.”

“So I heard.”

He put the box on the table hard enough to make my cup jump.

The keeper looked at the cup, then at Holl.

“Sorry,” he said.

She went back to the stove.

Holl sat opposite me and pushed the papers across the table.

“You said write it down.”

“I did.”

“No. I did.”

Right.

Prospective records.

Worker. Lot. Throughput. Ambiguous pieces. Returns or banding errors.

I had not thought about them yesterday.

That was probably healthy.

I unfolded the first sheet.

Holl had made columns.

Bad columns.

They were still columns.

“You did this yourself?”

“Iris started it.”

“She started it. I changed it because she writes too small.”

“Your writing is larger.”

“Better.”

“Those are not synonyms.”

He ignored me.

I read.

Six working days. Four lots. Two regular testers plus Holl on close pieces. Pieces sorted into three behavior bands. Set-asides counted. Rechecks counted separately on two days and not on the others because apparently measurement systems also required supervision.

There were return marks at the bottom.

Three.

I stopped.

“Three customer returns?”

“Three pieces returned. Two customers.”

“Why?”

“Wrong behavior.”

“Wrong band?”

“Yes.”

“Confirmed?”

Holl tapped the box.

I looked at it.

“No.”

“What?”

“You came here with rocks.”

“Yes.”

“My leg hurts.”

“You're sitting.”

“That is not the same as volunteering my table for magic testing.”

Holl stared at me.

I stared back.

This was satisfying.

He leaned back.

“Fine.”

That was less satisfying. I had expected resistance and prepared several excellent arguments.

“What do you want from me?” I asked.

“Look at the records.”

“Only?”

“Only.”

I pulled the second sheet closer.

There were numbers.

Numbers were dangerous because they looked like answers before anyone had asked a question.

Lot one: low ambiguity. Fast throughput. No returns.

Lot two: high ambiguity. Slow throughput. One returned piece.

Lot three: moderate ambiguity. Fast throughput. Two returned pieces.

Lot four: very high ambiguity. Very slow throughput. No returns yet.

I read again.

Then the worker lines.

Iris was faster than the other regular tester.

Not slightly.

Enough that I would have noticed if I had been paying her.

Her ambiguity rate was also higher.

Interesting.

The other tester set aside fewer pieces and processed fewer per hour.

Holl's rechecks converted some ambiguous pieces into saleable stock and rejected others.

“Which worker made the three returned calls?” I asked.

Holl pointed.

Two Iris. One other tester.

“Were those pieces marked ambiguous before sale?”

“No.”

“Close?”

“Don't know.”

“You don't know?”

“I didn't record every piece's original tray position and prayer history, Greg.”

“Reasonable.”

He narrowed his eyes.

“That sounded insulting.”

“It wasn't.”

It mostly wasn't.

I went back to the sheets.

The obvious answer was Iris was faster because she threw more uncertain pieces at Holl.

The second obvious answer was that this was bad.

The third obvious answer was that I had learned nothing from the last year.

“What happens to set-asides?” I asked.

“Holl tests them,” Holl said.

“You are Holl.”

“Yes.”

“What happens after you test them?”

“Band, reject, or hold.”

“Hold for what?”

“Better lot. Customer question. Sometimes I sell them as mixed suppression if somebody doesn't care.”

“At what price?”

“Less.”

“How much less?”

“Depends.”

“On?”

“Customer.”

Of course.

I looked at the lot totals again.

“Your expensive resource isn't the fixture.”

Holl's face changed slightly.

Not agreement. Attention.

“Keep going.”

I hated when people said that because it made me want to perform certainty.

I waited.

The keeper put bread between us without being asked. Holl took a piece. I took a piece. Nobody paid her immediately, which meant either trust or criminality.

“Maybe,” I said, “your expensive resource is you.”

“Obviously.”

“Not your skill generally. Your close-piece time.”

He chewed.

I pointed at lot four.

“This lot had the worst ambiguity and no returns.”

“Yet.”

“Yes. Yet. But you spent...”

I counted marks.

“Nearly twice as much recheck time on it as lot three.”

“Bad stone.”

“Maybe.”

“It was bad stone.”

“Fine. Bad stone. But if Iris is faster because she sends more close calls to you, that might be good or bad depending on what her time costs, what your time costs, what rejects cost, and what a wrong band costs.”

Holl stopped chewing.

I continued because stopping now would have been cowardice.

“And returns may not be the right error measure.”

“They're errors.”

“They are some errors. A customer can receive a piece at the edge of a band and never notice. Another customer can return a technically correct piece because their use is sensitive. A wrong piece might be consumed before anyone complains. A rejected piece might have been saleable. You don't see false rejects in returns.”

Holl looked at the sheets.

I looked too.

There it was.

The dangerous feeling.

I understand this.

Therefore I know what should happen next.

I could feel the sentence assembling.

Change the fixture.

Change the thresholds.

Give Iris a separate close category.

Price lots by expert-time burden.

Test a sample of rejects.

All plausible.

None mine yet.

“What decision are you trying to make?” I asked.

Holl looked up.

“Thought that was your question.”

“It is. Answer it.”

He considered.

“Whether to change anything.”

“Too broad.”

“Whether Iris is too loose.”

There.

Not the fixture.

Not the entire business.

Iris.

I read the numbers again with the actual question attached.

Different document.

“Then this doesn't answer it.”

Holl grunted.

“It tells you she's faster and sends you more close pieces. It tells you two returned pieces came from her calls. It doesn't tell you whether she makes more wrong calls per hundred clear decisions than the other tester.”

“Can calculate.”

“Not from this.”

“Why?”

“Because the lots differ.”

He frowned.

I tapped lot two, then three.

“If she handled more of the ugly material, comparing raw returns is nonsense. If she handled easier material, same problem the other direction. Also you recheck her ambiguous pieces. Those are not her final calls.”

Holl leaned forward.

“What do you need?”

Need.

Another dangerous word.

I nearly answered with a list.

Instead I asked, “What would you do if she is too loose?”

“Tell her to tighten.”

“And if that slows her down?”

“Fine if returns stop.”

“What if returns don't change?”

“Then I tell her to go faster again.”

I smiled despite myself.

“Good experimental design.”

“Don't call it that.”

“Fine. Business annoyance.”

“Better.”

I looked at the box.

“What are those?”

“The three returns and six pieces I pulled because I wanted comparison.”

“No testing.”

“You said.”

“Can I look at them without mana?”

Holl shrugged.

“Rocks don't bite.”

“Several rocks bite.”

“Not these.”

He opened the box.

Nine pieces of dull gray kestrin sat in cloth dividers. Cheap suppression stone looked disappointing even when it was causing expensive questions. The pieces differed in shape, surface, thickness. Two had chalk marks. One had a chipped corner.

I did not touch them.

“Which are returns?”

Holl pointed.

I looked.

Nothing visible distinguished them from the others.

Good.

Or useless.

Often the same thing.

“Do customers buy pieces or behavior?” I asked.

“Behavior.”

“You price by band.”

“Yes.”

“Do they care how close a piece is to the band edge?”

“Some.”

“Do you know which before sale?”

“Usually.”

Usually.

I rubbed my thumb against the bread crust.

“Then maybe there are two questions.”

Holl groaned.

“I came here for fewer questions.”

“Terrible choice.”

“What two?”

“Is Iris making worse calls? And are you selling the same tolerance to customers who don't actually need the same tolerance?”

He stared at me.

I immediately regretted the second question.

Not because it was bad.

Because it was interesting.

Interesting questions were how I acquired unpaid employment.

Holl reached for the papers.

“That's useful.”

“Maybe.”

“You always say maybe after the useful part.”

“Because you haven't tested it.”

“I'm not testing customers.”

“You already do. With invoices.”

He gave me a flat look.

I ate bread.

The keeper came past, saw the stones, and stopped.

“No magic.”

Holl and I both said, “No magic.”

She looked at me specifically.

“I said no magic.”

“You say many things.”

Then she left.

Holl smiled.

“Strong institutional authority.”

“You don't know the half of it.”

I pushed the papers back toward him.

“Don't change Iris from this.”

“I wasn't going to fire her.”

“I didn't say fire.”

“You thought it.”

“I thought you might blame the worker because worker is an easy variable.”

Holl's expression hardened.

“She is an easy variable.”

“Yes.”

“And sometimes the worker is the problem.”

“Yes.”

That mattered.

I had a tendency to become suspicious of obvious answers after discovering hidden ones. This was merely the inverse stupidity.

Holl tapped the page.

“So how do I know?”

I looked at the totals.

“You own the process.”

“I know.”

“You know the cost of a wrong band.”

“Yes.”

“You know what amount of recheck time annoys you enough to matter.”

“Yes.”

“Then pick a narrow comparison you can actually run without ruining the work.”

He waited.

I waited too.

He frowned.

“You're not going to tell me?”

“I can suggest.”

“Suggest.”

“Same lot. Split enough ordinary pieces between Iris and the other tester that material difference matters less. Keep their ambiguous piles separate. You recheck a small sample of each person's clear calls too, not only the pieces they flag. Then compare wrong clear calls, ambiguity, throughput, and your time.”

Holl considered it.

“Costs product.”

“Some.”

“Costs me.”

“Yes.”

“How much?”

“I don't know.”

He nodded.

That was the correct response to ignorance. Disturbing.

“And customer tolerance?” he asked.

“Ask them what decision the stone supports.”

“They'll tell me they need good stone.”

“Yes.”

“Useless.”

“Yes.”

“So?”

“So maybe ask what happens if the suppression is a little high or low.”

He looked at me.

“That sounds like work.”

“It is your business.”

“Thought you liked work.”

“I like other people's work at a safe distance.”

He laughed once.

The residual limb throbbed hard enough that I shifted in the chair.

Holl noticed.

Not dramatically. His eyes went down, then back up.

“You done?” he asked.

I wanted to say no.

The box was open.

Nine stones.

Three returns.

A business problem with actual data and a worker whose performance might be misread by the wrong denominator.

This was excellent.

Also my leg hurt.

“Yes.”

The word annoyed me less than expected.

Holl folded the sheets.

“That's it?”

“You asked me to look.”

“I did.”

“I looked.”

“What do I owe you?”

I blinked.

“For what?”

Holl stared at me.

Right.

Professional interaction.

I had somehow forgotten money while discussing somebody else's money.

“How long have you been here?” I asked.

The keeper answered from the stove.

“Forty minutes.”

Holl looked at her.

She shrugged.

“I have ears.”

I considered.

This was not Guild work. Holl had come to me. No transport. No magic. Judgment, not testing. Forty minutes.

“One copper.”

Holl reached into his purse.

Then stopped.

“Too little.”

I looked at him.

“You're arguing upward?”

“I pay Iris more than that for an hour when she's testing.”

“She's doing skilled production work.”

“So were you.”

“I ate your bread.”

“My bread?” the keeper said.

“Our bread,” I corrected.

“Two copper,” Holl said.

I almost objected.

Then didn't.

“Fine.”

He put two copper on the table.

The keeper took one.

I stared at her.

“Bread,” she said.

“That was not one copper of bread.”

“Table fee.”

“You have never charged a table fee.”

“New policy.”

Holl was already closing the box.

“You're encouraging her.”

“Yes.”

“Get out.”

He stood.

At the door he looked back.

“Same lot. Sample clear calls too.”

“Yes.”

“Don't change Iris yet.”

“Correct.”

“Ask customers what happens if they're wrong.”

“Approximately.”

He nodded.

Then he left with his stones and bad columns.

The room became quiet again.

I looked at the remaining copper.

One copper net after extortion.

Still more than yesterday's professional income.

Yesterday's professional income had been negative.

I had paid for transport to go nowhere useful and look at yellow cloth.

Today a testing shop owner had brought work to my breakfast table because something I had asked him to record had produced a question he wanted help answering.

The two facts did not cancel each other.

That seemed important enough that I refused to write it down.

I elevated my leg on the other chair.

The keeper put another piece of bread beside me.

“Free?” I asked.

“No.”

I ate it anyway.

*

By afternoon the swelling had reduced.

Not gone. Reduced.

I stayed downstairs.

This was partly discipline and partly because the stairs had become less interesting now that I knew I could use them under controlled conditions. Competence had ruined a perfectly good obsession.

I reread Holl's numbers from memory.

That was a mistake.

I did not have the papers.

Good.

I could reconstruct the broad pattern but not the exact counts. Also good. It prevented me from solving a business that was currently walking away from me in a wooden box.

I opened my notebook instead.

NORTH ROAD: WHITE FLOWERS IN DITCH.

DYE WORKS YELLOW IS OFFENSIVE.

CART VIBRATION COSTS MORE THAN EXPECTED.

Below that I wrote:

HOLL: COMPARE DECISIONS, NOT JUST PEOPLE.

I stared at it.

Too neat.

I crossed out HOLL.

Then I crossed out the whole sentence.

The keeper saw me.

“Bad?”

“Annoying.”

“What was it?”

“Something true enough to become false if I liked it too much.”

She considered that.

“Sounds like you.”

“Yes.”

I turned the page.

Blank.

Good.

Someone outside shouted about onions.

A cart rolled past.

Upstairs, a door opened and shut.

My leg hurt less than it had that morning.

I had one copper from work I had not gone looking for.

I had spent yesterday on a road for no reason that would survive an invoice.

Tomorrow remained offensively unassigned.

I left the page blank.

CHAPTER EIGHTY-SIX

The blank page lasted until nearly noon.

This was longer than expected.

I had assumed tomorrow would become assigned through ordinary violence. A Guild messenger. Holl returning with numbers despite being told to collect more than six days. Antonius deciding a one-hour task had siblings. Alden throwing something at a window. The keeper inventing a fee for remaining indoors.

Nothing happened.

My residual limb was less swollen than yesterday. The road soreness had settled into the dull kind that stopped being medically interesting and became personally annoying. Dressing dry. No heat. No redness. No drainage. Right thigh still sore. Lower back better. Hands almost ordinary if I did not squeeze anything hard.

I ate breakfast.

Then more breakfast because the keeper had made too much and claimed this was somehow my problem.

Then I sat.

The city continued without consulting me.

A wagon rattled past carrying empty baskets. Someone upstairs argued about a missing stocking. Two men outside spent five full minutes disagreeing about whether a barrel belonged at the front or back of a cart, then placed it in the middle. A woman came in to ask the keeper whether she knew anyone with a room for three nights. She did. Not here.

I considered going upstairs.

No.

I considered the Guild.

Dangerous. If I went there without a purpose, I would acquire one.

Arlo and Vessa were still under explicit instructions not to receive me. Their instructions, not mine, but enforcement seemed likely.

Edrin had nothing for me.

Holl had work he needed to do without my face appearing beside it.

Antonius knew where I lived.

Lyssa was working.

Sevren was probably already somewhere else because this was the defining feature of couriers.

Jorren was at the Guild yard.

That was not a reason.

I stood.

The keeper looked over.

“Guild?”

“No.”

“Where?”

“I don't know.”

Her eyebrows went up.

I disliked being interesting before leaving the room.

“Out,” I said.

“Strong plan.”

“Yes.”

I took my crutches and left before she could charge me for it.

*

Carrow was easier when I was not trying to cross it efficiently.

This was an irritating discovery because efficiency had previously been one of walking's major advantages.

With two crutches, a missing left foot, and no appointment, I could choose streets according to grade, crowd, surface, shade, benches, and whether a delivery wagon had converted the pavement into a temporary wall. There was no penalty for arriving late because there was nowhere to arrive.

I went south because the north road still existed and I did not need to prove it twice.

A baker had set cooling racks near an open window. I stopped long enough to smell bread and not buy any because I had eaten twice.

A cooper was shaving a hoop. Three children were using a gutter channel as a boat race. A dog slept with its head on a doorstep where anyone with sense would have moved it, which meant everyone stepped around the dog instead.

I did too.

At the next corner I heard somebody shout, “Too high.”

Then a hollow leather thump against wood.

Then Alden laughed.

I changed direction.

This was not an accident.

The south Guild yard had a side court I had seen before and ignored because it contained nothing worth being injured over. Today the main practice floor was occupied by shield work, so half a dozen Bronzes had migrated into the side court with two leather throwing balls, a chalked wall, and apparently no supervision.

Jorren stood with his back against the fence eating something from paper.

He saw me first.

“No.”

“I haven't asked anything.”

“You came toward Alden voluntarily.”

“That is not a question.”

“It is a diagnosis.”

Alden turned.

He had one of the leather balls in his right hand and sweat darkening the collar of his shirt.

“Greg.”

“No.”

His smile widened.

“I haven't asked anything.”

“You were going to.”

“Yes.”

“Then no.”

“Coward.”

I stopped beside Jorren.

“What is the game?”

Jorren closed his eyes.

Alden tossed the ball once and caught it.

“Three marks,” he said.

There were three chalk circles on the wall at different heights and distances from the center line. One low left. One chest-high center. One higher right.

“Rules?” I asked.

“Hit them.”

“In order?”

“Yes.”

“How many throws?”

“Three.”

“Scoring?”

“One point if you hit one.”

I waited.

Alden waited.

“That is the entire scoring system?”

“Yes.”

“No bonus for center?”

“No.”

“Distance?”

He pointed at a chalk line six paces from the wall.

“Same line.”

“Ball rotation?”

Jorren made a sound into his food.

Alden said, “You throw it.”

“Grip restrictions?”

“No.”

“Bounce permitted?”

“No.”

“Then why are there six people arguing?”

“Because Lio says the top mark is too small.”

Lio, already known to me and currently holding the second ball, said from the wall, “It is too small.”

“It is the same size it was yesterday,” Alden said.

“That does not make it good.”

This seemed reasonable.

I looked at Jorren.

“You play?”

“No.”

“Why are you here?”

“Lunch.”

He lifted the paper.

Apparently he had achieved what I was attempting.

Alden threw.

Low left. Hit.

Center. Hit.

High right.

The ball struck the chalk circle near its upper edge and dropped.

Alden turned toward me before it hit the ground.

“Three.”

“Two and a disputed boundary.”

“Chalk moved,” Alden said.

“Then your scoring surface is degrading during use.”

“Three.”

“Two.”

Lio said, “Three.”

“You just complained about the target.”

“I can dislike the target and still understand circles.”

Fair.

Alden held the ball out to me.

“No.”

“You walked over.”

“I was observing.”

“You've observed.”

I looked at the line.

Six paces.

The side court had packed dirt, reasonably flat. The wall was old timber backed by stone. The leather ball was roughly the size of my fist and stuffed enough to deform when it hit. No blades. No magic. No moving machinery. No road.

Still standing to throw would require one crutch or balancing on the right leg. Bad. Sitting would change the distance and release height. Also the chair would need to be behind the line.

I could ask for a chair.

That sounded like participation.

“No,” I said again.

Alden tossed the ball to Lio.

“Fine.”

This was unexpectedly annoying.

They played another round.

Lio hit two. A woman I knew by face but not name hit one. Another Bronze missed all three and blamed the ball. Alden hit two cleanly and one that I would have counted if I were not invested in his suffering.

I watched his shoulder.

He did not throw hard. That was the first thing.

The target was close enough that force mostly created rebound. The better throws left his hand smooth, with less visible effort than the misses. His feet did more than I expected. Small shift. Hip. Trunk. Shoulder. Release.

Old knowledge supplied a dozen throwing mechanics from weapons, stones, darts, improvised objects, and one ridiculous winter campaign involving frozen turnips.

None of those bodies were sitting down.

Interesting.

Alden caught me looking.

“Chair?”

I hated him.

“Yes.”

Jorren laughed so hard he nearly dropped lunch.

*

The chair came from the training annex.

Not a special chair. A normal wooden chair with one leg slightly shorter than the others because Carrow believed furniture should participate in uncertainty.

Alden set it behind the chalk line.

I moved it myself.

“Back another half pace,” I said.

“Why?”

“My hand starts closer to the wall than yours when seated.”

He considered that.

Then dragged the chalk line back with his heel instead.

“That works too.”

“Less furniture.”

I sat.

Crutches went on the ground to my right within reach, not leaning where somebody could kick them. Right foot flat. Left knee bent comfortably. Residual limb clear of the chair edge.

The game became different immediately.

Not harder exactly.

Different geometry.

Alden handed me the ball.

Leather. Dense stuffing. Slightly uneven seam. Enough weight to matter. Not enough to hurt the wall or anybody with reasonable luck.

“Low left,” he said.

“I know the order.”

“Wasn't sure after the questions.”

I threw.

The ball hit the wall a foot above the low circle.

Everyone became quiet for exactly long enough to be rude.

Alden said, “Good wall.”

“Shut up.”

I had thrown mostly with the arm.

Stupid.

My old body expected the left leg to receive part of the rotational shift even though I was sitting. Not weight-bearing, exactly. More like the movement map had included a base wider than the one physically available. My trunk had stopped halfway through because some part of it expected support that was not there.

That was a theory.

Observed fact: terrible throw.

I adjusted my right foot.

Center target.

Second throw hit low and right.

Better.

Third missed the high mark by less.

“Zero,” Alden said happily.

“Yes.”

“You want advice?”

“No.”

“Good. I didn't have any.”

I stood by pushing through the chair with one hand, caught myself, then stopped.

No. Why stand?

The next player could wait.

I stayed seated while Lio retrieved the balls.

Jorren came over chewing.

“You're making the face.”

“What face?”

“The one where the game stops being a game.”

“It has three targets and measurable outcomes.”

“Exactly.”

“I missed all of them.”

“Yes.”

“That is offensive.”

“Good.”

Alden called, “Again?”

I said, “Yes.”

Jorren pointed his food at me.

“Game.”

“I know.”

“No notebook.”

“I didn't bring it.”

He stared.

I had not realized this until he did.

Interesting.

“No notebook,” I agreed.

Second round.

Low left.

I let my torso turn farther before release and kept the right foot planted without trying to make it replace both legs.

Hit.

The ball landed inside the chalk and bounced almost straight back.

I caught it against my chest.

Alden's expression changed.

“Accident.”

“Yes.”

Center.

Miss.

High right.

Hit edge.

“Two,” Lio said.

Alden frowned.

“That last one was boundary,” Alden said.

“Chalk moved,” I said.

Lio pointed at me.

“He learns.”

The next round became competitive.

This was not my fault.

Alden had three points. Lio had two. I had two. The unnamed woman had two and clearly did not care about any of us, which made her dangerous.

I tried more force.

Worse.

I tried less.

Better.

I changed grip.

No meaningful difference.

I moved the chair three inches left.

Alden objected.

“Line is the line.”

“The chair remains behind it.”

“You're changing position.”

“You change your feet.”

“That is different.”

“Explain.”

He opened his mouth.

Closed it.

Jorren said, “Don't help him.”

Alden kicked the chair back three inches.

I stared at him.

“Now that's interference.”

“Play.”

I played.

The low target became easy first.

Not easy. Easier.

The center target exposed timing. The high target required more shoulder and less force than I thought. When I tried to generate power from the trunk, I shifted too far left and the chair rocked.

Once.

The missing foot planted itself in my body map to catch the shift.

Nothing touched the ground.

My left hip moved anyway.

The chair tipped half an inch.

My right hand shot to the seat edge and stopped it.

The ball dropped from my other hand.

Nobody laughed.

That was worse.

“I'm fine,” I said.

Alden nodded once.

Jorren had stopped chewing.

I reset the chair.

Pessa said from behind us, “You reached past what you had.”

Of course.

I turned.

She stood at the court entrance with a practice spear over one shoulder. She was sweaty enough to have been working.

“I know,” I said.

“After.”

I disliked the accuracy.

“Yes.”

She looked at the chalk circles, the ball on the ground, my chair, then Alden.

“What is this?”

“Game,” Alden said.

Pessa looked at me.

“Game,” I said.

“Good.”

That was all.

She pointed the spear at Alden.

“You're late.”

He looked toward the main yard.

“For what?”

She smiled.

Alden stopped smiling.

“Right.”

He handed me the ball.

“Hold that.”

“No.”

He was already following Pessa.

I now held the ball.

This was how property disputes began.

Lio said, “Your throw.”

Apparently it was also how games continued.

*

Without Alden, the game improved.

Not because he was bad.

Because he was annoying enough that beating him had become the objective, and his absence returned the objective to hitting chalk with leather.

I made three.

Then one.

Then two.

The unnamed woman made three twice in a row, accepted this with no visible emotion, and left when a Guild bell sounded.

Lio made two and complained that the ball was becoming soft.

I squeezed it.

It was becoming soft.

“Stuffing shifted,” I said.

Lio said, “Don't.”

“What?”

“Turn it into work.”

“I was describing the ball.”

“Greg.”

Apparently I had a reputation.

I threw again.

Missed low.

Center hit.

High hit.

The important part was not the score.

The important part was that by then my right shoulder had begun to tire in a way I recognized before it became pain. My hands were fine. My residual limb was quiet because I had been sitting. Right thigh did almost nothing. Trunk did more.

Different cost.

I noticed it.

Then I kept playing for one more round.

Not because I had failed to notice.

Because I wanted one more round.

This distinction felt dangerously like philosophy, so I refused to examine it.

I scored one.

Terrible decision.

Worth it.

Jorren finished his lunch and finally walked over.

“My turn.”

I handed him the ball.

“You said you don't play.”

“I said I wasn't playing.”

“That was forty minutes ago.”

“Yes.”

He stood behind the line.

Low left. Hit.

Center. Hit.

High right.

Hit.

Three throws. Three clean impacts.

No wasted motion.

I stared.

Lio stared.

Jorren handed the ball back.

“You asshole,” I said.

He smiled.

“I hit people for a living.”

“That is not the same skill.”

“Apparently close enough.”

“Again.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Lunch is over.”

He walked away.

I hated friendship.

*

I left before my shoulder made the decision for me.

This was partly because I was learning.

Mostly it was because Lio needed the chair back inside and I refused to be carried with it.

Standing after sitting that long required a moment. Right foot placed. One hand on chair. One on crutch. Rise. Balance. Second crutch. Good.

The residual limb had not swollen much while I played. It noticed the first ten crutch steps afterward, though. Blood shift. Pressure. Familiar pulse.

Manageable.

The right shoulder complained from throwing, not crutching. That was new enough to be interesting.

I did not have a notebook.

Excellent.

I stopped at a food stall and bought something fried around onions because the smell defeated whatever remained of my judgment.

The vendor wrapped it in paper.

“Careful, hot.”

I put the paper between my teeth while moving both crutches three steps to the side, then sat on a low wall.

This technique lacked dignity.

It worked.

I ate.

Alden found me halfway through.

He was sweaty again, which suggested Pessa had discovered what he was late for.

“How many?” he asked.

“Three.”

His face fell.

“Once.”

“Still.”

“Jorren made three first try.”

Alden's face changed in a much more satisfying way.

“What?”

“Yes.”

“He doesn't play.”

“That was also my understanding.”

Alden looked back toward the Guild as if betrayal might still be visible through two buildings.

“I hate him.”

“Yes.”

He took a piece of my fried onion without asking.

I slapped his wrist.

He got the onion anyway.

“Tomorrow?” he asked.

I almost asked what time.

Almost asked whether Pessa was training him first, whether the court would be free, whether the chair would be available, whether the same ball would be used, whether my shoulder would recover, whether repeated seated throwing had any useful transfer to knife work, combat, balance, future prosthetic use, crutch defense, or spellcasting.

All excellent questions.

None required yet.

“Maybe,” I said.

Alden nodded.

Then he stole another onion.

This time I caught his wrist.

He twisted free.

Progress for both of us.

*

Back at lodging, the keeper looked at my empty hands.

“No work?”

“No.”

“No road?”

“No.”

“No girl?”

“Lyssa has a name.”

“So no girl.”

“No.”

She looked at my shoulder when I lowered myself into the chair.

“What did you do?”

“Played a game.”

“With what?”

“Ball.”

She waited.

I waited.

“That all?” she asked.

“Yes.”

This answer felt suspiciously incomplete.

It was also true.

She put stew in front of me.

I ate.

Afterward I opened the notebook.

NORTH ROAD: WHITE FLOWERS IN DITCH.

DYE WORKS YELLOW IS OFFENSIVE.

CART VIBRATION COSTS MORE THAN EXPECTED.

The next page was blank.

I could write shoulder fatigue.

Seated rotation.

Reach boundary.

Phantom support assumption.

Chair position.

Release angle.

Three-mark scoring distribution.

Jorren is a bastard.

That one had merit.

I picked up the pencil.

Then put it down.

Tomorrow, if I went back, I could remember how the game worked.

If I forgot something, somebody would tell me.

Probably loudly.

I closed the notebook.

My right shoulder hurt.

My left foot felt as though it was tucked under the chair even though the chair had nothing under it except floor.

I moved the chair anyway.

The sensation did not change.

Fine.

I stole bread from the kitchen.

The keeper saw me.

She did not stop me.

Three points.

CHAPTER EIGHTY-SEVEN

My right shoulder objected to breakfast.

Not dramatically. It did not seize, tear, burn, or produce any of the symptoms that would justify using the word injury. It simply informed me, each time I lifted the spoon, that throwing leather balls at chalk circles had involved muscles I had not recently been using for throwing leather balls at chalk circles.

This was useful information.

It was also irritating because porridge was not heavy.

I changed hands.

The keeper watched me do it.

“No.”

“I haven’t asked anything.”

“You’re thinking about yesterday.”

“I think about most days.”

“You’re going back.”

“Maybe.”

She pointed the bread knife at my right shoulder. “No throwing.”

“I can play left-handed.”

“No.”

“That seems prejudicial.”

“That seems breakfast.”

I considered explaining that bilateral skill development had legitimate value.

Then I looked at the bread knife.

I ate.

The residual limb was better than it had been after the north road. Not normal, because normal had become a word with too many historical meanings, but the skin was dry, the swelling lower, and the deep ache from the cart had retreated into the sort of complaint that became louder only when I checked whether it was still there.

It was.

My missing left heel also itched.

That was less actionable.

By noon I had accomplished nothing except washing, eating, reading three pages of an old Guild notice I had already read, and deciding twice not to go watch Alden train.

The second decision was harder because it occurred while I was already halfway to the Guild.

I stopped at the corner.

The Guild was left.

The green door was right.

Straight ahead was a cooper arguing with a delivery boy about whether six hoops constituted a complete order when two of them were the wrong width.

I stood there long enough that the delivery boy noticed.

“Not you,” he said.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You looked like you were going to.”

“I was considering it.”

“Don’t.”

The cooper pointed at him. “See?”

I went right.

This was maturity.

Possibly.

The green door was open despite it being too early for most of the people who treated the place as an evening destination. Nessa was behind the counter with a rag over one shoulder and an expression suggesting she had already been disappointed by several objects.

Octavia sat at the back table with four cards face down in front of her and a little pile of copper bits at her elbow.

There were two other people at the table. I knew both by face and neither by name, which was ideal. Names created obligations.

Jorren occupied a chair beside them without cards.

He had a cup.

This was also ideal.

“You’re early,” Nessa said.

“For what?”

She looked at Octavia.

Octavia looked at me.

Jorren drank.

I disliked coordinated silence.

“What?”

“Sit,” Octavia said.

“No.”

“Good. Sit.”

“That is not how that works.”

“It worked.”

I looked down.

I had already moved toward the table.

Annoying.

The chair beside Jorren was ordinary, solid, and positioned so I could get both crutches against the wall without anyone stepping on them. I sat because standing indefinitely to prove that I had not been manipulated would have been a particularly expensive form of independence.

Octavia pushed four cards toward me.

“I don’t know this game.”

“Yes.”

“That usually matters.”

“Less than you think.”

Jorren said, “It matters.”

Octavia ignored him.

I looked at the cards.

They were narrow pasteboard, worn soft at the corners, each marked with one of four suits I recognized from other Carrow games. Cups. Nails. Birds. Towers. The values ran one through nine, except apparently not all values were present in all hands, which was either because the deck was incomplete or because I did not yet understand the deal.

Probably the second.

“How much?”

“One bit to stay in,” Octavia said.

“What am I buying?”

“The right to be wrong in public.”

“That seems overpriced.”

“One bit.”

I put down one bit.

Nessa called from the counter, “He’ll pay more.”

“I heard that.”

“You were meant to.”

Octavia dealt.

The game was called Four Doors, which was already suspicious because there were no doors involved.

Each player received four cards. One stayed hidden until the end. Three could be exchanged, one at a time, through a common row in the center. The goal was not simply to make the highest total. Matching suits mattered. Pairs mattered differently. Towers broke one kind of tie. Birds broke another. A hand that looked mediocre could become strong if the hidden card matched correctly.

I asked seven questions.

Octavia answered five.

“Why won’t you answer the other two?”

“Because one is strategy.”

“And the other?”

“Also strategy.”

“That seems arbitrary.”

“Yes.”

The first hand cost me one bit.

The second cost me two because I had misunderstood how aggressively one of the unnamed men valued a visible pair of nails.

The third I folded early.

Octavia looked disappointed.

“I had nothing.”

“You had a face.”

“I generally do.”

“It was a very informative face.”

I looked at Jorren.

He nodded.

“What did it say?”

Jorren considered. “You were about to explain why folding was correct.”

“That is not a face.”

“It is your face.”

I disliked this game.

I stayed.

By the fifth hand I understood enough to identify the first layer.

The cards mattered.

The visible row mattered.

What people took mattered.

What they declined mattered.

The order mattered.

Bet size mattered.

Speed mattered.

Eye movement mattered.

Posture mattered.

Breathing probably mattered, although trying to monitor breathing in three other people while remembering which towers had already appeared was excessive unless the expected return justified it.

It did not.

Probably.

Octavia won four bits from the man across from her by looking bored.

I watched carefully.

She did not look bored.

She performed bored.

The distinction was small enough that I only noticed because I had been watching her before she received the card that changed her hand.

Her shoulders had been loose.

Then they became loose on purpose.

Interesting.

The next hand I received two birds, a six of cups, and a useless tower.

Not useless objectively.

Useless to me.

The center row offered another bird.

I took it immediately.

Octavia glanced at me.

Mistake.

Not taking the bird. The speed.

I had announced that I liked it.

I could correct that.

On the next exchange, I waited.

Not naturally. I counted to three.

One.

Two.

Three.

Then I took a card I did not care about.

Octavia's mouth moved.

Not a smile.
