Worse.

Recognition.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You did something.”

“I breathed.”

“You breathed judgmentally.”

Jorren said, “She does.”

Octavia flicked one copper bit into the center.

The man across from her matched.

The woman beside him folded.

I matched.

I had a good hand.

Not excellent.

Good enough that the probability depended heavily on what Octavia had hidden, which meant the probability did not actually depend on what she had hidden because I did not know it.

This was the problem with probability when people used it conversationally. They usually meant confidence wearing arithmetic's coat.

Octavia exchanged one card.

Slowly.

I watched her fingers.

Nothing.

Her eyes.

Nothing.

Her shoulders.

Loose.

Naturally loose or deliberately loose?

I had one useful piece of evidence.

She had noticed me trying to manipulate timing.

Therefore she knew I was thinking about behavior.

Therefore any behavior she showed me might be chosen.

Which meant I needed to model what she believed I believed about what she believed I was trying to observe.

No.

That road ended in old men writing books about poker.

I had read some of those books.

Most were terrible.

Different game.

Same disease.

I looked at my cards.

Three birds.

Good.

I put in another bit.

Octavia matched.

The other man folded.

Now it was us.

She looked at me.

I looked back.

There was an obvious move available.

Appear uncertain.

I knew how to appear uncertain because I was uncertain almost constantly.

The difficulty was appearing uncertain in the correct way.

Actual uncertainty made me look at variables.

Performed uncertainty should probably look at the money.

I looked at the money.

Octavia said, “There.”

“What?”

“That.”

“What?”

“You moved your eyes.”

“Eyes move.”

“Not like that.”

I stared at her.

She grinned.

“You're pretending.”

“I am playing cards.”

“Yes.”

“That seems included.”

“It is.”

I considered the problem.

Then I realized I had stopped considering the hand.

This was probably also information.

I pushed in another bit.

Octavia did not.

She folded.

I won.

I felt immediate satisfaction.

Then suspicion.

“You folded because I had the better hand?”

“Yes.”

“Not because of the eye thing.”

“The eye thing told me you wanted me to think you were weak.”

“That should imply strength.”

“Usually.”

“So why fold?”

“Because your first bird was fast.”

I looked at the discarded row.

The first bird.

Five exchanges ago.

She had retained it.

Not the card. The fact.

“You knew I wanted birds.”

“I knew you were pleased by one.”

“That is not the same.”

“No.”

“But enough.”

“For that hand.”

I looked at Jorren.

He was smiling into his cup.

“This game is stupid.”

“Yes,” he said.

I played again.

The next hand I decided not to manipulate anything.

This lasted perhaps twelve seconds.

Then the man across from me raised, and I deliberately scratched my jaw because I had once read that inexperienced gamblers touched their faces when uncomfortable.

Octavia laughed so hard she had to put her cards down.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“That is obviously something.”

“You scratched.”

“My face itched.”

“No, it didn't.”

“You cannot know that.”

“You looked at me first.”

I had.

Damn.

The man across from me folded.

“Why did you fold?”

He shrugged. “Didn't like mine.”

“You weren't reacting to me?”

“No.”

This was insulting.

I lost that hand to Octavia.

I lost the next one because I spent too much attention deciding whether the woman beside her was genuinely impatient or performing impatience and failed to notice that I had discarded the only tower that would have protected my pair.

“Cards,” Octavia said.

“I know.”

“Do you?”

“I am learning.”

“You're studying the room.”

“The room is playing.”

“The cards are also playing.”

“The cards are cardboard.”

“They're beating you.”

Jorren made a small choking noise into his cup.

I pointed at him. “You are not participating.”

“I know.”

“You don't get to enjoy this.”

“I paid for the cup.”

“That does not include me.”

“It does today.”

Nessa called, “Table fee.”

I looked at her.

She held up one finger.

“No.”

“Outstanding balance.”

“You stole a copper yesterday.”

“Collected.”

“You invented the fee after I earned the money.”

“Administrative timing.”

Octavia said, “She's very powerful.”

“I have noticed.”

Nessa smiled without warmth.

I returned to the game.

The next hand, I got nothing useful.

Not secretly useful.

Actually bad.

A two of cups, a three of nails, a four of towers, and a seven of birds with no useful relationship between them.

I exchanged.

Still bad.

Again.

Worse.

The rational choice was to fold.

I knew this.

Octavia knew I knew this.

The others probably knew because I had spent the first three hands asking about expected losses from staying in.

I looked at my cards.

Then at Octavia.

She was watching me.

Not the hand.

Me.

I put in one bit.

Her eyebrows rose.

Interesting.

The man across from her folded.

The woman matched.

Octavia matched.

I exchanged my three of nails for a five of cups.

Still bad.

The woman took a tower.

Octavia declined the row entirely.

I put in another bit.

Now Octavia looked at my hands.

Not my face.

My hands.

I kept them still.

This was easier seated. There were advantages to having fewer available dramatic movements.

The woman folded.

Octavia stayed.

Of course she did.

We reached the last exchange.

I took nothing.

Octavia took nothing.

I had a terrible hand.

I pushed in two bits.

Jorren lowered his cup.

Octavia stared at me.

I had intended to look calm.

That was impossible because I was having fun.

Apparently those were different expressions.

She looked at the center.

At me.

At my cards.

At the discarded row.

Then she folded.

For half a second I did not move.

Then I collected the bits.

Octavia pointed at me. “Show.”

“No.”

“Show.”

“Rules say I don't have to.”

“I know the rules.”

“Then this seems resolved.”

“Greg.”

“No.”

Jorren said, “Don't.”

Octavia looked at him.

He shrugged. “He'll become unbearable.”

“I am already unbearable.”

“Worse.”

Octavia leaned back.

“Fine.”

I gathered the bits carefully.

My heart was beating faster than it had any right to.

Not fear.

Not exactly.

The peculiar bodily excitement of having stepped off a ledge that was only one inch high.

I had lied.

Badly, probably.

But successfully.

No.

Not lied.

Represented.

Also no.

I had made a choice intended to alter another person's model of my hand.

That was lying.

Cards made ethics conveniently cheap.

I smiled.

Octavia saw it.

“You had garbage.”

I said nothing.

Her eyes narrowed.

I waited.

This was difficult.

The urge to explain arrived immediately.

I wanted to tell her exactly why the hand had worked, which observations had mattered, which had not, why I had stayed in despite negative expected value, and why her attention shifting from my face to my hands had convinced me that she was uncertain enough to push.

I wanted to explain that the bluff had not been a general success. It had been local. Against her. In that hand. After I had established a pattern of overanalysis and obvious behavioral manipulation.

I wanted to explain all of it.

I did not.

Octavia's eyes narrowed further.

“Oh, fuck you.”

I laughed.

Jorren slapped the table once.

Nessa looked over.

“What?” Nessa asked.

“He didn't explain,” Jorren said.

Nessa frowned. “Is he sick?”

“I can explain.”

Octavia pointed at me. “No.”

The prohibition made it much harder.

I sat there with the explanation pressing against my teeth.

This was absurd.

Then Octavia started laughing.

Not because of the bluff.

Because she could see me suffering.

“You're awful,” I said.

“Yes.”

We played another hand.

I lost.

Then another.

Lost that too.

The bluff had not unlocked secret mastery.

This was disappointing but probably healthy.

By the time Lyssa came through the green door, I was down three bits overall and had developed a completely unjustified hatred of the four of towers.

She stopped beside the table.

“What are you doing?” Lyssa asked.

“Losing,” I said.

Octavia said, “Learning to lie.”

Lyssa looked at me.

I said, “That description lacks context.”

Octavia made a delighted sound.

Lyssa pulled out the empty chair beside me.

“I want the context.”

“You cannot have it.”

She sat.

“Why?”

“I am practicing.”

“Lying?”

“Not explaining.”

She looked at Octavia.

Octavia nodded solemnly.

Lyssa looked back at me.

“How's it going?”

“Poorly.”

“Why?”

I opened my mouth.

Closed it.

Lyssa smiled.

“That badly?”

“Yes.”

She stayed for three hands.

She did not play.

She watched.

This was worse than Octavia watching because I cared what Lyssa thought and because I had recently kissed her enough times to make her opinion physically salient.

I received a pair of cups.

Good enough to stay.

I exchanged once.

Improved.

Octavia watched my face.

I ignored her.

Lyssa watched my cards only when I tilted them enough for her to see, which was probably accidental until I noticed her doing it, at which point it became impossible to know.

I won one bit.

“Very impressive,” Lyssa said.

“Thank you.”

“Was that lying?”

“No.”

“Could've fooled me.”

I looked at her.

She smiled.

I liked her.

This was inconvenient.

The game continued.

My right shoulder began to ache from holding the cards too high.

That was ridiculous.

I lowered them.

My residual limb was fine. My hands were fine. My right leg had started to stiffen from sitting, so I shifted it forward and back under the table.

No catastrophe.

No revelation.

Just body.

After another hand, Lyssa stood.

“I have to go.”

“Where?”

“Work.”

“Oh.”

She looked at me.

I realized the question had sounded disappointed.

I was disappointed.

That was allowed.

Probably.

“I'll see you later?” she asked.

“Yes.”

No model.

No calendar check.

No calculation of whether later meant tonight or tomorrow or an unspecified socially acceptable interval.

Yes.

She bent and kissed my cheek.

Octavia made a noise.

Lyssa pointed at her without looking.

“Don't.”

Octavia raised both hands.

Lyssa left.

I watched the door for slightly too long.

Then I looked back at my cards.

Octavia was smiling.

“No.”

“I didn't say anything.”

“You were going to.”

“I was breathing.”

“Judgmentally.”

Jorren said, “She does.”

I lost another bit.

Eventually my shoulder moved from complaint to warning.

Not injury.

Enough.

I put my cards down.

“Done.”

Octavia looked at the pile in front of me.

“You're down four.”

“Three.”

“Four.”

“Nessa stole one.”

“Different ledger.”

“Same purse.”

Jorren stood.

“You going?”

“Yes.”

“Guild?”

I considered.

Alden might still be there.

The throwing game might still be there.

My shoulder had already voted.

“No.”

“Home?”

I looked outside.

Late afternoon light had turned the street gold along one edge and dirty gray along the other. A cart rolled past with empty baskets. Two children chased each other around a post. Someone farther down the street was singing badly while hammering something metal.

I did not want to go home yet.

“No.”

Jorren waited.

I waited too.

He shrugged.

“Food?”

“Yes.”

That was enough.

We went to find something fried.

I did not explain why.

This lasted almost six minutes.

Personal record.


CHAPTER EIGHTY-EIGHT

The keeper asked whether I still wanted my room.

This was a reasonable question.

I disliked it immediately.

“What?”

“Your room.”

“I know which room.”

“Good.”

She was standing at the bottom of the stairs with a folded sheet over one arm and a bucket beside her foot. I was sitting at the kitchen table with bread, cheese, and the six-legged clay horse from the night market.

The horse had migrated.

I had not moved it.

This meant the keeper had.

I pointed at it.

“Why is that here?”

“Rent.”

“That is not rent.”

“Decoration fee.”

“You cannot charge me for an object I own.”

“I can charge the object.”

The horse remained silent.

Coward.

The keeper nodded toward the stairs. “You still want it?”

My room.

Upstairs.

Bed. Window. Trunk. Two shirts I did not particularly like. One shirt I did. A stack of paper. A chipped cup. Three objects I had kept because they might become useful and had not yet justified their continued existence.

My life, apparently.

“Yes.”

“You haven't slept there in four nights.”

“Five.”

She waited.

I hated when people let my corrections improve their argument.

“The downstairs room is working,” she said.

“It is storage.”

“You sleep in it.”

“That does not alter its architectural identity.”

“It has a bed.”

“It has boxes.”

“Your upstairs room also has boxes.”

“Fewer.”

She shifted the sheet to her other arm.

“I'm asking because rent comes tomorrow.”

Ah.

Money.

The least philosophical of all forces.

“How much difference?”

She named it.

I knew the amount already. I had been paying it.

That was not what I had asked.

“How much cheaper downstairs?”

She named that too.

I calculated.

Then I stopped.

Then I calculated anyway because refusing arithmetic on principle was stupid.

The difference was not trivial.

It was also not ruinous.

I could keep the upstairs room.

Probably.

Exact purse remained a thing I had avoided reconstructing because the answer changed every time I ate, rode somewhere, lost at cards, bought a blue shirt, or allowed Nessa to invent taxation.

I had enough.

That was a number.

Not a precise one.

Still useful.

The keeper watched my face.

I wondered whether Octavia had permanently damaged my relationship with faces.

“What?”

“You're doing sums.”

“Yes.”

“Want downstairs?”

“No.”

That came out before the rest of the sums finished.

Interesting.

The keeper nodded.

That was all.

No argument.

No warning about stairs.

No speech about practicality.

She picked up the bucket.

I became suspicious.

“You agree?”

“With what?”

“Keeping the room.”

“You pay for it.”

“Yes.”

“So keep it.”

“You just asked whether I wanted it.”

“Yes.”

“And now you have no opinion.”

“I have lots of opinions.”

“About this.”

She considered.

“Your room has better light.”

That was not the opinion I expected.

She started up the stairs.

“Wait.”

She stopped on the second step and looked back.

“I want to go up.”

“Now?”

“Yes.”

She looked at my shoulder.

My right shoulder was better than yesterday. Not perfect. Raising my arm high still produced a dull objection, but normal crutch use had been fine all morning.

She looked lower.

The residual limb had behaved. Dry. Less swollen. No heat. No new redness. The north road had mostly stopped collecting interest.

Then she looked at my face.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You are all doing that now.”

“Doing what?”

“Looking at my face.”

“I've always looked at your face.”

“Not analytically.”

“I promise I am not doing that.”

“That sounds like something someone doing it would say.”

She went upstairs.

I finished breakfast.

Not because she had won.

Because stair practice immediately after eating bread too fast was a poor decision.

There were fourteen steps.

Twelve, landing, two.

The rail ran ash-smooth beneath my left hand, three posts, wall return. Lerris Vane had built it properly. The stringer had been inspected. Nothing was secretly waiting to kill me.

This was useful to remember because my body had developed opinions about stairs independent of engineering.

The keeper came back down with the old sheet.

“You still going?”

“Yes.”

“Then stop staring.”

“I am assessing.”

“You know the stairs.”

“That does not eliminate assessment.”

“It has been seven minutes.”

I stood.

Crutches first.

Right foot planted.

Left knee bent, residual limb clear.

The ascent had become familiar enough to have sequence but not familiar enough to become automatic. That was probably good. Automatic was where my missing foot occasionally rejoined the workforce without authorization.

I put one crutch where I wanted it, hand to rail, weight through right leg, then up.

Pause.

Reset.

Again.

The first four were easy.

Easy was relative.

Easy meant I did not have to negotiate with each muscle individually.

By six, my right thigh was working.

By eight, my left hand had tightened on the rail.

At ten, the keeper said, “Slow.”

“I am slow.”

“Slower.”

This was insulting because she was correct.

I stopped.

Not dramatically.

Just stopped.

My right leg trembled once, then settled.

The old version of me would have categorized the tremor.

Fatigue.

Motor control.

Load.

Recovery interval.

Potential failure mode.

The current version did all of that too.

He was not dead.

He had simply acquired a chair-shaped appreciation for pauses.

There was no chair.

I leaned into the rail and crutch.

The missing left foot felt planted one step below me.

It was not.

I looked down at the actual geometry.

Right foot.

Wood.

Crutch.

Rail.

No left foot.

Good.

“Ready?” the keeper asked.

“Yes.”

Two more.

Landing.

Turn.

The turn remained stupid.

Stairs should not require choreography.

Two final steps.

Then upstairs.

I stood in the narrow hall breathing harder than fourteen steps deserved.

The keeper did not comment.

This was kindness.

Or boredom.

Either was acceptable.

My room smelled closed.

Wood, old cloth, a little dust, the faint dry smell of paper.

The window was shut.

The bed was made badly.

My trunk sat at the foot of it.

Nothing had happened.

This surprised me.

Not intellectually.

I had not expected burglary, fire, structural collapse, spontaneous fungal occupation, or the development of a small upstairs government.

But unused rooms acquire a strange quality. They stop feeling like places and begin feeling like stored versions of places.

I moved to the bed and sat.

The mattress compressed.

Still mine.

Apparently.

The keeper put the clean sheet on the trunk.

“Need anything?”

“No.”

“Coming down before dinner?”

“Yes.”

She looked at me.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“That was a look.”

“That was me checking whether you were going to try descending alone.”

“I wasn't.”

“Good.”

She left.

I waited until her steps disappeared.

Then I said, “I could.”

The room did not believe me.

I opened the window.

Carrow entered immediately.

Not the city.

The noise.

Cart wheels.

Someone calling prices.

A dog objecting to something with moral certainty.

Hammering from two streets over.

A woman laughing below.

The smell of bread, smoke, horse, river damp, and something fried badly enough that it might still be worth eating.

My upstairs window had a different city than the downstairs storage room.

This was obvious.

Height changed sightlines.

The storage room had wall, alley feet, and whatever portion of the sky happened to survive between buildings.

Up here I could see roofs.

Not many.

Enough.

A slice of Guild roof farther away.

A chimney with three cracked bricks.

Laundry moving between buildings.

Two birds fighting over something on a gutter.

I sat on the bed and watched them.

One bird won.

The other returned six seconds later.

Poor strategic learning.

I approved.

My papers were where I had left them.

I pulled the stack from the trunk.

Old notes.

Work.

Magic.

Money.

Names.

Questions.

The kind of paper archaeology that could consume an afternoon if I let it.

I found one page from before West River.

A list.

Not important enough to remember writing.

Things to ask Edrin.

A Guild job possibility.

Something about Arlo and Vessa's regulator.

A note to price better paper.

At the bottom:

STAIRS AT LODGING?

I stared at it.

I had apparently once considered stairs a property feature.

Technically they still were.

I turned the page over.

Blank.

Good.

I put it aside.

There were newer notes too.

NORTH ROAD: WHITE FLOWERS IN DITCH.

DYE WORKS YELLOW IS OFFENSIVE.

CART VIBRATION COSTS MORE THAN EXPECTED.

I had written those downstairs.

They looked different up here.

Not because the words changed.

Because I had a window.

I moved the papers.

The blue shirt hung from a peg.

I touched it.

Still blue.

Excellent.

Good.

The damaged left boot was not here. Tam had the salvage leather.

My right boot sat under the bed beside nothing.

That arrangement looked wrong.

I looked away.

Then back.

Still wrong.

Fine.

Some wrong things were just true.

I took the right boot out, checked the sole, found nothing requiring attention, and put it back.

The empty space remained.

I considered moving something into it.

No.

That would be worse.

I lay back on the bed.

This was not medically optimal posture for everything.

It was, however, extremely good.

My right shoulder relaxed.

My right leg stretched.

The residual limb rested without pressure.

The ceiling had a water stain shaped like a coastline from a country that did not exist.

Or perhaps did.

My future geographic memory was unreliable enough that I could not safely rule out ceiling countries.

I closed my eyes.

I woke to someone knocking.

Not the door downstairs.

My door.

I opened my eyes.

Light had moved across the floor.

I had slept.

This was unacceptable.

“Who?”

“Me.”

Lyssa.

I sat up too fast.

My residual limb swung.

My missing foot struck the floor.

The sensation was complete enough that my stomach dropped before my eyes corrected it.

Nothing hit.

Nothing hurt.

Old map.

I breathed once.

“Wait.”

I looked at myself.

Hair.

Fine.

Shirt.

Not blue.

Why was I not wearing the blue shirt?

Because I had not expected Lyssa.

This was a weak excuse.

I crutched to the door and opened it.

She stood in the hall with one hand against the wall and a folded paper packet under her arm.

“You're upstairs.”

“Yes.”

“I noticed.”

“How?”

“Stairs.”

“Strong evidence.”

She looked past me.

“I've never seen your room.”

This was true.

That seemed suddenly important.

Not objectively.

Still.

“Do you want to?”

She smiled.

“Yes.”

I moved aside.

This required more geometry than the gesture deserved.

Crutch.

Door.

Right foot.

Do not block entry with body.

Do not create dramatic invitation accidentally.

Lyssa entered.

She looked around.

There was not much to look at.

Bed.

Trunk.

Window.

Peg.

Paper.

Cup.

One chair.

The six-legged horse was downstairs, which damaged the room's cultural standing.

“This is nicer,” she said.

“Than storage?”

“Yes.”

“That is an extremely low comparison.”

She went to the window.

I watched her look out.

This was different from looking out myself.

Possibly because she had hair that moved when the air came in.

That was not analytically relevant.

I sat on the bed.

“What is that?”

She held up the paper packet.

“Food.”

“Why?”

“You said I'd see you later.”

“I did.”

“This is later.”

Good.

Very strong system.

She opened the packet.

Fried dough.

Honey.

I stared.

“You brought this upstairs?”

“I carried it.”

I looked at my crutches.

Then at the food.

Then at her.

“Yes,” she said.

“I didn't say anything.”

“You did with your face.”

Octavia had ruined everything.

Lyssa sat beside me.

Not touching at first.

Then our shoulders touched.

My right one complained faintly.

I shifted.

She noticed.

“Throwing?”

“Yes.”

“You went back?”

“No.”

“Cards?”

“Yes.”

“How do cards hurt your shoulder?”

“I was holding them too high.”

She laughed.

I ate fried dough.

Honey got on my thumb.

Lyssa took the piece from my hand and ate the rest.

This was theft.

I permitted it.

We talked about nothing important.

Her work.

A customer who had changed her mind three times about a hem and then blamed the cloth.

A man downstairs who had tried to sell the keeper onions too soft to survive the day.

Jorren's theory that fried fish became health food if eaten while walking.

My counterargument that walking while eating fried fish introduced risk without altering nutrition.

Lyssa rejected both positions.

The light moved.

At some point she put her head against my shoulder.

Left shoulder.

Competent woman.

I looked out the window.

The roofs had gone orange.

I thought about rent.

Not the amount.

The room.

I could have moved downstairs.

Cheaper.

Easier.

More practical.

I had not.

There were reasons.

Privacy.

Light.

Air.

Belongings.

A door that was mine to close.

A place Lyssa had not seen before because it belonged to a part of my life that had become temporarily difficult to reach.

All defensible.

I could make the case.

I did not.

Lyssa said, “What?”

“Nothing.”

“You did a whole thing.”

“I did not.”

“You went quiet.”

“That is allowed.”

“It is.”

I waited.

She waited.

I realized she was not asking.

Good.

I ate another piece of fried dough.

Eventually the keeper called from below.

“Greg!”

“Yes?”

“You coming down?”

“Yes.”

“When?”

I looked at the window.

Then at Lyssa.

“Soon.”

The keeper made a sound that traveled up the stairs and conveyed skepticism without language.

Lyssa smiled.

“You need help?”

“No.”

That answer came too quickly.

I corrected it.

“Not with the stairs. I need her spotting.”

Lyssa nodded.

No offense.

No insistence.

No attempt to become useful.

Also good.

We stood.

I took the crutches.

At the door, Lyssa kissed me.

Not my cheek.

Brief.

Then again, less brief.

My body did not attempt to step anywhere.

Progress.

Or sitting had trained it.

No.

Do not build theory from two kisses and a card game.

She pulled back.

“I'll go first.”

“Why?”

“So I'm not standing behind you on the stairs.”

That was sensible.

I disliked how many people around me were sensible without needing my assistance.

She went down.

The keeper came up to the landing.

I followed with the rail, crutch, right foot, pause.

Descent still required more attention than ascent.

At the landing my right thigh trembled.

I stopped.

Nobody spoke.

Then I continued.

At the bottom, I sat immediately.

Not because I had failed.

Because there was a chair.

The keeper handed me water.

Lyssa took the remaining fried dough.

“Hey.”

“You were busy.”

“That does not transfer ownership.”

“It transferred possession.”

I looked at the keeper.

“Do something.”

“Table fee.”

“This is not a table.”

“Stair fee.”

“You cannot keep inventing fees.”

She smiled.

Lyssa laughed.

I drank the water.

Upstairs, my room remained upstairs.

Fourteen steps away.

Still inconvenient.

Still mine.

Rent due tomorrow.

I would pay it.


CHAPTER EIGHTY-NINE

Rent took less time than deciding to pay rent.

I gave the keeper the money after breakfast.

She counted it once.

I watched.

She looked up.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You're watching me count.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because it is money.”

“You think I steal?”

“Yes.”

She nodded. “Fair.”

Then she put the coins away and handed me a folded scrap of paper.

I looked at it.

“What is this?”

“Guild.”

That was not an answer.

The paper had my name on one side.

GREGORY.

Under it, in smaller writing:

IF HE COMES BY, ASK HIM TO WAIT.

No signature.

No task.

No rate.

No explanation.

I turned it over.

Blank.

“When did this arrive?”

“Morning.”

“Who brought it?”

“Boy.”

“Which boy?”

“One with legs.”

I looked at her.

She looked at me.

“That was unnecessary.”

“I thought it narrowed it.”

“It did not.”

I put the note in my pocket.

I did not leave immediately.

This was deliberate.

Possibly petty.

Mostly I wanted another piece of bread.

The Guild was busy when I arrived.

Not dramatic busy.

Ordinary busy.

The front hall had six people waiting, two people arguing, one person pretending not to argue while speaking louder than everyone else, and Merrin behind the front desk with three stacks of paper arranged in the particular order of someone who would know if another person moved one sheet half an inch.

He saw me.

“Good.”

“That is unusually welcoming.”

“Sit.”

There was a stool behind the side end of the desk.

I looked at it.

Then at him.

“No.”

“Yes.”

“What am I doing?”

“Nothing.”

“That is rarely paid.”

“It isn't.”

“Then I object more strongly.”

Merrin took a ledger from under the desk.

A man at the front of the line said, “I've been here twenty minutes.”

Merrin said, “Then you know how the line works.”

The man stopped speaking.

Useful skill.

Merrin pointed at the stool.

“I need to go upstairs.”

“For what?”

“Not your business.”

“Then why am I involved?”

“You aren't.”

“This is becoming circular.”

“Sit there. If anyone asks where I am, say upstairs. If anyone hands you anything, do not accept it. If anyone wants a decision, you cannot make one. If anyone says they were told something, tell them to wait.”

“How long?”

“Ten minutes.”

“That is suspiciously specific.”

“Greg.”

I sat.

Merrin left.

The line looked at me.

I looked at the line.

This was a mistake.

Not mine.

Yet.

The stool was acceptable.

No back.

Too high for my left knee to rest comfortably without the residual limb hanging, so I shifted sideways and planted my right foot. Both crutches fit against the desk within reach.

The first man stepped forward.

“I need a replacement token.”

“I cannot make decisions.”

“It isn't a decision.”

“Then why do you need the Guild?”

He stared at me.

I reconsidered.

“Wait for Merrin.”

“Where is he?”

“Upstairs.”

“How long?”

“Approximately ten minutes.”

The man looked at the stairs.

Then at me.

“You new?”

“No.”

“Clerk?”

“No.”

“What are you?”

“Temporarily seated.”

The woman behind him laughed.

He did not.

He stepped aside.

The woman came forward.

“I was told to leave this.”

She held out a sealed envelope.

I did not take it.

“Wait for Merrin.”

“I don't need Merrin. I need to leave this.”

“I was specifically told not to accept anything.”

“With you?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“I assume experience.”

She looked at the envelope.

Then at me.

Then tucked it back under her arm.

“Fine.”

Good.

Two people successfully not helped.

The third person was easier.

“Where's Merrin?”

“Upstairs.”

“Fine.”

He left.

Excellent.

I began to understand clerical work.

The fourth person ruined it.

He was carrying a wooden tally board with six small brass tags clipped along one edge.

“I need Bay Three released.”

“I cannot make decisions.”

“Merrin already released it.”

“Then it is released.”

“He didn't mark it.”

“Then wait for Merrin.”

“The cart is outside.”

“Still wait.”

“The driver's charging.”

“That sounds unfortunate.”

He stared at me.

I could see the problem.

That was dangerous.

Bay Three was one of the covered receiving bays on the east side. I knew enough about Guild traffic to know that holding a cart outside cost money and blocked street space. If Merrin had actually approved the release and merely failed to mark the board, waiting ten minutes was pointless.

I also knew Merrin had told me not to make decisions.

Very clear.

Almost offensively clear.

The man put the tally board on the desk.

“Look. Vale consignment. Empty return crates. Nothing sealed.”

I looked.

That was also dangerous.

The tags were ordinary brass.

One marked VALE.

One marked RETURN.

One marked BAY 3.

The rest meant less to me.

“If Merrin released it,” I said, “why are you here?”

“Because the yard won't open the chain without the mark.”

“Correctly.”

“Yes.”

“So wait.”

He exhaled through his nose.

“Fine.”

He moved aside.

I felt good.

This lasted eleven seconds.

A girl came through the front door carrying a basket of folded cloth.

Not a child.

Younger than me, probably.

She looked at the line, looked at me, and said, “Where do I put Guild wash?”

I had no idea.

I could infer.

That was worse.

“Wait for Merrin.”

She stared at me.

“With wet cloth?”

I looked at the basket.

It was not wet.

“Is it wet?”

“No.”

“Then yes.”

She stared longer.

“Who are you?”

“Temporarily seated.”

The woman with the envelope laughed again.

The girl put the basket on the floor and sat on it.

Fine.

The next man wanted to know whether a Bronze named Tavin had checked in.

I knew Tavin.

I did not know whether he had checked in.

“Wait for Merrin.”

“Can you look?”

“No.”

“You're behind the desk.”

“That has proven misleading.”

“Ledger's right there.”

He pointed.

The ledger was right there.

I looked at it.

Merrin had not told me not to look at the ledger.

He had told me not to accept things or make decisions.

Looking was not deciding.

I reached toward it.

Then stopped.

The man watched my hand.

I thought of Octavia.

Not because this was performance.

Because being watched altered the decision.

If I opened the ledger, I would know whether Tavin had checked in.

Possibly.

If the ledger was current.

If I read the right column.

If Tavin used the same registry for whatever this man meant by checked in.

Knowledge would arrive faster than authority.

That was familiar.

I put my hand back.

“Wait for Merrin.”

The man sighed.

Good.

I was excellent at this.

Then the front door opened and Jorren came in.

He saw me behind the desk.

Stopped.

Looked at the line.

Looked back at me.

“No.”

“I agree.”

“What happened?”

“Merrin went upstairs.”

“And left you?”

“Yes.”

Jorren looked toward the ceiling.

“He's brave.”

“I have made no decisions.”

The Bay Three man said, “He won't even make the one already made.”

Jorren looked at him.

Then at me.

“What one?”

“Do not assist.”

“I wasn't.”

“You were about to.”

“I was not.”

Jorren smiled.

I disliked him.

He moved to the side wall and leaned against it.

“What do you need?” I asked.

“Nothing.”

“Then why are you here?”

“Now? This.”

He folded his arms.

Spectator.

Traitor.

The line advanced through attrition rather than service.

One person left.

Two more arrived.

A woman asked whether the Guild bought damaged spearheads.

“Wait for Merrin.”

A man asked whether the east yard was open.

I knew it was.

I had seen carts entering when I arrived.

“Yes.”

He thanked me and left.

Jorren said, “Decision.”

“That was observation.”

“You answered.”

“He asked a factual question.”

“What if the yard closed after you came in?”

I looked toward the door.

It had been perhaps fifteen minutes.

No.

Twelve.

Maybe.

“Then I would be wrong.”

“Yes.”

“That does not make it a decision.”

“Feels like one if he gets there and it's shut.”

I hated this.

The girl sitting on the wash basket said, “East yard's open.”

“Thank you.”

“My sister's there.”

“Excellent.”

Jorren nodded. “Now you have a source.”

“I had a source.”

“You had a memory.”

I looked at him.

“Why are you here?”

He smiled.

I looked away.

Merrin still had not returned.

Ten minutes had become something else.

I considered going upstairs.

Impossible.

Not physically impossible.

Administratively impossible.

Leaving the desk defeated the purpose of being at the desk.

Also stairs.

No.

The Bay Three man tapped his tally board.

“Cart's still charging.”

“I know.”

“You could send someone upstairs.”

I looked at the line.

No one volunteered.

Jorren remained useless.

“Go get him,” I said.

The Bay Three man blinked.

“Me?”

“Yes.”

“I can't go upstairs.”

“Why?”

“Yard boots.”

I looked down.

Mud.

Substantial mud.

Guild front hall had rules about that.

Fine.

I looked at Jorren.

“No,” he said.

“I did not ask.”

“You looked.”

“That is apparently legally binding now.”

The woman with the envelope said, “I'll go.”

I looked at her shoes.

Clean.

“Good.”

She started toward the stairs.

Then stopped.

“Can I leave this with you while I go?”

She held out the envelope.

“No.”

She laughed.

“Worth trying.”

She went upstairs carrying it.

This was delegation.

Probably.

I had not made a decision about Guild business.

I had made a decision about who could climb stairs.

No.

She had volunteered.

Important distinction.

The front door opened again.

A man came in fast enough that the room changed.

Not running.

Purposeful.

He went straight to the desk.

“Who has west shed keys?” he asked.

I did not know.

“Wait for Merrin.”

“Can't.”

“Why?”

“Latch broke. Door's swinging into the lane.”

That was different.

“How bad?”

“Bad enough I came inside.”

Useful scale.

“Is anyone holding it?”

“Yes.”

“Then wait.”

“They need the keys.”

I looked around.

Everyone was looking at me.

Of course.

I could solve this.

Not the latch.

The information.

Keys had locations.

People knew locations.

The Guild was a system.

I knew enough of it to route a question.

Merrin upstairs.

Yard staff outside.

Jorren standing against wall because he was a bad person.

“Jorren.”

“No.”

“This is not clerical.”

“What is it?”

“Door.”

He looked at the man.

“West shed?”

“Yes.”

“Keys hang in the yard office.”

The man turned.

Then paused.

“Which hook?”

Jorren shrugged. “Ask yard.”

The man left.

Solved.

Not by me.

Annoying.

I felt the shape of the error before I knew what it was.

I had assumed the front desk was the information center because the desk looked like the center.

Jorren knew because he worked here.

The yard knew because they used the keys.

Merrin might not have been necessary at all.

The next person stepped forward.

I held up a hand.

“Before you speak, is there someone other than Merrin who actually owns your problem?”

The man considered.

“Probably.”

“Excellent.”

He left.

Jorren laughed.

“This is much better.”

“I am improving throughput.”

“You're sending everyone away.”

“Those can be identical under certain conditions.”

The girl on the wash basket raised her hand.

I pointed at her.

“Who owns wash?”

“Kitchen.”

“Why are you here?”

“Kitchen told me front hall.”

“Why?”

She shrugged. “They don't want the basket in the kitchen.”

I stared.

System failure.

Or family dynamics.

Impossible to distinguish.

“Wait for Merrin.”

She lowered her hand.

The woman returned from upstairs.

“Merrin says he's coming.”

“Did he say when?”

“No.”

“Did you ask?”

“No.”

I closed my eyes.

She put the envelope on the desk.

I opened my eyes.

“No.”

“You didn't accept it.”

“It is touching the desk.”

“Not your hands.”

“That is not the standard.”

“What standard?”

“Merrin's.”

“He said don't accept it?”

“Yes.”

“You didn't.”

I looked at the envelope.

Then at her.

She smiled.

Octavia had contaminated the population.

I did not touch it.

Merrin returned three minutes later.

He came down the stairs carrying a narrow ledger and looking more annoyed than when he left.

He stopped at the bottom.

Looked at the line.

Looked at me.

Looked at the envelope.

“I didn't accept it,” I said.

The woman said, “True.”

Merrin picked it up.

He looked at the Bay Three tally board.

“Why is this still here?” Merrin asked.

The man made a sound I would have enjoyed if it were not aimed partly at me.

“You told me not to make decisions.”

“I released Bay Three before I went upstairs.”

“He said that.”

“So?”

“You didn't mark it.”

Merrin stared at me.

I stared back.

“Could I have marked it?”

“No.”

“Could I have told the yard to release it?”

“No.”

“Then why are you looking at me like that?”

“Because you could've sent him to Dena.”

I stopped.

“Dena can mark it?”

“She owns bay board when I'm off desk.”

I looked at the Bay Three man.

He looked exhausted.

“Did you know that?” I asked.

“Yes.”

“Why didn't you go to Dena?”

“She was in south yard.”

“Why didn't you say that?”

“You didn't ask.”

I looked at Jorren.

He was enjoying himself too much.

Merrin marked the board.

The man took it and left at speed.

Merrin pointed at the wash basket.

“Kitchen.”

“They sent her here.”

Merrin looked at the girl.

“Why?”

“Cook says front hall keeps losing cloth.”

Merrin's face changed.

Not much.

Enough.

“Put it behind the counter.”

I moved my crutch.

The girl slid the basket behind the counter.

Done.

Merrin handled the replacement token in less than a minute.

The damaged spearhead question went to stores.

The Tavin question went to a different registry, not the ledger I had almost opened.

Good.

Very good.

The east yard was still open.

I retained that victory.

Within six minutes, the line was gone.

Merrin sat in his chair.

I remained on the stool.

Jorren remained against the wall.

“Why did you need me?” I asked.

Merrin opened the narrow ledger.

“Because someone had to tell people I was upstairs.”

“That did not require this.”

I gestured at the desk.

“You made it require this.”

“I followed your instructions.”

“Mostly.”

“I made no decisions.”

“You sent a woman upstairs.”

“She volunteered.”

“You told a man to find someone who owned his problem.”

“That was excellent.”

“It was.”

I paused.

“Really?”

“Yes.”

That was suspicious.

Merrin wrote something.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“What are you writing?”

“Work.”

“About me?”

“No.”

I leaned.

He closed the ledger.

“Greg.”

“Fine.”

I sat back.

My right shoulder was fine.

My right thigh had stiffened from the high stool.

The residual limb did not like hanging, so I had kept the knee bent and shifted sideways for most of the time. Not painful. Not ideal.

I stood carefully.

Crutches under arms.

No.

Not under arms.

Hands.

Always hands.

I had corrected that enough times in my head that it had become irritating.

Jorren pushed off the wall.

“You done clerking?”

“I was never clerking.”

Merrin said, “Correct.”

“Thank you.”

“You'd be terrible.”

I looked at him.

“You left me there.”

“For ten minutes.”

“It was thirty.”

“Twenty-seven.”

“That is not better.”

“Upstairs took longer.”

“What was upstairs?”

“Not your business.”

Still.

Good.

I liked that less than I respected it.

I looked at the empty front hall.

There was an obvious conclusion available.

Something about knowing the system from the outside versus knowing who held authority inside it.

Something about desks creating false centers.

Something about questions belonging to people before they belonged to procedures.

Something about how quickly I had wanted to become useful when my assigned task had been to say one sentence and wait.

All true.

Probably.

I did not need all of them.

“What do I get?” I asked.

Merrin looked up.

“For what?”

“Twenty-seven minutes.”

“You sat.”

“I performed queue control.”

“You obstructed queue control.”

“I prevented unauthorized decisions.”

“By you.”

“Exactly.”

Jorren said, “Pay him.”

Merrin looked at him.

“Why?”

“I want to see what number he argues with.”

I considered this.

“Never mind.”

Jorren's face fell.

Excellent.

I turned toward the door.

Merrin said, “Greg.”

I looked back.

He tossed something.

Bad choice.

My right hand was on the crutch.

My left hand was also occupied.

The object hit my chest and dropped.

I stared at the floor.

One copper bit.

Jorren started laughing.

Merrin said, “Substitute clerk.”

“I was not a clerk.”

“Then give it back.”

I bent badly.

Stopped.

No.

I was not picking a copper off the floor while holding two crutches with two people watching.

Jorren picked it up.

He held it out.

I took it.

“Thank you.”

He nodded.

Merrin had already returned to his ledger.

I put the bit in my pocket.

One bit was not enough to matter.

That was not the point.

I had been paid for sitting somewhere I did not belong, answering almost nothing, and eventually learning to redirect questions toward people who knew more than I did.

There were worse professions.

I went outside.

The east yard was still open.

I checked.


CHAPTER NINETY

I wanted a chair.

Not a special chair.

This distinction became important.

I wanted an ordinary wooden chair with four legs, a back, a seat, and no moral purpose.

The chair in my upstairs room had all of those things except comfort.

Comfort had not mattered much before because I had mostly used it for putting clothes on.

Now I was spending more time upstairs.

Reading.

Writing.

Looking out the window.

Occasionally allowing a woman to bring me fried dough.

The chair had developed ambitions beyond its construction.

After twenty minutes, the front edge pressed behind my right thigh. After thirty, my lower back began negotiating. The left side of the seat did nothing useful for the residual limb, which was not the chair's fault because the chair had been built for a customer with the standard inventory of lower legs.

Still.

I wanted a better chair.

This was how I ended up in a furniture shop arguing against improvements.

The shop sat three streets east of the lodging house, open to the road through a pair of wide doors. Half the front room was chairs. The other half was tables pretending not to be chairs.

Wood shavings curled across the floor.

A woman at a workbench was fitting a stretcher between two chair legs.

I knew her by face.

She knew me by face.

This was increasingly common in Carrow and mildly alarming.

“You're the stair rail,” she said.

“I am not.”

“The one with the rail.”

“Yes.”

“Lerris made it.”

“Yes.”

She looked at my crutches.

Then at me.

“Chair?”

“Yes.”

She stood.

I immediately became suspicious.

“Ordinary chair.”

She stopped.

“I haven't said anything.”

“I am establishing scope.”

“Sit.”

She pointed to a chair.

I sat.

It was too low.

“Not that one.”

“You told me to sit.”

“I was learning.”

“About me?”

“About the chair.”

Good answer.

I stood.

This took more effort than I wanted it to.

Low chairs were traps disguised as furniture.

Right foot under me.

Hands.

Push.

Crutch.

Balance.

The woman watched.

I disliked that.

Not because she was staring.

Because she was competent enough that I could see her measuring without measuring.

“How high's yours?”

I told her approximately.

She held a hand beside her hip.

“That?”

“Probably.”

“Probably is bad furniture.”

“I can measure it.”

“Do that.”

She moved to another chair.

Higher.

Flat seat.

Straight back.

Arms.

“No arms.”

“Why?”

“They interfere with crutches.”

“Getting up?”

“Sometimes. Also placing them beside me.”

She looked at the chair.

Then moved it away without argument.

Excellent.

Third chair.

No arms.

Higher seat.

Slight backward angle.

I sat.

Better.

Not good.

The front edge still met my right thigh in the wrong place.

I shifted.

She watched.

“What?”

“You're sitting crooked.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

I looked down.

My left knee was bent. The residual limb stayed clear of the seat edge, but to do that comfortably I had rotated slightly right.

“Because if I sit square, the left side presses here.”

I touched the back of my thigh above the knee.

“Not the end?”

“No.”

She nodded.

This was good.

No dramatic pause.

No expression about tragedy.

Just location.

She crouched and looked at the seat.

“Could cut the left front corner back.”

“No.”

She looked up.

“Why?”

“I want a chair.”

“That would still be a chair.”

“I want an ordinary chair.”

“Ordinary chairs fit ordinary bodies badly all the time.”

“That is not helping your sales argument.”

“It is helping my chair argument.”

I stood.

She moved to a fourth.

“Try.”

I did.

This one had a woven seat.

Higher again.

The weave gave slightly under my weight.

Better on the right thigh.

Worse under the left because the edge sagged differently when I shifted.

“No.”

She nodded.

Fifth.

Wood.

Broad seat.

Almost level.

Back upright enough that I could write at a table without folding forward.

I sat square.

Interesting.

The seat was deep enough that the left thigh rested without the front edge reaching the sensitive area behind the knee. The residual limb hung free without contact.

My right foot planted.

I could stand from it without using the back of my right calf against the seat.

I stood.

Sat.

Stood again.

The woman said, “That's annoying.”

“What?”

“You found one.”

“You wanted me to find one.”

“I wanted to sell you work.”

“Ah.”

She was honest.

I liked her.

This was dangerous.

“How much?”

She named a price.

I disliked her.

“That is a chair.”

“Yes.”

“Not a horse.”

“No.”

“It has four legs and no ability to move itself.”

“Correct.”

“That should reduce cost.”

“Horse eats.”

“This does not.”

“Exactly.”

I looked at the chair.

Good chair.

Too expensive.

Not impossibly expensive.

More than I wanted to spend.

“How much for the ugly one?”

She looked around.

“Which ugly one?”

I pointed.

A chair near the wall had a broad seat, one repaired back spindle, and a dark stain across one side that looked like someone had died while eating stew.

“That isn't ugly.”

“It is visibly guilty.”

“Old tavern chair.”

“Why is it here?”

“Repair.”

“For the tavern?”

“No. They replaced the set. I bought six.”

“How many left?”

“Two.”

“Why?”

“Because they're good chairs.”

I crutched over.

She moved it clear for me.

I sat.

The seat was broad.

Height good.

Back slightly too curved.

The repaired spindle did not matter.

The stain was definitely stew.

Probably.

I shifted left.

No edge pressure.

Right foot planted.

I stood.

Easy enough.

“How much?”

She named a lower price.

Still not low.

“Why is the new one so much more?”

“New wood. New labor. Matching stock. Finish.”

“This has labor.”

“Repair labor.”

“And old wood.”

“Yes.”

“Which has survived long enough to demonstrate structural competence.”

She stared at me.

“That is the worst way anyone has ever asked for a discount.”

“It is a valid point.”

“No.”

“Old furniture has evidence.”

“Old furniture has old joints.”

“Which you repaired.”

“One spindle.”

“What about the joints?”

“Checked.”

“So evidence.”

She folded her arms.

I had become a customer.

This was different from being useful.

I had no jurisdiction.

No professional standing.

No reason she should care what I thought except that I had money and she wanted some of it.

This was refreshing.

“How much if I carry it?”

She looked at my crutches.

I looked at the chair.

“That was a test.”

“You failed it.”

“I agree.”

“Delivery's one bit.”

“One bit?”

“Three streets.”

“I can see my lodging from the corner.”

“Then carry it.”

I looked at her.

She smiled.

Octavia had also ruined smiles.

“Half bit.”

“There is no half bit.”

“Then free.”

“One bit.”

“I will ask Jorren.”

“Then Jorren can carry it.”

“He might.”

“Good.”

This was not going well.

I stood beside the chair.

I wanted it.

This fact had become irritatingly simple.

There were other chairs.

I could keep using the one upstairs.

I could ask the keeper whether there was another chair somewhere in the lodging house.

I could buy nothing.

I could wait.

I could spend the money.

The chair was not an investment.

It would not increase earning capacity in any defensible way.

It would not unlock a professional category.

It was not medical equipment.

It was not magical.

It was not even attractive.

It was comfortable.

I sat again.

Yes.

Damn.

“I'll take it.”

The woman nodded.

“One bit delivery.”

“I object.”

“Noted.”

“I am not paying delivery.”

“Then don't.”

“I want the chair.”

“Then solve your problem.”

I stared at her.

She returned to the workbench.

Conversation over.

I sat in my purchased chair while she worked.

This was strange.

I had not paid yet.

Possession was conceptually unstable.

“Can I leave it here?”

“For how long?”

“Until I find someone to carry it.”

“Today.”

“Yes.”

“Fine.”

“What if tomorrow?”

“Storage fee.”

“You people are inventing fees.”

“Who is people?”

“Nessa. Keeper. You.”

“Sounds like a you problem.”

Possibly.

I paid for the chair.

Not delivery.

Principle mattered.

Then I left to find Jorren.

He was not at the Guild.

This was inconvenient but reasonable because Jorren did not exist to transport my furniture.

Alden was there.

Worse.

He was coming out of the side yard with a practice shield under one arm and sweat darkening his shirt.

He saw me.

“Game?”

“No.”

He looked offended.

“I bought a chair.”

His expression changed.

“What?”

“I need to move a chair.”

“Why?”

“Because I bought it.”

“Why?”

“To sit.”

He stared.

This was fair.

“Where?”

I told him.

“Where to?”

“Lodging.”

He looked at my crutches.

“Yes,” I said.

“I didn't say anything.”

“You did.”

“With my face?”

“Everyone is doing this now.”

Alden laughed.

“I have training.”

“Now?”

“In a little.”

“How little?”

He looked toward the yard.

“Enough to carry a chair?”

“Probably.”

“Then no.”

“What?”

“You will be late.”

“I can carry a chair three streets.”

“I believe you.”

“Then?”

“I do not want Pessa arriving at my lodging to kill me because I converted your training time into furniture logistics.”

“She won't kill you.”

“Good.”

“She'll make me run.”

“Worse.”

Alden considered.

“After?”

“When?”

“After training.”

“That is an actual time category?”

“No.”

“Excellent.”

He went back inside.

I stood outside the Guild.

I could wait.

I did not want to wait.

This was partly because the chair was mine now and remained somewhere else.

Ownership creates ridiculous urgency.

I went to the green door.

Octavia was not there.

Nessa was.

“No.”

“I haven't asked.”

“You need something carried.”

I stared.

She pointed at my face.

“Fuck all of you.”

She laughed.

“Jorren?”

“Not here.”

“Sevren?”

“Road.”

“Octavia?”

“Freight office.”

“I know.”

“Then why are you here?”

“I was checking.”

“For people.”

“Yes.”

“Very moving.”

I left.

I considered the freight office.

No.

Octavia had work.

Sevren had work.

Jorren had somewhere he was not.

Alden had training.

Lyssa had work.

This was becoming a survey of other people's schedules.

Good.

Healthy.

Annoying.

I went back to the furniture shop.

The woman looked up.

“No porter?”

“No.”

“One bit.”

“No.”

I sat in the chair.

She returned to work.

I watched her fit the stretcher.

She used a mallet, not hard, tapping the joint into alignment before checking the square.

Competent.

I liked watching competent people work even when they were extorting me.

After several minutes, she said, “You planning to live there?”

“Temporarily.”

“Storage fee.”

“I paid for the chair.”

“Not the floor.”

“This is coercion.”

“This is a shop.”

I looked toward the street.

A handcart passed.

Not useful.

Two laborers passed carrying a rolled rug between them.

Potentially useful.

No.

They were working.

A boy passed with nothing.

Too small.

A woman carrying three baskets.

Obviously no.

I could hire someone.

That would cost money.

Probably more than one bit.

The furniture woman knew this.

Her delivery price was reasonable.

That made the argument worse.

“I will pay one bit.”

She nodded.

I hated her.

“Who delivers it?”

“My nephew.”

“When?”

“After lunch.”

“It is after lunch.”

“Then later after lunch.”

“That is not a time.”

“You bought a chair, not a clock.”

I closed my eyes.

“Fine.”

“Where?”

I gave the lodging house.

She knew it.

Of course.

Carrow was not enormous.

“Upstairs?”

I opened my eyes.

“Yes.”

“One bit is door.”

“No.”

She pointed at the chair.

“Three streets.”

“Yes.”

“Door.”

“Yes.”

“Stairs are different.”

“How much?”

She named another bit.

“No.”

“Then door.”

“I need it upstairs.”

“Then two.”

“That doubles delivery.”

“Stairs.”

“There are fourteen.”

“That's stairs.”

“Twelve, landing, two.”

She stared at me.

“That is still stairs.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

I did not like her.

I liked her less because she was right.

Carrying a chair upstairs was not the same job as carrying it three streets on level ground.

I had spent weeks learning that stairs were not decorative vertical hallways.

Of course labor changed.

“Two bits.”

“Yes.”

“Delivered upstairs.”

“Yes.”

“No damage to rail.”

She looked offended.

“I'm furniture.”

“That does not answer rail.”

“It answers enough.”

“Does your nephew know how to carry through a turn?”

She put the mallet down.

“Do you want the chair?”

“Yes.”

“Do you want it upstairs?”

“Yes.”

“Then stop interviewing the stairs.”

I paid two bits.

This felt like defeat.

It was not.

I had bought a service.

That was different.

Probably.

I went home.

The chair arrived an hour later.

The nephew was a man older than me.

This was one of those family words that survived age.

He carried the chair upside down over one shoulder.

I stayed out of the way.

The keeper opened the door.

“What's that?”

“Chair.”

“We have chairs.”

“I bought this one.”

She looked at it.

Then at me.

“Why?”

“It is better.”

“For what?”

“Sitting.”

She considered the existing downstairs chair.

Then the new one.

“Fair.”

The nephew carried it upstairs.

I did not follow immediately.

There was no reason.

He knew the room.

The keeper showed him.

I heard the chair touch the wall once.

Not hard.

Then steps.

Then nothing.

Then steps down.

He emerged empty-handed.

“Done.”

“Rail?”

He looked at me.

“Still there.”

Good.

I thanked him.

He left.

The keeper looked at me.

“You paid delivery?”

“Yes.”

“How much?”

“No.”

She smiled.

“Too much.”

“No.”

“Then you'd say.”

“I bought labor.”

“That bad?”

“Go away.”

She did.

I waited until my legs, plural in the grammatical sense, felt ready.

Then I went upstairs with the rail.

Slow.

Known sequence.

No drama.

At the top, the chair sat by the window.

It looked wrong.

Not because it was ugly.

It was.

Because it looked like it had always been there.

Broad seat.

Old repaired spindle.

Dark stew stain.

I moved it six inches.

Better.

Sat.

Right foot planted.

Left thigh supported without pressure where I did not want pressure.

Back against wood.

Window open.

Carrow beyond it.

Good.

I had spent money on a chair and then spent more money because I could not carry it home or upstairs.

There were several ways to interpret this.

Dependence.

Adaptation.

Luxury.

Logistics.

Waste.

Preference.

Economic participation.

I could make any of them work.

The chair did not care.

I sat in it until dinner.


CHAPTER NINETY-ONE

Hessa sent for me the next morning.

I did not assume this meant magic.

This was maturity.

It lasted until I reached her door.

Then I assumed it meant magic.

The note had been brief.

COME AFTER BREAKFAST.
BRING NOTHING.

Bring nothing was either very good or very bad.

If she wanted me to cast, I did not need equipment.

If she wanted to tell me I was still not casting, I also did not need equipment.

Efficient woman.

I knocked.

“Come.”

Hessa was at the long table by the window with three cups, a shallow ceramic dish, and a bowl of water.

No crystals.

No wire.

No chalk.

No measuring frame.

No Barrier plates.

Nothing interesting.

I looked at the table.

Hessa looked at me.

“No.”

“I didn't ask.”

“You arrived asking.”

“That is unfair.”

“Sit.”

I sat.

The chair was worse than mine.

This was now a category of knowledge I possessed.

Hessa pushed one of the cups toward me.

Tea.

I picked it up.

“Why am I here?”

“To answer a question.”

“Mine?”

“Eventually.”

She took a drink.

I waited.

This was another skill I had been developing.

Not well.

“What question?”

Hessa put her cup down.

“Does it still feel like your foot is there?”

“Yes.”

“How often?”

“Depends.”

“On?”

“Attention. Movement. Sometimes nothing I can identify.”

“Pain?”

“Sometimes.”

“What kind?”

I looked at the shallow dish.

Empty.

“Cold. Burning. Cramping. Pressure. Position.”

“Position?”

“Yes.”

“Explain.”

“Sometimes the foot feels planted. Sometimes twisted. Sometimes like the ankle is bent. Once I woke up and felt the whole foot hit the floor.”

“After it was gone.”

“Yes.”

“Any sensation while using magic?”

“No.”

She looked at me.

I corrected.

“I haven't used magic.”

“Good.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

“Yes.”

“Then stop sounding offended.”

“I am not offended.”

“You are.”

“I am interested aggressively.”

“That is offended with paperwork.”

I drank tea.

She was improving.

Or I was easier to mock.

Probably both.

Hessa reached for the bowl of water.

She put one finger into it.

Then withdrew it.

“Cold.”

“I can see condensation.”

“Good.”

She slid the bowl toward me.

“Right hand.”

I put two fingers in.

Cold.

“Left.”

I switched.

Cold.

“Right foot.”

I looked at her.

She looked back.

“That seems difficult.”

“Your right foot, Greg.”

“Oh.”

I took off my right shoe.

The floor was cool.

Hessa moved the bowl down.

I put my toes in.

Cold.

She nodded.

“Left foot.”

I stared at her.

“No.”

“Correct.”

I stared harder.

She pulled the bowl back onto the table.

“What was that?”

“A question.”

“That was not a question.”

“It answered one.”

“Which?”

“Whether you would try.”

I opened my mouth.

Closed it.

Opened it again.

“That is insulting.”

“It is.”

“I would not put a nonexistent foot in water.”

“You nearly stood on one.”

“That was different.”

“You tried to step on one while kissing a girl.”

“That was private.”

“Nerin told me.”

“Of course he did.”

“Medical information.”

“Then why do you know about the kissing?”

“He enjoyed that part.”

I made a note to kill Nerin.

Later.

Hessa tapped the table.

“Your body can attempt an old movement before your attention corrects it.”

“Yes.”

“I wanted to know whether instruction could do the same.”

“And?”

“You noticed.”

“Obviously.”

“Good.”

She took another drink.

I waited.

The question I wanted to ask was sitting directly behind my teeth.

I let it stay there.

Hessa noticed.

Of course.

“Ask.”

“Can I cast?”

“No.”

There it was.

I had expected it.

Still unpleasant.

“When?”

“I don't know.”

“Why not?”

“Because I don't know what changed.”

“Channels?”

“Maybe.”

“Body map?”

“Maybe.”

“Neither?”

“Maybe.”

“That is not satisfying.”

“It is accurate.”

I put my shoe back on.

This took longer than it used to.

Not much.

Enough.

Hessa waited.

No assistance.

Good.

When I finished, she said, “I can check some things without having you cast.”

I stopped.

“What things?”

“Basic channel response.”

“Now?”

“Yes.”

That was magic.

Technically.

Not casting.

Still.

My pulse increased.

Nineteen was inconvenient.

Fifty-something years of memory and the body still reacted to permission like a dog hearing a cupboard open.

“What do I do?”

“Nothing.”

“That is becoming a theme.”

“Sit square.”

I adjusted.

She came around the table.

“Hands on your thighs.”

I did.

“Close your eyes.”

“No.”

“Greg.”

“Why?”

“So you stop trying to help.”

“I can stop trying to help with my eyes open.”

“No, you can't.”

Fair.

I closed them.

The room changed.

Not magically.

Sound.

Street outside.

Cart wheel over stone.

Someone calling something about onions.

Hessa's steps.

Then her hand touched my right shoulder.

Two fingers.

Light pressure.

Nothing.

She moved to my left shoulder.

Nothing.

Upper arm.

Forearm.

Wrist.

I knew this kind of examination only broadly.

Not enough to predict it.

Good.

She touched the center of my chest.

Something moved.

Not power.

Attention.

No.

That was too vague.

I felt the familiar internal readiness that came before drawing mana, except smaller and incomplete, like hearing the first note of a song and knowing the next one without singing it.

“Don't.”

“I didn't.”

“You started.”

“I thought.”

“You started.”

I opened my eyes.

Hessa's fingers were still against my shirt.

“What did you do?”

“Very little.”

“What?”

“Close your eyes.”

I did.

Annoying woman.

She repeated it.

Shoulder.

Arm.

Wrist.

Chest.

This time I did not follow the sensation.

It remained.

Faint.

Not imagined.

Probably.

She moved her fingers lower along the right side of my ribs.

The readiness shifted.

Then hip.

Right thigh.

Knee.

Nothing at the shin.

Ankle.

Nothing.

Foot.

Nothing.

Obviously.

She moved back up.

Left hip.

Left thigh.

Knee.

Then stopped.

I knew where her hand was from pressure through the trousers.

Below the knee there was no contact.

There could not be.

But my left foot felt cold.

I opened my eyes.

Hessa was standing beside me.

Her hand was nowhere near the residual limb.

“What?”

She withdrew.

“What did you feel?”

“Cold.”

“Where?”

“Left foot.”

Her face did not change.

That was worse than if it had.

“Did you do that?”

“I touched your left knee.”

“That is not what I asked.”

“No.”

“Did you use magic?”

“A little.”

“On the knee?”

“Near it.”

“What kind?”

“Not yours.”

“Obviously.”

“Then why ask?”

“Specificity.”

She returned to her chair.

I looked at my missing lower leg.

Nothing visible.

No glow.

No sensation now.

“Again.”

“No.”

“Hessa.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because once is information.”

“Twice is better information.”

“Sometimes.”

“Usually.”

“Not when the subject is already leaning into the result.”

“I am sitting.”

“You know what I mean.”

I did.

I hated that.

“What does it mean?”

“I don't know.”

“Does it mean the channel is still there?”

“I don't know.”

“Does it mean the body map carries channel expectation?”

“I don't know.”

“Does it mean your magic triggered phantom sensation without any channel below the knee?”

“I don't know.”

“Could you tell the difference?”

“Not today.”

I leaned back.

Bad chair.

My chair was better.

This was not relevant.

Hessa watched me.

“You're disappointed.”

“No.”

“Good.”

“I am furious.”

“Better.”

“Because this is useful.”

“Yes.”

“And you are stopping.”

“Yes.”

“Because I want to continue.”

“Partly.”

“That is vindictive.”

“Partly.”

I stared at her.

She smiled.

Very slightly.

I had not known Hessa could do that.

Disturbing.

“Other reason?”

“You have spent weeks learning what your body does when you aren't directing it.”

I said nothing.

“Today I need to know what it does when you aren't directing magic.”

I looked at the empty ceramic dish.

“What was that for?”

“Nothing.”

I looked at her.

She shrugged.

“Gives you somewhere to look.”

“That is evil.”

“It worked.”

I had spent the first five minutes trying to infer a test from a dish.

Fine.

Excellent.

“What did you learn?”

“That you can feel a basic channel prompt through the trunk.”

“I knew I could feel magic.”

“Before.”

“Yes.”

“Before is not now.”

Right.

She continued.

“You responded along the right side in a way I expected.”

“What does expected mean?”

“Broadly intact.”

My pulse increased again.

She raised one finger.

“Do not turn that into cleared.”

“I wasn't.”

“You were.”

“I was turning it into encouraging.”

“That is allowed.”

Good.

“And left?”

“Your response above the knee was present.”

“Broadly intact?”

“Broadly.”

“Below?”

“I did not test below.”

“You can't touch below.”

“I don't need to touch skin to test every channel response.”

That stopped me.

I knew that.

Of course I knew that.

But the sentence opened several doors at once.

Hessa saw it happen.

“No.”

“I have a question.”

“You have twelve.”

“Can channels persist through absent tissue?”

“I don't know.”

“Has anyone studied amputation?”

“Yes.”

That was new.

I sat forward.

“Who?”

“People.”

“Hessa.”

“Not here.”

“Where?”

“Different places.”

“What did they find?”

“Different things.”

“That is aggressively unhelpful.”

“It is also true.”

“Give me one.”

She considered.

“Some practitioners report changed flow after limb loss. Some report no meaningful change. Some cannot return to prior forms. Some can. Some develop pain with channel use. Some don't. Records are bad.”

“Why?”

“Because people lose limbs in wars, accidents, monsters, infections, failed magic, punishment, work. They are not all mages. The mages are not all trained the same. The injuries are not the same. The amputations are not the same. The follow-up is not the same. And most people care whether the patient can live, not whether a Barrier architecture remains elegant.”

I sat back.

That was fair.

Also rude.

“Below-knee specifically?”

“Some.”

“Barrier specialists?”

“I don't know.”

“Dynamic support?”

“I don't know.”

“Counter-architecture?”

“Greg.”

“Right.”

I stopped.

Barely.

This was the first time since the amputation that the problem had become larger than me in a useful way.

Not unique.

Not solved.

Not even especially well documented.

But other people had lost limbs and used magic afterward.

Some had returned.

Some had not.

Some differently.

That should have comforted me.

Instead it made me want records.

“Do not go looking for records.”

I looked at Hessa.

“I didn't say anything.”

“You leaned.”

“That is not speech.”

“It is with you.”

“Are there records in Carrow?”

“No.”

“Guild?”

“No.”

“Private?”

“Greg.”

“Fine.”

She let the silence sit.

I could feel my left foot again.

Not cold.

Present.

Heel on floor.

It was not on the floor.

I looked down.

The sensation weakened when I looked.

Interesting.

No.

Not interesting.

Not yet.

Hessa followed my gaze.

“Now?”

“Foot feels planted.”

“Pain?”

“No.”

“Position only?”

“Yes.”

“After the test?”

“Yes.”

“Did it start before you looked?”

“Yes.”

She nodded.

That was all.

No conclusion.

I wanted one badly enough that my teeth hurt.

“When do we test again?”

“Three days.”

“Why three?”

“Because I said three.”

“Physiological reason?”

“Scheduling.”

“Oh.”

She had work.

Of course.

“Same test?”

“Some of it.”

“Casting?”

“No.”

“Mana draw?”

“Maybe.”

I looked at her.

She pointed at me.

“Maybe means maybe.”

“I know.”

“You don't.”

“I do.”

“Say it.”

“Maybe means maybe.”

“Again.”

“Fuck you.”

“Good enough.”

I laughed.

I had not intended to.

Hessa's mouth moved again.

Almost smile.

She stood.

Done.

I stood too.

Hands to crutches.

Right foot planted.

Left knee bent.

The phantom foot tried to remain on the floor for half a second as my body rose.

It produced a strange stretching sensation through an ankle that did not exist.

I stopped.

Not because I was falling.

Because I wanted to notice.

Then I finished standing.

Hessa watched.

“Anything?”

“Old geometry.”

“Meaning?”

“Foot thought it stayed down while I stood.”

“Thought?”

“Felt.”

“Better.”

I adjusted the crutches.

“When you write this down, don't write ‘channel response below knee.’”

“I wasn't going to.”

“What will you write?”

She looked at me.

“Patient annoying.”

“That lacks diagnostic precision.”

“Patient consistently annoying.”

“Better.”

I went to the door.

“Greg.”

I turned.

“No casting.”

“I know.”

“No experiments.”

“I know.”

“No trying to reproduce what I did.”

“I don't know what you did.”

“That has never stopped you.”

Also fair.

I opened the door.

“Hessa.”

“What?”

“Three days?”

“Yes.”

I nodded.

That was enough.

Outside, Carrow continued without caring that my left foot had felt cold when a mage touched my knee.

A cart blocked half the street.

Someone had dropped onions.

A dog was eating one and regretting it.

I stood in the doorway for a moment with both crutches planted.

Three days.

Not clearance.

Not a theory.

Not even a result I could name safely.

But it was the first appointment about magic that ended with another appointment about magic.

I went home before I could improve it.


CHAPTER NINETY-TWO

I lasted until noon before becoming unbearable.

This was not entirely about magic.

Possibly forty percent.

The rest was because I had no work, Hessa had told me not to experiment, my chair was comfortable enough to make staying upstairs plausible, and therefore I needed to leave before I invented a reason to disobey someone.

I went to the Guild.

This was not work.

I told myself that twice.

The side yard was loud before I reached it.

Not the throwing court.

The larger training yard beyond it.

Wood striking wood.

Boots.

Someone shouting, “Again.”

Then Alden swearing.

I went around the corner.

Pessa had six Bronzes in the yard.

Alden was one.

Lio was another.

The other four I knew by face and not well enough to name.

Good.

No introductions required.

They were working in pairs with padded practice weapons and short round shields.

Not fighting.

Drilling.

One attacked.

One moved.

Reset.

Again.

Simple enough to look simple.

That usually meant it was not.

I stopped by the wall.

Pessa saw me.

“Watching?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

That was all.

No invitation.

No chair.

No adaptation.

Excellent.

I leaned against the wall with both crutches planted.

For perhaps thirty seconds.

Then my hands objected.

I shifted.

Pessa noticed.

Of course.

She pointed with her chin toward a stack of empty grain sacks beside the shed.

“Sit if you're staying.”

“I can stand.”

“Didn't ask.”

I sat on the lowest sack.

Not elegant.

Comfortable enough.

Alden saw me during reset.

He grinned.

Then Pessa hit his shield with the flat of her practice blade.

“Eyes.”

He turned back.

I enjoyed this.

The drill changed.

Attackers now had three options.

High cut.

Low cut.

Straight shove with shield.

Defender did not counter.

Only moved, covered, reset.

Alden was fast.

Too fast sometimes.

He anticipated the high cut before it came and moved early.

Pessa stopped him.

“You guessed.”

“I was right.”

“You guessed.”

“He lifted his shoulder.”

“Then read the shoulder.”

“I did.”

“No. You decided before he finished telling you.”

Alden looked toward me.

I raised both hands.

Bad idea.

One crutch fell sideways.

It hit the wall.

Everyone looked.

I retrieved it.

“Continue.”

Pessa's face did not move.

Alden laughed.

She hit his shield again.

Good.

I watched.

This was familiar in a way that made my chest hurt.

Not because I missed having two legs.

I did.

But that was too simple.

I missed being inside the problem.

Watching combat was not combat.

Watching magic was not magic.

Watching work was sometimes work because analysis could be the work.

This was not.

Pessa changed pairs.

Lio defended against Alden.

Alden attacked high.

Lio moved.

Reset.

Low.

Move.

Reset.

Shield shove.

Lio absorbed too much of it instead of clearing.

Pessa corrected his angle.

Again.

The pattern accumulated.

Not the movements.

The timing.

Pessa was teaching them not to choose before the information existed.

That sounded like several things I had recently experienced.

I refused to make a philosophy out of it.

Alden attacked.

Lio moved late.

Their shields struck.

Lio stumbled.

Recovered.

Pessa said, “Again.”

No speech.

No concern.

Correct.

I wanted to try.

The desire arrived whole.

Not theoretical.

Not “I should determine whether.”

Not “future combat capability requires.”

I wanted a shield in my hand.

I wanted Alden to come at me.

I wanted to be inside the timing.

This was inconvenient.

Pessa looked over.

She had seen something.

“What?”

I said, “Nothing.”

“Good.”

She returned to the drill.

I hated competent people.

After another ten minutes, the six Bronzes broke for water.

Alden came over.

“You look miserable.”

“I am enjoying myself.”

“Worse.”

“Yes.”

He drank.

Sweat ran down his neck.

Nineteen-year-old body reacted to the smell of effort with recognition.

Not attraction.

Memory.

Training yards had a smell.

Dust, leather, old wood, sweat, metal somewhere even when the weapons were padded.

My body knew it before my mind did.

“You want in?” Alden asked.

“Yes.”

Pessa, across the yard, said, “No.”

I looked at her.

“I wasn't asking you.”

“You were going to.”

“I was answering Alden.”

“He can't put you in my drill.”

Alden said, “I could.”

Pessa looked at him.

He drank water.

I said, “I know I can't do the footwork.”

“Correct.”

“I could defend seated.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because this drill is movement.”

“I can move seated.”

“Not the movement I'm teaching.”

“What if we change the drill?”

“No.”

There it was.

I felt the old response rise.

Not anger exactly.

Architecture.

Fine.

If this drill required lower-body movement, construct another drill isolating upper-body read, shield angle, weapon line, seated recovery.

Perfectly reasonable.

Pessa watched my face.

“Don't invent drill.”

I stared.

“You've said that before.”

“You needed it again.”

Alden laughed into his cup.

I ignored him.

“I want to train.”

“Good.”

That stopped me.

Pessa came over.

She took Alden's cup from him, drank from it, handed it back.

He looked offended.

She did not care.

“I want to train,” I repeated.

“I heard,” Pessa said.

“You said no.”

“To this.”

“What can I do?”

“I don't know.”

That answer landed harder than no.

“You don't know?”

“No.”

“You are literally the movement expert.”

“Yes.”

“And I am missing a lower leg.”

“Yes.”

“This seems within the category.”

“Does it?”

I opened my mouth.

Pessa pointed at the yard.

“What are they training?”

“Reading committed movement before choosing response.”

“Partly.”

“Maintaining balance under changing line.”

“Partly.”

“Distance.”

“Yes.”

“Shield positioning.”

“Yes.”

“Recovery.”

“Yes.”

“Then isolate the parts I can do.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because you just made a list from watching twenty minutes and decided the list is the thing.”

I stopped.

Alden stopped smiling.

Good.

Pessa continued.

“You want to train?”

“Yes.”

“Train what?”

“Combat.”

“That's not a thing.”

“It is absolutely a thing.”

“No. It's a pile of things people call one thing after they already know the pile.”

I hated this.

“What do you want to be able to do?”

“Fight.”

“Still not a thing.”

“Survive violence.”

“Better.”

“Protect myself.”

“Better.”

“Protect other people.”

“Different.”

“Use a sword.”

“Different.”

“Use Barrier support with movement.”

“Not cleared.”

“I know.”

“Then not today.”

I gripped the crutch handle.

My palm hurt slightly.

Not injury.

Pressure.

Pessa saw.

She always saw.

“What do you want today?”

I looked at the yard.

Alden and Lio.

Shields.

Padded blades.

Dust.

Timing.

“I want someone to come at me and not feel like the answer is to leave.”

Silence.

Not dramatic.

Just enough.

Pessa nodded once.

“That I can work with.”

Alden said, “Now?”

“No.”

He looked disappointed.

I was disappointed.

Pessa said, “You came here to train?”

“No.”

“What did you come here for?”

“To not be upstairs.”

“Then watch.”

“That is cruel.”

“Watch with a question.”

“What question?”

She pointed at the pairs reforming.

“When do they know enough to move?”

I looked.

“That is your drill.”

“Yes.”

“So you are giving me work.”

“No.”

“What is it?”

“Watching.”

“That sounds like unpaid work.”

“Leave.”

I stayed.

Alden went back into the yard.

The drill resumed.

I watched with the question.

When do they know enough to move?

Annoyingly good question.

The high cut began in the shoulder.

No.

Sometimes.

One of the unnamed Bronzes lifted his shoulder for both high and straight attacks.

His hip told more.

Lio's shield shove committed through the rear heel before the shield moved.

Alden's low attack was readable in his eyes if you knew him, which was useless against strangers.

Pessa corrected that.

“Stop looking at the target.”

Alden said, “I'm not.”

“You are.”

He swore.

Again.

I watched.

The answer was not one moment.

Of course not.

Enough depended on cost of being wrong.

Move too early and the attacker changed line.

Move too late and line arrived.

Some defenses tolerated uncertainty better than others.

That was more interesting.

I leaned forward.

My phantom left foot felt planted.

I noticed.

Did nothing.

The sensation stayed for several breaths.

Then faded.

Not magic.

Not relevant.

Maybe relevant to movement later.

Not now.

I watched.

Pessa changed the drill again.

Now defenders could counter after the first movement.

Everything became messier.

Alden improved immediately.

Lio improved more slowly and then more reliably.

One of the others kept overcommitting to counters and got shoved backward twice.

Pessa did not stop him the first time.

She stopped him the second.

Why?

Because first could be noise.

Second was pattern.

Maybe.

I wanted to ask.

I did not.

This was difficult.

After another twenty minutes, Pessa called the session.

The Bronzes scattered toward water, shade, food, other work.

Alden dropped beside me on the sacks.

“You watched the whole thing.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Pessa made me.”

“I did not,” Pessa said from across the yard.

“You weaponized curiosity.”

“That sounds like your problem.”

Alden leaned his shield against the wall.

“Tomorrow?”

Pessa said, “No promises.”

He looked at me.

I understood the question was not about the throwing game this time.

Maybe.

“Are you training tomorrow?” I asked Pessa.

“Yes.”

“Can I watch?”

“Yes.”

“Can I do anything?”

“Maybe.”

My heart did the cupboard thing again.

I disliked being nineteen.

“What?”
