Then at me. Then at it. This was already a better experiment than thread because the dog clearly wanted something. Also worse because dogs had opinions. It stood. Took one step toward the wall.

Stopped. I did nothing. The dog sat again.

“Your controls are terrible,” I told it.

Its tail moved once. Could be wind. I laughed before I could stop myself. A man passing with a sack looked at me.

“Dog won't eat pear.”

“I can see that.”

“He'll eat sausage.”

“I don't have sausage.”

“Then you've designed badly.”

He kept walking. I stared after him. Everyone in Carrow had become Hessa. Unacceptable. My forearm felt normal. Hands normal. Residual limb quiet. Phantom toes appeared briefly when I shifted. Ordinary. Tomorrow no magic.

Fine. I finished the pear. The dog watched the core. I held it out. It sniffed. Did not take it. Non-replication.

“Fuck you too.”

The dog left. I laughed. Then went home.

CHAPTER 128

THE MESSENGER

I went to the theatre because I wanted to. This was becoming suspicious. No Hessa. No magic. No Guild task. No courier cart. The theatre door was open.

Inside, somebody was shouting:

“Not the blue one.”

A different voice shouted:

“They are both blue.”

“Not that blue one.”

I entered. Two painted doors stood onstage. Both blue. One darker. Probably. The soot-shirt worker was carrying a brass handle in her teeth. She saw me. Pointed at the darker door. Then pointed at the floor beside it.

I went there.

“What?”

She removed the handle.

“Hold this.”

She gave me the door. Not metaphorically. It was lighter than it looked. Canvas over frame. I braced it with one hand while keeping a crutch under the other arm. Bad arrangement. She looked.

“No.”

“Yes.”

“No.”

She took the door back.

“Sit.”

There was a chair near the stage edge. I sat. She put the door beside me.

“Hold from there.”

Better.

“Why?”

“Because I need the hinge.”

“Which hinge?”

“The one you are covering.”

I moved my hand. She took the hinge.

“Excellent.”

“That was not useful.”

“It was eventually.”

Good morning. Teren was at his usual place with pages. He looked up.

“Gregory.”

“Teren.”

“Can you read?”

“Yes.”

“Today?”

“Probably.”

He held out three folded pages. I took them.

“What am I?”

“Messenger.”

I looked at the page. The title at the top was not the play title. Just scene number and a word I did not know. I pointed.

“What is that?”

“Scene change note.”

“It looks like a name.”

“It isn't.”

“What does it mean?”

“Blue room after court.”

“That is four words.”

“It saves space.”

“It failed.”

“For you.”

“Then it failed.”

Teren took the page back, looked at the note, and said:

“No.”

He gave it back.

The servant actor called from the floor:

“Gregory has discovered notation.”

“I can read notation.”

“Today?”

“Fuck you.”

The woman said:

“Please keep him. He improves morale.”

Teren said:

“He is not mine.”

Good. Correct. I looked at the page again. There was a messenger. Four lines.

“No.”

Teren blinked.

“What?”

“I mean what am I doing?”

“Reading messenger.”

“That sounds like what I am.”

“For six minutes.”

“Why?”

“Because we are working the entrance.”

I looked toward the stage. The recurring woman was there in a dark skirt over rehearsal clothes. The servant actor was lying on the floor. Not dead. Probably. Another man stood by the blue door.

Actual actors. No missing person. No emergency. Teren pointed.

“You enter from there.”

He pointed to the darker blue door.

“Walk to the table.”

There was no table.

“There is no table.”

“There will be.”

“Where?”

The woman pointed at a chalk rectangle on the floor.

“There.”

“Why not put the table there?”

“Because they're painting it.”

Reasonable. I looked at the page. Messenger entered. Crossed to table. Delivered letter. Four lines. Exited.

“Why me?”

Teren had already looked back at his pages.

“Because you are here.”

That answer was becoming dangerous. The servant actor sat up.

“Gregory has been promoted.”

“To what?”

“Temporary furniture.”

“I am messenger.”

“Temporary messenger furniture.”

The woman said:

“Start before he develops standards.”

I stood. Crutches. Pages. Letter. Too many things. Teren noticed.

“Pages stay with me.”

Good. He took them back.

“You know the lines?”

“No.”

“You just read them.”

“That is not the same thing.”

He held them where I could see. Fine. The letter was a folded scrap. I tucked it under two fingers on my right crutch handle.

Teren said:

“No.”

Everyone said no here.

“What?”

“You need to hand it over.”

“Yes.”

“You have trapped it.”

I looked. True.

“Pocket.”

I put it in my shirt pocket.

The woman onstage said:

“Messenger does not arrive with royal correspondence folded into his armpit.”

“It is my pocket.”

“Worse.”

“Why?”

“Because then I watch you dig for it.”

“You are supposed to be listening to the message.”

“I can do both.”

“That seems like your problem.”

“It becomes yours when I laugh.”

The servant actor said:

“She will.”

“I won't.”

“You already are.”

She was. Barely. Fine.

The servant actor said:

“Put it in your teeth.”

I looked at him. He grinned.

Soot-shirt worker, still by the door, said:

“Don't.”

Fine. I held the letter in my right hand and used the crutch grip with the heel of that hand. Possible. Awkward. Teren watched.

“Can you cross like that?”

“Yes.”

“Do it.”

I entered. Wrong door.

“Other blue,” three people said.

I backed out.

“Both blue.”

The woman said:

“Not to us.”

Second attempt. Correct blue door. Across stage. Three unrailed steps existed at the front. I did not use them. No reason. The chalk table was farther than it looked from the wing. The stage also had more traffic than it appeared to from a chair.

A stool waited just outside my path. A rolled carpet occupied part of the wing. Someone crossed behind the painted wall carrying a lamp. None of this was in the four lines. I reached the chalk table.

Stopped. Read from Teren.

“My lady, a message from Lord…”

I looked at the name. Teren supplied it.

“Varen.”

“Varen.”

The woman held out her hand. I continued reading. She kept holding out her hand. I kept reading.

“Letter,” she said.

“Oh.”

I gave it to her. The servant actor made a small choking sound. Probably laughter. I finished the lines.

“Then go,” Teren said.

“I have another line.”

“After she reads.”

I looked at the page. Yes. Pause. Right. The woman opened the letter. Read silently. Looked at me. I said my final line. Too late.

“Again,” Teren said.

No criticism. Just again. I went back. Third attempt. Correct door. Cross. Line. Letter before she had to ask. Pause. Final line. Exit. I turned toward the wrong side.

“Other way,” Teren said.

I changed direction.

The servant actor said:

“Messenger knows the kingdom. Not the building.”

“Fuck you.”

The woman laughed.

Teren said:

“Again.”

Fourth. I was enjoying this. That was inconvenient. The problem was not the lines. The problem was everything around the lines. Door. Crutches. Letter. Where she stood. When her hand appeared. How long she read.

Where I was supposed to leave. I had four lines and somehow there were twelve failures available. Excellent. Also my right crutch made a sound on one board. Small. Wood tip against a slightly raised seam.

Click. Every crossing. I noticed it on the fifth attempt. Of course I did. I looked down.

Teren said:

“No.”

“I haven't done anything.”

“You are about to.”

“The board is raised.”

“Yes.”

“My crutch catches it.”

“Does it stop you?”

“No.”

“Then later.”

“It changes the sound.”

The servant actor said:

“Messenger has hooves.”

I looked at him.

“No horse.”

Nobody understood why that was funny to me. Better. I crossed again. Click. The woman did not react. Neither did anyone else. I tried placing the crutch half an inch left next time. No click.

That made my step worse.

Teren said:

“Why did you do that?”

“Board.”

“Stop.”

Fine. Click returned. Apparently messenger had one hoof. Again. This time I remembered the exit. The woman did not hold out her hand. I almost handed her the letter anyway. Stopped. She looked at me.

I looked at her. She said her line. Then held out her hand. I gave it.

Afterward I said:

“You changed it.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I was late.”

“You did that intentionally?”

“No.”

I stared. She shrugged.

“I forgot.”

“That is worse.”

“Did you survive?”

“Yes.”

“Then again.”

Teren said:

“From the argument before entrance.”

I started to leave.

“No. Stay.”

“I am not in the argument.”

“You are outside the door.”

“So I wait?”

“Yes.”

“Doing what?”

“Being outside the door.”

“That is not an action.”

The servant actor said:

“Think messenger thoughts.”

I hated him. I stood behind the blue door. The argument began. Louder than expected. The woman crossed. The man by the door slammed a cup onto the nonexistent table. There was no cup.

He slapped his palm against the chalk rectangle instead.

Teren said:

“Cup.”

Soot-shirt worker tossed him a wooden cup. He caught it. Argument continued. I waited for my line. No. Entrance. I waited for the argument to end. It did not.

The woman shouted:

“Then let him come tell me himself.”

That sounded like entrance. I entered.

Teren said:

“Too early.”

I stopped. The actors did not. The man turned toward me.

“Who the hell are you?”

Not on my page. I looked at Teren. He made a small circular motion. Continue. Right. The woman looked at me too. I had no line yet.

The servant actor, now standing near the wall, whispered:

“Messenger thoughts.”

Fuck him. I looked at the letter. Then at the man.

Then said:

“I was told to deliver this.”

Not the line.

The man snapped:

“Then deliver it.”

I crossed. The woman held out her hand. I gave her the letter. She opened it.

Teren said:

“Now.”

I found the actual first line.

“My lady, a message from Lord Varen.”

The woman looked at the letter already in her hand. Then at me.

“That much I gathered.”

Everyone laughed. I did too. Which made the next line impossible.

Teren said:

“Again from entrance.”

I went back.

“Was that wrong?” I asked.

“Yes,” Teren said.

The woman said:

“It worked.”

Those were different answers. Good.

“Which matters?”

“Right now?” Teren said. “Wrong entrance.”

The woman said:

“Right now? Do it again.”

No philosophy. Fine. We did it again. I waited longer. Correct entrance. Correct line. Correct letter. Correct pause. Correct exit. Boring. Not actually. Cleaner. Then the blue window failed. Same painted window from before.

Or one like it. The evening blue appeared across it. Flickered. Went gray. Nobody stopped. Soot-shirt worker pulled one side lamp lower. Another worker shifted a pale panel. The woman continued arguing with the man.

The window stayed gray. The scene still happened. I watched for half a second too long. Teren tapped my page.

“You're next.”

Right. Messenger. I entered. Correct door. Forgot the letter. I reached the chalk table. Hand empty. The woman held out hers. Nothing. I stopped. Teren said nothing. The servant actor's face became delighted. I could go back.

No. Too late. I looked at the woman. She looked at my empty hand.

Then she said:

“Well?”

I put my hand into my shirt pocket. Nothing there. Obviously.

I said:

“I was told to place it directly in your hands.”

Her eyebrows moved.

“Then?”

“I appear to have been lied to.”

The servant actor folded in half. The woman held it. Barely.

The man said:

“Search him.”

That was not on anything.

“No,” I said.

“Suspicious.”

“I am on crutches.”

“Perfect disguise.”

The woman lost. She laughed.

Teren said:

“Stop.”

Everyone stopped. I expected correction. Teren pointed at the wing.

“Letter.”

The soot-shirt worker held it up. I had left it on the chair.

“Yes.”

“Get it.”

I went.

The servant actor said:

“Coward.”

“You were not being searched.”

“I would have committed.”

“To what?”

“Anything.”

Probably true. I returned with the letter.

Teren said:

“Again.”

We did it. No one explained what I should have done when the prop vanished. Apparently the answer was not whatever I had done. Also apparently it had not killed the scene. Both could be true.

At the next pause I asked the woman:

“What was I supposed to do?”

“When?”

“Without the letter.”

“Oh.”

She thought.

“Depends.”

“That is not useful.”

“It is exactly useful.”

“What would you have done?”

“If I were you?”

“Yes.”

“Probably swear.”

“Onstage.”

“Quietly.”

I waited. She relented.

“Could have said it was stolen. Could have made him send you back. Could have crossed without handing anything and let me decide. Could have stopped if Teren stopped us.”

“Which is correct?”

“Whichever lets us get to the next thing without making a worse problem.”

“That is not correct.”

“No.”

She smiled.

“It's rehearsal.”

Then somebody called her and she left. That was all the instruction I got. I disliked it. I also wanted another missing letter. The blue window came back while we were halfway through. Nobody applauded.

It was simply blue again. I noticed the effect more this time. Not how. Just that the room looked later. The painted wall had not changed. The window had. The woman's face picked up a little blue on one side.

Then I had to enter. I entered. After six minutes, which was actually closer to thirty, Teren took the pages.

“Done.”

“That was not six minutes.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“We kept using you.”

“That is not a unit of time.”

“It is here.”

The servant actor came over.

“You were terrible.”

“Yes.”

“Better than last time.”

“I did not have a last time.”

“You read merchant.”

“That was seated.”

“Still terrible.”

“Thank you.”

He clapped my shoulder. Not hard.

“Tomorrow?”

There it was again. Everyone in this city had one question.

“I have Hessa.”

“After?”

“I don't know.”

“Fine.”

He left before I could decide whether that was invitation. The woman was arguing with soot-shirt worker about the blue door. Not the window. Door.

“It reads black from the side.”

“It reads blue from front.”

“Half the house is side.”

“Not half.”

“Enough.”

They moved the door. Turned it. Moved a lamp. Still blue. Different blue. I watched. Soot-shirt worker saw me.

“No.”

“I did not say anything.”

“You leaned.”

This was spreading.

“I was looking.”

“Dangerous.”

The woman said:

“Gregory.”

“Yes?”

“Stand there.”

She pointed to a place off the stage. I went.

“Blue?”

I looked. The door was almost black.

“No.”

“Thank you.”

Soot-shirt worker moved the lamp.

“Now?”

“Blue.”

“Done.”

“That seems audience-specific.”

They both looked at me. I regretted speaking.

The woman said:

“It seems blue from where people sit.”

“Yes.”

“That is generally where we need it.”

Right. I shut up. Soot-shirt worker grinned.

“Learning.”

“No.”

“Good.”

They went back to work. I stayed. Not because needed. That distinction was getting weaker. Later somebody gave me a piece of bread. I did not know whose. I ate it. A young crewman carried the chalk table in while I was chewing.

Actual table. I moved my chair without being asked. He put it exactly over the rectangle. Almost. One leg missed by two inches. I noticed. He noticed me noticing.

“Don't.”

“I didn't.”

“Good.”

He shoved the table once. Done. The servant actor dropped the cup again. Different scene. This time nobody laughed because apparently he was supposed to. I could not tell anymore. That was fun. My palms got warm.

I sat before they hurt. Nobody commented. The blue window worked. Then failed once. Then worked. Nobody asked me to care. I did not. Mostly. When I finally left, the soot-shirt worker was changing the hinge on the darker blue door.

I said:

“Wrong blue?”

She said:

“Fuck off, Gregory.”

I laughed all the way to the street. No magic. Tomorrow Hessa. But not yet. For now I had been a messenger for thirty minutes. Badly. I wanted to do it again.

CHAPTER 129

THE LIMIT

The threads were gone. I noticed before I sat down. The frame was gone too. No tile. No copper beside it. No white sleeve. No gray sleeve. Hessa had a cup of tea. This was worse.

“You stopped.”

“Sit.”

“You stopped the thread test.”

“Sit.”

I sat. She checked my hands first. Palms normal. No tenderness from yesterday. Right calf normal. Residual limb quiet. Phantom foot present in the usual impossible way, mostly heel this morning. Thumb fine. Fingers fine.

Wrist fine. Grip. Again. Fine. Hessa wrote. I waited. She drank tea.

“You stopped.”

“Yes.”

There. I did not like how quickly she said it.

“Why?”

“Because I reviewed the three attempts.”

“And?”

“The apparatus is not giving me enough interpretable signal to justify spending more of your safe attempts on it right now.”

I stared at the empty table.

“One failed replication.”

“One failed replication after two ambiguous attempts.”

“The second was better than ambiguous.”

“It was more interesting.”

“That is not the same word.”

“Correct.”

“The near thread moved toward me during REACH while the far thread didn't.”

“Yes.”

“That is a differential observation.”

“Yes.”

“Then the next test should repeat it.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because we did.”

“Once.”

“Yes.”

“That is not enough.”

“No.”

“Then repeat again.”

“No.”

I hated this. Hessa put down her cup.

“What answer are you trying to get?”

“Whether I moved it.”

“Can this apparatus tell us?”

“Eventually.”

“Maybe.”

“Then why stop?”

“Because your attempts are not free.”

“I am fine.”

“You are fine after the attempts we have done.”

“Yes.”

“That does not make the next ten free.”

“I said one.”

“You will say one after that.”

“Only if it is useful.”

“You currently think another thread attempt is useful.”

“It is.”

“I don't.”

There it was. Jurisdiction. Annoying. Clean. I looked at the empty table again.

“So what did the three tests establish?”

“That thread moves.”

“Excellent.”

“Hessa.”

“You asked.”

She ignored me.

“First, they established that suspended thread in this room is sensitive to more things than we can cheaply isolate.”

“Yes.”

“Air movement. Heat. vibration. twist. static. position. breathing. room traffic.”

“Yes.”

“Second, they established that two threads exposed to much of the same room can still behave differently without your magic.”

“Yes.”

“Third, we observed one movement during REACH that was interesting enough to repeat.”

“Yes.”

“We repeated it.”

“It didn't happen.”

“Correct.”

“That does not disprove it.”

“Correct.”

I stopped. She waited. That was the problem. She was not saying impossible. She was saying not enough. Harder to argue with.

“Fourth,” she said, “the reliable part of all three external attempts was not external.”

I looked at her.

“Your control.”

“Yes.”

“You established the small alteration where instructed. You maintained the underlying draw. You attempted a directional change without broadening into the older response. You did not recruit your hand. You did not chase sensation when the apparatus did something interesting. You RETURNed when told.”

“Mostly.”

“What does mostly mean?”

“I argued afterward.”

“Afterward is allowed.”

Good.

“Your internal sequence is becoming more repeatable than the external observation.”

“Yes.”

“So that is what we test today.”

I looked at the empty space where the frame had been.

“Did you throw it away?”

“No.”

“Where is it?”

“Cabinet.”

“Why?”

“Because if I leave it out, you will spend the entire assessment looking at it.”

“I am looking at where it was.”

“Yes.”

“That proves nothing.”

“It proves I know you.”

I did not answer. She pulled the three old pages from beneath a newer sheet. I recognized the white and gray labels in the margins.

“You kept the notes.”

“Obviously.”

“Show me.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because you will argue with my abbreviations.”

“I can read.”

“That has not protected me before.”

“Hessa.”

She turned the first page toward herself, not me.

“Attempt one. Single thread. Baseline movement. One movement toward arm during bounded external question, another later movement with multiple room confounds. No attribution.”

“Two movements.”

“I said one during the bounded question.”

“The other was still during maintained draw.”

“Which is why it is written down.”

Second page.

“Attempt two. Paired threads. Baseline differential behavior demonstrated before draw. During REACH, closer thread moved toward arm while farther did not at that same moment. Later farther moved independently.”

“Yes.”

“Attempt three. Same general setup. During shape, closer moved away, farther moved shortly after. During REACH, no recorded movement from either.”

“Yes.”

She stacked the pages.

“If I only owned the second page, I would repeat.”

“You did.”

“If I owned the first two, I would repeat.”

“You did.”

“If I own all three, I have to ask whether a fourth attempt is the best use of your current tolerance.”

“And you decided no.”

“Yes.”

“What would make you return to it?”

“Better reason.”

“That is vague.”

“A stronger external signal from some other bounded question. Better control. More mature shaping. A reason to think the thread's sensitivity is useful instead of merely noisy.”

“Or time.”

“Possibly.”

“So not abandoned.”

“No.”

That helped more than it should have. I did not want the thread. I wanted the possibility to remain alive. It did. Annoyingly. I looked around.

“No apparatus.”

“Your arm is the apparatus.”

“That sounds medically threatening.”

“It should.”

She brought out the copper. Relief was embarrassing. Not because copper did anything important. Because it belonged to the sequence I knew. Hessa noticed.

“You expected it.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“You always use copper.”

“Not always.”

“Recently.”

“Yes.”

“What does that tell you?”

“That you are predictable.”

“Good.”

“No, that was an insult.”

“I know.”

She set it down well away from the old thread position. I watched her choose the place.

“Is that placement part of the test?”

“No.”

“Then why there?”

“Because my tea is here.”

I looked at the tea. Reasonable constraints continued ruining elegant interpretation.

“What question?”

“Whether you can produce the same bounded directional change and RETURN at a different right-forearm target without an external object to pull your attention.”

“That is less interesting.”

“To you.”

“Yes.”

“I know.”

“Why remove the target?”

“Because I want to know whether REACH is currently an instruction you can execute internally, or whether the thread is part of what makes the response happen.”

I sat straighter. That was better. Not thread. Still a question.

“What direction?”

“Not toward the old thread position.”

“Why?”

“Because you have practiced that direction three times.”

“Two.”

“Three external attempts.”

“The first geometry differed.”

“Greg.”

“Fine.”

She marked my forearm. Charcoal. Small target closer to the upper outer side than the recent wrist-near work. Not elbowward. Not the familiar broad direction. Different. I looked.

“Outward?”

“Toward that mark.”

“There is no object.”

“The mark is an object.”

“External object.”

“No suspended target.”

“You know what I mean.”

“Yes.”

“Can I look at it?”

“Before draw. Not during.”

“Why?”

“Because I want your report, not you steering with your eyes.”

“That is not how mana works.”

“Good. Then it should not matter.”

I disliked that answer. She checked position. Right forearm supported. Hand relaxed. Fingers visible. Copper was present after all. On the other side of the table. Not part of a thread apparatus. Just copper.

Familiar. Hessa placed two fingers above the new charcoal mark.

“Question is small.”

“Yes.”

“One draw.”

“Yes.”

“One shape.”

“Yes.”

“One directional instruction.”

“Yes.”

“One RETURN.”

“Yes.”

“If the response broadens, changes direction, recruits hand or wrist, produces thumb or finger symptoms, produces unusual left response, pain, cold, numbness, weakness, or anything you cannot describe, you stop.”

“Yes.”

“No external effect question.”

“Yes.”

“No casting.”

“Yes.”

“No spell.”

“Yes.”

“No Barrier.”

“Yes.”

“No proving anything.”

I looked at her.

“That one was unnecessary.”

“No.”

“Fine.”

“Draw.”

I did. Minimal. Copper answered. Right forearm. Stable. No hand. No thumb. No left.

“Report.”

I did.

“Shape.”

Localized. The altered region came slower than last time. Not much slower. Enough to notice. I said so.

“Continue only if stable.”

I waited. It settled. Small. Near the charcoal mark but not on it.

“Location?”

I described it. Hessa touched the skin outside the region. No change.

“Hold.”

Held. Then she moved her fingers. Not toward the mark. Away. Two inches farther up and outward. I looked at her.

“That is not the mark.”

“No.”

“You said toward the mark.”

“I changed the instruction.”

“That seems bad.”

“Can you follow it?”

Maybe. That was different. Not REACH toward something. REACH from the altered region toward a direction Hessa indicated in space over my arm. No thread. No fixed destination. Just direction.

“Smallest extension,” she said. “Toward my fingers. No force. Maintain draw.”

I did. Or tried. The near edge sharpened. Wrong edge. Toward the charcoal mark. I stopped.

“Hessa.”

“Report.”

“It went toward the mark.”

“Did you intend that?”

“No.”

“Stop directional instruction. Hold.”

Held. Interesting. Bad. Interesting. She moved her fingers away.

“RETURN.”

I returned. The alteration reduced. Underlying draw remained. No hand. No thumb. No broadening.

“Hold.”

Held.

“Release.”

Released. Hessa checked everything. Again. Fine. I looked at the charcoal mark.

“You tricked me.”

“No.”

“You established a target and then changed it.”

“Yes.”

“That was intentional.”

“Yes.”

“So you were testing whether I was following the instruction or the prepared target.”

“Yes.”

“That is a trick.”

“It is a test.”

“You could have told me.”

“That would change the test.”

I hated that she was right. Mostly.

“What did I do?”

“You shaped near the prepared target.”

“Yes.”

“When I redirected the directional instruction, your first altered edge sharpened toward the prepared target instead of toward my indicated direction.”

“Yes.”

“So I failed.”

“You did not execute the changed direction as instructed.”

“That is failure.”

“For that question, yes.”

Clean. Again. I appreciated it. Also hated it.

“Did the altered region move at all?”

“The edge changed.”

“Toward the prepared mark.”

“By your report.”

“You did not feel it?”

“No.”

“Copper?”

“Changed with draw and shape. Nothing I would distinguish during the directional instruction.”

“So no independent confirmation.”

“No.”

“Could I have simply reported what I expected?”

“Yes.”

I looked at her.

“That is a problem.”

“Yes.”

“You believe me?”

“I believe you are trying to report accurately.”

“That is not the same.”

“No.”

Good. More problems. I had missed having enough problems.

“Can you touch the edge while I do it?”

“Not today.”

“Why?”

“Contact changes sensation.”

“Could still be useful.”

“Yes.”

“Then next time.”

“Maybe.”

“You hate commitments.”

“I make them when I have enough information.”

“That is a lie. You committed to no magic tomorrow very quickly.”

“That decision has excellent evidence.”

I laughed despite myself. She wrote something.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You wrote because I laughed.”

“I wrote because your hand stayed relaxed while you laughed.”

I looked at my right hand. Still open on the support.

“That matters?”

“Maybe.”

“You just did it.”

“What?”

“Made everything information.”

“Everything is information.”

“That is convenient.”

“Only if I don't care what it says.”

I recognized that. She knew I recognized it. Neither of us mentioned the last time.

“What does that mean?”

“I don't know yet.”

“Hessa.”

“It may mean the prepared target strongly organizes what you are doing.”

“Yes.”

“It may mean changing directional instruction after shaping is harder than beginning with the intended direction.”

“Yes.”

“It may mean you anticipated the old sequence.”

“Yes.”

“It may mean my instruction was poor.”

I looked at her.

“Again?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“One attempt.”

“I am fine.”

“One attempt.”

“But this is internal.”

“Yes.”

“And it failed.”

“Yes.”

“So repeat.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because failure is data before it is an invitation.”

That sentence was offensive. I leaned back.

“Tomorrow?”

“No magic.”

“Again?”

“Yes.”

“How many days?”

“One.”

“Then assessment?”

“Yes.”

“What are you going to test?”

“I don't know.”

“You absolutely know.”

“I have questions.”

“Which?”

“No.”

“Hessa.”

She picked up her tea. Cold now, probably.

“Today I learned something I did not know.”

“That I follow charcoal instead of fingers.”

“Possibly.”

“That sounds stupid.”

“It sounds like learning.”

“I knew the charcoal was the target.”

“Exactly.”

I stopped. She drank. I thought about it. I had built the shape around the mark before she changed the instruction. Of course the response favored it. Maybe. Or I had simply failed to redirect.

Or REACH was not direction at all and I had been interpreting noise. Or the thread had mattered. Or Hessa's fingers were a terrible target. Many possibilities. I started listing them. Hessa held up a hand.

“No.”

“I have four.”

“Keep them.”

“I can tell you.”

“I know.”

“You do not know mine.”

“I know enough.”

“That is arrogant.”

“Yes.”

Fair. I looked at my forearm. Charcoal still there. Nothing else.

“Are we farther from external effect than we were?”

“That is not how I would describe it.”

“How would you?”

“We stopped spending attempts on a poor measurement.”

“That is farther.”

“It is different.”

“It feels farther.”

She considered that.

“Yes.”

Good. At least she allowed that. I expected the feeling to disappear once named. It did not. Three days ago I had been staring at a thread that might have moved because of me.

Today Hessa had put the thread in a cabinet and made me fail to follow two fingers. Objectively, that felt like retreat. Also objectively, my arm had done something small on command and then stopped when told.

Again. The second fact was less exciting. It was also the one Hessa trusted. I knew which one I preferred. That did not change which one she trusted. I rubbed neither arm. Kept hands still.

Not because instructed. Habit.

“Am I getting better?”

“At the parts we can currently observe reliably.”

“That is a Hessa answer.”

“Yes.”

“Which parts?”

“Minimal draw. Localized shaping. maintaining draw while altering. RETURN. avoiding the older broad response. avoiding motor recruitment.”

“Directional control?”

“Unclear.”

“External?”

“Unestablished.”

“Casting?”

“No.”

“I know.”

“Good.”

“Barrier?”

“No.”

“I know.”

“Good.”

I sighed. She smiled. Actually smiled. Small. Cruel woman.

“Go live tomorrow.”

“I lived yesterday.”

“You were a messenger.”

I froze. Hessa looked at me.

“How do you know that?”

“Teren's sister buys herbs from the woman downstairs.”

I stared.

“What?”

“She mentioned the theatre had acquired a tall messenger on crutches who forgot his letter.”

I closed my eyes. No. Absolutely not.

“That was rehearsal.”

“I assumed.”

“I was not acquired.”

“I assumed.”

“I am not a messenger.”

“You were yesterday.”

“For thirty minutes.”

“That seems sufficient.”

“This city is too small.”

“Carrow is not small.”

“Then people need to stop talking.”

“No.”

I stood. She pointed at my forearm.

“Wash the charcoal off later.”

“Yes.”

“No magic tomorrow.”

“Yes.”

“No practicing directional attention.”

I stopped.

“What does that mean?”

“You know exactly what it means.”

“I cannot stop looking at things.”

“You can stop sitting at a table trying to recreate today's task without mana.”

“That would not be magic.”

“It would be rehearsal.”

I stared. She raised an eyebrow. I refused to give her that.

“No.”

“Good.”

I left. Outside, the morning had become bright. Not warm. Bright. I walked three streets before realizing I was heading toward the theatre. I stopped. Hessa tomorrow was no magic. Theatre was allowed. That was not why I had turned.

Probably. I looked west. Then east. Then at the street ahead. No test. No conclusion. No thread. My right forearm felt completely ordinary. I went to buy lunch.

At the bread stall, the seller said:

“Messenger.”

I nearly left Carrow.

CHAPTER 130

THE EXTRA

The bread seller called me Messenger again. I ignored him. Mostly. Then I went to the theatre. That proved nothing. The door was open. Inside, nobody needed a messenger. This was disappointing. I had not admitted I wanted to do it again.

Apparently my body had. I stood just inside. Teren was arguing with a page. Not a person. The page. He had three versions open across his knees.

The recurring woman was onstage with the servant actor and another woman I had seen twice but never spoken to. The soot-shirt worker was halfway up a short ladder adjusting something above a painted doorway.

Nobody looked at me. Fine. I went to my usual chair. Basket of fake fruit. Again. I moved it. Teren looked up.

“Gregory.”

“Teren.”

“Chair is wrong.”

“It is the same chair.”

“Not for today.”

“Why?”

“Sightline.”

He pointed two chairs left. I moved. No argument. That felt suspicious. The servant actor noticed.

“Messenger.”

“No.”

“You came back.”

“Yes.”

“For messenger.”

“No.”

“Liar.”

The recurring woman said:

“He forgot the letter. Of course he came back.”

“I did not forget it today.”

“You don't have one.”

“Exactly.”

She smiled. Then went back to the scene. I watched. No messenger. Apparently the play contained other events. Unreasonable. The scene involved three people at a supper table. Actual table today. Not chalk. Wood.

Three cups. One bowl. A plate with nothing on it. The servant actor was supposed to enter late. He kept entering too early. I enjoyed this.

Teren said:

“Again.”

Servant actor returned to the wing.

The woman at the table said:

“You're enjoying this too much.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

They reset. The scene ran. The servant actor entered. Late this time. Better. Then he sat in the wrong chair. The other woman stopped.

“That is mine.”

“Not in the scene.”

“It is now.”

“You have two.”

“I have one body.”

The recurring woman said:

“Keep going.”

They did. The servant actor shifted the cup instead of the chair. The other woman took the cup back. He took the bowl. She took the bowl too.

The scene became a silent war over table objects while the recurring woman delivered a serious line about inheritance. Teren stopped them.

“None of that.”

The servant actor said:

“She started it.”

The other woman said:

“He sat wrong.”

The recurring woman said:

“You're both children.”

Teren said:

“Again.”

Before they reset, a woman from backstage appeared holding the missing belt from earlier.

“Whose?”

Three people answered. Different names. She stared at them.

“Excellent.”

She hung it over the blue door.

The soot-shirt worker shouted:

“Not there.”

“Then come get it.”

“No.”

The belt stayed. The servant actor looked at me.

“Professional environment.”

“Yes.”

“Highly disciplined.”

“Obviously.”

“Do you feel inspired?”

“Deeply.”

He went back to his mark. The belt remained on the door for the next three runs. Nobody who had claimed it took it.

At the fourth run, the woman at the supper table reached the doorway, saw the belt, and used it. She put it around her waist mid-scene. Nobody stopped. The servant actor's eyes widened. She ignored him.

After the scene, somebody backstage shouted:

“That's mine.”

The table woman removed it.

“Then why was it on my door?”

No answer. She handed it to soot-shirt worker. Soot-shirt worker threw it backstage without looking. Someone caught it. I had no idea who owned it. This was apparently less important than everyone had claimed.

I laughed. Nobody cared. Good. The soot-shirt worker climbed down. She had a strip of painted cloth in one hand.

Someone behind her said:

“That's mine.”

She kept walking. The voice followed.

“That's the west-wall strip.”

“It is brown.”

“It is west-wall brown.”

She stopped. Turned. A narrow man with paint on both wrists came out from behind the doorway. He pointed at the strip like she had stolen a child.

“That matches the alley set.”

“It matches this.”

“It absolutely does not.”

They held the strip against the doorway. I looked. Same. Probably. The paint-wrist man looked at me.

“You.”

“No.”

“Which?”

I looked again.

Soot-shirt worker said:

“Don't recruit civilians.”

“He is not civilian anymore.”

“I am absolutely civilian.”

The servant actor called from stage:

“Messenger.”

“Fuck you.”

Paint-wrist man held the strip higher.

“Door or alley?”

I compared. There was a tiny warmer red under the doorway brown. The strip had more gray.

“Alley.”

He pointed at soot-shirt worker.

“Thank you.”

She looked at me.

“Traitor.”

“You asked indirectly.”

“I did not ask.”

“Good.”

She took a different strip from his arm. He objected. She ignored him. This appeared to be a supply system. I liked it. Mostly because nobody was winning. The soot-shirt worker finally turned to me.

“Gregory.”

“Yes.”

“Hold.”

I held. Seated. Learning. She compared the cloth to the painted doorway. Different brown. Slightly. Maybe.

“Wrong?”

I asked.

“Yes.”

“They look the same.”

“No.”

I looked again. One warmer. One grayer.

“Close.”

“Close is wrong under front light.”

“Why?”

She stared at me. I stopped. Not a lesson day. She took the cloth.

“Need darker.”

Went away. I watched rehearsal. No messenger. After maybe twenty minutes, Teren handed me a page. I looked at him.

“What?”

“Read the landlord.”

“Why?”

“Because I need to hear the cut.”

“Where?”

“From chair.”

I looked. Six lines. Older man. Angry about rent. Good. I could do angry about money. Probably. The recurring woman stood at the table. She read opposite me. I started. Too quiet.

“Louder,” Teren said.

Of course. I started again. Louder. Too much. The servant actor covered one ear.

“Landlord is furious.”

“Fuck you.”

Teren said:

“Less.”

I tried. The line sounded normal. The recurring woman answered. I missed the next line because I was looking at the page and not listening. Teren tapped his own copy. I found it. Again.

Second pass better. Third pass, Teren cut half my second line while I was saying it.

“Stop after ‘three months.’”

I stopped. The recurring woman continued. My next line now came sooner. I missed it.

“Again.”

We did. This was not messenger. Still fun. Then Teren changed the cut back.

“Why?”

“Testing.”

“That is rude.”

“Yes.”

The servant actor whispered:

“Hessa.”

I looked at him.

“How do you know Hessa?”

“I don't.”

“Then why?”

“You made the face.”

Everyone had the face now. Fine. We ran the little landlord exchange again. I got through it. Teren took the page.

“Good.”

That meant done. I wanted another. Apparently I had standards now. I sat. The recurring woman went back to the table scene. Someone backstage dropped something metal. Loud. Everyone onstage flinched. The recurring woman did not stop.

She continued the line. The other woman did too. The servant actor turned the flinch into looking toward the doorway. For half a second it looked intentional.

Then Teren said:

“Again from before the drop.”

The metal thing clattered again because somebody kicked it while retrieving it.

The servant actor called:

“Commitment.”

Someone backstage shouted:

“Fuck off.”

Good theatre. The scene restarted. I found myself listening for the drop. It did not happen. Disappointing. At break, the servant actor came over with two cups. One had water. One smelled like something worse.

He gave me water.

“Landlord.”

“No.”

“Messenger Landlord.”

“No.”

“Gregory of Rent.”

“No.”

He sat on the floor. I looked at him.

“Why floor?”

“Chair is cursed.”

“It is a chair.”

“Exactly.”

I drank.

He said:

“You keep coming.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

I looked at him. He waited. Not serious enough to be dangerous.

“It's funny.”

He nodded.

“Mostly.”

“That is not what I said.”

“I know.”

He drank the bad cup. Made a face.

“What is that?”

“Tea.”

“No.”

“Exactly.”

We sat. Around us, people moved furniture. The soot-shirt worker returned with darker cloth. The blue window was not blue. Nobody cared yet. Someone argued about a missing belt. Someone else said the belt was under the red bench.

There were two red benches. Apparently this building had learned nothing from blue doors. I smiled. The servant actor saw.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“Dangerous.”

He stood. Break over. I expected to keep sitting. Instead the recurring woman pointed at me.

“Gregory.”

“Yes?”

“Stand there.”

She pointed near the painted doorway. I stood.

“What am I?”

“Person.”

“That is broad.”

“You can manage.”

The servant actor said:

“Debatable.”

She ignored him.

“When she crosses, move aside.”

The other woman stood at the table.

“Why?”

“Because she needs the path.”

“That is not acting.”

“No.”

Good. I stood. The scene began. The other woman crossed. I moved aside. Too early. Also wrong direction. I had moved toward the painted doorway because it was closer. She had planned to cross behind me.

Now I was in the path twice. She stopped.

“Why are you following me?”

“I am avoiding you.”

“You are extremely bad at it.”

“I noticed.”

“Again.”

Teren did not even say it. She did. Apparently everyone had authority over again now. We reset. The second attempt I waited too long. She had to angle around my right crutch. Not dangerous.

Ugly. She finished the cross anyway.

Then turned at the table and said:

“Your crutch is louder than you are.”

“That seems false.”

“Not from here.”

Teren looked up.

“She's right.”

“About volume?”

“Yes.”

“This is becoming personal.”

The servant actor said:

“Landlord Messenger Furniture has a sound problem.”

“I will kill you.”

“Not in this scene.”

“Again.”

I went back. She changed path. I moved again. Now I was in her way. She stopped. Looked at me.

“Choose.”

“I was getting out of the way.”

“Once.”

Right. Again. This time I waited until she committed to a path. Moved once. Fine. Then the servant actor entered from behind me and nearly hit my crutch. He avoided it. Kept scene.

Afterward he said:

“Your leg is in my kingdom.”

“Crutch.”

“Same problem.”

“Then use another door.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Mine.”

Of course.

Teren said:

“Gregory, half a step left.”

I moved. Servant actor tried entrance. Clear.

“Again.”

We repeated. That was all. I had become scenery with opinions. Excellent.

Then the recurring woman added:

“When I say ‘bring him in,’ cross to table.”

“Who?”

“You.”

“As what?”

“Person.”

“That is not enough.”

“It is today.”

“What do I do at table?”

“Stand.”

“Why?”

“Because I am talking to you.”

“Do I have lines?”

“No.”

The servant actor said:

“Messenger has been demoted.”

I looked at him.

“Landlord outranks messenger.”

“Person is below both.”

Unclear hierarchy. We ran it.

The woman said:

“Bring him in.”

I crossed. Too fast.

“Again.”

Too slow.

“Again.”

I stopped at wrong side of table.

“Again.”

I looked at Teren. He was not smiling. Not annoyed either. Just pages. Again. I crossed. Stopped where she could see me without turning away from the other actor. She said her line to me.

I had no response. I looked at her. She continued. That was apparently correct. Strange. Next run she stood closer. I stopped in the old place. Now I was too far away. She looked at the distance between us.

Then at me. I stayed. She said the line louder.

Afterward:

“Why didn't you move closer?”

“You moved.”

“Yes.”

“You said stop there.”

“I said stop where I can talk to you.”

“That is not a location.”

“It is today.”

I looked at Teren. He was writing. No help.

“So I choose?”

“Yes.”

“Based on what?”

“Where I am.”

“That changes.”

“Yes.”

“That is terrible.”

She smiled.

“Again.”

I moved closer next time. Too close. She stepped back while continuing the scene. I noticed and adjusted half a step. Teren did not stop us. That was apparently acceptable. Not correct. Acceptable. The distinction was becoming irritatingly useful.

Next pass I nodded. She stopped.

“No.”

“What?”

“Don't.”

“Why?”

“Because then I have to answer the nod.”

“That makes no sense.”

“It makes enough.”

I stared. She smiled.

“Again.”

Fine. No nod. Just stand. Harder than expected. My face wanted to do something. My body wanted to acknowledge. Instead I stood. She spoke. I listened. Then she turned away. Scene moved. Teren did not stop.

That felt like success. Tiny. Embarrassing. Good. Later, the soot-shirt worker needed the path. I moved before she asked. She noticed.

“Learning.”

“No.”

“Yes.”

“No.”

She carried the darker cloth up the ladder. The painted doorway changed almost imperceptibly. Under the front lamp, the patch disappeared. I could not see where old brown ended and new began. That was satisfying.

Not magic. Paint. Good. The afternoon kept going. No messenger. I stopped caring. Mostly. I read landlord twice more when Teren needed it. I stood as Person during three runs. One time I forgot to move when the other woman crossed.

She shoulder-checked me lightly. Kept going. I apologized after.

She said:

“Move next time.”

“Yes.”

That was all. One time the servant actor came through his door too fast and caught the edge of the painted flat with his sleeve. The flat shifted. Soot-shirt worker grabbed it. The actor kept going.

I almost looked at the flat. Did not. Because the recurring woman was speaking to me. I stayed where I was. Afterward I looked. The flat was fine. Soot-shirt worker had already wedged it.

No one praised me for not turning around. Obviously. It was not impressive. That felt good too. The next run the flat did not shift. The run after that, the cup rolled off the table.

Different failure. The recurring woman caught it against her skirt with one hand and kept speaking. The other woman took it from her without looking. Servant actor reached for it one line later because his hand expected the cup to be there.

Nothing. He converted the reach into pointing. Nobody laughed. The scene continued.

Afterward he said:

“I saved that.”

The recurring woman said:

“You nearly murdered a cup.”

“I saved the scene.”

“You pointed.”

“Heroically.”

Teren said:

“Again.”

I laughed. Servant actor pointed at me.

“See? Audience.”

“I am not audience.”

“You laughed.”

“Against my will.”

“Counts.”

I did not know whether it counted. I did know I wanted the next run. At the end Teren collected pages.

“Tomorrow?”

“Hessa.”

He nodded. No after. Interesting. The recurring woman passed me carrying the empty plate. She stopped. Looked at me.

“You came back.”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

That was all. Small. Ordinary. Somehow better than being needed. I liked that.

Then:

“Messenger.”

“I was not messenger.”

“Landlord?”

“Briefly.”

“Person?”

“Yes.”

She nodded solemnly.

“Promotion.”

“Fuck you.”

She laughed. I left. My palms were warm. Right calf tired. Not bad. Residual limb quiet. I sat on the low wall outside before walking home. Not because ordered. Because I wanted to. People passed.

Nobody called me Messenger. Excellent. Then the bread seller across the street saw me. He raised one hand. I raised a finger. He laughed. I did too. No magic today. Tomorrow Hessa. Today I had been a landlord, a person, and occasionally furniture.

None of them mattered. I wanted to go back.

CHAPTER 131

THE DIRECTION

Hessa had removed the charcoal. Not from my arm. From the table. There was no charcoal stick beside the copper. No little marks waiting to become important. I noticed this before I sat down.

Hessa noticed me noticing.

“Good morning.”

“No target.”

“Good morning, Greg.”

“Good morning. No target.”

“Sit.”

I sat. Yesterday had left me with warm palms, a tired right calf, and the disturbing discovery that being called Person could require several attempts. This morning the palms were normal. Right calf normal.

Residual limb quiet. Phantom foot present, mostly toes today. No pain. No thumb. No finger urge. Grip normal. Hessa checked twice anyway.

“You went back.”

I looked at her.

“Theatre.”

“Yes.”

“You were not a messenger.”

I narrowed my eyes.

“Teren's sister?”

“No.”

“Herb woman?”

“No.”

“Bread seller?”

Hessa wrote something.

“That is not an answer.”

“You are becoming easier to track than you think.”

“That sounds threatening.”

“It is mostly gossip.”

“Worse.”

She put the page aside. No more theatre. Good. She turned my right forearm palm-down on the support. Different position from last time. Not dramatically. Enough. I looked for charcoal again. Nothing.

“What question?”

“Direction first.”

I sat straighter.

“You think the prepared target pulled the response.”

“I think it may have.”

“So no prepared target.”

“Yes.”

“And you tell me direction before shape.”

“Yes.”

“That isolates whether changing direction after shaping was the problem.”

“No.”

I stopped.

“It helps distinguish it.”

“Yes.”

“That's what I meant.”

“No, it isn't.”

“Hessa.”

“Words matter when you are trying to decide what an observation excludes.”

“Fine.”

She pointed to a broad neutral patch on the outer half of my forearm. No mark. No suspended object. No thread. Her finger did not touch.

“Localized alteration in this region.”

“That is still a target.”

“A region.”

“A target region.”

“Yes.”

“So you did not remove targeting.”

“No.”

“You removed a fixed destination.”

“Yes.”

Better.

“What direction?”

“Toward your wrist.”

I looked at my wrist.

“Not elbowward.”

“Correct.”

“Why wrist?”

“Because your older unwanted pattern had a familiar elbowward component, and I do not want today's question tangled with it.”

“Good.”

“Also because you have a wrist.”

“That is less rigorous.”

“It is extremely well established.”

I almost laughed. Hessa did not. Probably on purpose. She reached for a narrow folded towel instead and slid it under my forearm. I watched her square the edges.

“You changed the support.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“The old one has charcoal on it.”

“That matters?”

“To the experiment? Probably not.”

“Then why mention it?”

“You asked.”

The towel raised my forearm perhaps half an inch. I flexed nothing. Still, the angle felt different enough that I noticed.

“Same arm position?”

“Close.”

“Close is not same.”

“No.”

“Does that become a confound?”

“Everything becomes a confound if you demand enough precision.”

“That sounds irresponsible.”

“It means I record it.”

She did. I looked at the page.

“You are writing towel.”

“Yes.”

“This is humiliating magic.”

“It is medicine with ambitions.”

That was worse. She moved the copper into view. Not close to the arm. Same familiar role. Observation. Not target.

“One draw?”

“Yes.”

“One shape?”

“Yes.”

“One directional instruction?”

“If the shape is stable.”

“RETURN.”

“Yes.”

“Release.”

“Yes.”

“No second trial.”

“Yes.”

“You decided that already.”

“Yes.”

“Even if it works?”

“Yes.”

“Even if it fails?”

“Yes.”

“Annoying.”

“Yes.”

She checked my hand position. Fingers relaxed. Wrist neutral. Elbow supported.

“Do not look at your wrist during the directional instruction.”

“Why?”

“I do not want you moving the hand or changing muscle tension while visually steering.”

“I wasn't going to.”

“Good.”

“Where do I look?”

“At the wall.”

I looked. Blank plaster. Excellent target.

“Before draw,” Hessa said, “tell me the full instruction.”

“Minimal draw. Localized alteration in the region you indicated. If stable, smallest asymmetry toward the wrist. No force. No broadening. Maintain underlying draw. Stop if anything changes outside the bounded response or if I cannot describe it.”

“RETURN on command.”

“Yes.”

“What direction?”

“Toward wrist.”

“Again.”

“Toward wrist.”

She waited. I waited. Nothing clever happened.

“Draw.”

I drew. Minimal. The copper changed. Right forearm. Familiar now. Not easy. Familiar. Those were different. No hand. No thumb. No left.

“Report.”

I did.

“Hold.”

Held.

“Shape in the indicated region.”

I shaped. The localized alteration appeared. Small. Not a point. Not a line. A patch with edges that were easier to describe than the center. It came slightly faster than last time. I reported that too.

“Stable?”

“I think.”

“Think or know?”

I waited. The patch did not broaden. No hand response. No movement.

“Know enough to continue.”

“Good. Direction.”

Toward wrist. I had known the direction before the draw. No charcoal. No fingers appearing afterward. No thread. Nothing to chase. I tried to let the smallest part of the altered edge favor the wrist side.

Something changed. I stopped doing anything more.

“Report.”

“Wrist-side edge sharpened.”

“Moved?”

“No.”

“Extended?”

“Maybe.”

“Maybe is allowed.”

“Center unchanged. Elbow-side edge unchanged. Wrist-side edge feels more distinct.”

“Anything else?”

“No.”

“Hand?”

“No.”

“Wrist?”

“No.”

“Thumb?”

“No.”

“Fingers?”

“No.”

“Left?”

“No.”

“Hold.”

I held. The wrist-side edge remained easier to find. Or I remained better at finding it because I expected it. That possibility arrived immediately. I told her.

“Good.”

“That was not good.”

“It was accurate reporting.”

“Possibly.”

“Still accurate.”

She watched my hand. I watched the wall. This was an absurd way to do magic. Probably healthy.

“RETURN.”

I returned. The localized alteration reduced. The wrist-side distinction softened with it. Underlying draw remained. No broadening. No motor urge. No wrist movement. No thumb. No unusual left response.

“Hold.”

Held.

“Release.”

Released. Hessa checked my hand before I could turn my arm over. Grip. Fingers. Thumb. Wrist. Temperature. Sensation. Fine. She wrote. I waited. She wrote more. I hated this part.

“Well?”

“You completed the sequence.”

“That is not the question.”

“It is one question.”

“The directional question.”

“Your report was consistent with a small directional asymmetry toward the instructed side.”

I stared at her.

“That sounds successful.”

“It sounds consistent.”

“Hessa.”

“You reported a sharper wrist-side edge. I did not independently observe the edge.”

“The copper?”

“Changed with draw and shaping. I saw nothing during the directional instruction that I would separate from that.”

“So still self-report.”

“Yes.”

“But unlike last time, it went the instructed direction.”

“By your report.”

“Yes.”

“Yes.”

I waited for more. She did not provide it.

“Does that increase your confidence?”

“In what?”

“That I can direct it.”

“A little.”

There. Small enough to be insulting. Real enough to matter.

“How little?”

“I am not giving you a number.”

“Qualitative scale.”

“No.”

“More than yesterday?”

“Yes.”

“Less than localized shaping?”

“Much less.”

“Less than RETURN?”

“Yes.”

“More than external effect?”

She looked at me.

“That is not a useful comparison.”

“Why?”

“Because one is an internal report about control and the other is a claim about effect outside the body.”

“Both are uncertain.”

“In different ways.”

Fine. I looked at the blank forearm. No charcoal. Nothing to point at afterward. The absence made the report feel less satisfying than Ch129. Then I realized that was backward. A mark had given me something visible to organize around.

Today Hessa had deliberately taken that away. I wanted to ask whether that made today's attempt harder. I asked.

“Possibly,” she said.

“Because there is less reference.”

“Possibly.”

“Could you mark the region after I shape instead of before?”

“Why?”

“So the mark cannot organize the initial response, but we still get a visual reference for where I reported it.”

Hessa considered that.

“Maybe.”

“Good idea?”

“Maybe.”

“You are abusing that word.”

“It is doing useful work.”

“What did removing the mark tell you?”

“Not enough yet.”

“It went toward the wrist.”

“Today.”

“You wanted direction first.”

“Yes.”

“And it worked better than changing direction after shape.”

“Today.”

“That distinction is becoming irritating.”

“It should remain irritating for a long time.”

“Do you think the charcoal caused the failure?”

“No.”

“You said it may have.”

“I still say it may have.”

“Then why no?”

“Because today's result does not tell me that it caused yesterday's result.”

“Ch129.”

“Yes.”

“Two days ago.”

“Yes.”

“Yesterday was theatre.”

“I know.”

“Good.”

She gave me a look. I had won something. Unclear what.

“Possible explanations,” I said.

“No list.”

“You hate lists.”

“I hate your lists before I finish my notes.”

“That is more specific.”

“Yes.”

I waited. She finished the line.

“Now?”

“No.”

“Hessa.”

“You already know them.”

“I want to know yours.”

“Fine. One: giving direction before shaping may help you organize the response.”

“Yes.”

“Two: removing the prepared charcoal destination may have mattered.”

“Yes.”

“Three: wristward may simply be easier than the direction I chose last time.”

I had not thought of that.

“Why?”

“I don't know.”

“Anatomy?”

“Possibly.”

“Old pattern?”

“Possibly.”

“Position?”

“Possibly.”

“Expectation?”

“Possibly.”

“You enjoy this.”

“No.”

“Liar.”

She continued.

“Four: your report may be biased by knowing the intended direction.”

“Yes.”

“Five: there may be a small real directional response that you can currently produce more reliably when the direction is established before shaping.”

I looked at her. She looked back.

“That one was last.”

“Yes.”

“You did that on purpose.”

“Yes.”

“Because it is least established.”

“Yes.”

I liked it anyway. That was my problem. I could already feel my attention trying to promote the fifth explanation because I liked it. The other four became obstacles instead of possibilities. I knew that habit.

Knowing it did not stop it.

“Hessa.”

“Yes?”

“If I had reported elbow-side instead, what would you have done?”

“Written elbow-side.”

“Would that lower your confidence?”

“In directional control under today's instruction, yes.”

“Would you think I followed some hidden prepared target?”

“There was no hidden prepared target.”

“Good.”

“Why good?”

“Because I was checking.”

She stared at me.

“You think I hid charcoal from you?”

“Not charcoal.”

“What?”

“I don't know. A scratch. A vein. Something you selected.”

“I selected a region of your arm.”

“So yes.”

“No.”

“Technically yes.”

“Greg.”

“Fine.”

She wrote again.

“What now?”

“Suspicious of clinician.”

“You did not write that.”

“No.”

I leaned enough to try to see. She covered the line with her hand. Rude.

“Repeat next assessment?”

“Maybe.”

“Same direction?”

“Maybe.”

“Opposite direction would be better.”

“Why?”

“Because if wristward is anatomically easier, opposite direction tests whether I can choose rather than merely produce a favored asymmetry.”

Hessa stopped writing. I waited.

“That is a reasonable question,” she said.

Excellent.

“So next time.”

“I said reasonable.”

“Hessa.”

“I did not say next.”

Cruel.

“What would be better?”

“I need to decide whether changing direction is worth another safe attempt before I have more ordinary repeatability at direction-first shaping.”

“So repeat wristward.”

“Maybe.”

“Then opposite.”

“Maybe.”

“Then external.”

“No.”

I had known that one. Worth trying.

“What about the thread?”

“No.”

“I did not ask to use it.”

“You were about to.”

“I was going to ask whether better directional control would be one of your reasons to reconsider it.”

Hessa paused.

“Yes.”

I waited.

“That is all?”

“That is all.”

“So if this becomes repeatable...”

“Then one reason to revisit an external question becomes stronger.”

“Not necessarily thread.”

“Correct.”

“Good.”

“Why good?”

“Because I am learning.”

She looked unconvinced. Fair. She checked my arm again. Still fine.

“What is the count?” I asked.

“Sixteen successful minimal draws.”

“Twelve shapes.”

“Yes.”

“Directional attempts?”

She paused.

“You are trying to create a category.”

“I am trying to count.”

“You have several attempts involving directional instruction under different conditions.”

“Four external REACH-type attempts?”

“Three external.”

“I know. I mean including internal.”

“No.”

I frowned.

“Why no?”

“Because you are about to make unlike things look alike by giving them one number.”

That was unfair. Also accurate.

“Ch129 changed direction after shaping.”

“Yes.”

“Today direction established before shaping.”

“Yes.”

“Both directional.”

“Yes.”

“So two internal directional questions.”

“If you want to write that in your notebook, you may.”

“Will you?”

“No.”

“What will you write?”

She turned the page slightly. Not enough for me to read all of it. Enough to see separate lines. Of course.

“Conditions,” she said.

“That is not a count.”

“Correct.”

I sat back. This was why she owned the room. Not because she was always right. She had been wrong before.

She had changed tests, changed language, shelved the thread after being interested enough to repeat it, and admitted when her own instruction might have been poor. That mattered more than pretending the sequence had been inevitable.

I preferred inevitable sequences. They were cleaner. Reality remained badly managed. Not because she was always right. Because she refused to let convenience become evidence when she could help it. I still wanted the number.

I would probably write one. Carefully.

“Tomorrow?”

She considered me. I hated when she did that.

“No magic.”

I blinked.

“Again?”

“Yes.”

“One day?”

“Yes.”

“Assessment after?”

“Yes.”

“Why rest after one clean internal attempt?”

“Because it remains an altered response in the same recovering system.”

“No symptoms.”

“Good.”

“Clean RETURN.”

“Good.”

“Clean release.”

“Good.”

“So why not tomorrow?”

“Because the absence of a problem is not a reason to increase frequency every time you notice the absence.”

I stared at her.

“That sounds prepared.”

“It is. You keep asking the same question.”

Fair.

“What am I allowed to do?”

“Live.”

“I know.”

“Apparently you need repetition.”

I looked toward the door. Theatre existed in that direction eventually. So did Lyssa, depending on where she was working. So did Sevren. So did the Guild. So did lunch. A surprisingly crowded category.

I had gone to theatre yesterday expecting one thing and been used as three other things instead. That thought belonged to yesterday. I left it there. Mostly.

What mattered now was that none of those places required me to know whether the wrist-side edge had been real. The fact was almost offensive. Carrow would continue functioning without a conclusion.

Hessa said:

“Greg.”

“Yes?”

“Do not spend tomorrow deciding whether today's wrist-side edge was real.”

“I cannot promise not to think.”

“I did not ask that.”

“What did you ask?”

“Do not turn the day into an unrecorded extension of this assessment.”

I considered arguing. Did not.

“Fine.”

“Good.”

I stood. My forearm looked completely normal. No charcoal to wash off. That was mildly unsatisfying. At the door I stopped.

“Hessa.”

“Yes?”

“That is not what I asked.”

“It is the answer you are getting.”

He said:

“Landlord.”

I stopped. He grinned. Absolutely fucking not. I pointed at him.

“No.”

He laughed hard enough to lean on the stall. I kept walking. Tomorrow, no magic. After that, Hessa again. Today the answer was not yes. It was not no either.

It was a sharper edge on the side I had been told to choose, observed by exactly one person from inside his own arm. Terrible evidence. Better than Ch129. I could live with that.

THE HOUR

I wanted to see Lyssa. Again. This was less annoying than the first time. Not unannoying. Less. No magic today. Hessa had been explicit. No draw. No shaping. No direction. No sitting at a table pretending I was not practicing.

I stopped chewing.

“No.”

He smiled.

“How?”

“Bread man.”

“I hate him.”

“For what?”

“Gregory.”

“Lyssa.”

The crate man looked between us.

“Your landlord?”

I closed my eyes. Lyssa laughed.

“No.”

“Messenger?”

“No.”

Lyssa laughed harder. I looked at her.

“You know?”

“Apparently.”

“This city is diseased.”

The crate man said:

“I heard you forgot the letter.”

“No.”

“Yes.”

She looked pleased. Also busy. Good.

She pointed at the crate.

“What is it?”

“Not yours.”

“Correct.”

The crate man said:

“Glass.”

Lyssa looked at him. He shrugged.

“No.”

“Thank you.”

Lyssa checked a folded scrap. Then the crate. Then the scrap again.

“Six?”

“Six.”

“You said five.”

“I said six.”

He pointed to the side. A charcoal six. Lyssa stared.

“That was not there yesterday.”

“It was.”

“No.”

I looked at the six. Then at Lyssa. Then at the man. Not my problem. Wonderful.

Lyssa said:

“Fine. Six. Same price.”

He said:

“More glass.”

“Your mistake.”

“Your order.”

“Your six.”

“Your glass.”

They continued. I stood nearby. Not adjudicating. Eventually Lyssa paid something. The man looked unhappy. Lyssa looked satisfied. Probably both had won enough. She took one side of the crate. I looked at the other.

“No.”

“I didn't say anything.”

“You leaned.”

This was everywhere now.

“Yes.”

“And a crate full of glass.”

“Yes.”

“No.”

“Fine.”

The crate man called a boy from inside. The boy took the other side. Lyssa and the boy carried it twenty feet to a handcart. I followed. Useful. Very. The crate went onto the cart.

Lyssa checked the wheels.

“Where are you taking it?”

“Two streets.”

“I can walk two streets.”

“I know.”

“Good.”

She took the cart handles. I walked beside her. The cart rattled. Glass clicked inside. I wanted to know how it was packed. Did not ask. Progress. Probably.

“No.”

“That's disappointing.”

“I read six lines.”

“No.”

She grinned. We crossed a narrow street. A wagon waited. Lyssa pulled the cart over the curb edge. One wheel stuck. I moved around.

“No.”

She rocked the cart once. Wheel cleared. Good. I kept walking. Two streets became three because the destination was around the back of a building. Lyssa stopped at a side door. Knocked. A woman opened it.

Looked at the crate.

“Six?”

Lyssa looked at me. I looked away.

The woman said:

“I know.”

The woman looked inside the crate.

Lyssa blinked.

“No.”

Lyssa stared. The woman smiled. Negotiation began again. I sat on a low step because this was going to take time. Eventually the sixth piece stayed. More money changed hands. Lyssa came out.

“No.”

“Yes.”

“Incorrect.”

She stopped. He held out a narrow wrapped parcel.

“When?”

“Now.”

“How far?”

“Dyer's row.”

She looked at the sun.

“No.”

He blinked.

“No.”

He named a number. Lyssa shook her head. He raised it. She shook her head again.

“Maybe.”

He looked at me. I immediately hated that.

The man frowned.

“It is light.”

Lyssa looked at me. Not annoyed. Maybe pleased. The man tried again.

Lyssa considered. For one second I thought she would take it. Then she looked toward the south street.

“Maybe.”

“Yes.”

She raised one eyebrow. Fine.

“Yes.”

She held up one of the straps on her work bag. The stitching at the lower end had started to separate. I had not noticed.

“Most.”

“How long has it been failing?”

“Today.”

“That did not happen today.”

“It became a problem today.”

“New strap.”

“Stitch.”

“New strap.”

“Stitch.”

“It will tear again.”

He looked at her. She looked back. I stayed out of it. Mostly.

He said:

“Brown.”

Lyssa said:

“Black.”

“Brown matches.”

“You hate it.”

“It doesn't match.”

“Yes.”

“Then?”

I had been surrounded by theatre workers too long.

“Nothing.”

“Don't do that.”

She pulled again. Still held.

“Good.”

“What?” Lyssa asked.

“Yes.”

She smiled.

“No.”

“Landlord.”

“Stop.”

“Yes.”

I had not planned past that. Good.

“Food?”

“I have an hour.”

“Before?”

“Work.”

“Where?”

“South.”

“Can I come?”

She thought.

“No.”

Clean.

“Why?”

“Fine.”

No apology. Better. She tilted her head.

“You okay with that?”

“Yes.”

“I have one face.”

I hated everyone.

“Food.”

“Food.”

We bought meat pies from a stall near the fountain. Not the paper-bird square. Different fountain. Carrow had too many fountains. The pie seller knew Lyssa. Not well.

Enough to say:

“Late today.”

Lyssa said:

“Glass.”

The seller nodded as though that explained time. Apparently it did. He looked at me.

“Landlord?”

“No.”

Lyssa said:

“Yes.”

I looked at her. The seller handed me my pie.

“Rent's due.”

“I will burn this stall.”

“Then no pie.”

“Fine.”

I paid. Lyssa was still laughing when we reached the bench. We sat. Lyssa took the better side.

“That is mine.”

“You sat slowly.”

“I have crutches.”

“Excuses.”

I moved one crutch between my knees. The other leaned beside me. Not ideal. Stable enough. Lyssa bit into her pie.

“Did the magic do anything?”

I looked at her. She raised one eyebrow.

“You don't have to tell me.”

“It did something small.”

“Good?”

“Unclear.”

“That's your favorite.”

“It is not.”

“You say it a lot.”

“Hessa says it.”

“Then it's hers.”

“Fine.”

She waited. Did not ask again. Good. For almost a minute we ate without speaking. That should not have been notable. It was. Lyssa watched people crossing the square. A woman with three baskets.

A man carrying a chair upside down over one shoulder. Two children following a dog that clearly did not belong to them. I watched Lyssa. Not secretly enough. She looked over.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You are staring.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“I wanted to see you.”

That landed differently than I expected. Her expression softened. Not dramatic. Just less guarded.

“You found me.”

“Yes.”

“Again.”

“Yes.”

She looked back at the square. Then leaned her shoulder into mine once. Small. I liked it. I told her anyway.

“Thread is done.”

“Done?”

“For now.”

“Because?”

“It did not repeat cleanly.”

She nodded. No interpretation.

Lyssa chewed.

“What does that mean?”

“Maybe.”

She pointed at me with the pie.

“Unclear.”

“Fuck you.”

She smiled.

Then:

“Are you allowed magic today?”

“No.”

“I am not.”

“Good.”

That was the entire medical discussion. Excellent. She ate. A pigeon landed near our shoes. My phantom toes curled. Not actually. Sensation. Brief. Ordinary. I shifted my right foot instead. Lyssa noticed.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You moved.”

She looked down.

“See?”

“Friends.”

She fed that one too. Soon there were five.

Lyssa laughed so hard she almost dropped the pie. Good. We stayed. No purpose. The hour became forty minutes. Then thirty. Lyssa checked the sun. I noticed.

“Soon.”

“Now?”

“Not yet.”

She leaned back. Her shoulder touched mine. Stayed. I liked that. No analysis. Almost.

“I don't know.”

“Landlord duties.”

“No.”

“Messenger?”

“No.”

“Person?”

I looked at her.

“How do you know that?”

She smiled.

“No.”

“Lyssa.”

“No.”

“That one happened yesterday.”

“Yes.”

“Yes.”

“Yes.”

“Unfair.”

“You were very serious.”

“So does Person.”

“No.”

“Did you have a line?”

“No.”

“Stood.”

She waited.

“And?”

“Moved.”

She waited.

“Badly.”

There. She smiled.

“Did you like it?”

I looked at the fountain.

“Yes.”

“More than landlord?”

“Different.”

“Messenger?”

“I forgot the letter once.”

“I know.”

“Everyone knows.”

“Yes.”

“This is humiliating.”

“You keep going back.”

“Yes.”

“So maybe humiliation isn't fatal.”

She laughed.

“I don't know.”

“Good.”

There. Easy. I looked at her. She looked back. No joke. Not heavy either. Just true.

“I do.”

She nodded.

“Good.”

“What?”

“Yes.”

“Romantic.”

“Consequences.”

She stared at the bird.

“Yes.”

“Fuck.”

I laughed. The bird left. We watched it go. Lyssa checked the sun again. Now. She stood. I stayed seated. Before she left, a girl about twelve came running across the square.

“Lyssa.”

“Morning?”

The girl nodded.

“She said afternoon.”

“Before midday.”

The girl shrugged in the universal way of people carrying messages they did not own.

“Fine.”

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You want to know.”

“Yes.”

“Tomorrow work.”

“Where?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because then you'll start planning my route.”

“It happened today.”

“With everything.”

“South?”

“South?”

“Yes.”

“Inside?”

“Yes.”

“Stairs?”

“Yes.”

“Too many people?”

“Yes.”

“Fine.”

She looked at me.

“What are you doing?”

“Probably walking.”

“Strong plan.”

“I have a notebook.”

“Dangerous.”

She leaned down and kissed me once more. Then straightened.

“Tomorrow?”

There it was. Again. I looked at her.

“I have Hessa morning.”

“I know.”

“After?”

“Maybe.”

She rolled her eyes.

“You keep saying maybe.”

“You keep asking tomorrow.”

“Yes.”

Fair. I thought.

“I could find you after.”

“If I'm not there?”

“Then you aren't.”

“Good.”

“Landlord.”

“Fuck you.”

She walked away laughing. I sat another minute. My palms were warm but fine. Right calf ordinary. Residual limb quiet. Phantom foot present, heel against nothing. No magic. Good. I stood. The day was not finished.

I could go theatre. Guild. Home. Nothing. I chose nothing for a while. Walked without deciding. At one corner I passed the paper-bird seller. He recognized me. Held up a yellow bird. I looked at it.

The one on my table was yellow too.

“Not today,” I said.

He shrugged. No offense. Good. I kept walking. The thread did not enter my head. Not for several blocks. When it did, it was not first. Lyssa was. Annoyingly simple. Again.

CHAPTER 133

THE OTHER WAY

Hessa had removed the charcoal. Again. I liked that. Which probably meant I had developed opinions about blank forearms. Not ideal.

“Sit.”

I sat. Morning baseline was boring. Excellent. Hands normal. Right calf normal. Residual limb quiet. Phantom foot present in the vague way it usually was when I thought about it and less present when I did not.

No thumb. No fingers trying to participate. No unusual cold. No pain. Hessa checked anyway. She always checked anyway. Then she put the folded white towel beneath my right forearm. Copper sat farther up the table.

Not near enough to be interesting. I looked around. No threads. Still.

“Disappointed?” Hessa asked.

“No.”

“You looked.”

“I have eyes.”

“Tragic.”

I rested my arm. The outer forearm was unmarked. No charcoal target. No line. No point. Nothing to accidentally obey. Good. Hessa sat across from me with her notes. She had rewritten something. I could tell because one strip of paper had been pasted over another.

“What did you change?”

“My wording.”

“Why?”

“Because I wrote that you directed the edge wristward.”

“That is what happened.”

“That is what you reported.”

I looked at her. She looked back.

“Fine.”

“Good.”

“I hate your notes.”

“They are not for your emotional comfort.”

“I know.”

She put the pen down.

“Last time I told you the direction before shaping.”

“Yes.”

“You reported a small asymmetry toward your wrist.”

“Yes.”

“Today I want the same sequence with one change.”

“Elbowward.”

She stared at me.

“That was my guess.”

“Stop guessing.”

“You said one change.”

“I did.”

“And opposite direction is the cleanest.”

“Probably.”

I smiled. She did not.

“Your confidence is unattractive.”

“That seems unrelated.”

“It isn't.”

I stopped smiling. Mostly. Hessa touched two fingers lightly to the table near my elbow. Not my arm. Just direction.

“Elbowward.”

“Yes.”

“Not toward my fingers.”

I frowned.

“I am indicating a direction. If I move my hand, the direction does not move with it.”

“Good.”

“You understand?”

“Yes.”

“Say it.”

“Toward my elbow. Not toward your hand.”

She moved her hand away. Good. No target. No destination. Only direction. That was cleaner. Probably. Hessa watched me.

“One draw.”

“One shape.”

“One directional instruction.”

“One RETURN.”

“One release.”

“Yes.”

“No external question.”

“Yes.”

“No attempt to make the effect larger because you think a larger effect would be easier to report.”

“I was not going to.”

“You thought it.”

“I think many things.”

“That is the problem.”

I breathed. Not special breathing. Just enough to stop talking.

“Draw.”

I reached. Carefully. The draw came more easily than it had weeks ago. That did not mean easy. It meant familiar. A narrow opening. A small pull. Mana. Contained. No broad flood. No rush into the left.

No fingers. No thumb. No urge to move my hand. I held. Hessa watched my face more than my arm.

“Stable?”

“Yes.”

“Anything else?”

“No.”

“Hold.”

I held. The temptation was to prepare for the next instruction. I noticed that. Then I noticed that noticing it was also preparation. Annoying.

Neutral region. Outer right forearm. Small. Localized. Not direction yet. That mattered. I let the familiar alteration form. Not a point. Not a patch exactly. An area with an edge I could feel more clearly than I could describe.

The center changed first. Then the boundary became legible. Not visible. Mine. Internal.

“Report.”

“Localized.”

“Size?”

“Small.”

“That is not size.”

“About the same as last time.”

“Comparison is not size.”

I almost opened my eyes. They were already open. I had been staring at the wall.

“Two fingers across. Maybe less.”

“Shape?”

“Uneven oval.”

I waited. Checked. Not pushed. Checked.

“No.”

“Certain?”

“No.”

“Useful.”

She wrote. I hated that too.

“Hold.”

I held. The edge stayed. No broadening. No elbow pull. No wrist pull. Nothing external. Copper remained copper. Wonderful object. Hessa waited long enough that I started wondering whether she had forgotten the next instruction.

She had not.

“Smallest directional change toward your elbow.”

I did not move. That was the first thing. No hand. No wrist. No fingers. No shoulder. Inside. Elbowward. The previous wristward attempt wanted to become relevant. I tried not to use it. Impossible.

Memory existed. Fine. I did not reverse it. There was nothing to reverse. This was a new shape. Elbowward. For several breaths nothing happened. Or nothing I could distinguish happened. I felt the center.

The wrist-side edge. The elbow-side edge. The elbow-side edge seemed softer than the wrist side. Wrong. Maybe. I waited. Hessa said nothing. I wanted to fix it. That was dangerous wording. Not fix. Observe.

Then the elbow-side boundary sharpened. A little. I thought. The wrist side stayed where it was. The center stayed. Elbow side clearer. Not farther. Clearer. Maybe.

“Report.”

“Elbow-side edge changed.”

“How?”

“Sharper.”

“Extension?”

“I don't know.”

“Other edges?”

“Wrist side same.”

“Center?”

“Same.”

“Anything else?”

“No.”

“Motor?”

“No.”

“Force?”

“No.”

“Broadening?”

“No.”

“Left?”

“No.”

“Hold.”

“Yes.”

“Same?”

“I think.”

“Think or know?”

“Think.”

“Good.”

She waited.

Then:

“RETURN.”

I reduced. The elbow-side distinction softened first. Then the rest. The localized alteration diminished without sliding. No familiar broad response. No hand urge. No thumb. No fingers. No wrist. No elbow movement. Underlying draw stayed.

“Report.”

“Reduced.”

“Gone?”

I checked.

“Maybe a little center.”

“Hold.”

I held. It faded.

“Now?”

“Gone.”

“Draw?”

“Still.”

“Release.”

I released. The draw closed. Nothing chased it. Nothing jumped left. Nothing moved outside me. Hessa waited. Then checked my hand. Forearm. Wrist. Thumb. Asked about fingers. Asked about phantom foot. Asked about the left.

“No.”

“You would enjoy it.”

“Yes.”

I leaned back.

“Yes.”

“That is the second time your report has favored the instructed side.”

“Opposite sides.”

“Yes.”

“So.”

“More than last time.”

“That is not a number.”

“Can I direct it?”

“I am not writing that either.”

She turned the page enough that I could read the line. REPORTED ASYMMETRY FOLLOWED OPPOSITE INSTRUCTED DIRECTION UNDER OTHERWISE SIMILAR DIRECTION-FIRST CONDITION.

Below it:

“That is obnoxious.”

“It is accurate.”

“Yes.”

“That is usually why you dislike things.”

“No.”

“Yes.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because I have not decided.”

“We could alternate.”

“We could do many stupid things in orderly patterns.”

“That is unfair.”

“It is extremely fair.”

She closed the notes.
