There were several variables. Lyssa stopped at a doorway and knocked. I nearly continued past her.

"What?"

"Work."

"Oh."

A young man opened the door. He saw Lyssa. Then me.

"No."

I looked at him. Lyssa said, "He's not coming in."

"Good."

"What is inside?"

"Gregory."

"I am asking spatially."

The young man looked at Lyssa.

"Does he do this?"

"Yes."

"Constantly?"

"Not constantly."

"Frequently."

"Thank you."

Lyssa handed him the folded wet cloth. He frowned.

"This is wet."

"Yes."

"Why?"

"Because everyone is difficult."

He accepted that. Apparently this was a professional category. Lyssa took a small packet from her bag and gave it to him. He gave her another. Then he looked at me again.

"Landlord?"

"No."

Lyssa said, "Shopkeeper now." I turned.

"What?"

The young man smiled.

"Oh. That was you?"

No. Absolutely not.

"How do you know?"

"My sister was there."

"At the market hall?"

"Yes."

"What did she say?"

Lyssa leaned against the doorframe. The young man thought.

"That the king was terrible."

Correct.

"And?"

"The princess was good."

Correct.

"And?"

"The man with one foot threatened somebody about debt."

"That was not a threat."

He laughed.

"She said it was."

"It was consultation."

That made him laugh harder. Lyssa looked delighted. I hated public performance.

"Did she say anything about the sword?"

"The talking one?"

"Yes."

He shrugged.

"Funny."

"That is all?"

"What else would it be?"

I opened my mouth. Closed it. Fair. The young man shut the door. Lyssa waited. I started walking. She caught up.

"Funny."

"Stop."

"The talking one."

"Lyssa."

"Shopkeeper."

"That is not my name."

"It was last night."

"No."

She laughed. I let her. For three streets. Then she said, "You're going." I looked at her.

"Where?"

She did not answer. That was irritating.

"I have not decided."

"You came to find me after Hessa."

"I have done that before."

"Yes."

"I wanted to see you."

"I know."

"And I needed to tell you."

She looked at me. There. That had escaped. Fine.

"Tell me what?" she asked.

"The theatre leaves tomorrow."

Her face changed only slightly. Not fear. Not surprise exactly. Attention.

"How long?"

"Five days. Maybe six."

"Where?"

I told her. She knew the road but not the town.

"Why?"

"Theatre."

"I got that."

"There is also a municipal hall."

Lyssa stared at me.

"What?"

"You're leaving for a building?"

"The roof was rebuilt twice."

She kept staring.

"The original load paths are strange."

"Gregory."

"I wanted to see it years ago."

"How many years?"

I stopped. Ah.

"Many."

She understood. Not everything. Enough. The street moved around us. A woman squeezed past carrying a basket of onions. Somewhere behind us, a hammer struck metal in a steady rhythm. Lyssa stepped closer to the wall so we were not blocking the lane.

"And the theatre happens to be going there."

"Yes."

"Tomorrow."

"Yes."

"For five days."

"Maybe six."

"You're going."

"I said I haven't decided."

She reached out and straightened the edge of my coat where Hessa's stiff paper had made it bulge.

"You put the drawing in here."

"Yes."

"You came straight to find me."

"Mostly."

"You asked someone where I was."

"Yes."

"You're telling me before you told me you've decided."

"I have not decided."

Lyssa nodded.

"Fine."

That was too easy.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"No."

She started walking again. I followed.

"You're doing the thing."

"What thing?"

"Where you stop arguing because you think you already know."

"I don't know."

"You do."

"No."

"Lyssa."

She turned into the next square. I followed, irritated enough that I almost clipped a fruit crate.

"Lyssa."

She stopped beside a fountain. Not the pigeon fountain. Good.

"What do you want me to say?"

"I don't know."

"Then why are you angry?"

"I am not angry."

"You're hitting the ground harder."

I looked at my right crutch. Traitor.

"I am explaining that the decision is not made."

"Okay."

"You don't believe me."

"I believe you haven't said it."

"That is different."

"Yes."

I waited. She waited. People crossed between us and the fountain. A little boy leaned over the basin until his mother pulled him backward by his shirt.

"Do you want me to tell you not to go?" Lyssa asked.

"No."

"Do you want me to tell you to go?"

"No."

"Do you want me to be upset?"

I frowned.

"No."

She looked at me for another second.

Then softer:

"Do you want me to care?"

That was a much worse question.

"I know you care."

"Then?"

I looked away. A horse was drinking from the far side of the fountain. Its driver held the reins loosely and picked something from his teeth. Five days. Maybe six. Not long. I had traveled farther for worse reasons. I had also died. Different trip.

"I wanted to tell you," I said.

"I know."

"Before."

"I know."

"I don't know what you're doing tomorrow."

"Work."

"Obviously."

"Morning north side. Afternoon maybe west."

"Maybe?"

She smiled.

"Contagious."

I ignored that.

"I leave early if I go."

"If."

"Yes."

"Fine."

I looked at her. She did not rescue me. Good. Annoying.

"Could I see you tonight?"

"Yes."

Immediate. No bargaining. Something in my chest loosened enough that I noticed it.

"Where?"

"My room."

I blinked. Lyssa raised an eyebrow.

"You've been there."

"Yes."

"You look surprised."

"I am not."

"You are."

"I was calculating stairs."

"No, you weren't."

I smiled despite myself.

"Some."

"Liar."

"Fine."

She stepped close and kissed me. Not long. Public enough that a woman passing with a basket looked at us and then politely looked somewhere else. Lyssa drew back.

"Go tell your theatre."

"I haven't decided."

"Then go inspect the wagon for six hours until the decision becomes official."

"That is insulting."

"Will you?"

I thought about the south-road wheels. The loading. How much weight I could actually move. Whether there was space to ride if my hands got bad. Where the crutches would go. What happened if the town had stairs everywhere. Whether Teren had assumed I was coming or merely offered. Whether the servant actor could throw his voice from a moving wagon. No. That last one was irrelevant. Probably.

"I should ask about the road."

Lyssa nodded.

"And the wagon."

"Yes."

"And sleeping arrangements."

"Yes."

"And whether they expect me to carry anything."

"Yes."

"And how many shows."

"Yes."

"That is not the same as deciding."

"No."

She was smiling.

"Stop."

"I didn't say anything."

"You're doing it with your face."

"I have one face."

"That is my line."

"It is everyone's line now."

She kissed me again. Then she stepped away and adjusted her work bag.

"I have to go."

"Where?"

"North."

"You said morning north."

"It is still morning."

I looked at the sun. Barely.

"That assessment took longer than I thought."

"You talked."

"Hessa talks."

"Sure."

"She does."

Lyssa started backward for two steps.

"Tonight."

"Yes."

"Don't arrive after I'm asleep."

"What time?"

She gave me a look. Right. Not everything required measurement.

"Before late."

"Good."

She turned.

"Lyssa."

She looked back. I nearly said I was going. The words were there. Instead I said, "The black patch is still ugly." She looked down at her bag. Then at me.

"Five days might improve your taste."

"Six would not."

She laughed and walked away. I watched longer than two seconds this time. She did not turn around. Good. I headed for the theatre. Not because I had decided. I needed information. The theatre doors were open when I arrived. A flat painted like a stone tower was halfway into the alley, blocking most of it. The soot-shirt worker stood on the wagon bed with a coil of rope around his neck, shouting at someone inside.

"Not that one. The other ugly one."

A voice answered, "They're both ugly."

"The tall ugly one."

"That is not better."

I stopped beside the wagon. One rear wheel had been removed. Good. South-road wheels. The servant actor was underneath it. I could see his boots.

"Teren?"

"Inside," the soot-shirt worker said.

"Why is the wheel off?"

The boots under the wagon moved.

"Because it was bad."

"How bad?"

The servant actor slid out on his back. His shirt was dusty and his hair had something black in it.

"Bad enough."

"That is not a measurement."

"It is for wheels."

He sat up.

"You coming?"

I looked at the missing wheel.

"I have questions."

He smiled.

"Coming."

"Questions."

"Ask."

"How long on the road tomorrow?"

"Depends."

"On?"

"Road."

I stared at him. He wiped his hands on his trousers.

"Three hours to first stop if the axle behaves. Eat. Another three, maybe four. We sleep there."

"Where?"

He named a village I knew.

"Then?"

"Shorter second day."

"That makes the trip longer than five days."

"Five or six there and back if nothing goes wrong."

"That is impossible."

"Then six."

"Teren said five maybe six."

"He lies optimistically."

Useful.

"Sleeping?"

"Inns if rooms exist. Hall floor if they don't. Wagon once, probably."

"Probably?"

"Gregory."

"What?"

"You are asking theatre people for certainty."

Fair.

"Shows?"

"Two planned. Maybe three."

"Shopkeeper?"

"If Meren remains dead."

"He isn't dead."

"Then he should arrive."

"Do I have a role if he does?"

The servant actor looked at me.

"Sword."

"Yes."

"And whatever breaks."

"That is not a role."

"It is the oldest role."

The soot-shirt worker shouted from the wagon, "Can the oldest role lift a wheel?"

"No," I said.

"Then he's decorative."

"Fuck you."

"See? Actor."

The servant actor laughed. I looked at the wagon bed.

"Where do I sit?"

He pointed.

"Front if Teren loses the argument. Back if he wins."

"What argument?"

"Seats."

"With whom?"

"The wagon owner."

"Why?"

"Wagon owner wants cargo where people go."

"That seems backwards."

"Yes."

"Can I secure crutches?"

"We'll tie them."

"Where?"

He pointed to a rail. I inspected it. Solid enough. Probably.

"And if my hands get bad?"

"You ride."

"I am already riding."

"You ride more."

"I mean during loading."

"Then don't load."

"That makes me a hindrance."

He looked at me. Not joking now.

"No. It makes you a man who doesn't load."

"I can carry some things."

"Then carry some things."

"And when I can't?"

"Don't."

"That is not efficient."

He shrugged.

"We have actors."

"That does not answer anything."

"It answers most things."

From inside, Teren shouted, "Sword!" I looked toward the door. The servant actor grinned.

"See?"

I went in. Teren was at a table covered in pages, receipts, two apples, a broken buckle, and a small pile of coins. He did not look up.

"You're coming."

"I have questions."

"Tomorrow before sunrise."

"That is not a question."

"Bring food."

"I haven't said yes."

"Bring food anyway."

"How many shows?"

"Two."

"He said maybe three."

Teren looked toward the alley.

"Who?"

"The king."

"Never trust kings."

"He said you lie optimistically."

Teren considered.

"Fair."

I put both hands on the table edge.

"Where am I sleeping?"

"Wherever we all sleep."

"That is not useful."

"No."

"Do you know whether the municipal hall has stairs to the stage?"

Teren finally looked at me.

"No."

"Back entrance?"

"No."

"Dressing rooms?"

"No."

"Floor height?"

"No."

"Chair?"

"Yes."

"You don't know the rest."

"I know chairs."

"How?"

"Town has people."

I stared. The troupe's faith in chairs was becoming theological. Teren picked up an apple.

"Gregory."

"What?"

"Are you coming?"

I looked at the pages. The receipts. The broken buckle. The coins. Outside, someone hammered the wheel back into existence. Tonight I was going to Lyssa's room. Tomorrow before sunrise the wagon left east. Hessa's drawing sat inside my coat. There were no good reasons left to pretend the decision required another category.

"Yes," I said.

Teren bit into the apple.

"Good. Bring food."

That was all. No welcome. No contract. No speech about the road. He pushed a packet of pages toward me.

"What is this?"

"Third show."

I stared at him.

"You said two."

"Maybe three."

"Fuck you."

"Learn page twelve."

I took the packet. Apparently I was traveling.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 141

## THE PACKER

Page twelve had seventeen lines. This was an unreasonable number of lines for a page Teren had handed me less than a day before leaving Carrow. I read them once at the theatre. Then again while someone dragged a painted tree past my chair and struck the doorframe hard enough to remove a branch. Nobody stopped. The tree continued outside with one fewer branch. I looked at the script. The role was a clerk. Of course it was.

Not a useful clerk. A comic clerk who had lost a document and spent most of the scene insisting the document had never existed. I understood the profession immediately.

"Do I need to learn all of this?"

Teren was tying pages into separate packets with red string.

"Page twelve."

"There are seventeen lines on page twelve."

"Yes."

"Why only page twelve?"

"Because if we do the third show, that scene is changing."

"Into what?"

"I don't know."

"You handed me lines for a scene you know is changing."

"Yes."

"That seems inefficient."

Teren pulled the knot tight with his teeth.

"Learn page twelve."

I took the packet home. By late afternoon I had packed three times. The first packing was practical. The second was because the first packing had been wrong. The third was because I had removed half the things from the second packing and could no longer remember why I had included them. Travel had been easier when other people decided what I carried. That was not a good argument for other people deciding things. I put the bag on the bed. Two shirts. One spare pair of trousers. Underclothes.

Cloth for the residual limb. Extra wrapping. Small repair kit. Soap. Cup. Food for the morning. Money. Script. Hessa's drawing. No. The drawing came out. I looked at it. Wrist-side boundary dark. Upper edge less certain. Broken lower line. It was information.

It was also exactly the kind of information I would look at in a wagon until I convinced myself the bumps in the road had revealed something about mana. I put it in the drawer. Then I took it out. Hessa had told me to take it. That did not mean she had told me to carry it east. I put it back in the drawer. Closed the drawer. Opened it. The drawing remained there. Good. I closed it again.

The room was warm. Evening light came through the window and caught the dust over the bed. Somewhere downstairs, someone was cooking onions in too much fat. The smell climbed through the floorboards and made the bread on my table seem inadequate. I looked at the bag. Crutches. Those were difficult to forget.

I added a second length of cord for tying them to the wagon rail. Then a third. No. Two. I removed one. There was a knock.

"Come in."

The door opened. Lyssa looked at the bag on the bed. Then at the folded shirt in my hands.

"You're packing."

"No."

She closed the door behind her.

"What are you doing?"

"Determining what to bring."

"That is packing."

"I haven't finished."

"That is still packing."

She carried a small paper parcel and a bottle. Her hair was pulled back loosely, though several curls had escaped around her face. She had changed clothes since the morning, simpler and softer, and the black-patched work bag was gone. I looked at the parcel.

"What is that?"

"Food."

"I have food."

She looked at the piece of bread on my table.

"No."

"That is bread."

"That is sadness with a crust."

"It was cheap."

"I can tell."

She put the parcel beside it. I opened it. Cheese. Two small meat pies. Dried fruit. Something wrapped separately in waxed paper. I opened that too. Sweet cake. I looked at her.

"This is too much."

"Then leave some."

"I won't."

"I know."

She sat on the edge of the bed, which made the bag tilt toward her.

"What are you bringing?"

I showed her. She picked up one shirt.

"This one?"

"Yes."

"It has a hole."

"It is small."

She put it on the floor.

"Lyssa."

"You have another."

"I have two others."

"Then why are you taking the one with a hole?"

"Because travel damages clothing."

"So you brought damaged clothing in preparation."

"Yes."

She stared at me.

"That makes sense."

"Thank you."

"I hate it."

She put the shirt back in the bag. I sat beside her. The mattress dipped. My left leg ended where it ended, and the empty space beyond it was no longer strange enough to notice every time. Lyssa noticed other things. She picked up the extra wrapping cloth.

"Enough?"

"Yes."

"For six days?"

"Yes."

"What if it gets wet?"

I looked at her. She smiled.

"Fuck you."

"You need more."

"I can buy cloth."

"In the town?"

"Yes."

"You've never been there."

"There will be cloth."

"Theatre has chairs. Town has cloth."

"Exactly."

"This is how civilizations collapse."

I added another piece. Not because she was right. Because there was room. She watched me do it and said nothing. I disliked successful silence.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"You're pleased."

"No."

"You are."

"I brought you food. I'm miserable."

I laughed. She leaned back on her hands. For a while we packed without making it important. She rolled the spare trousers tighter than I had. I objected, then kept them that way. I found a loose stitch on the bag strap and repaired it while she ate half of one meat pie despite claiming they were for me.

"You are stealing my travel food."

"I bought it."

"You transferred ownership."

"No contract."

"Verbal."

"No witness."

"I am a witness."

"Interested party."

I pointed the needle at her.

"You've spent too much time around me."

"Five days will fix it."

"Maybe six."

"Even better."

I tied off the stitch. The room became quieter as the street outside changed from work to evening. Wheels were less frequent. Voices carried farther. Somebody below laughed loudly, then shushed themselves for reasons that were not apparent. Lyssa took the clerk pages from the table.

"What is this?"

"Third show."

"You said there were two."

"There are two."

She looked at the pages.

"This says three."

"There may be three."

"You're leaving before sunrise for a trip that may be five or six days to perform two or three shows in a building you've never seen."

"Yes."

"And you know seventeen lines."

"On page twelve."

She flipped the page.

"There are more after twelve."

"I was instructed not to learn those."

"That seems dangerous."

"Thank you."

She handed it back.

"Do the voice."

"No."

"What voice?"

"I don't know yet."

"You have a voice."

"I have several."

She smiled.

"I knew it."

"That woman was wrong."

"Do the clerk."

"I haven't built him."

"Built?"

"Voice. Pace. How he answers."

"You could just talk."

"That would be me."

"You're playing a clerk."

"Yes."

"Have you considered that clerks can sound like people?"

I looked at her.

"That is radical."

"I know."

I picked up the page. The scene began with another character demanding a permit. The clerk denied that permits were issued in that office. The other character produced a permit issued by that office. The clerk explained that this proved the permit had already been issued and therefore there was no need to issue one. I liked him. That was concerning. I read the first line in a narrow, fussy voice. Lyssa's face changed.

"No."

"What?"

"Don't."

"Why?"

"You sound like a dying bird."

"He is bureaucratic."

"He is sick."

I tried lower.

"Now he sounds old."

"He could be old."

"Is he?"

"I don't know."

"Then why are you making him old?"

I lowered the page.

"You are interfering with my process."

"Yes."

I read it in my normal voice. Lyssa listened.

"Again."

I did.

"Slower."

"Why?"

"Because he knows the other person has to wait for him."

I looked at the page. Oh. I read it again. Not slow exactly. Unhurried. The permit seeker had urgency. The clerk did not. The line changed. Lyssa pointed.

"That."

"I know."

"You didn't."

"I was about to."

"You were a dying bird."

"That was exploratory."

She laughed. I read the next exchange. By the fourth line I stopped performing the clerk and started answering as if the permit seeker were wasting my time. That worked better. Annoyingly. Lyssa stretched out across the bed on her stomach, chin on her hands, while I went through the page. She interrupted whenever I sounded false. She did not use that word. Her words were worse.

"No."

"Too much."

"Why are you doing that?"

"Normal person."

"That one."

"Again."

Once she said nothing. I stopped.

"What?"

"Continue."

"You reacted."

"I breathed."

"You breathed differently."

She rolled onto her back.

"You are impossible."

"Was it good?"

"It sounded like you believed him."

"Believed what?"

"That the missing document is someone else's problem."

I looked at the line. Yes. That was the clerk. Not fussy. Not old. Protected. He lived inside a system where inconvenience moved downhill and he had arranged to be uphill. I read the next line. Lyssa closed her eyes.

"Better."

I kept going. At the end of page twelve she sat up.

"Again?"

"No."

I looked at her.

"No?"

"You know it enough to ruin it if you keep going."

I stared.

"That is what Teren said."

"I am smarter than Teren."

"You don't know Teren."

"I don't need to."

Fair. I put the pages down. The bag was packed. Mostly. There were still decisions available if I wanted them. Another shirt. More food. Different cord. A small knife. The drawing. I did not touch the drawer. Lyssa stood. For a moment I thought she was leaving. Instead she took my crutches and moved them away from the bed.

"What are you doing?"

"Making room."

"For what?"

She looked at me. Oh.

"That was a stupid question."

"Yes."

She came back and stood between my knees. I put my hands on her hips. She touched the side of my face. Neither of us said anything useful. Then she kissed me. The first kiss was easy. The second was not. I pulled her closer. She shifted one knee onto the bed beside me, careful of my left side without looking at it, and kissed me until I stopped thinking about page twelve. That took less time than expected. When we separated, she rested her forehead against mine.

"Before sunrise?"

"Yes."

"That's disgusting."

"It is."

"You'll be terrible."

"I am good in the morning."

"No one is good before sunrise."

"Farmers."

"Miserable."

"Bakers."

"Miserable with bread."

I smiled. She kissed the corner of my mouth.

"Come back."

The words were quiet. Not dramatic. Not a demand. I felt them anyway.

"It's five days."

"Maybe six."

"Six."

"Gregory."

"I'll come back."

She nodded. Then immediately reached past me and pulled the bag closer.

"What?"

"You forgot socks."

I stared at her.

"I did not."

She opened the bag. I had forgotten socks.

"Fuck."

"I know."

I got up. Lyssa sat in the warm hollow I left on the mattress while I crossed to the drawer. The socks were in the second drawer. The drawing was in the first. I opened the second. Took three pairs. Closed it. Lyssa watched me.

"What?"

"Nothing."

I put the socks in the bag. She did not ask what was in the other drawer. Good. I tied the bag shut. Then untied it because the sweet cake was still on the table. Lyssa laughed.

"Shut up."

"I didn't say anything."

I packed the cake. Retied the bag. This time I left it closed. Tomorrow before sunrise I would get into a wagon with actors, scenery, bad wheels, too many scripts, and no reliable answer about where I would sleep. I was looking forward to it. That seemed unwise. I went back to Lyssa. There was still an evening left.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 142

## THE PASSENGER

Before sunrise, Carrow smelled like horses. Not only horses. Wet stone. Cold ash. Yesterday's beer outside a tavern that had closed recently enough for two men to still be arguing beside it. Bread somewhere I could not see. River damp under everything. But mostly horses.

I arrived at the theatre with my bag over one shoulder and discovered that I was late. I was not late. The sky was black. Teren had said before sunrise. This was before sunrise. The problem was that theatre people apparently interpreted departure times the way they interpreted scripts. The alley was already full.

One wagon stood backed almost to the theatre doors, canvas rolled over its top rails. Another waited crooked behind it with a horse that looked personally offended by the hour. Scenery leaned against both walls. A painted window rested upside down on a crate marked COSTUMES, and somebody had put three swords into a basket with a cabbage. I stopped. The cabbage was real.

"Why?"

The soot-shirt worker looked up from a coil of rope.

"What?"

I pointed. He followed my finger.

"Oh."

He took the cabbage out.

"Thank you."

He put it on a chair. That was not better.

"Gregory!"

Teren appeared in the theatre doorway carrying a lamp in one hand and a boot in the other.

"Why do you have one boot?"

"Not mine."

"Whose?"

He looked at it.

"No idea."

He threw it into the wagon. A woman inside shouted, "Fuck you."

"Found your boot."

"I was wearing the other one."

"Then you're halfway done."

Teren disappeared again. I stood in the alley with my bag. This was the organization I had joined. No. Not joined. Traveling with. Important distinction. The servant actor was sitting on the rear edge of the first wagon drinking something from a tin cup. He had a blanket around his shoulders and looked much less cheerful than usual.

"You came," he said.

"I said I would."

"People say things."

"What are you drinking?"

"Regret."

"Is it hot?"

"Not anymore."

He moved his cup and made space beside him. I did not sit.

"Where are the crutches going?"

He pointed toward the wagon rail. I inspected it. Someone had already tied a broom there.

"That is where you said."

"Yes."

"There is a broom."

"We'll move the broom."

"Where?"

He looked at me over the cup.

"Gregory."

"What?"

"The broom will survive."

I set my bag down. The extra cord was in the top section because I had planned properly. I found it immediately. That felt good. Then I spent several minutes trying to determine the best way to secure two crutches to a wagon that was still being loaded by people who did not respect fixed geometry. Every time I chose a position, someone needed the rail.

"That's scenery."

"I can see that."

"Then move."

"I am attaching mobility equipment."

The soot-shirt worker had one end of the painted tower on his shoulder.

"You can attach it after the tower."

"The tower blocks the rail."

"Only until we unload it."

"That is tomorrow."

"Exactly."

I stared at him. He stared back. The tower won. I moved. A second actor I knew mostly as a guard carried a crate past us.

"Put them inside."

"Where?"

He jerked his head toward the wagon. I looked. The inside contained three people, four costume trunks, rolled fabric, a basket of kitchen things, two spears, one painted moon, and the cabbage. The cabbage had returned.

"No."

The guard shrugged.

"Then walk."

"Fuck you."

"Morning."

He kept going. The recurring woman arrived from the street carrying two bags and a long wrapped bundle. Her hair was tied up badly. She looked awake in the technical sense only. She saw me.

"You're here."

"Yes."

"Why?"

I frowned.

"You told me there were shopkeepers in other towns."

She stared for a second. Then remembered.

"Oh."

She handed me one of her bags. I nearly dropped it.

"What is in this?"

"Shoes."

"How many feet do you have?"

"Depends on the show."

She walked into the theatre with the other bag. I looked at the one she had left me. It was heavier than my travel bag. The servant actor sipped his regret.

"Princess."

"I know."

"Do you?"

"No."

I carried the shoe bag three awkward steps and put it beside the wagon. That counted as loading. Useful. The theatre emptied itself by degrees. Not neatly. Nothing came out in the order I would have chosen. A small table emerged before the legs that belonged to it. Costumes came before the trunk meant to hold them. A rolled backdrop was carried into the alley, returned inside because it was the wrong one, then brought out again because apparently the wrong one was coming too.

I stopped trying to understand the whole operation. That helped.

"Greg."

I turned. Teren stood beside the second wagon with a paper in his hand. Not Gregory. Greg. I waited. He looked at the paper.

"You're in this one."

"Which?"

"Second wagon."

"Why?"

"First is full."

"It was full twenty minutes ago."

"Now it is more full."

"Where do I sit?"

He pointed. There was no seat.

"There."

"That is a crate."

"Yes."

"What is in it?"

"Curtain weights."

"How heavy?"

"Enough."

"I am not sitting on curtain weights for three hours."

Teren looked into the wagon.

"Move the weights."

"To where?"

He looked around. I waited. Teren pointed at the first wagon. The servant actor shouted, "No." Teren pointed at the alley. The soot-shirt worker shouted, "No." Teren looked at me.

"You see the problem."

"Yes."

"Good."

"That does not solve it."

"No."

He walked away. I hated theatre. A little later, the curtain weights went under the rear bench, the rear bench moved forward, two costume trunks traded wagons, the painted moon went flat beneath a stack of fabric, and the crate became a seat after all. Not the curtain-weight crate. A different crate. This one contained cups. I sat carefully. It held. Good.

My crutches were finally tied along the inner rail beside me, handles forward, cuffs wrapped in a scrap of cloth so the wood would not knock against the wagon every time we hit a rut. I had used one cord. The soot-shirt worker had watched me finish, tugged the knot once, and added a second knot above mine.

"What was wrong with mine?"

"Nothing."

"Then why?"

He had already walked away. I left both knots. The sky had begun turning from black to gray by the time the horses moved. There was no announcement. No speech. No count. Someone shouted that a lantern was still inside. Someone else shouted that it could stay there. The first wagon rolled forward anyway. Our driver swore. The horse moved.

The wagon lurched hard enough that I caught the rail with both hands. A cup inside my crate rattled. Then another. Then all of them. We rolled out of the alley. That was departure. I looked back once. The theatre doors were still open.

Teren stood in them with the lamp, shouting at someone I could not see. For one alarming moment I thought we had left him. Then he ran after the wagon carrying the unidentified boot. He climbed onto the back of the first wagon while it was moving. Nobody reacted. Carrow passed slowly around us. Shuttered shops. Dark upper windows. A baker carrying a tray through a side door. A woman sweeping yesterday out of a doorway.

The streets I knew looked narrower from the wagon because I was not choosing where to put my feet or crutches. I was simply being carried through them with cups under my ass. The city gate appeared. We went through. No one stopped us. Then Carrow was behind us. I turned forward. The road was terrible. Not immediately. For perhaps fifty yards it was acceptable. Then the paving ended. The wagon dropped into a rut. Every cup beneath me jumped. I jumped with them.

"Oh."

The guard actor sitting across from me opened one eye.

"First wagon trip?"

"No."

He closed his eye.

"This one."

"Yes."

He smiled without opening his eyes. I adjusted my position. My left side did not like the crate edge. I shifted. My right foot needed somewhere to brace, but every useful surface already belonged to luggage or another person's boots. The recurring woman sat near the front with her back against a costume trunk, knees drawn up beneath a blanket. She had somehow acquired the cabbage. She was eating it. Raw. I watched. She noticed.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"You're staring."

"I was determining whether it was a prop."

She took another bite.

"It is now."

The cabbage had a bite missing from one side. I looked away. The road shook us east. For the first hour, nobody was interesting. This surprised me. Theatre people were extremely interesting inside a theatre. On the road they slept. The guard actor slept with his head against the side rail and woke every time it struck him. The recurring woman slept with the cabbage in her lap. A thin older man I had seen playing fathers and magistrates put his hat over his face and disappeared completely.

The driver did not sleep. Good. I tried to read page twelve. Impossible. The words moved. I knew they were not moving. That did not help. I got through four lines before the wagon struck a stone and the script hit me in the mouth. I folded it. The clerk could wait. The countryside east of Carrow was flatter than I remembered.

Fields spread beyond low walls and hedges, wet with morning. Smoke rose from farmhouses in thin gray lines. We passed a boy driving goats the opposite direction. He stared at the painted tower sticking above the first wagon. One goat stared too. The boy waved. Someone in the first wagon waved back with a severed wooden hand. The boy stopped waving. I laughed. The recurring woman opened one eye.

"What?"

"Nothing."

She closed it. A mile later the servant actor climbed from the first wagon to ours. While both were moving. I watched him step onto the rear rail, catch the side of our wagon, and swing across the gap.

"No."

He landed beside the driver.

"What?"

"You cannot do that."

"I just did."

"That does not make it safe."

"It makes it possible."

"That is not the same thing."

He climbed over a trunk and sat on the floor near my crate.

"Move your foot."

"I only have one available."

"That one."

I moved it. He stretched his legs into the space.

"Why are you here?"

"King snores."

"The guard snores."

The guard opened his eyes.

"No."

"You do."

"No."

"You were."

"I was breathing."

"With your throat closed."

The guard shut his eyes again. The servant actor leaned his head against the crate. For a while we rode in silence. Then, without moving, he said, "Your sword was better late." I looked at him.

"At the market hall?"

"Yes."

"Why?"

"You stopped trying."

"I did not."

He opened one eye.

"You did."

"I was still performing."

"Not what I said."

I waited. He closed his eye again.

"That is not useful criticism."

"Wasn't criticism."

"What was it?"

"Observation."

"Hessa does that."

"Who?"

"Never mind."

The wagon hit another rut. His head knocked against the crate. He swore. I smiled.

"Do you always travel like this?"

"No."

"What changes?"

"Worse roads."

"That is not what I meant."

"I know."

He sat up and rubbed the back of his head.

"Sometimes we have three wagons. Sometimes one. Sometimes horses. Once a boat."

"A boat?"

"Bad."

"Why?"

"Actors."

"That explains nothing."

"It explains the boat."

The recurring woman spoke without opening her eyes.

"He vomited on the king."

The servant actor pointed at her.

"Different king."

She smiled beneath the blanket. I looked between them.

"How many kings have there been?"

"Too many," she said.

"Four," he said.

"Six."

"Those two don't count."

"They wore crowns."

"One was a child."

"Still king."

The older man beneath the hat said, "Seven." Everyone looked at him. He did not move the hat. The servant actor frowned.

"Who was seven?"

"Pel."

"Pel wasn't king."

"Winter show."

"Oh."

The servant actor leaned back.

"Seven."

The hat remained over the older man's face. I looked at the road. This was apparently history. Not important history. Better. By the second hour my hands were fine. My shoulders were not. Neither was my ass. The crate had developed corners it had not possessed when we left. I shifted again. The recurring woman noticed.

"You can take the floor."

"I am not sitting on the floor."

"Why?"

"Getting up."

She looked at the space beside her. Then at my crutches. Then back at me.

"Right."

No apology. No pity. She moved one of the shoe bags and pushed a folded blanket toward me with her foot.

"For the crate."

I took it.

"Thank you."

"Don't make it strange."

"I said thank you."

"Exactly."

I put the blanket beneath me. Better. Much. I did not tell her how much. She knew. The sun came up properly. The fields turned gold-green. Mist stayed low in the ditches. Birds moved ahead of the wagon and then settled behind us again, irritated by the interruption.

At some point I realized I had not thought about mana since leaving Carrow. Then I had. Annoying. I looked at the road instead. The first stop appeared as a cluster of buildings around a crossroads, with a stable, a well, and an inn whose sign had lost enough paint that the animal on it might have been a fox or a burning dog. The first wagon pulled in. Ours followed. When we stopped, everyone became alive at once. Blankets came off. Bodies unfolded.

The guard actor climbed over me before I could object. The recurring woman stood on the wagon bed and stretched until her back cracked. The servant actor jumped down. I reached for my crutches. The knots were still tight. Both of them. Good. I untied the first. The second had pulled hard under vibration and would not loosen. I worked at it. Nothing. The soot-shirt worker appeared beside the wagon.

"Problem?"

"No."

He watched me pull at the knot.

"Problem."

"It tightened."

"Yes."

"You tied it."

"I improved it."

"You trapped my crutch."

He climbed onto the wheel hub, reached over the rail, and pulled one short end I had not noticed. The knot fell open. I stared. He handed me the crutch.

"What was that?"

"Slipped hitch."

"Show me."

"Later."

He jumped down. I looked at the cord. Then at him.

"Later when?"

"Not now."

He walked toward the stable. The servant actor passed carrying two cups.

"Welcome to theatre."

"That was rope."

"Everything is theatre if Teren hasn't paid you."

I got down from the wagon. Right foot. Crutches. Weight. My body objected to becoming vertical. Not pain. Stiffness. A deep complaint through my back and shoulders, plus the unpleasant certainty that the crate had permanently altered the shape of me. I stood still. The recurring woman landed beside me.

"You alive?"

"Yes."

"Good."

She walked toward the inn with the cabbage. I took one step. Then another. My body remembered walking. Mostly. Three hours. We had another three or four after this. I looked at the wagons. At the road east. At the cup crate. The servant actor came back and handed me one of the cups.

"What is it?"

"Regret."

I drank. Tea. Cold. Terrible. I drank again. The first wagon horse sneezed. Somewhere inside the inn, Teren was already arguing about food. I smiled into the cup. The road was awful. I was glad I had come.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 143

## THE STOP

The road was awful. I was glad I had come. Both facts remained true while I stood beside the wagon drinking cold tea and waiting for my back to remember that it had not, in fact, been constructed out of curtain weights.

The crossroads inn had a yard of packed dirt with a stable on one side and the main building on the other. Chickens moved through both jurisdictions without respecting either. A low stone wall surrounded the well. Someone had tied a red cloth to the bucket handle, perhaps to make it easier to find, though the bucket was attached to a rope and directly above a well. The sign over the inn creaked in the breeze. I still could not tell what animal it showed.

"Fox," I said.

The servant actor followed my eyes.

"Dog."

"It has a tail."

"Dogs have tails."

"That tail is on fire."

"Sunset."

"It is coming out of the animal."

"Art."

I drank the tea.

"Who painted it?"

"No idea."

"Then why are you defending it?"

He shrugged. "Dog." The recurring woman passed us carrying the remains of the cabbage.

"Horse."

We both looked at her. She kept walking.

"That is not a horse," I said.

"Now you're defending it," the servant actor said.

I hated him. Teren came out of the inn. He was no longer carrying the boot. This suggested either progress or abandonment.

"Food," he said.

Everyone moved. I stayed where I was. Teren stopped.

"What?"

"Are we buying it?"

"Yes."

"Individually?"

"No."

"Is it included?"

"In what?"

"The trip."

Teren stared at me. I realized there had never been a discussion of what the trip included because there had never been a discussion of the trip at all.

"Do I owe you money?"

"Probably."

"How much?"

"Later."

"No."

Teren sighed. Behind him, the guard actor tried to pass through the door. Teren did not move. The guard said, "Food."

"I know."

"You're in the door."

"I know."

"Move."

Teren stepped aside. The guard went in. I said, "How much?"

"For what?"

"The trip."

"You're working."

"Am I being paid?"

"Yes."

That was new.

"How much?"

Teren rubbed his face.

"Gregory."

"What?"

"It is morning."

"It has been morning for hours."

"Not to me."

"You organized the departure."

"I made a mistake."

He looked toward the road as if Carrow might still be close enough to return to.

"Food now. Money later."

"That is how people get cheated."

"Then keep count."

"I will."

"I know."

He went inside. The servant actor leaned toward me.

"You're definitely theatre now."

"I am not."

"You asked about pay after getting on the wagon."

"That is bad practice."

"Yes."

I followed Teren inside. There were two steps. I disliked them immediately. Not because they were high. Because the first was shallow and the second was not, which was worse than two equally bad steps because it encouraged confidence before betrayal. I took the first. Adjusted. Took the second. The servant actor waited behind me without offering help. Good. Then he tripped over the threshold. Better.

The inn was warmer than outside and smelled of porridge, smoke, onions, horse leather, and people who had been traveling longer than we had. Long tables filled most of the room. A fire burned low in a wide hearth despite the day already warming.

Our troupe occupied one end of a table as if they had been starving for weeks. Bowls appeared. Bread appeared. Nobody seemed to know whether the bread belonged to us. They ate it anyway. I sat at the end where I could put my crutches against the wall. The older actor with the hat was already there. Without the hat over his face, he had a face. I had known this. I had seen him perform. Still, it felt strange.

He had a narrow gray beard and deep lines around his mouth. He was cutting an apple into slices with a small knife.

"Pel," he said.

I looked at him.

"What?"

"Seventh king."

"Oh."

He ate a slice. I had not asked.

"Was he good?"

"No."

"Why did he count?"

"Crown."

That was consistent. A bowl of porridge landed in front of me. The woman carrying it said, "Spoon."

"Yes."

She put one down.

"Anything else?"

"What is the animal on the sign?"

She stared at me.

"Food first."

Then she left. The older actor smiled at his apple.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"You know."

"Yes."

"What is it?"

"Food first."

I ate. The porridge was better than the tea. This was not difficult. There were bits of onion and something salty in it, and the bread was fresh enough that I stopped worrying about whether it belonged to us. The recurring woman sat across from me. She had removed her blanket and looked more awake. The cabbage was gone.

"Did you finish it?"

"What?"

"The cabbage."

She looked under the table. Then beside her.

"Oh."

"You lost a cabbage?"

"It wasn't mine."

"You ate half."

"That doesn't establish ownership."

I looked at her. She smiled. Lyssa would like her. Probably. That thought arrived without warning. I ate more porridge. The guard actor came back with a second bowl.

"You already ate."

"No."

"I watched you."

"That was first breakfast."

"Are we walking to the village?"

"No."

"Then why do you need two breakfasts?"

He sat beside the recurring woman.

"Body."

That was apparently sufficient. Teren arrived last. He carried no food. Instead he had a conversation with the innkeeper in a low voice near the counter. I watched. Coins. Paper. The innkeeper shook his head. Teren said something. The innkeeper shook his head harder. Teren pointed toward us. The innkeeper looked at us. His expression did not improve.

"What is he doing?" I asked.

The servant actor tore bread with his teeth.

"Being Teren."

"Does that mean negotiating?"

"Sometimes."

"Does he owe money?"

"Always."

"That is not funny."

"It is if it isn't yours."

I kept watching. Teren produced another coin. The innkeeper took it. Teren returned to the table.

"What did that cover?" I asked.

He sat.

"Food."

"For everyone?"

"Yes."

"Then why did you say I probably owe you?"

"Because you probably do."

"How can both be true?"

He reached for bread. I moved it away. Teren looked at me.

"How much am I being paid?"

"Gregory."

"No."

The recurring woman said, "Oh, good." The guard actor kept eating. Teren leaned back.

"For the trip?"

"Yes."

"Depends how many shows."

"No."

"No?"

"You cannot answer a current pay question with a future number of shows unless there is a rate per show."

"There is."

"What?"

Teren looked around the table. Nobody helped him. The servant actor looked delighted. Teren named a number. I considered it.

"Per show?"

"Yes."

"Travel?"

"Food while moving. Sleeping if I arrange it. You buy anything else."

"Do I get paid if the third show doesn't happen?"

"For two shows."

"Yes."

"What if I perform Shopkeeper in addition to Sword?"

"That is still a show."

"What if I perform Clerk?"

"Still a show."

"So roles do not change pay."

"No."

"That encourages doing as little as possible."

The recurring woman raised her spoon.

"Finally."

Teren pointed at her.

"Don't."

I said, "What about loading?"

"What about it?"

"Work."

"You want to be paid for loading?"

"If loading is required."

"Do you want to load?"

"No."

"Then don't."

"That does not answer the principle."

The guard actor said, "Please stop." I looked at him. He had nearly finished the second bowl.

"Why?"

"I want to hear myself chew."

Teren tore off bread.

"You are being paid the same as the others for the shows. Food on travel days. Sleeping where I put you. If the town adds a show, you get another show payment."

"What if I don't appear in it?"

"Then no."

"Reasonable."

Teren blinked. Apparently he had expected more. I took the bread back and handed it to him.

"Thank you."

"You're welcome."

The servant actor looked disappointed. I ate. The innkeeper passed our table. I caught his attention.

"What animal is on the sign?"

He stopped. Everyone near me became quiet. The innkeeper looked toward the front door.

"Boar."

The servant actor said, "Bullshit." The innkeeper looked at him.

"You painted it?"

"My brother."

"Then your brother painted a fox."

The innkeeper's expression changed.

"Boar."

"It has a tail."

"Boars have tails."

"Not that tail."

The recurring woman said, "Horse." The innkeeper looked at her as if she had insulted his mother. The older actor continued eating apple.

"Dog," he said.

The servant actor pointed at him.

"Yes."

I said, "The tail is on fire." The innkeeper walked away. Nobody resolved it. That was probably best. Outside, the horses were being watered. The soot-shirt worker had one wheel blocked with a stone and was underneath the wagon again. I approached. He saw my crutches first. Then me.

"Don't."

"I haven't done anything."

"You have questions."

"Yes."

"Later."

"This is later."

He stopped moving under the wagon. That was satisfying. After a moment he slid out. His name remained a problem. I had spoken to him enough times that asking now would be embarrassing. That was not a reason not to ask. It was a reason I had not asked. He sat up and wiped grease from his fingers with a rag.

"What?"

"The knot."

He looked at the wagon rail.

"You remembered?"

"Yes."

"Good."

He reached for a loose piece of rope beside him. The rope was thicker than my cord and dirty enough that I did not want it near clothing. He looped it around the rail.

"Over."

I watched.

"Under."

"Yes."

"Back through."

"Yes."

He pulled. The knot tightened. Then he pulled the short end. It released. I stared.

"Again."

He did it again. Slower. I watched the path of the rope instead of his hands. Over. Around. Bight through. Load on one part. Release on another.

"Let me."

He handed me the rope. I put one crutch under my arm and used both hands. The first attempt was wrong. I knew before I pulled.

"Wrong."

"Yes."

I undid it. Second attempt. Also wrong. He did not speak. That was irritating. Third. I formed the loop, passed the bight, loaded it. It held. I pulled the release. It opened.

"Oh."

He took the rope.

"Done."

"That was three attempts."

"You know it."

"I can reproduce it once."

"Then reproduce it later."

"That is poor instruction."

"I fix wagons."

"What is your name?"

He looked at me. There. I had done it. He wiped his hand on the rag again and held it out.

"Davin."

I shook it.

"Greg."

"I know."

"Apparently."

Davin went back under the wagon. I stood there.

"Davin."

"No."

"I was only going to ask about the wheel."

"No."

Fine. I walked toward the well. A girl of perhaps ten was standing beside it staring at the first wagon. Specifically at the painted tower. She had a bucket in both hands. Her mother, or someone performing the role, was filling another bucket. The girl looked at me.

"Are you with them?"

"Yes."

"What are you?"

I considered.

"Passenger."

She frowned.

"That isn't in plays."

"Sometimes."

"Are you an actor?"

"No."

Davin laughed from under the wagon. I looked toward him. The girl followed my gaze.

"Are you?"

"Sometimes."

"What do you play?"

"A sword."

She stared at me.

"No."

"Yes."

"You don't look like a sword."

"I don't have the costume on."

This was technically true because there was no costume. She looked at my left trouser leg. Then at the crutches. Then back at my face.

"How?"

"With my voice."

"Oh."

She accepted this immediately. Children were better audiences than adults in some ways and much worse in others.

"Do you fight?"

"No."

"Swords fight."

"This one complains."

She smiled.

"What does it say?"

I looked toward the inn. Teren was nowhere visible. Good. I used the Sword voice.

"Put me down."

The girl's eyes widened. Her mother turned. I continued.

"You are holding me incorrectly."

The girl laughed. Her mother looked from me to the wagon.

"Is that from the show?"

"Not exactly."

"Do it again," the girl said.

I almost did. Then stopped. Not because of magic. Not because of rules. Because I could feel myself reaching for the exact sound that had made her laugh. Last one. I looked at the servant actor's observation from the wagon. You stopped trying. Annoying. The girl waited. I said, in the Sword voice, "No." She laughed harder. Oh. I smiled.

"Why no?" she asked.

"Contract dispute."

She did not understand that. Her mother did. The mother laughed. Different line. Different audience. Same sword. Maybe. I did not pursue it. The mother picked up both buckets.

"Come on."

The girl followed her. She turned once and waved. I waved back. Davin slid out from beneath the wagon.

"You're an actor."

"No."

"Fine."

He checked the wheel. I went to use the privy. It was behind the stable. There were three steps down into a narrow patch of mud, then one step up into a structure built by someone who hated knees. I stood at the top of the first step. This was not theatre. This was architecture. Architecture was worse. I managed. Nobody learned anything. Good.

By the time we loaded again, the sun was fully up and the inn yard had become crowded with carts. A merchant wanted our second wagon moved. Teren wanted the merchant to wait. The merchant had money. The innkeeper therefore wanted Teren to move. We moved. This involved everyone pretending to know where everything belonged. I tied my crutches to the rail with the slipped hitch. Davin walked past. He tugged it once. Did not add a knot. That was better than praise.

I sat on the blanket over the cup crate. The recurring woman climbed in with two apples.

"No cabbage?"

"Lost it."

"You ate it."

"Not all of it."

"Then where is the rest?"

She looked toward the inn.

"Traveling."

I decided not to ask. The servant actor returned to the first wagon because apparently the king had stopped snoring while awake. We rolled east. The second stretch of road was worse. Not dramatically worse. Persistently worse. Ruts came in pairs. Dust rose behind the first wagon and settled over us. The sun warmed the canvas and made the inside smell like cloth, wood, leather, old paint, apples, and the guard actor's boots.

"Your boots smell."

His eyes opened.

"No."

"That is not a matter of opinion."

He looked down.

"They're boots."

"They smell like something died inside them."

"Feet."

The recurring woman covered her nose with the edge of her blanket.

"Take them off."

"That would be worse."

She considered.

"Keep them on."

He smiled. I read page twelve again. This time I could manage it. Not because the road improved. Because I stopped trying to read every word. I knew the scene now. Permit. Denial. Existing permit. Therefore no need for permit. The logic was stupid. The clerk was not.

He understood the only important fact: the other person needed something from him. I read the lines silently. The recurring woman watched me.

"What?"

"You move your mouth."

"No."

"You do."

"I am not speaking."

"Still moving."

I stopped. She smiled.

"Do you know the clerk scene?"

"Yes."

"Who are you?"

"Apparently the clerk."

"No. Who are you with?"

I looked at the packet. There were names written above the scene. One had been crossed out. Another written in. Then crossed out. A third written smaller.

"I don't know."

She took the pages.

"That's Iven."

"Which?"

She pointed.

"The permit man."

"Who is Iven?"

"Guard."

I looked at the guard actor. He was asleep again.

"That is Iven?"

"Yes."

I had been traveling with him for five hours.

"Why did nobody tell me?"

"You didn't ask."

I looked at her.

"What is your name?"

She smiled slowly. Oh, fuck.

"You don't know."

"I know who you are."

"That is not my name."

"You've never told me."

"You've never asked."

"That is different."

"How?"

I considered several answers. None survived.

"Fine. What is your name?"

"Serra."

I repeated it.

"Serra."

"Yes."

"You knew mine."

"Everyone knows yours."

"That is becoming concerning."

She handed the pages back.

"Iven," I said, pointing across the wagon.

He opened one eye.

"What?"

"Your name is Iven."

"Yes."

"Good."

He closed his eye. Serra laughed. I looked toward the front wagon.

"The servant actor."

Serra frowned.

"Who?"

"The man who was king last night."

"Oh. Marek."

"Marek."

"Yes."

"Older actor?"

"Orin."

"Davin I know."

"You learned Davin before me?"

"He taught me a knot."

"I gave you a blanket."

"That did not require identification."

Serra threw an apple at me. I caught it against my chest. Barely.

"That could have gone under the wagon."

"Then you'd know where the cabbage went."

I ate the apple. Names changed things slightly. Not enough to explain. Iven remained asleep. Serra remained irritating. Marek was now in the first wagon somewhere, probably doing something unsafe. Orin's hat was visible above a stack of fabric. Davin rode beside the driver of the first wagon after apparently deciding the wheel would remain attached. Teren was not visible. This did not mean he had been lost. Probably. We stopped once because a strap broke. Not ours. The first wagon. Everyone got down except me and Iven.

Iven remained asleep. I stayed because nobody asked me to get down and because climbing in and out of the wagon for a five-minute repair seemed stupid. Davin and another crew worker pulled a chest sideways. Serra held a section of canvas out of the dirt. Marek stood on the wheel and passed rope over the load. Teren appeared from nowhere. Good. Still present. The repair took twelve minutes. I timed it. Not deliberately. I happened to know when we stopped.

When we started again, I noticed the broken strap had not been repaired. It had been replaced by rope arranged in a pattern I did not understand. I considered asking Davin later. Then stopped myself. Not every rope needed to become mine. That was a strange thought. I ate dried fruit. The road continued.

Around the sixth hour, conversation returned because everyone had slept enough to become annoying again. Marek came back to our wagon at a stop slow enough to cross without jumping. Progress. He sat beside Iven. Iven opened his eyes.

"No."

Marek sat anyway. Serra said, "Greg doesn't know anyone's name."

"I know names."

Marek looked at me.

"Mine?"

"Marek."

He seemed disappointed.

"Her?"

"Serra."

"Old man?"

"Orin."

From the first wagon, Orin's voice carried back.

"Not old."

I looked at Marek.

"How did he hear that?"

Marek shouted, "Old!" Orin raised one hand above the wagon side. One finger. Serra laughed. I did too.

"Davin," I said.

Marek nodded.

"Teren."

"Yes."

"Iven."

Iven said, "Unfortunately."

"Who am I missing?"

Marek looked around.

"Most of us."

"How many?"

"Depends."

"On what?"

"Show."

I sighed. Serra leaned toward me.

"You'll learn."

"I have been there for weeks."

"Yes."

"I know roles."

"Exactly."

That was true. Princess. Servant. Guard. Older actor. Soot-shirt worker. I knew what people did around me before I knew what they were called. That was not entirely unusual. It was still embarrassing.

"Do you know Lyssa's name?" Serra asked.

I looked at her.

"How do you know Lyssa?"

"You said it."

"When?"

"Sleeping."

I stared. Marek became very interested.

"I did not."

Serra smiled.

"You did."

"What did I say?"

"Lyssa."

"That is not evidence of anything."

"I didn't say it was."

"What else?"

"Nothing."

I looked at Iven. He shrugged.

"I was asleep."

"You are always asleep."

"Good system."

Marek said, "Who's Lyssa?"

"No one."

Serra's eyebrows rose. I corrected.

"Not no one."

Marek smiled.

"Excellent recovery."

"Fuck you."

"Is that Lyssa?"

"No."

Serra laughed so hard she had to turn away. I regretted learning their names. The village appeared late in the afternoon. At first it was only smoke beyond trees. Then roofs. Then a narrow road with houses pressed closer together than the farms we had passed all day. My body had stopped complaining individually. Everything had joined into one general objection. Shoulders. Back. Right hip. Hands slightly tired but not bad. Residual limb warm from sitting and wrapping and the day. No new pain. No new symptom. Just travel.

I knew enough now not to call ordinary discomfort nothing. I also knew enough not to turn it into prophecy. The wagons slowed. Children appeared first. They always did. One ran beside us for half the street, shouting questions at the painted tower. A dog barked at the horse. The horse ignored it.

A woman outside a shop recognized the theatre before she recognized any of us.

"Players?"

Marek leaned over the wagon side.

"Unfortunately."

She laughed.

"Performing here?"

"No."

"Then keep moving."

"We intend to."

Teren shouted from the first wagon, "Marek."

"What?"

"Stop advertising."

"I denied everything."

We turned into the yard behind an inn smaller than the crossroads place. Much smaller. I looked at the building. Then at the troupe. Then at the building again.

"No."

Serra followed my gaze.

"Yes."

"There are too many of us."

"Yes."

"There cannot be enough rooms."

"No."

"Where are we sleeping?"

She smiled.

"Now you're traveling."

The wagons stopped. I reached for my crutches. The slipped hitch released on the first pull. Good. I untied the second. Climbed down. My right leg nearly folded. Not fully. Enough that I caught myself hard on both crutches. Serra was beside me immediately but did not touch me.

"You good?"

"Yes."

I waited. My leg steadied.

"Again," she said.

"I said yes."

"You said it fast."

I looked at her. Hessa would like Serra. That was terrible. I shifted my weight carefully. Right leg held.

"Stiff."

"Good?"

"Not good. Ordinary."

She nodded. Then picked up her shoe bag and walked away. No hovering. Also good. The innkeeper came into the yard. Teren met him. They spoke. The innkeeper looked at the wagons. Then at us. Then at the inn. His expression became familiar.

"No," he said.

Teren said, "We booked."

"You booked eight."

"We are eight."

I counted. We were not eight. The innkeeper counted too.

"You are twelve."

Teren looked around as if four of us had appeared spontaneously. Marek raised his hand.

"I'm not staying."

Teren looked at him.

"Where are you going?"

"I don't know yet."

"That doesn't help."

"Iven can sleep outside."

Iven said, "No." Orin climbed down from the first wagon.

"Stable."

Everyone looked at him. He put on his hat.

"I've slept in worse."

Teren said, "No one is sleeping in the stable." The innkeeper said, "Two can." Teren turned.

"You just said no."

"I said you booked eight."

"How many rooms?"

"Three."

"How many beds?"

"Eight."

"How many stable spaces?"

The innkeeper looked toward the stable.

"For people?"

"Yes."

He considered.

"Four."

Teren looked at us. Nobody volunteered. I looked at the inn. There were stairs visible through the open door. Narrow ones. Steep. Of course. Marek followed my eyes.

"Stable?"

I looked at him.

"You just said you weren't staying."

"I found somewhere."

"Where?"

"Stable."

I laughed. Teren pointed at both of us.

"No."

"Why?"

"Because if the legendary sword gets kicked by a horse, I have paperwork."

"I am not sleeping with the horse."

"Good."

"I said with the horse."

Teren closed his eyes. Serra walked past him.

"I'm taking a bed."

"Serra."

"I brought shoes."

"That is not a reason."

"It is to me."

Iven followed her.

"Bed."

Orin said, "Stable." Marek said, "Stable." Davin said, "Wagon." Teren looked at him.

"You're not sleeping in the wagon."

"I am."

"You drove half the day."

"Yes."

"You need a bed."

"I need you to stop talking."

The innkeeper watched all of this. Then looked at me.

"What do you do?"

I leaned on my crutches.

"Passenger."

He nodded.

"Stable."

I laughed hard enough that my shoulders hurt. The road had been awful. The inn was too small. My body was tired. Nobody knew where I was sleeping. Tomorrow we would do it again. I had been away from Carrow for less than a day. It felt farther than that. Not worse. Just farther. Teren was still arguing when I picked up my bag. I went to inspect the stable.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 144

## THE STABLE

The stable was better than the inn. This was not praise. It was larger. The roof did not leak in any place I could immediately identify. The floor was packed earth with straw over it, and the horses occupied stalls along one wall behind wooden partitions polished by years of rubbing shoulders and teeth against them. It smelled exactly like a stable. Strongly. Marek stood in the middle aisle with his hands on his hips.

"Good."

"No."

"You haven't seen the loft."

"I don't need to."

"There's hay."

"That is generally where hay goes."

Orin passed us carrying his bag.

"Loft is warmer."

I looked up. A ladder rose through a square opening in the ceiling.

"No."

Orin followed my eyes.

"For you, yes."

"No."

"I meant no loft."

"Oh."

He kept walking. Marek looked up at the ladder, then at me.

"Could carry you."

I stared at him. He smiled.

"I could kill you."

"From down here?"

"I have reach."

He laughed and went to inspect a stall. I moved farther inside. The first empty stall had a latch I could operate easily and enough clear floor for a bedroll. The second had a broken board near the bottom. The third contained tack, two sacks, a bucket, and something under a cloth that I did not investigate because travel had already taught me that unidentified objects became my problem if I looked at them too long. The stable door was wide. The privy was across the yard. No stairs. Good.

The inn had stairs to every room. Stable. I had slept in worse places. That sentence carried more history than I wanted at the moment. I set my bag in the first empty stall. Marek appeared behind me.

"You picked."

"Yes."

"Good one."

"Why?"

"Far from Orin."

Orin's voice came from the next stall.

"I can hear you."

Marek lowered his voice.

"He snores."

"I do not."

"Everyone snores."

"I don't," I said.

Serra's voice came from the stable entrance.

"Lyssa."

I closed my eyes. Marek laughed. I turned. Serra had changed shirts. I had not seen her leave the yard. Her hair was loose now, and she carried a shallow wooden basin under one arm with two damp cloths hanging over the edge.

"You're in the stable?"

"Yes."

She looked at my stall.

"Good."

Marek pointed at me.

"He chose it himself."

"I assumed."

"Why?"

"Because nobody else would inspect three stalls before putting down a bag."

"I inspected two."

Serra looked toward the third.

"What is in that one?"

"I don't know."

"You didn't inspect it?"

"Something under a cloth."

Marek immediately walked toward it.

"No," I said.

He stopped.

"Why?"

"I don't want to know."

Serra nodded.

"Good."

Marek looked between us.

"You've both become boring."

He lifted the cloth. A saddle. He stared at it. I stared at him.

"Happy?"

"No."

He put the cloth back. Serra went toward the inn.

"Where are you going?"

She looked over her shoulder.

"Work."

"What work?"

She raised the basin. I waited.

"That explains nothing."

"It doesn't need to."

She left. Marek watched her go. Then looked at me.

"You ask many questions."

"Yes."

"Does Lyssa like that?"

I picked up a handful of straw. He moved. Good. The sleeping problem was solved in less than ten minutes. Not by Teren. Teren was still inside arguing with the innkeeper about the difference between booking eight beds and booking space for eight people, which appeared to be a distinction only Teren recognized. Davin solved it.

He walked into the stable, looked at the loft, looked at the stalls, then pointed.

"Orin loft. Marek loft. Greg stall. Me wagon."

"Why are you deciding?" Marek asked.

"Because you're talking."

Marek accepted that.

"Who else?"

"Pell and Nessa stable."

I did not know either of them.

"Who?"

Davin pointed toward the yard. A broad woman with cropped brown hair was carrying a costume trunk by one handle while a younger man carried the other. They were arguing. Not about the trunk.

"You changed it."

"I fixed it."

"You cut six inches."

"It dragged."

"It was supposed to drag."

"Then it was stupid."

"It was a mourning dress."

"She's mourning. She isn't sweeping."

The woman stopped. The younger man nearly kept going and had to back up.

"You do not cut a principal costume without asking."

"I asked."

"You asked after."

"I asked whether you noticed."

"That is not asking."

Davin pointed again.

"Pell. Nessa."

"Which is which?"

He looked at me.

"The one yelling is Nessa."

Both were yelling. Davin walked away. Useful. The broad woman saw us.

"Davin!"

He did not turn.

"You cut this?"

"No."

"Who did?"

The younger man said, "I did." She rounded on him again. Davin continued toward the wagon. I watched. That argument had started somewhere before the village. Probably before Carrow. Possibly before I had ever walked into the theatre. Neither person knew I existed. Good. I moved my bag deeper into the stall. Marek had gone. Orin was unfolding a blanket in the next stall.

"Who are Pell and Nessa?"

"Costumes."

"That is not names."

"Yes."

"Which?"

Orin looked toward the yard.

"Pell is the boy."

"He is not a boy."

"Everyone under thirty is a boy."

"How old are you?"

"Not old."

He shook out the blanket. I left him alone. My stall needed almost nothing. That was suspicious. I found a nail on the partition where I could hang my bag. Another lower hook held a coil of old lead rope. I moved that. There was a feed box in the corner, low enough to sit on but not wide enough to sleep on. Straw. Blanket. Bag. Crutches against the partition where I could reach them from the ground. The getting-down part would be manageable.

The getting-up part would be annoying. I tested it before becoming tired enough to make the test dishonest. I lowered myself to the blanket. Right foot planted. One hand on the feed box. Other on a crutch. Down. Fine. I sat. The floor was hard beneath the straw. I lay back.

The stable roof had dark beams crossing it and a gap near the eaves where evening light came through. A horse exhaled. Something small moved in the straw. I sat up. No. Not because of the horse. The something small. I looked. Nothing. Probably mouse. Fine. I had slept with worse. Again. History. I reached for the crutches and got up. Harder than down. Not impossible. My shoulders objected.

I ignored them only long enough to finish standing, then stopped ignoring them. Tired. Expected. I adjusted my grip. No sharp pain. Good. A horse in the nearest occupied stall watched me.

"What?"

It chewed.

"Useful."

It kept chewing. The stable door opened. A girl came in carrying two buckets. Not the crossroads girl. Different child. She looked at me. Then at the horse.

"Move."

I moved. She took the buckets into the stall. The horse immediately became interested in her.

"You work here?"

She looked at me like the answer was visible.

"Yes."

"Which horse is ours?"

She pointed with her chin.

"Those two."

"How are they?"

"Tired."

"Anything wrong?"

"No."

"Wheel horse?"

"What?"

"Nothing."

I had been around Davin too long. She poured water.

"Don't feed them."

"I wasn't going to."

"People do."

"Why?"

"People are stupid."

She could not have been more than twelve.

"Fair."

She moved to the next horse. I returned to my stall. She did not ask why I had one leg. That was pleasant. She did ask, "You actors?"

"Some."

"You?"

"Apparently."

She shrugged. Less interesting than horses. Also pleasant. Dinner happened in shifts because the inn did not have room for all of us at once. I learned this when Marek appeared at the stable door and shouted, "Second food!"

"What?"

"Second group."

"I ate at the crossroads."

"So did everyone."

"That was hours ago."

"Yes."

I looked at the light. It was later than I thought. Travel did strange things to time. We went inside. The two steps remained badly designed. I hated them with greater confidence now. The room had changed since arrival. Local people filled half the tables. A farmer and two women were playing cards near the fire. Someone had brought a baby. The baby was winning an argument with everyone. Our first group was leaving. Serra came down the stairs carrying a bundle of cloth. Not dinner. Not socializing. Cloth.

"Where were you?"

"Upstairs."

"Doing what?"

She looked at the bundle. I sighed.

"Fine."

She stopped beside me.

"You know the blue dress?"

"No."

"Yes, you do."

"I know several blue dresses."

"The court one."

"Princess?"

"Not mine. The other one."

"Then no."

"Pell cut the hem."

"I heard."

Serra frowned.

"You heard?"

"Stable."

"Oh."

She looked toward the door.

"Nessa is going to kill him."

"Which is Nessa?"

"Costumes."

"Yes. Which person?"

Serra pointed toward the stairs. A narrow woman with dark hair was coming down carrying pins in her mouth. Not the broad woman. I looked at Serra.

"Davin lied."

"About what?"

"He said the one yelling was Nessa."

Serra laughed.

"Everyone was yelling."

"Yes."

"Nessa."

The narrow woman reached the bottom. She removed the pins from her mouth.

"Serra."

"What?"

"Where is Pell?"

"Stable?"

"No."

"Wagon?"

"No."

"Dead?"

"Not yet."

Nessa went out the door. Serra watched her.

"Soon."

"Who was the broad woman?"

"Rinna."

"What does she do?"

"Depends."

Of course. Serra went upstairs again with the cloth. She had not eaten. I noticed because I was hungry. That was probably not the only reason. Marek pushed me toward the table by placing one finger against my shoulder. I moved before he could make it annoying. Dinner was stew. Real stew. Meat, potatoes, carrots, something green. Iven was already seated. Awake. This was concerning.

"You're awake."

He looked at me.

"Eating."

"Does that require consciousness?"

"No."

He ate. Orin sat beside him. Davin was not there. Neither was Teren. Marek took the bench across from me.

"Where is Teren?"

"Problem."

"What problem?"

"Money."

"His or ours?"

"Yes."

I looked toward the counter. Teren was speaking to a man I had not seen before. The man wore a dark coat too clean for the stable yard and held a folded paper. Neither looked angry. That made it more serious. Teren read the paper. Read it again. Said something. The man answered. Teren's shoulders changed. Not much. Enough.

"What is that?" I asked.

Marek looked.

"Oh."

"Oh what?"

"Don't know."

"You reacted."

"I know him."

"The man?"

"Yes."

"Who?"

Marek tore bread.

"Owner's agent."

"Whose owner?"

"Hall."

"Here?"

"No. East."

I stopped.

"The municipal hall?"

"No."

"Then which hall?"

"The one we're performing in."

I looked at him.

"We are not performing in the municipal hall?"

"No."

I had assumed. That was stupid. The theatre was going to the eastern town. The municipal hall was in the eastern town. I had combined them.

"They're different buildings."

"Yes."

"How far apart?"

"No idea."

"Do you know anything about the municipal hall?"

"No."

I ate stew. Fine. Still there. Different building. Good.

"What does the agent want?"

Marek shrugged.

"Teren."

"That is not an answer."

"It is from here."

He pointed with bread. Teren and the agent were still talking. Nobody at our table seemed interested. Orin ate. Iven ate. Marek stole one of Iven's potatoes. Iven stabbed his hand with a spoon. Marek withdrew. Teren's problem remained Teren's problem. I watched anyway. The agent unfolded another paper. Teren laughed once. Not happily. Then he saw me looking. He pointed at my bowl. Eat. I looked down. Fine. I ate. Halfway through dinner, Nessa came back in. She had Pell by the sleeve.

Pell was younger than I had thought. Still not a boy. Maybe twenty-five. He looked furious. Nessa sat him at the far end of the table.

"You will fix it."

"I improved it."

"You shortened it."

"It was dragging in dirt."

"It drags on stage."

"The stage isn't dirt."

"Exactly."

Pell looked at me. Not because he knew me. Because I was there.

"Do you think a mourning dress should drag?"

I had a spoon halfway to my mouth.

"No."

Nessa said, "Don't ask him."

"You asked me."

"I did not."

Pell pointed at me.

"He agrees."

"I don't know the dress."

"See?"

"That is not support."

Nessa said, "It is cut for the actress's height, the shoe, and the scene. It drags by design. The hem moves when she turns." Pell said, "It catches."

"Because you put her in the wrong shoe."

"I didn't put her in anything."

"You packed the shoe."

"That is not the same thing."

Rinna appeared behind them. Broad woman. Not Nessa. Good. She put a plate down.

"You packed the rehearsal shoe."

Pell looked at her.

"No."

"Yes."

"That was Serra."

From the stairs, Serra shouted, "Fuck you." Rinna shouted back, "Blue ribbon!" Serra's voice came down.

"Black ribbon!"

Nessa closed her eyes. Pell smiled. Rinna looked toward the ceiling.

"Shit."

The argument changed direction. Immediately. Now it was about shoes. I ate. Nobody asked me anything else. Excellent. After dinner I went back outside. The light had softened. The village street beyond the yard was still active, though quieter than Carrow would have been at the same hour. A cart rolled past carrying empty baskets. Somewhere nearby, a man was singing badly while hammering something.

Davin sat on the rear wheel of our wagon with a plate balanced on one knee. He was eating cold stew.

"You missed dinner."

"No."

"You're eating outside."

"Yes."

"Why?"

He pointed at the wagon. One of the canvas ties had torn. Of course.

"You could eat inside."

"No."

I stood beside him. He kept eating. The tear was small. A crew problem. Not mine. I looked away from it deliberately. Davin noticed.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"You looked."

"I decided not to ask."

"Good."

He ate. I stayed.

"Why are you still here?" he asked.

"I don't know."

"Good."

We sat in silence. Or he sat. I stood. That became irritating after a while, so I moved to an overturned bucket. Better. The inn door opened. Teren came out with the clean-coated agent. They crossed the yard without looking at us. The agent said, "He wants the old terms."

"He can want them," Teren said.

"He owns the hall."

"He owns a roof and a floor."

"And the seats."

"We bring half the seats."

"You bring benches."

"Seats for people with realistic expectations."

The agent did not laugh. They went toward the road. I looked at Davin. He ate.

"What old terms?"

Davin scraped the bottom of the plate.

"Don't know."

"You heard."

"Yes."

"And?"

"Don't know."

Fair. The agent and Teren stopped near the gate. I could not hear them now. Teren had both hands in his coat pockets. The agent talked. Teren listened. This was different from Teren talking to actors. He did not interrupt. Not once. I wondered how bad that was. Davin stood.

"Hold this."

He handed me the plate. I took it. He climbed into the wagon and started untying the torn canvas. I held the plate.

"This is work."

"Yes."

"You said I didn't have to load."

"This isn't loading."

"What is it?"

"Holding a plate."

I considered dropping it. I did not. Davin replaced the torn tie with cord. Not the slipped hitch. Different knot. I watched despite myself. He noticed.

"Don't."

"I didn't ask."

"Your face did."

"I have one face."

"No."

He climbed down and took the plate. I laughed.

"Thank you," he said.

"You're welcome."

Teren came back alone. He walked past us.

"Teren."

He stopped.

"What?"

I had several questions. Hall. Terms. Agent. Seats. Whether our shows were changing. Whether this affected pay. Whether the third show existed. He looked tired. Not road tired. Different.

"Nothing," I said.

He nodded once and went inside. Davin looked at me.

"What?"

"Nothing."

Good. The stable became crowded after dark. Not with sleepers. With work. Apparently the innkeeper objected to costume repairs in the rooms because Nessa had spilled dye in one before.

"Once," Nessa said.

The innkeeper stood in the stable doorway.

"Purple."

"It came out."

"It is still purple."

"It is less purple."

"No dye."

"We are sewing."

"No fire."

"We don't need fire."

"No paint."

"That was Rinna."

Rinna said, "Once." The innkeeper looked at all of them.

"No."

Then he left. Nessa set up on an overturned crate. Rinna sat on a stool. Pell sat on the floor with the mourning dress spread across his knees. Serra brought down three pairs of shoes and placed them in a row. I sat in my stall and watched the stable become a workshop. Nobody invited me. Nobody needed to. Marek lay in the straw outside Orin's stall and shuffled cards. Iven had disappeared. Davin was still outside. Teren was somewhere in the inn. The costume argument continued without repeating itself.

This was impressive.

"The black ribbon is the performance shoe," Serra said.

"No," Rinna said. "Black ribbon is second act."

"Second act is the performance."

"Blue ribbon is court."

"The mourning scene is court."

"No. After court."

Pell held up the dress.

"Does any of this matter if I put the six inches back?"

Nessa looked at him.

"How?"

He hesitated.

"Fabric."

"Which fabric?"

He hesitated longer. Nessa smiled without warmth.

"Exactly."

Pell put the dress down. I looked at the hem. It had been cut cleanly. Very cleanly. That seemed like part of the problem. Marek dealt cards onto the straw.

"One."

I looked at him.

"What?"
