"Playing?"

"No."

He dealt another hand anyway. Orin emerged from his stall.

"Yes."

"You don't know the game."

"I know all games."

Marek looked at me.

"He cheats."

Orin sat.

"Only when losing."

"That is cheating."

"Then don't let me lose."

I joined. The game involved four cards, two hidden, one shared, and rules Marek explained differently each time I asked.

"This is not a real game."

"It is."

"Then explain scoring."

"Highest pair unless road."

"What is road?"

"Three in sequence."

"You said four cards."

"Shared counts."

"Then why did Orin win with two queens?"

"Pair."

"I had three in sequence."

"No."

"Yes."

"You had four, five, six."

"Road."

"Wrong suit."

"You did not say suit mattered."

"Obviously suit matters."

Orin took the coins. I stared at him. He smiled.

"You cheat."

"I won."

"Those are not mutually exclusive."

Marek dealt again. Serra sat beside us while Nessa and Pell worked. She took my cards from my hand.

"Hey."

"You're holding them where everyone can see."

"I am not."

"I can see."

"You are beside me."

"So can Orin."

Orin said nothing. That was evidence. Serra rearranged my cards and gave them back.

"Don't help him," Marek said.

"He needs it."

"I do not."

"You lost to Orin."

"Apparently everyone does."

"Correct," Orin said.

We played. I lost again. Less badly. The costume people argued. A horse shifted in its stall. The stable girl came through once to check water and looked at all of us with open contempt.

"You're loud."

Nessa said, "Sorry." Marek said, "We're artists." The girl said, "You're loud." Then she left. Marek looked offended.

"Children used to respect theatre."

Orin took another coin.

"No."

At some point Serra stopped playing and went back to the shoes. At some point Rinna and Pell stopped arguing and started sewing. At some point Nessa left without explanation and came back with bread. She handed half to Pell. He took it. Neither apologized. The mourning dress lay across both their knees while they worked. I watched the hem grow again. Not six inches. Different fabric. A narrow strip on the inside. It would not be the same dress it had been. Maybe that was the point.

I lost another hand.

"Fuck."

Marek grinned.

"You're improving."

"I lost."

"Closer."

"That is not improvement."

Orin took my coin.

"It is in theatre."

I looked at him. He smiled. I did not ask. Later, when the stable had quieted, I washed. Not fully. There was a basin behind a partition near the tack room and water cold enough to hurt my fingers. I cleaned road dust from my face, neck, hands, and right foot. Then I took care of the residual limb. Private enough. Not completely. Travel rarely was.

I sat on the feed box in my stall with the blanket hung partly across the opening. The skin was warm and irritated in two places but intact. I checked properly. Not Hessa-properly. Greg-properly. No breakdown. No swelling I disliked. No new pain. I cleaned it. Dried it. Rewrapped. Outside the blanket, people continued having lives. Marek and Iven argued quietly about who had cheated at cards. Orin denied being involved. Serra was upstairs again. Nessa and Rinna had taken the repaired dress inside. Pell had gone somewhere.

Davin still intended to sleep in the wagon. Teren had not appeared for over an hour. Nobody asked what I was doing. Good. When I finished, I moved the blanket. Marek was sitting against the opposite stall wall. He looked at me.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Good."

He went back to shuffling cards. I pulled on my trouser leg.

"Where is Teren?"

"Meeting."

"With the agent?"

"Probably."

"At night?"

"Hall owners don't become nicer in daylight."

I considered asking what the old terms were. I didn't. Instead I said, "Do we still have two shows?" Marek shrugged.

"Ask Teren."

"When?"

"When he knows."

That was the end of it. Interesting. My acting problem had become very small. I liked that less than expected. I took out page twelve. Marek glanced at it.

"Clerk?"

"Yes."

"Don't."

"I am only reading."

"Fine."

I read. He shuffled. After several lines, he said, "Too fast." I looked up.

"You said don't."

"I changed my mind."

"Why too fast?"

He dealt cards to himself.

"Don't know."

"That is not useful."

"Then ignore me."

I read again. Slower. Not because he said. Because Lyssa had. The clerk had nowhere to be. The permit seeker did. Marek stopped commenting. I finished the page.

"Better?"

He shrugged. I hated actors. I put the script away. The stable lights went out by degrees. One lantern remained near the door. Orin climbed to the loft despite claiming the stall earlier. Marek followed. The ladder creaked.

"Don't fall," I said.

Marek looked down.

"Catch me."

"No."

"Then don't tell me what to do."

He disappeared into the loft. Iven had somehow acquired a bed inside. Traitor. Pell took the other stable stall. Rinna went inside. Nessa went inside. Serra had a room. Davin climbed into the wagon. I was alone on the stable floor except for Pell, horses, and whatever small thing lived in the straw. I lay down. The floor remained hard. The straw remained straw. My shoulders remained tired. I put my bag beneath my head. Bad. I replaced it with folded clothing. Better. The horse nearest me shifted. Leather creaked.

Someone in the loft whispered. Someone else said, "Shut up." Silence.

Then:

"Lyssa."

I sat up. Marek laughed from the loft.

"Fuck you."

Orin said, "Sleep." I lay back down. I was smiling. That was irritating. The stable door opened. Teren came in carrying no lantern. He stopped until his eyes adjusted. I could barely see him.

"Teren?"

"Go to sleep."

"What happened?"

"Tomorrow."

"Are the shows still happening?"

A pause.

"Yes."

"How many?"

"Gregory."

"Fine."

He moved farther into the stable. Not toward a stall. Toward the ladder.

"Marek," he said quietly.

No answer.

"Marek."

"What?"

"Come down."

"Why?"

"Need you."

There was movement above. Marek appeared at the opening.

"For what?"

"Tomorrow."

That was all. Marek came down. He did not joke. Teren looked toward the stall where Pell slept.

"Pell."

A groan.

"What?"

"Up."

"Why?"

"Costume."

Pell swore. He got up. Neither Teren nor Marek looked at me. Good. They went outside. Pell followed, still pulling on one boot. The stable door closed. I lay in the dark. Whatever had happened with the hall was not mine. Not yet. I listened to the horses breathe. After a while, I slept.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 145

## THE ARRIVAL

I woke to someone saying, "No." Not loudly. Firmly. The kind of no that had already been said several times. I opened my eyes. Gray morning light came through the stable door. My shoulder hurt because folded clothing was not a pillow no matter how carefully I arranged it. Straw had found its way inside my shirt. One horse was chewing. The voice came from outside.

"No," Nessa said again. "If you put him in that, he looks like a priest."

Pell answered, "He is supposed to look respectable."

"Respectable is not priest."

"It has a collar."

"Exactly."

I lay still. There was movement in the yard. Harness leather. Buckles. A bucket set down hard. Someone coughed. Marek said, "I could be a priest."

"No," Nessa and Pell said together.

I smiled. Then I remembered they had been awake after I went to sleep. I sat up. My body objected. Not one part. All of it. The objection was less severe than yesterday's first attempt to stand after the wagon, but more comprehensive. Back, shoulders, right hip, hands. My residual limb felt warm under the wrapping. I sat for a moment. The horse chewed.

"Good morning."

It ignored me. I checked the limb before standing. No new problem. Warm. Mild irritation. Same places. Fine. Not nothing. Fine. I dressed properly, repacked the blanket, and used the feed box to get upright. The stable was mostly empty. Orin's loft blanket was gone. Pell's stall held a heap of fabric and one shoe. Not his shoe. Probably. I took my bag and went outside. The yard had changed. Yesterday we had arrived as a pile. This morning we were becoming wagons again.

Davin and Rinna were already loading. Rinna stood inside the second wagon arranging trunks while Davin passed them up. Neither spoke much. I carried my bag toward them. Davin looked at it.

"Keep."

"What?"

"With you."

"Why?"

"Need room."

"For?"

He pointed at a long wooden box near the inn wall. I had not seen it yesterday. It was narrow, nearly as long as I was tall, with iron corners and fresh rope around it.

"What is that?"

"Box."

"I can see that."

"Good."

He lifted one end. Rinna took the other. I moved aside. They carried it toward the first wagon.

"Can I help?"

"No."

"Why?"

"Rinna knows where it goes."

Rinna did not look at me. Good. I kept my bag. Near the stable door, Nessa had Marek standing in a dark coat that did, in fact, make him look slightly like a priest. He looked tired. Not wagon tired. He had shadows under his eyes and a small cut near his jaw I had not seen yesterday. Pell knelt at his feet pinning the coat hem. Nessa stood back.

"No."

Marek looked down at himself.

"I like it."

"You like everything if someone tells you not to."

"Not true."

"Take it off."

Pell looked up.

"Then what?"

"The gray."

"The gray is packed."

"Unpack it."

"Davin will kill me."

"Then die usefully."

Pell stood. He saw me.

"Morning."

"Morning."

That was all. He went toward the wagon. I looked at Marek.

"What happened to your face?"

He touched the cut.

"Oh."

"Yes."

"Door."

"What door?"

Nessa pulled the coat off him.

"Don't."

I looked at her. She bundled the coat over one arm.

"He'll tell it badly."

"I can tell my own injury."

"You walked into a door."

Marek looked at me.

"Door."

Fine.

"What were you doing?"

Nessa said, "Greg."

"What?"

"Food."

She pointed toward the inn. I looked at Marek. He smiled.

"Food."

I went. Teren was not at breakfast. Neither was Serra. That was noticeable because Serra's place from dinner had a cup sitting at it, untouched. Iven was eating eggs. Of course. Orin had bread, cheese, and something pickled. I sat.

"Where is everyone?"

Iven looked around.

"Here."

"No."

"Yes."

"Teren."

"Gone."

"Where?"

He ate egg. Orin said, "Town."

"What town?"

"The one we're going to."

I stopped.

"Teren left already?"

"Agent had a horse."

"When?"

"Early."

"Why?"

Orin spread something on bread.

"Problem."

"What problem?"

He looked at me. I waited.

"Hall."

"Yes. What about it?"

He bit the bread.

"I don't know."

Iven said, "Door." I looked at him.

"What?"

"Marek."

"Yes."

"Door."

"I know."

"He walked into it."

"I know."

Iven smiled. This was useless. I ate. The eggs were good. The innkeeper passed and put a small paper on the table.

"Your man owes."

I looked at it.

"Which man?"

He pointed toward the yard. There were several men.

"Teren?"

"Yes."

"For?"

"Four extra."

"Stable?"

"People."

I looked at the paper.

"Why are you giving this to me?"

"He left."

"I am not responsible for him."

The innkeeper looked at my crutches. Then at me. Then at the paper. I slid it toward Orin. Orin slid it back.

"No."

"I don't know Teren's accounts."

"Neither do I."

Iven moved his plate away from the paper. The innkeeper said, "Someone pays." I looked toward the door. Davin was visible through it, lifting the long box.

"No."

The innkeeper waited. I considered paying simply to end the conversation. That was exactly how one became responsible for things.

"No," I said.

He took the paper.

"Your company."

"I am a passenger."

Iven laughed into his eggs. The innkeeper walked away. Orin looked at me.

"Learning."

"Nothing was learned."

"Good."

I ate the rest of breakfast. Serra came in as I finished. She was dressed for travel but carried no food. There was a dark mark on one sleeve and her hands smelled faintly of something sharp when she reached for my cup.

"That is mine."

She drank.

"What is on your sleeve?"

"Dye."

"I thought the innkeeper banned dye."

"He did."

I waited. Serra drank again.

"Did you dye something?"

"No."

"Then why are you covered in dye?"

"Nessa."

"That explains almost nothing."

"It explains enough."

She put the cup down.

"Do you have food?"

"I ate."

"For the road."

"Yes."

"Good."

She turned to leave.

"Serra."

"What?"

"Where were you?"

She looked at me.

"When?"

"Breakfast."

"Busy."

"With?"

She smiled.

"Gregory."

Fine. She left. I sat for another moment. Other people had apparently completed half a day before I finished eggs. I did not like mornings. Outside, Pell was carrying the gray coat. Marek wore a shirt. Better. Nessa had moved on to someone else entirely.

A woman I had not met stood on a crate while Nessa adjusted a red overskirt. Rinna argued with Davin about whether a trunk could be turned sideways.

"Not if the lid opens."

"It doesn't need to open."

"It will."

"When?"

"Before yours."

"That is not an answer."

"It is to me."

Davin turned the trunk sideways. Rinna swore. I went to the second wagon. The cup crate was gone. I stopped. My seat. Not a good seat. Still. Gone. In its place was a narrow bench attached along the side. I looked at Davin.

"What happened?"

"Cups moved."

"Why?"

"Box."

The long box was now in the first wagon.

"That is not this wagon."

"No."

"Then why did the cups move?"

"Weight."

"What weight?"

Davin pointed at the rear axle. I looked. Then at him.

"Did something change?"

"Yes."

"What?"

He walked away. I hated opacity. I put my bag under the new bench. My crutches went on the same rail. Slipped hitch. First try. I pulled the release. Opened. Retied. Good. Nobody noticed. Better. Marek climbed into the wagon wearing the gray coat. I stared. He sat across from me.

"Why are you dressed?"

"Because Nessa hates joy."

"Are you performing in the wagon?"

"Maybe."

"That is not funny."

"I know."

He leaned his head back. His eyes closed. I looked at the cut again. Door. Fine. Serra climbed in next. Then immediately climbed out.

"Wrong wagon."

"Where are you going?"

"First."

"Why?"

"Shoes."

Of course. She disappeared. Iven arrived with bread.

"Move."

"There is an entire bench."

"Your bag."

I moved it. He sat. Orin chose the first wagon. Pell rode with us, carrying a sewing kit on his lap. Nessa did not ride. I noticed when the first wagon started moving.

"Where is Nessa?"

Pell threaded a needle.

"Staying."

I looked back. Nessa stood in the inn yard beside Rinna. Rinna was staying too. They had three trunks between them.

"What?"

Pell bit the thread.

"Coming later."

"How?"

"Cart."

"Why?"

"Work."

I waited. Pell started sewing something gray.

"Mourning dress?"

"No."

"What?"

"Coat."

"Marek's?"

"No."

I stopped asking. The wagons rolled out of the village. Teren was gone ahead. Nessa and Rinna were behind. Davin drove the first wagon with someone else beside him. Our driver was a man I had not learned the name of. The troupe had become pieces. Nobody had asked me whether that was acceptable. It was. Mostly. The second day road was shorter and better. Not good. Better.

The land rose gradually. Fields gave way to more trees, then open stretches again. We crossed a narrow stone bridge over water clear enough to see the bottom. Marek slept. Iven ate. Pell sewed. I watched the road. After an hour, I said, "What happened with the hall?" Nobody answered. I looked at Pell. He kept sewing.

"Marek?"

His eyes stayed closed.

"Door."

"That is not what I asked."

"Good."

Iven smiled. I looked at Pell again.

"Were you working on something for the hall last night?"

"Yes."

"What?"

"Costume."

"I know that."

He held up the gray fabric.

"Then why ask?"

I sighed. Pell looked at me. Not unfriendly. Just tired.

"Teren will tell you if it changes you."

"That is a terrible sentence."

"It works."

"Does it change Marek?"

"Yes."

Marek opened one eye.

"Unfortunately."

"How?"

Pell said, "Greg."

"What?"

"I'm trying not to stab myself."

I stopped. He sewed. That was fair. A while later Marek woke on his own. He stretched, winced at the cut on his jaw, and looked out at the road.

"Where are we?"

Pell named a farm. Marek nodded as if that meant something.

"You know it?"

"No."

"Then why did you nod?"

"Polite."

He looked at me.

"You're staring."

"I have questions."

"No."

"You don't know them."

"I know you."

"Fine."

I looked at the gray coat.

"Why are you dressed?"

Marek looked down.

"Oh."

"Yes."

"Meeting."

"With?"

"Hall."

"Owner?"

"Maybe."

"Why you?"

He smiled.

"Face."

Pell snorted. Marek looked offended.

"What?"

"Your face walked into a door."

"It remains handsome."

Pell kept sewing. I looked between them.

"Are you pretending to be someone?"

Both stopped. Not dramatically. Enough. Interesting. Marek said, "No." Pell said, "Don't." I held up both hands.

"Fine."

They resumed. I looked at the road. I had learned something. Not what. Good enough. Around midday, the eastern town appeared from a ridge. Not all at once. First a church tower. Then roofs. Then a pale strip of wall and clustered chimneys in a shallow valley where two roads met. Larger than I had expected. Smaller than Carrow.

The roofs were mostly red or brown tile rather than dark slate. A river curved along the southern edge, broad enough for barges. Beyond it, low hills rose in patches of green and exposed stone. I leaned forward. The municipal hall would be somewhere in there. Probably. I did not know what it looked like. That was inconvenient. The road descended. Traffic increased. Farm carts. A wagon of timber. Two riders. A woman walking six geese. The geese had better road discipline than actors.

We passed through an outer market without a wall or gate. Stalls had spread along both sides of the road. Someone sold copper pans. Someone else sold onions in braided ropes. A boy carried a tray of cups between wagons and nearly lost all of them when our horse shifted. I reached instinctively. Too far. The cups survived without me. Good. People noticed the scenery. A painted tower was difficult to hide. Children followed for half a street. One shouted, "Players!" Marek opened his eyes.

"No."

The child laughed. Apparently that worked everywhere. The town tightened around us. Stone buildings, timber upper floors, narrow fronts, signs projecting over the street. The road changed from packed dirt to uneven paving. My body recognized the improvement before my eyes did. The wagon still shook. Different frequency. Better. We turned twice. I lost direction immediately. That annoyed me. I had studied maps of the region years ago. Maps did not include a bakery cart blocking an alley. The first wagon stopped. Ours stopped behind it. I looked ahead.

A man in an apron was shouting at Davin. Davin pointed at the wagon. The man pointed at the alley. Davin pointed at the painted tower. The man pointed at the sky. I could not hear the words.

"Problem?" I asked.

Our driver said, "Bakery." That was his first contribution to the trip.

"Thank you."

Marek climbed down.

"Where are you going?"

"Meeting."

"We aren't there."

"I am."

He walked into the alley. Pell grabbed the back of his coat.

"Not that way."

Marek stopped. Pell pointed across the street. Marek changed direction. No shame. They disappeared between buildings. I looked at Iven.

"Do you know where they're going?"

"No."

"Good."

The bakery cart moved. We continued. The performance hall was on a wider street near the river. I knew it was the performance hall because Teren was standing outside it arguing. Comforting. The building was older than the shops around it but not ancient. Two stories. Broad front doors. Tall windows. A faded carved emblem above the entrance that might once have been painted. A man in a clean dark coat stood with Teren. The agent. Another man stood beside him. Older. Better coat. Owner, probably. Teren saw the wagons.

He did not wave. He pointed toward the side street. Davin turned the first wagon. We followed. That was the entirety of our welcome. The side entrance was narrow. Not catastrophically. Enough. The first wagon stopped beside a double door. Crew appeared from inside. Not ours. Three local workers. One woman, two men. They began opening the wagon before Davin had fully climbed down. He slapped one man's hand away from a rope. The man shouted. Davin shouted back. I could not hear the words. They were probably about knots.

Rinna would have enjoyed this. I untied my crutches. The slipped hitch opened. I got down. My right hip was stiff. Less than yesterday. Progress. No one cared. Good. A local worker came toward the second wagon.

"Costumes?"

Pell was gone.

"Some."

"Which?"

"I don't know."

He stared at me.

"What do you do?"

I considered saying passenger.

"Actor."

The word came out before I decided whether it was accurate. The worker nodded.

"Then move."

He climbed into the wagon. Apparently actors were obstacles. Also comforting. I moved. Inside the side door was a corridor. Narrow. Then a turn. Then three steps down. Of course. I took them. The hall smelled like dust, old wood, lamp oil, and damp stone. Not the same as Carrow's theatre. Larger backstage. Worse floor. People moved everywhere. Local crew carried benches. One of our people rolled fabric through a doorway. Someone shouted for Nessa. Someone else shouted that Nessa was not here. That caused a third person to swear.

I stood against the wall. Present. Irrelevant. Excellent. Teren appeared.

"Greg."

I straightened.

"Yes."

"Stage."

"Where?"

He pointed. I followed the direction.

"Why?"

"Sword check."

"What check?"

"Voice."

That was all the attention I received. He turned away.

"Teren."

He stopped.

"Clerk?"

"Later."

"Shopkeeper?"

"Maybe."

"What happened with the hall?"

"Later."

"How many shows?"

"Two."

"Third?"

"Dead."

"Why?"

"Gregory."

"Fine."

He was already moving. I went to find the stage. The corridor opened behind a curtain. Not our curtain. A heavy brown one with patched lower corners. Beyond it was a stage larger than the market hall platform and smaller than Carrow's theatre stage. Real wings. Good. Shallow. Less good. The house beyond was empty except for workers moving benches. I stepped onto the stage. The floor flexed under my right crutch. I stopped. Pressed again. Not dangerous. Loose board. I marked it mentally.

A local woman stood in the house with a ledger. She looked up.

"Speak."

"What?"

"Speak."

"Why?"

"Teren said voice."

Right. I used my normal voice.

"Where?"

She pointed to the back wall.

"Again."

I projected. Not Sword. Me.

"Again."

Louder. She wrote.

"What are you measuring?"

"Whether they hear you."

"Who?"

She pointed. A man at the back raised one hand.

"I hear him."

She wrote again.

"Now sword."

I stared. She looked at me.

"Teren said sword."

Of course. I used the Sword voice.

"I object to this procedure."

The man at the back laughed. The woman did not.

"Again."

I almost repeated it. Stopped.

"Put me somewhere respectable."

The man at the back laughed again. The woman wrote.

"Fine."

"That is the test?"

"Yes."

"What did you write?"

"Fine."

"I can see that."

"Then we're done."

She looked toward the wing.

"Next!"

A woman I did not know walked past me carrying a wooden crown. My assessment was over. Three seconds from Teren. Two lines from me. A local woman had decided I was fine. I stepped offstage. Behind me, someone else began speaking. Nobody watched me leave. I liked this place. Possibly. I went back toward the side door.

Davin was in the corridor arguing with a local worker about the long box.

"Not flat."

"It fits flat."

"Not flat."

"Why?"

Davin put both hands on the box. The worker put both hands on the other end. Neither moved. I approached.

"Can I help?"

Both said, "No." Good. I kept going. Outside, Teren was still with the owner. Serra had arrived somehow. Not with us. She stood near the front doors speaking to a woman in a yellow scarf. They were not arguing. The woman touched Serra's arm. Serra's face changed. Not much. Enough. Then they walked away together. I stopped. I had no idea who the woman was. Serra did not see me. Or saw me and had somewhere else to be. Either was possible. I looked down the street.

The river was visible at the far end between buildings. Somewhere in this town was the municipal hall. I could ask. Later. Right now the theatre was unloading without me. That was fine. I went back inside. A local worker handed me a bundle of wooden cups.

"Kitchen."

I looked at him.

"Where?"

He pointed. I took them. Apparently I had found my role.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 146

## THE HAND

The kitchen was not a kitchen. It had once been. There was a hearth, a blackened chimney, a long scarred table, and shelves built into one wall. There was also no food, no cook, and no reason for twelve wooden cups to be there. I stood in the doorway holding them.

A local woman was on her knees beneath the table tightening something with a short iron tool.

"Cups?"

She did not look up.

"Washroom."

"I was told kitchen."

"This used to be kitchen."

"Then why call it kitchen?"

She stopped tightening. I waited. She looked out from beneath the table.

"Because that's what it's called."

Fine.

"Where is the washroom?"

"Past green room. Left. Down."

"Down?"

"Three."

Of course. I carried the cups. The corridor behind the stage formed a shape that made sense only if the building had been constructed in several arguments. The old kitchen sat behind the house wall. A narrow passage ran from it toward the stage, widened suddenly around a door marked with faded green paint, then narrowed again before reaching three steps down to a stone-floored room with a pump and two basins. The green room was not green. I checked. Brown walls. One yellow chair. Two benches.

A cracked mirror. Someone had written LIAR into the plaster beside the mirror.

Below it, in smaller writing:

WHICH ONE?

I liked this building. The washroom contained a boy washing cups. Not ours. Different cups. He looked at mine.

"Those clean?"

"I don't know."

He took one. Smelled it.

"Wine."

"I didn't put wine in it."

"I didn't say you did."

He dumped all twelve into a basin. My job ended. I remained. The boy looked at me.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Then move."

Right. I moved. Backstage had become more crowded while I was gone. The long wooden box was now standing upright against a wall. Davin had won. Or lost differently. Two local workers were arguing beside it.

"Can't stay there."

"Not staying."

"It is there."

"For now."

"Now is when I need the wall."

"What for?"

"Wall."

I passed them. Neither noticed me. Onstage, a man stood on a ladder adjusting a lamp bracket while the ledger woman shouted numbers from the house.

"Two left."

"Your left?"

"Stage left."

"I'm not on stage."

"Then mine."

He moved the bracket.

"No."

He moved it back.

"Too far."

He looked down.

"You said two."

"I said two before you moved four."

"I moved two."

"You moved four."

"I know my hand."

"You don't know inches."

This continued. I stopped near the wing. The loose floorboard was still there. Someone had put a chalk X on it. Good. Not my problem. A local worker came behind me carrying a bench.

"Move."

I moved. Another carried the other end. They set it near the wing.

"No," the ledger woman called.

Both men stopped.

"House."

One said, "You said stage."

"I said spare to stage, cracked to house."

"This is spare."

"That is cracked."

The man looked at the bench. He pressed one hand against it. The seat shifted.

"Cracked."

They picked it up again. I moved farther out of the way. This was harder than work. I found Pell in a dressing room. Not deliberately. I was looking for somewhere to put my bag. The dressing room had six pegs, three mirrors, two stools, and clothing on every available surface. Pell stood with his back to the door, sewing the gray coat Marek had worn that morning. I stopped.

"You said that wasn't his."

Pell looked over his shoulder.

"It wasn't."

"Now it is?"

"No."

He went back to sewing. I looked at the coat. Same gray. Different coat. Fine.

"Can I put my bag here?"

"No."

"Why?"

"Women's room."

"There are no women."

"There will be."

"Where is men's?"

"Other side."

"Which other side?"

Pell pointed with the needle. I followed. Before I left, I said, "Did Marek's meeting happen?"

"Yes."

"What happened?"

"Meeting."

I waited. Pell looked at me.

"Teren will tell you if it changes you."

"I hate that."

"I know."

I left. The men's dressing room was smaller. Four pegs. One mirror. One stool. Iven was asleep on the stool. His head rested against the wall.

"How?"

His eyes opened.

"What?"

"Never mind."

I hung my bag.

"Are we rehearsing?"

"Probably."

"When?"

He closed his eyes.

"Later."

I was beginning to understand why Teren liked him. I went back into the corridor. Someone shouted, "Hand!" I stopped. Nobody came.

"Hand!"

Louder. A local worker leaned through a doorway.

"You."

He pointed at me.

"Me?"

"Yes. Hand."

I looked at my hands.

"What?"

"Need one."

He disappeared. I followed because curiosity remained a disease. The room beyond was storage. Not a room. A cavity. Shelves reached almost to the ceiling. Props filled them without visible system: clay jugs, wooden fruit, metal plates, three crowns, a bird cage, rope, folded flags, a false beard on a jar, two shields, and an entire painted fish.

The local worker stood on a stool holding a crate above his head.

"Take."

I put one crutch against the wall.

"Both hands?"

"One."

"That crate needs two."

"Not crate."

He nodded toward a small wooden hand sticking out of it. Of course. I took the hand. He lowered the crate.

"Thanks."

I stared at the wooden hand.

"What now?"

"Third shelf."

"Which third?"

He pointed. I put it beside a ceramic chicken. He looked.

"No."

"You pointed there."

"Other third."

"There cannot be two third shelves."

He pointed across the room. I moved the hand.

"Why is there a hand?"

"Play."

"Which?"

He was already climbing back onto the stool.

"No idea."

I put it down. The wooden hand remained a hand. No destiny. Excellent. When I returned to the stage, Teren was there. Not available. There was a difference. He stood near the front with the hall owner, the agent, the ledger woman, and a local man holding a carpenter's square. Papers lay on the stage floor between them. The owner said, "That was the agreement." Teren said, "Eight years ago."

"The terms didn't expire."

"The company did."

"You are the company."

"I bought a name and three trunks."

"You bought obligations."

"I bought mildew."

The agent said something quieter. Teren rubbed his forehead. The ledger woman looked bored. The carpenter measured the edge of the stage. Nobody looked at me. I moved into the wing. Marek entered from the opposite side. Still in the gray coat. The cut on his jaw had been cleaned. He saw Teren. Stopped. The owner saw Marek. His expression changed. There. Something. Recognition? Dislike? I could not tell. Marek's posture changed too. Not much. He became straighter. Older. No. Not older. More expensive. That was stupid. Still true.

The owner said, "You." Marek smiled.

"Me."

Teren closed his eyes. The agent looked at the floor. Interesting. The owner said, "I was told you weren't with them." Marek spread his hands.

"I wasn't."

"You are now."

"Apparently."

Teren said, "This is not helping." Marek looked at him.

"You asked me to come."

"I asked you to stand there."

"I am standing."

"Quietly."

"Ah."

Marek became quiet. The owner looked at the gray coat. Then at Teren.

"You knew."

Teren said, "Last night."

"Knew what?" I whispered.

Someone beside me said, "Shh." I turned. Serra. She had returned without my noticing. The yellow-scarf woman was not with her. Serra wore different earrings. I had not noticed earrings before.

"You're back."

She looked at me.

"Apparently."

"Who was---"

She put one finger against my lips. Not gently.

"Shh."

I stopped. Onstage, the owner picked up one of the papers.

"I won't have this."

Teren said, "You already agreed to the performances."

"Under the old terms."

"Which you are trying to resurrect because you saw the name on the bills."

"You use the name."

"I own the name."

"Then you own the debt."

Teren's face went still. Debt. There. Not enough. The agent said, "Master Coln." Owner. Name. Coln. Good. Coln ignored him.

"You bring him into my hall wearing that coat."

Marek looked down at himself.

"I was told gray."

Teren turned.

"Marek."

"What?"

"Quiet."

"Right."

Serra's finger was still near my mouth. I moved my head away. She lowered her hand.

"What is happening?" I whispered.

"Old shit."

"What old shit?"

She looked at me.

"Old."

That was useless. Coln said, "Two shows. Half gate against balance." Teren laughed.

"No."

"You want the hall?"

"Not at that price."

"You already brought the wagons."

"I can take them away."

Davin's voice came from behind us.

"No."

Everyone turned. Davin stood in the corridor with a coil of rope. Teren stared at him. Davin said, "Loaded wrong now." There was silence. Marek coughed into his hand. Serra looked down. I bit the inside of my cheek. Teren said, "Thank you, Davin." Davin nodded and left. Coln did not understand why this was funny. That made it better. Teren looked back at him.

"Not half gate."

Coln named a lower fraction. Teren named another. They argued. Numbers. Old balance. Use of hall. Damage deposit. Lamp oil. Bench rental, despite Teren's earlier claim that we brought half the seats. We apparently did. Not enough. The old terms began to become visible. Not one thing. A pile.

Some previous version of the troupe had performed here under an arrangement involving a debt, gate share, hall expenses, and apparently Marek. Marek remained standing quietly. Almost. At one point Coln said, "And he does not go upstairs." Marek said, "That was one time." Teren turned. Marek raised both hands. Quiet. I looked at Serra. She whispered, "Door." I stared at her. She smiled. Marek's cut. No. Different door. Probably. I did not ask. Eventually Teren and Coln moved into the house with the agent. The ledger woman followed.

The carpenter did not. He remained onstage measuring. Marek relaxed. Immediately. His shoulders dropped. He looked like Marek again. Serra walked out.

"Marek."

He looked at her. She pointed at the coat.

"Off."

"Why?"

"Not yours."

"I know."

"Then off."

He started unbuttoning it. I approached.

"What was that?"

Marek looked at me.

"Meeting."

"I know."

He removed the coat. Underneath, his shirt was wrinkled.

"What debt?"

"Old."

"Yes. Everyone says that."

"Because it is."

"Yours?"

He looked at Serra. Serra said, "Don't." Not to me. To him. Marek stopped. Interesting.

"Fine," I said.

Marek handed Serra the coat. She inspected the sleeve.

"Pell fixed this?"

"Yes."

"Badly."

"Tell him."

"I will."

She left. Marek watched her go. I watched him.

"Who was the woman in the yellow scarf?"

He looked at me.

"What woman?"

Good. He genuinely did not know.

"Never mind."

Teren returned ten minutes later. He walked directly past me.

"Teren."

"No."

"I only---"

"No."

He pointed at the stage.

"Shopkeeper."

"What?"

"Shopkeeper. Fifteen minutes."

"Meren?"

"Not here."

"Is he coming?"

"No idea."

"Clerk?"

"Dead."

"I know the third show is dead."

"No. Clerk dead."

"The scene?"

"Yes."

"Why?"

"No permit desk."

"That is not a reason."

"It is today."

He was already walking away.

"Teren."

He turned. I had one useful question.

"Do I use the market version?"

"Mostly."

"Mostly what?"

"Don't threaten the front row."

Then he left. Three seconds. Maybe four. Fine. I found Iven. He was awake. Again concerning.

"You're debtor."

"Yes."

"Fifteen minutes."

"I know."

"How?"

"Teren told me."

"When?"

"While you were watching the adults fight."

I stared.

"You were there?"

"No."

Of course. We rehearsed Shopkeeper. Not the whole scene. Entrances first. This stage had actual wings, but the right wing was shallow enough that my crutches could be visible if I waited where I normally would. A local stage worker named nothing-to-me pointed.

"Back."

"I need room."

"Back."

"If I go farther back, I can't see the cue."

"You don't need to see."

"I need to hear?"

He pointed upward. A narrow opening in the wall carried sound from the stage strangely well. I stood behind it. Iven spoke from center. Clear.

"Oh."

The worker had already left. Fine. We tried the entrance. The stage floor flexed in different places. The chalked loose board was avoided by everyone without discussion. My crutch tip slipped once on a patch of old paint. I stopped. Tested. Dry. Smooth. I adjusted. Iven waited.

"Good?"

"Yes."

"Again?"

"Yes."

We went back. Second entrance better. The scene itself was worse. Not terrible. Flat. I knew the lines. Iven knew the lines. We both knew where the laughs had been at East Market Hall. That was the problem. I could feel them sitting there like furniture. Eleven days. Floor. Double. Almost stand. Consultation. Every line had a memory attached. The empty hall did not care. Iven said, "You are doing the thing."

"What thing?"

"The face."

"What face?"

"Thinking."

"I am always thinking."

"Bad for you."

We started again. Halfway through, someone rolled the long wooden box behind the curtain. It made a scraping sound. I stopped. Iven did not.

"You've had eleven days to improve it," I said.

He answered. The box scraped again. I looked toward the wing. Iven snapped his fingers.

"Here."

"I am here."

"No."

We continued. The scene improved slightly when I became irritated with him. Useful. Not profound. Afterward, Iven said, "Fine."

"Everyone says fine here."

"Fine."

He left. I stood onstage. The house was still mostly empty. A few local workers placed benches. The carpenter was now on his knees near the front edge marking something. I looked up. The ceiling beams were old. Not municipal-hall old. Still interesting.

One central truss had been reinforced with newer timber on only one side. I stared. Why one side? Load? Repair? Water damage? The carpenter looked up.

"You."

"Yes?"

"Off."

"What?"

"Need stage."

Right. I left. Present. Irrelevant. The old kitchen had become a real kitchen again somehow. Not through architecture. Through food. Someone had brought bread, cheese, onions, and a pot from somewhere. The woman who had been under the table now stood cutting bread. I entered. She pointed.

"Cups."

"I delivered them."

"Where?"

"Washroom."

She stared.

"You told me washroom."

"I told you washroom to wash them."

"Yes."

"Then bring them back."

I closed my eyes. Of course. I went down the three steps. The boy had washed them. Good. I carried them back. The woman put them on the table.

"Thanks."

"What is your name?"

"Edda."

"Greg."

"I know."

"Why?"

She pointed at my leg. I looked down.

"That is fair."

She handed me bread.

"Eat."

I ate.

"Do you work here?"

"Yes."

"What do you do?"

"Today?"

"Yes."

She looked around the old kitchen.

"Bread."

That was an excellent answer. I ate more. Through the doorway, people crossed the corridor. Pell carrying gray cloth. A local worker with a ladder. Davin with rope. Iven with nothing. Marek without the coat. Serra passed once with the yellow-scarf woman. I saw only the woman's back this time. They were talking quickly. Serra did not look in. Teren crossed in the other direction with Coln. Still arguing. Nobody came to explain anything. Good. Edda cut onions. I said, "Where is the municipal hall?"

She pointed with the knife.

"North square."

"How far?"

"Ten minutes."

"Which direction is north?"

She looked at me. I had deserved that.

"From here."

"Front door, left. Fountain, right. Up hill. Big ugly building."

"Twice-rebuilt roof?"

She stopped cutting.

"You're interested in the roof?"

"Yes."

"Why?"

"Load paths."

She stared.

"Actor?"

"Apparently."

She went back to onions.

"Big ugly building."

I smiled. Ten minutes. Close. I could go. Not now. Teren appeared in the doorway.

"Greg."

I swallowed bread.

"Yes."

"Five."

"Five what?"

"Minutes."

"For?"

"Shopkeeper."

"I thought fifteen."

"That was ten minutes ago."

It had not felt like ten minutes. I put the bread down. Edda handed it back.

"For after."

I took it. Teren was already gone. I followed. The stage was ready enough to rehearse. Not ready. Enough. Serra had returned. She stood in the wing adjusting one earring. I looked at her. She looked at me.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Good."

Then she stepped onto the stage and became the Princess. Someone called for the King. Marek answered from somewhere upstairs. Coln shouted, "No." Marek shouted back, "I'm changing." Coln said something I could not hear. Serra closed her eyes. Teren shouted, "Marek!"

"I know!"

The hall had known them before I arrived. That was becoming obvious. I had no idea what had happened here eight years ago. I had no idea who the woman in the yellow scarf was. I did not know why Nessa and Rinna were coming later, what was inside the long box, whether Meren would arrive, or what exactly Teren had agreed to with Coln. I did know my entrance. Mostly. I put the bread in my pocket. Iven took his place. Teren pointed at me.

"Shopkeeper."

Three seconds. Enough. I went to work.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 147

## THE REHEARSAL

I went to work. Then I missed my entrance. Not by much. Enough. Iven was onstage being poor at paying debts when my cue came through the opening in the wall. Clear. Perfectly clear. I heard it. I knew it. I waited because in Carrow there had been another line before mine. There was not another line here. Teren had cut it ten minutes earlier while I was eating bread. Iven waited. The hall waited. I realized. I moved. Too fast. My right crutch hit the edge of the wing.

The sound was enormous. Not actually enormous. It felt enormous. I entered late with one crutch still vibrating. Iven looked at me.

"Master, before you become unreasonable---"

"I already am."

That was not the line. Iven paused. I knew the correct line. He knew I knew it.

"Good," he said. "Then perhaps we can skip ahead."

Someone laughed backstage. Not Teren. Teren said, "Stop." We stopped. He was in the house with three pages in one hand and a pencil in his mouth.

"Again."

"From where?"

"Entrance."

"I didn't know you cut---"

"Now you do."

That was my acting note. I went back. The local worker standing near the wall opening moved aside for me. I positioned my crutches. Waited. Iven started. This time I entered correctly. Then I overplayed the first laugh. Not deliberately. That made it worse.

"You've had eleven days to improve it," I said.

I waited. Not long. Long enough. There was no audience. No laugh. Only an empty hall, local workers, Teren, Serra in the opposite wing, and someone hammering upstairs despite Coln's apparent objection to anyone using upstairs. The pause sat there. Dead. Iven continued.

"You wound me."

"No. Then you would owe me for the floor."

I did it again. The shape of the old laugh. Waiting for something that was not there. Teren said, "Greg."

"Yes."

"Don't."

"What?"

He looked at me. Then at the pages. Then toward the front doors, where Coln's agent had appeared again.

"Don't do that."

He walked away. Excellent. Iven waited.

"What am I doing?"

"The thing."

"You said that before."

"Yes."

"What thing?"

He shrugged.

"Waiting for ghosts."

I looked at him. That was irritatingly specific.

"Again."

We started. This time I rushed. Better than waiting. Worse in another direction. Iven interrupted me in the middle of a line.

"No."

"What?"

"You're stepping on me."

"I am not near you."

"Words."

"I know what stepping on a line means."

"Then stop."

I took a breath.

"Again."

"From?"

"Beginning."

He looked toward the house. Teren was gone.

"Fine."

We started again. It was mediocre. That was all. Not secretly good. Not almost there. Mediocre. I knew because I had felt the scene work before. This did not. When we finished, Iven said, "Food?"

"I just ate."

"I didn't."

He left. I remained onstage. Serra crossed behind me carrying the wooden crown.

"Was that bad?"

"Yes."

"Good."

"Why good?"

She stopped.

"I didn't say good for you."

Then she kept going. Fine. The rehearsal moved on without solving me. Marek came down from upstairs wearing a different coat. Not gray. Blue. Coln saw him.

"Why were you upstairs?"

Marek stopped at the bottom of the stairs.

"Changing."

"I said you do not go upstairs."

"You said that before I needed trousers."

"There is a dressing room downstairs."

"Occupied."

"By whom?"

Marek looked toward the women's room. Coln looked too. Nessa's voice came from inside.

"Don't."

I turned. Nessa was here. So was Rinna. I had not seen them arrive. A cart must have come while I was failing. Three costume trunks blocked half the corridor. Rinna stood over one with her hands on her hips. Pell was inside the dressing room. Serra had vanished. Nessa stepped out holding the mourning dress. The hem looked normal. I had never seen it before the cut, so this meant nothing. Coln said, "Who are you?"

"Nessa."

"That room is not included."

Nessa looked behind her.

"At what?"

"In your hire."

She stared.

"It's a room."

"Upstairs rooms are excluded."

"This is downstairs."

Coln pointed toward a different door.

"That one."

Nessa followed his finger.

"Then why are you telling me?"

Coln looked at Teren. Teren was not there. This seemed to happen often. The agent stepped between them.

"Master Coln means the upper wardrobe and two rear rooms are not part of the present agreement."

Nessa said, "Fine." No argument. She turned.

"Pell. We don't have wardrobe."

Pell's voice came from inside.

"Fuck."

Rinna said, "Wagon." Nessa said, "Too far." Rinna said, "Old kitchen." Edda shouted from somewhere, "No." Nessa shouted back, "Temporary."

"No."

"Corner."

"No."

"Under table."

"No."

Nessa looked at Rinna.

"Green room."

A local worker passing by said, "No." Nessa closed her eyes. The mourning dress remained over one arm. This problem had nothing to do with me. I enjoyed it for almost thirty seconds. Then Rinna pointed at me.

"Greg."

"No."

She blinked.

"I didn't ask yet."

"I know."

"Hold this."

She handed me the mourning dress. Of course. I held it. Nessa and Rinna went to inspect the green room. Pell came out carrying a box of pins. He saw me with the dress.

"Don't let it touch the floor."

"I know."

"You don't."

"I can infer."

"Keep the hem up."

"I am."

"Other side."

I lifted the other side.

"Higher."

"Pell."

"What?"

"I have one free hand."

He looked at my crutch.

"Oh."

He took the dress.

"Thanks."

That was the end of my involvement. Good. I went looking for Teren. Not because of the costume room. Because my Shopkeeper was bad. I found him in the house near the back row speaking with the ledger woman.

"No," she said.

"Why?"

"Sound dies under balcony."

"There is no balcony."

She pointed upward. A shallow gallery projected from the rear wall. Teren looked at it.

"That is a gallery."

"Yes."

"Different."

"No."

He rubbed his face. I waited. The ledger woman said, "If you put musicians there, they lose stage."

"We don't have musicians."

"Then don't."

"Excellent."

She walked away. Teren saw me.

"No."

"I haven't asked."

"Good."

"Shopkeeper is bad."

"Yes."

I stared.

"You watched?"

"Some."

"What am I doing?"

"Too much."

"That is not specific."

He looked toward the stage. Someone shouted his name. Then someone else shouted it from backstage. Teren pointed at me.

"Stop trying to make it good."

He turned. I said, "That is terrible advice."

"Then ignore it."

He left. I stood among empty benches. The hall owner walked past me carrying a ledger. Not the ledger woman's ledger. Different ledger. He did not look at me. I went back to the stage. A rehearsal had started without me. Not my scene. Marek and Serra. King and Princess. The Sword was not in it. I stayed in the wing. Marek crossed downstage. Serra stopped him.

"No."

"What?"

"Too far."

"I am at the mark."

"Wrong mark."

She pointed with her toe. There were three chalk marks near each other. Marek looked down.

"Who did that?"

A local worker said, "Me."

"Why three?"

"Chair. Table. You."

"Which is me?"

The worker pointed. Marek moved. Serra restarted. No Teren. They ran the scene themselves. Marek missed a turn. Serra corrected him without stopping. He adjusted. She changed her path around the chair because the wing was shallower. He changed his next cross to give her space. Neither discussed it. They had done this longer than I had. That was obvious. Halfway through, Serra skipped a line. Marek answered the line she should have said anyway. She stopped.

"No."

"You skipped."

"I know."

"Then why stop?"

"Because you covered."

"Yes."

"Don't."

"Why?"

"I need to know I skipped."

Marek considered.

"Fine."

They went back. That was interesting. Not for me. For them. I stayed quiet. They ran it again. Better. Then Serra's yellow-scarf woman appeared in the house. She stood near the back. Serra saw her. Missed her next line. Marek waited. Serra recovered. The woman in yellow did not react. When the scene ended, Serra walked offstage without looking at Marek. She went directly into the house. The yellow-scarf woman met her halfway. They spoke. Too far for me to hear. Serra folded her arms.

The woman said something. Serra looked away. Marek came into the wing. He saw them. His expression changed.

"You know her."

He looked at me.

"Yes."

"Who is she?"

"No."

"That is not an answer."

"It is."

He picked up a cup. Empty. He put it down.

"Is she family?"

Marek looked at me. Then at Serra.

"No."

"Friend?"

"Greg."

"What?"

"Not yours."

I stopped. He was right. I disliked how often that happened. The yellow-scarf woman touched Serra's arm again. Serra pulled away this time. Not violently. Clearly. The woman said something else. Serra left through the front doors. The woman remained. Marek watched. I watched Marek. He noticed.

"Don't."

Fine. I went to find food. Edda had onions in the old kitchen. Still.

"How many onions are there?"

"Too many."

"What are they for?"

"Tonight."

"Are we eating here?"

"Yes."

"Where are we sleeping?"

She looked at me. I had not asked Teren. I had forgotten.

"Not here."

"Useful."

She handed me an onion.

"What?"

"Peel."

"I am an actor."

"Congratulations."

I peeled onions. This was better than Shopkeeper. Edda cut them. I peeled. Another local woman came in and started washing a pot. They talked over me. Not to me.

"Did he come back?"

"No."

"He said he would."

"He says."

"You going?"

"No."

"You said that last time."

"I went last time."

"Exactly."

"That's why no."

The second woman laughed. Edda did not. I peeled another onion. I had no idea who they meant. Good. After five onions, my eyes watered.

"This is hostile."

Edda said, "Actor."

"Yes."

"Use it."

"For what?"

She smiled. I hated everyone. Rinna came in.

"Need table."

"No," Edda said.

"Five minutes."

"No."

"Two."

"No."

Rinna looked at me. I shook my head. She left. Edda handed me another onion. The rehearsal resumed after the costume rooms were reorganized into some arrangement I did not understand. Nessa had taken half the green room. The local crew hated this. Edda had successfully defended the old kitchen. Marek was no longer wearing blue. Serra had returned. The yellow-scarf woman had not. Nobody mentioned it. Teren called Shopkeeper. I wiped onion from my hands. Iven appeared from nowhere.

"Again?"

"Yes."

"You smell."

"Onions."

"Good."

"Why good?"

"Debt."

"That makes no sense."

He entered. I waited in the farther wing position. The cue came through the wall. I entered. Correctly. That was the only part I did correctly. The first exchange was flat again. Then Iven changed a line. Not much.

"Master, before you become unreasonable, I have a very good explanation."

Very good. Different. I answered.

"You've had eleven days to ruin it."

Wrong line. Not written. Iven smiled.

"Ten."

"What?"

"It was ten yesterday."

I stared. He stared back. Oh.

"Then you've wasted today too."

Somebody in the house laughed. Not an audience. Crew. I did not wait. We continued. Iven changed another line. I answered differently. The scene loosened. Then I got greedy. I reached for the consultation line because I knew it worked. I set it up. Too clearly. Iven saw me doing it. He refused.

Instead of asking whether I was threatening him, he said, "You are a deeply unpleasant man." I had nothing. My prepared answer died. I stared. Iven waited.

"Pay me."

He laughed. Actually laughed. Not acting. Teren said, "Good. Stop." I looked toward the house. He was halfway down an aisle with Coln.

"That was good?"

"Enough."

"Why?"

He kept walking. Three seconds. Iven came beside me.

"You tried to make me say it."

"Yes."

"No."

"I know."

"Good."

He left. I stood there. Mediocre first. Better second. Still not solved. Fine. The Sword rehearsal was worse. Serra was different after whatever had happened with the yellow-scarf woman. Not worse. Different. Quieter. Her Princess entered without the earlier sharpness. I expected the version from Carrow. Wrong. My first line came too hard. She looked at the sword. Not at me. The silence after my line was wrong. I filled it. Also wrong.

"Do you intend to carry me like that all evening?"

Serra turned.

"That isn't your line."

"I know."

"Then why did you say it?"

I had no answer. Teren shouted from the house, "Keep going." We kept going. Badly. I tried to find the rhythm. Serra did not give me the old rhythm. She moved slower. Held the sword differently. At one point she sat instead of crossing. I missed the cue because I was waiting for the cross. Silence. Serra said, "Sword?"

"Yes."

"That was your cue."

"I know."

"Apparently not."

Marek laughed backstage. I said, "Fuck you." Teren said, "Sword doesn't say fuck you."

"I wasn't Sword."

"Good."

We restarted. Second time, I watched Serra. Too much. I followed every movement. That made me late in a different way. She stopped.

"Greg."

"What?"

"I'm not going to do the same thing tonight."

"I know."

"No. You know now."

That hurt. Fair.

"Why?"

She looked at me. Not angry. Tired.

"Because I don't want to."

That was all. Teren called from the house.

"Again."

Serra took her starting place. I did too. Third time, I stopped trying to predict her. Not completely. Enough. She entered. Picked up the sword. Held it. I waited for the line. Not the movement. The line came. I answered. Better. Then I missed another cue later anyway. Not everything improved at once. Good. We finished. Serra left immediately. No note. No conversation. She went backstage, took her coat, and disappeared through the side door. I looked at Marek. He was changing a belt.

"Don't."

"I didn't ask."

"Your face."

"I have one face."

"No."

Davin said that too. Conspiracy. Teren climbed onto the stage. Everyone who was nearby looked at him. Not because he was important. Because he had the schedule.

"Tonight," he said. "Doors at seven. First show tomorrow afternoon. Second tomorrow night."

Someone said, "Both tomorrow?"

"Yes."

Nessa said, "No." Teren looked at her.

"Why no?"

"Red dress isn't done."

"Which red dress?"

Nessa stared. Teren corrected.

"Right. Red dress. When?"

"Tomorrow morning."

"Good."

"No. Noon."

"Show afternoon."

"I know."

"Can it be morning?"

"No."

"Can the show be evening?"

Coln said from the house, "No." Nobody had known he was there. Teren closed his eyes. Nessa said, "Then she wears blue." Rinna said, "Blue is court." Nessa looked at her.

"Not anymore."

That solved something. Or created something. Teren continued.

"Tonight is setup and open rehearsal. No full show."

I raised my hand. He ignored me.

"Food here. Sleeping at the River House, three streets west. Rooms are arranged."

I lowered my hand. That had been my question.

"Greg."

I looked up.

"Yes?"

"Shopkeeper tomorrow afternoon. Sword both."

"Shopkeeper night?"

"Maybe Meren."

"He's coming?"

"Maybe."

"When will you know?"

Teren looked at me. I knew.

"If it changes me."

Pell laughed from the wing. Teren frowned.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Good."

He moved on.

"Upstairs is closed except costume changes with permission."

Marek raised his hand.

"No," Teren said.

Marek lowered it.

"Do not argue with Coln. Do not move his benches. Do not touch the front lamps. If you break anything, tell Davin before Coln sees it."

Davin said, "Tell me before you break it."

"Better."

Teren looked around.

"Questions?"

Everyone spoke at once. Not me. Nessa wanted time. Rinna wanted storage. Pell wanted to know which blue dress. Iven wanted food. Orin wanted the room list. A local worker wanted our tower moved. Coln wanted the tower out of the corridor.

Davin said the tower was only there because Coln would not let him put the long box against the wall. Coln said the box should be flat. Davin said, "No." That continued. I stepped offstage. Nobody noticed. Outside, late afternoon had turned the river bright between buildings. I had time. Maybe. Ten minutes to the municipal hall. Ten back. Unless rehearsal started again. Unless someone needed me. Unless Teren changed something. I looked inside. Everyone was arguing. Good. I went to the old kitchen. Edda was stirring the pot.

"Municipal hall."

She pointed with the spoon.

"Front, left. Fountain, right. Uphill."

"I remember."

"Then why tell me?"

"I wasn't asking."

She looked at me.

"Actor."

I took the bread she offered. Then I went outside. For the first time since arriving, nobody gave me anything to carry. I turned left.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 148

## THE ROOF

I turned left. This immediately became difficult because left contained a cart. The cart contained cabbages. A man was unloading them directly into a shop while another man stood in the street objecting to the location of the horse.

"Move him."

"Where?"

"Not there."

"That isn't a place."

"It is if you move him."

I waited. Nobody moved the horse. I went around the cart. The street rose gently away from the river, which meant Edda's directions were probably correct. The paving was better here than near the market and worse than directly outside the performance hall. Flat stones had been laid down the middle with narrower gutters on either side, except where repairs had replaced stone with brick, and where repairs to the repairs had apparently been made with whatever was available. I liked it. Not walking on it. That was worse.

My right crutch landed on a brick edge and slipped half an inch. I corrected. Slower. The bread in my pocket was becoming flatter every time my coat pulled across it. I ate it. Problem solved. The first fountain was wrong. I discovered this after turning right. Edda had said fountain, right. There was a fountain. I went right. The street descended. That was suspicious. I continued for another minute because perhaps the hill curved. It did not. A woman sold flowers beneath a striped awning.

"North square?"

She pointed behind me.

"Other fountain."

"Of course."

"You want the court?"

"Municipal hall."

"Court's in the hall."

"I want the building."

She looked at me.

"Yes."

"No. I mean I want to see the building."

She looked at my crutches. Then at my face.

"It's not going anywhere."

"I know."

"Back. Second fountain. Up."

"Thank you."

She had already turned to another customer. I went back. The horse with the cabbages was still there. The men were still arguing. Good. The world remained stable. The second fountain was larger. Not dramatically. Enough that I should have known. Four stone fish spat water into a round basin. One fish had lost most of its face and produced a stronger stream than the others. A boy was filling a bucket. Two women sat on the rim talking. A dog drank from the lower overflow. Right. Up.

The hill became less theoretical. I stopped after half a block. Not because I had to. Because there was a low stone wall beside a baker's shop and sitting on it was clearly more efficient than pretending the hill did not exist. I sat.

My hands were tired from rehearsal and two days of travel. Not bad. The web between thumb and forefinger on my right hand had a tender place from the crutch grip. I opened and closed my fingers. Fine. A man came out of the bakery with a tray. He looked at me.

"You waiting?"

"No."

He waited.

"For someone?"

"No."

"Then why are you on my wall?"

I looked down.

"Is it your wall?"

"Yes."

"Sorry."

I started to stand. He sighed.

"No, stay."

I stopped. He went back inside. Fine. A few minutes later he came out again and put a cup on the wall beside me. Water.

"Thank you."

He nodded. No conversation. Excellent. I drank. From where I sat, the town changed with the slope. The river appeared between roofs below. Beyond it, the road we had come in on crossed the flatter southern ground. I could see part of the market, the church tower from the ridge, and one of our painted wagon pieces sticking above a wall near the performance hall. I could not see the performance hall itself. Good. I finished the water. The baker came out for the cup.

"Hall?"

I pointed uphill. He nodded.

"Ugly one."

"Yes."

He took the cup. Apparently everyone agreed. I continued. The municipal hall appeared before the square did. The roof gave it away. I stopped in the middle of the pavement. Someone behind me said, "Move." I moved. Then stared. The building was ugly. Not badly ugly. Interesting ugly.

It occupied the uphill side of a broad square and looked as though three different buildings had agreed to share a front wall. The lowest level was stone, pale originally, darkened by age and weather. The central entrance had an arch large enough for a wagon, though the doors inside it were newer and narrower. On either side, tall rectangular windows had been cut or enlarged at different times. The left pair matched. The right pair almost matched.

Above that, the second story was plaster over masonry with heavy timber visible in places where the plaster had failed. And the roof--- The roof was wrong. I smiled. There were two ridgelines. Not separate roofs. One roof that had become two answers.

The western half rose at a steeper pitch and carried newer tile. The eastern half was lower, broader, and sagged slightly between supports despite obvious repair. A short raised section crossed the center where the two systems met, like someone had built a small roof to stop the larger roofs from arguing. Drainage ran everywhere. Stone gutters. Copper gutters. One wooden channel that could not possibly be original. Two downspouts on the west. Four on the east. One of those emptied onto a lower roof. Why? I crossed the square.

Slowly. The front facade had cracks. Old ones. Most had been filled. A vertical repair line beside the central arch told me the opening had once been wider or differently shaped. The stone above it changed color three courses up. I moved to the left. From there I could see the western roof better. New timber projected beneath the eaves. Not decorative. Ends of rafters. Thicker than expected.

The wall below had three shallow buttresses that did not continue around the corner. Added. Probably after the first roof problem. Maybe before. I wanted the records. That was unreasonable. I wanted them anyway. A bell rang inside. People began coming out. I moved away from the door. Not a few people. Many. A man carrying rolled papers. Two women arguing about a property boundary. A family with a boy who looked furious. Three laborers. A clerk with ink on both cuffs.

An older woman who stopped directly in the doorway to continue an argument with someone still inside.

"Twenty-seven years," she said. "You cannot discover a drainage right after twenty-seven years."

A voice from inside answered, "We didn't discover it."

"You wrote it yesterday."

"We recorded it yesterday."

"That is discovering with ink."

I liked her. The clerk with ink cuffs saw me staring at the roof.

"Court?"

"No."

"Registry?"

"No."

"Tax?"

"No."

He waited.

"Roof."

He looked up.

"Yes."

"I came to see it."

He looked at me.

"Why?"

"It's been rebuilt twice."

"Three."

I stared. He kept walking.

"Wait."

He did not. I followed. This was difficult because he had two legs and no interest in me.

"Three?"

He stopped at the edge of the square.

"Roof?"

"Yes."

"Three."

"I heard twice."

"Then you heard twice."

"That doesn't answer---"

He crossed the street. A wagon passed between us. When it cleared, he was gone into a side lane. I stood there. Three. Interesting. I went inside. Nobody stopped me. This was less exciting than it sounded because the entrance opened into a public hall full of people who had better things to do. A long counter divided the room. Three clerks worked behind it. A line formed in front. Benches ran along one wall. Doors led deeper into the building. One door had a guard.

Another had a sign I could not read from where I stood. The ceiling was high. I looked up. Wrong again. The main beam ran east-west. I had expected north-south from the exterior roof. Unless--- I moved sideways. A woman in line said, "There's a line."

"I'm not in it."

"Then don't stand in it."

I moved. The beam was not centered. It sat nearly two feet west of the room's centerline. A second, smaller beam ran parallel near the east wall. Both disappeared into plaster. The western one was older. Dark timber. The eastern one looked newer. Not new. Newer. I followed it with my eyes.

"Sir."

I looked down. A clerk behind the counter was watching me.

"Yes?"

"What do you need?"

"Nothing."

She waited.

"The roof."

"No."

"I haven't asked yet."

"No roof."

"I only want to know when it was rebuilt."

"Records."

"Good. Where?"

"Records office."

"Where?"

She pointed to the guarded door. The guard looked at me.

"Can I---"

"No."

The clerk had already called the next person. I moved to a bench. Apparently records existed. Excellent. Apparently I could not have them. Less excellent. I sat and looked at the ceiling. That was still free. A man beside me held a bundle of papers tied with blue string. He noticed.

"Leak?"

"What?"

"You looking for leak?"

"No."

He looked up.

"There's one there."

He pointed. There was. A pale stain spread from the plaster near the newer eastern beam.

"That's not under the roof valley."

He looked at me.

"What valley?"

"Outside. Where the roof sections meet."

"Water moves."

"Yes."

He returned to his papers. Fair. I studied the stain. If water entered higher on the roof, it could travel along a rafter before appearing there. Or the gutter behind the raised center section leaked. Or there was another roof surface I could not see from the square. I wanted upstairs. The stairs were behind the guard. Of course. I sat for another minute. Then a door opened beside the counter. Not the guarded one. A woman emerged carrying a stack of ledgers. Behind her I could see a corridor.

And stairs. Different stairs. I stood. The woman nearly walked into me.

"Sorry."

She adjusted the ledgers. One began sliding. I caught the bottom edge.

"Thanks."

She looked at my crutch tucked under my arm. Then at the ledgers.

"Can you open that?"

She nodded toward the door. I opened it. She passed through. I held it. The corridor beyond smelled like dust and wax. The stairs rose at the far end. I looked. The woman looked back.

"You coming?"

"Can I?"

"Why?"

"Roof."

She stared.

"No."

Fair. I let the door close. I had not been invited into a secret architectural kingdom. Disappointing. Reasonable. I went outside. The square had changed again. A vegetable seller had arrived. Children chased each other around the fountain. The older woman with the drainage argument was now arguing with a man holding a measuring chain. I walked around the building.

The western side street was narrow enough that I could touch the hall wall with one crutch and nearly touch the opposite building with the other. I did not test this. The buttresses were clearer here. Three added supports. The middle one was thicker. Above them, the roof pitch changed approximately over the second. Not coincidence. Probably. The stone around the middle buttress had been cut back. Retrofit. I crouched slightly to look at the base. Bad idea. Not dangerous. Awkward. I straightened. A door opened beside me.

A man carrying a bucket stepped out.

"Don't piss there."

"I wasn't."

He looked at me.

"I was looking at the buttress."

He looked at the buttress.

"Why?"

"It was added."

"Yes."

"When?"

"Before me."

"How long have you worked here?"

"Eleven years."

"Do you know why?"

"Wall leaned."

I stopped.

"Which way?"

He pointed across the alley.

"Out."

"Because of the roof?"

He shrugged.

"Because wall leaned."

He walked away with the bucket. That was enough to make me happy for several minutes. The wall had leaned. The buttresses were added. The roof changed above the middle support. Cause and response. Maybe. I continued around the back. The rear was worse. Better. Much better. The public front had been repaired to look intentional. The back had not. Old stone met newer brick. Two windows had been filled. A third had been shortened when a roofline dropped across it.

There was a low annex attached to the eastern side, probably after the main building, and the eastern roof emptied partly onto it. That explained one downspout. Not the stupid one. The stupid one emptied directly onto a tiled slope, where the water had carved a dark path through moss. I stood looking at it.

"Terrible."

Someone beside me said, "Yes." I turned. An old man sat on an overturned crate beside the rear door. Not troupe old. Actually old. Gray beard. Brown coat. One boot unlaced. He held a small knife and was cutting an apple.

"Why would they do that?"

He bit a slice.

"Cheap."

"That cannot be the whole answer."

"It usually is."

I looked at the downspout.

"They rebuilt the roof three times?"

He cut another slice.

"Depends what you call rebuilt."

"What do you call rebuilt?"

"Roof comes off."

"All of it?"

"Enough."

"That is not a definition."

He smiled.

"You work here?"

"No."

"Then why are you here?"

"My daughter does."

"What does she do?"

"Complains."

I waited. He ate apple.

"What actually happened to the roof?"

"Which time?"

Excellent. I moved closer. He pointed the knife at my crutches.

"Sit if you're staying."

There was another crate. I sat. He cut apple. I waited. He did not speak.

"You said which time."

"Yes."

"Which times?"

"Old roof burned."

I knew about the fire.

"First rebuild."

"Maybe."

"Maybe?"

"Wasn't here."

"Neither was I."

"Then we're equal."

Fine. He pointed upward with the knife.

"After fire, they put it back wrong."

"How?"

"Too much roof."

I frowned.

"That means nothing."

"It held snow."

"All roofs hold snow."

"That one held the wrong snow."

I stared. He smiled around the apple.

"You know roof?"

"A little."

"Then look."

I looked. The eastern half. Broader pitch. Longer run. If the post-fire roof had extended farther than the original---

"They changed the span."

"Maybe."

"Why?"

"Wanted bigger room."

That made sense. Too much sense.

"They removed supports?"

"Maybe."

"You keep saying maybe."

"I wasn't there."

Good.

"Then the wall leaned."

"Later."

"And they added buttresses."

"Probably."

"You know that?"

"My daughter says those are buttresses."

"They are."

"Then yes."

"What was the second rebuild?"

"Storm."

"Roof failed?"

"Part."

"Which part?"

He pointed vaguely west.

"Other side."

"The steeper roof."

"Sure."

"You don't know."

"No."

I laughed. He offered me apple. I took a slice.

"Third?"

"Council."

"What did the council do?"

"Argued."

"That does not rebuild roofs."

"It does eventually."

He cut another slice.

"Leak. Rot. Money. More arguing. New wood."

"When?"

"Six years?"

He thought.

"Seven."

"That would be the western rafters."

He shrugged. Maybe. I ate the apple. This was not reliable information. It was wonderful.

"Do you know who has the records?"

"Clerks."

"They won't let me in."

"Good."

"Why good?"

"Means they're working."

"That is optimistic."

"My daughter is a clerk."

"Which one?"

He smiled.

"Complains."

Of course. The rear door opened. A woman leaned out.

"Papa."

He looked over. Ink on both cuffs. The clerk from the square. She saw me.

"Oh, for fuck's sake."

I smiled.

"He said three."

"I know what he said."

"You didn't tell me."

"I was going home."

The old man offered her apple. She took it.

"Why is he here?"

"He likes roof."

"I know."

"Strange boy."

"I know."

I objected.

"I am sitting here."

They ignored me. She looked at the sky.

"You have ten minutes."

I stopped.

"For what?"

She pointed at me.

"Not upstairs. Not records. Not anywhere with a locked door. I will show you the council chamber because if you keep circling the building someone will report a suspicious cripple and then I have paperwork."

I stared.

"Really?"

"Ten minutes."

I stood too quickly. My right shoulder objected. I ignored it. No. I acknowledged it and stood anyway. The old man said, "Roof boy."

"I have a name."

He cut apple.

"Roof boy."

Fine. The clerk opened the rear door. I followed. Her name was Mara. I learned this because someone in the corridor said, "Mara, did Fen sign---"

"No."

"Did you ask?"

"Yes."

"What did he say?"

"No."

"Then what do I tell---"

"I don't care."

She kept walking. I liked Mara. The back corridor was narrower than the public room and older than the front suggested. Stone showed through the plaster at shoulder height. The floor sloped slightly toward the east.

"Is that settlement?"

"No."

"How do you know?"

"Because the floor has always been shit."

"That does not exclude settlement."

She kept walking.

"Ten minutes."

We passed the guarded door from the other side. The guard looked at me. Then Mara.

"No."

Mara said, "Chamber." He sighed.

"Ten."

Everyone agreed on ten. We climbed a staircase. Slowly. Not because Mara slowed. She did not. The stairs turned tightly at the middle landing. My crutches fit, barely. The inside corners of the treads were worn down from centuries of feet. At the top, Mara waited. Not looking concerned. Just waiting. I appreciated that.

"Council chamber."

She opened double doors. I forgot my hands hurt. The room was large. Larger than the ground-floor public hall. That was the problem. Immediately. The ceiling rose into the eastern roof. There were no central columns. None. The span crossed almost the entire building. I moved inside.

The council table occupied the center, long and dark, surrounded by mismatched chairs. Tall windows faced the square. The rear wall had been patched in at least four different materials. Above us, roof timbers crossed at angles that did not agree with the walls. I smiled.

"Oh."

Mara leaned against the door.

"Ten minutes."

"They took the columns out."

"I don't know."

"They must have."

"Why?"

"The ground floor beam isn't centered because it is carrying something that used to land differently."

She looked up. I moved toward the middle. A heavy tie beam crossed overhead. Newer than the rafters around it. Iron straps reinforced both ends. One strap had been doubled.

"There."

"What?"

"The load changed."

Mara said nothing. I traced it. Not with my hands. Eyes. Roof down to tie. Tie to wall. Wall to--- But the eastern wall had the newer parallel beam below. The western side had buttresses. Different fixes for different consequences. They had not rebuilt one bad roof three times. They had kept changing the building underneath it. Or around it. Or both.

"Why remove the columns?"

Mara said, "Council wanted a larger chamber."

"When?"

"Before I was born."

"After the fire?"

"Probably."

"Before the wall leaned?"

"I don't know."

"Do you have drawings?"

"No."

"You do."

"No for you."

I laughed. She checked the corridor clock.

"Six minutes."

I moved to the eastern wall. A vertical timber disappeared behind paneling. I crouched to see where it met the floor. Mara said, "Don't." I stopped.

"Why?"

"Because council meets here and if you break your neck under the table I have paperwork."

"I am not going under the table."

"You looked like you were."

"I was looking at the post."

"From standing."

Fine. I stood. The post did not align with the window spacing. Added. Almost certainly. I looked at the roof again. It was not elegant. It was not a hidden masterpiece. It was a series of decisions. Some good. Some cheap. Some forced by fire, weather, money, politics, or people wanting a bigger room. The building had survived them. Not unchanged. Not correctly. Just continuously. I loved it. Mara watched me.

"You're smiling."

"Yes."

"It's a roof."

"Yes."

"Bad roof."

"Complicated roof."

"It leaks."

"That is separate."

"It is literally the roof."

I considered.

"Fair."

She checked the time.

"Two minutes."

I turned slowly once more. Not to memorize it. Impossible. Just to see. The mismatched rafters. The iron straps. The western tie. The added eastern post. A patch where plaster had cracked around one joint. Water stain near the rear. Chairs stacked against a wall. A broken window latch. Someone had left a cup on the council table. A building used by people. Not a diagram.

"Time."

I went. Downstairs was slower. My shoulders had tightened while I stood in the chamber. At the rear door, Mara held it open.

"Thank you."

"You get ten minutes."

"I got more."

"Don't tell anyone."

"I think the guard knows."

"He doesn't count."

The guard, somewhere inside, shouted, "I heard that." Mara closed the door. Her father was still on the crate. He had finished the apple.

"Well?"

I looked up at the roof.

"Too much roof."

He smiled.

"See?"

"That still means nothing."

He laughed. I started back toward the square.

"Roof boy."

I turned. He tossed something. I nearly dropped a crutch trying to catch it. Apple. Whole.

"Thank you."

He waved me away. I went downhill. Much easier. The town had moved toward evening while I was inside. Shop awnings came down. Lamps appeared in windows. The fountain fish continued spitting water with complete indifference to municipal architecture. I found the wrong fountain first. Again. That was impressive.

By the time I reached the river street, my shoulders were tired enough that the performance hall looked farther away than it had any right to. I stopped. Across the street was a bench. I used it. The apple sat in my lap. I could see the hall entrance from there. People were going in. Not many. Open rehearsal. Right. I had not checked the time. That was stupid. I stood. A voice behind me said, "Gregory." I turned. Serra stood in the street. Alone. No yellow scarf.

She looked at the apple.

"Where did you get that?"

"Roof."

She stared. I pointed uphill.

"Municipal hall."

"That explains less."

"I saw the roof."

"Was it good?"

"Yes."

"Good."

She kept walking toward the theatre. I fell in beside her. Not quickly. She adjusted to my pace after half a block without saying anything. I did not ask where she had been. She did not ask why a roof had given me an apple. The performance hall doors were open. Inside, someone shouted for the Princess. Serra sighed.

"They found me."

"You walked in the front door."

"Still."

Someone shouted for the Sword. I looked at her. She looked at me.

"Apparently they found you too."

I put the apple in my pocket. Then we went inside.
