------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 149

## THE AUDIENCE

Then we went inside. Nobody was ready. This did not prevent people from watching. The front doors stood open to the river street, and the house had perhaps thirty people scattered through it. Not seated properly. Scattered.

Three children occupied the front bench and were arguing over the middle. Two women sat halfway back with baskets at their feet. A man in a work apron had chosen an aisle seat and was eating something from folded paper. Several local crew members had stopped pretending they were not watching. Mara was there. I stopped. Municipal Mara. Ink cuffs. She sat near the back with her father. He saw me.

"Roof boy!"

The entire hall did not turn. Enough people did. I closed my eyes. Serra looked at me.

"Roof?"

"Don't."

Her mouth moved. Not a smile. Worse. The old man raised one hand. I did not wave. Mara did. Traitor. Someone backstage shouted, "Sword!"

"I know!"

Serra was already moving.

"Princess!"

"I know!"

We went opposite directions. That felt appropriate. The backstage corridor had become narrower because it contained more people, more clothing, and one large painted wall that had not been there when I left. I stopped. The wall stopped me too.

"Why is this here?"

A local worker behind it said, "Move."

"I can't."

"Then back."

I backed. The wall advanced. I flattened against the real wall. It passed. Davin came behind it holding the bottom edge.

"Where is it going?"

"Stage."

"Why?"

"Wall."

"That isn't---"

He was gone. Fine. I found the men's dressing room. My bag was under the stool. Iven was not asleep on it. Improvement. Marek was buttoning a brown vest while Pell knelt beside a trunk looking for something.

"Have you seen the narrow belt?" Pell asked.

"No," Marek said.

"You wore it."

"When?"

"Carrow."

"That was days ago."

"Yes."

"Then no."

Pell looked at me.

"No."

"I didn't say anything."

"Good."

I put my crutches against the wall long enough to check my coat. Apple. Still there. Less round. I took it out. One side had a bruise where I had apparently leaned against something. Marek reached. I moved it away.

"No."

"Food."

"Mine."

"Where did you get an apple?"

"Roof."

He stopped.

"What?"

"Nothing."

I put it in my bag. The apple had survived architecture. It did not need theatre. Teren appeared in the doorway.

"Greg. Sword first."

"What about Shopkeeper?"

"Later."

"How much later?"

"After Sword."

"That is not---"

He was gone. Marek said, "Good talk."

"Fuck you."

"Better."

Pell found the belt under Marek's coat. He stared at it. Marek looked down.

"Oh."

Pell hit him with it. Not hard. They continued dressing. I went to the wing. The house had grown. Maybe forty now. People entered without ceremony. Some paid something at the front. Some apparently did not. A woman came in, saw someone she knew, crossed two rows to sit beside her, and immediately began talking. This was not an audience. It was a town temporarily facing the same direction. Teren stood in the center aisle.

"Start with the road scene."

Someone onstage said, "Which road?"

"The second."

"We cut the second."

"No, we cut the first half of the second."

"So the third?"

Teren looked at his pages.

"No."

A child in front laughed. Teren looked at him. The child stopped. Then Teren smiled. The child smiled back.

"Second road," Teren said. "From the toll."

Actors moved. No curtain. No announcement. A local worker carried a chair across the stage while the scene began. The audience did not care. Or they understood. I did not. The road scene started. Orin entered wearing half a costume. Proper coat, ordinary trousers. Iven followed with a hat I had never seen. They spoke. Teren stopped them after four lines.

"No. Bench is wrong."

A local worker said, "Bench is there."

"I know."

"You asked there."

"Yesterday."

"This is today."

The worker stared. Teren pointed.

"Two feet."

The worker and another man moved the bench. The audience watched. The children in front whispered. Orin stayed in character while the bench moved around him.

"You see," he told Iven, "this is what happens when public works receive funding."

A few people laughed. Teren said, "Don't add." Orin said, "Of course." They restarted. He did not add it. That impressed me more than the joke. The scene ran. A woman entered late and sat beside Mara. Mara's father said something to her. She laughed. Not at the play. Fine. Nobody was obligated. Teren stopped the scene twice. Once for blocking. Once because Iven's hat fell off. Iven picked it up. Teren said, "Again from bridge." Iven said, "There is no bridge."

"Line."

"Oh."

They continued. The audience stayed. Mostly. The man with folded-paper food left halfway through. A mother came in with a baby. Two boys left. Three older men took their seats. The room changed. Not dramatically. Enough. Then Teren called Sword. My stomach tightened. That was stupid. I had performed for more people at East Market Hall. This was not a performance. That made it worse. At a performance, mistakes belonged to the show. Here, Teren could stop me. Everyone would know why. Serra came into the wing.

She wore the blue dress. Not Princess blue. Different blue. Nessa was behind her adjusting a sleeve.

"Arm."

Serra lifted it.

"Other."

She changed arms. Nessa pinned something. Serra looked at me.

"You look ill."

"I am fine."

"Good."

Nessa said, "Don't move."

"I am not moving."

"To her."

"Oh."

Serra's face remained neutral. Nessa finished.

"Don't catch this on him."

She pointed at my crutch. Serra looked at the sleeve. Then at me.

"Move."

"I am not even near you."

"Future."

Nessa left. Serra rolled one shoulder. I said, "Are you doing it the same?" She looked at me. I knew immediately that this was the wrong question.

"No."

"Right."

"Greg."

"What?"

"Listen."

"I know."

She stared.

"No. You know now."

I hated callbacks when I deserved them. Teren shouted, "Princess!" Serra entered. I stayed behind the wall opening. Could not see her. Good. Maybe. The scene began before the Sword entered. Her voice carried through the opening. Different again. Not as quiet as afternoon rehearsal. Sharper. But not East Market sharp. I tried not to build a version of her before my cue. That required more effort than it should have. Line. Line. Movement I could hear but not see. Then my cue. I spoke.

"Careful."

Too serious. I knew it as soon as it left me. Serra paused. The audience did too. Then she said, "You object?" Not the written line. I answered.

"I prefer thieves with steadier hands."

A laugh. Small. Front somewhere. My body noticed it. Immediately. Dangerous. Serra said, "You prefer thieves?"

"I have limited experience."

Another laugh. More. There. I felt myself reach. Not for a line. For the feeling. The room had opened slightly. I wanted to keep it open. Serra moved. I heard fabric. Her next written line came. I answered too quickly. Stepped on the end. The laugh vanished. Good. Punishment immediate. Serra continued. I settled. For three exchanges, we were fine.

Then she crossed somewhere I could not see and changed the way she held the sword. I knew because my next line expected the blade to tilt. It did not. Silence. Not cue silence. My silence. I had used movement again. Fuck. Serra waited. The audience waited. I said the line late. Teren called, "Stop." There it was. Everyone watched. Not everyone. The baby did not. Mara's father was scratching his beard. A woman in the third row was whispering. Still. Enough. Teren stood.

"Greg."

"Yes."

"You can't see her."

"I know."

"Then why are you watching her?"

"I am not."

Serra looked toward the wing. I could feel it. Teren said, "You're waiting for movement."

"Yes."

"Don't."

"I know."

"Good. Again."

That was it. No lecture. The audience heard all of it. Excellent. We restarted. A child in front said, "He can't see her?" His mother whispered something. The child said, louder, "Why not?" Teren said, "Because he's a sword." The child considered.

"Oh."

We continued. This time I listened. Actually listened. Not for the cue I remembered. For Serra. Her breath came through the opening before one line. The scrape of her shoe before another. Not useful. Then words. Useful. I answered the words. Better.

We reached the place where the Princess threatened to return the Sword to the King. At East Market Hall, I had looked toward Marek as King, waited, and said no. Big laugh. I remembered it. Of course I remembered it. Serra said, "Perhaps I should return you to His Majesty." There. The old opening. Marek was onstage. I could not see him. I could imagine him picking at his sleeve. I almost did the old thing.

"To him?"

A few people laughed. Not many. I heard Marek make a small offended sound. Different. I waited. Too long. Ghost. Fuck. Then a man in the audience coughed. The laugh was gone. I said, "No." Nothing. Dead. Not catastrophic. Dead. Teren did not stop us. Worse. We continued. I could feel my face heating though nobody could see it. Good. Sword. No face. Serra changed the next line.

"You seemed more certain a moment ago."

That was for me. Not Princess. Both. I answered, "I had less information." A laugh. Not large. Real. I did not wait.

"Most kings improve with distance."

Marek said, "I can hear you." That got a bigger laugh. I answered immediately.

"That is unfortunate."

Bigger. There. Again. The room opened. I wanted it. I knew I wanted it. Marek stepped in.

"I could have you melted."

Written? No. Probably not. I said, "Into what?" He paused. I heard the audience shift. Marek said, "Something useful." Good. Very good. I had an answer. Three answers. All bad because I was choosing. The pause lengthened. Serra saved us.

"A spoon."

The front children exploded. Not polite laughter. Actual children losing control. One slapped the bench. Marek looked at her. I could not see it. I heard his silence. Then he said, "Why a spoon?" Serra answered, "He would finally serve someone." The adults joined. I laughed. Sword should not. I did. Teren said, "Stop." We stopped. The laughter faded. Teren pointed at Serra.

"Keep spoon."

Marek said, "Absolutely not."

"Maybe."

"Then why say keep?"

"So I remember."

"That is not what keep means."

Teren pointed at me.

"Greg."

"Yes."

"Don't laugh."

"I know."

"Also don't wait for the old no."

"I know."

"Good."

Three seconds. He sat. Serra came offstage. I moved out of her way. She looked at me.

"Spoon."

"Fuck you."

"Not mine."

"Might be."

She smiled. Not much. Enough. Then the yellow-scarf woman entered the hall. Serra saw her. The smile disappeared. Not because of me. Good. The woman took a seat near the side wall. Serra looked away. Nessa caught Serra before she could leave.

"Sleeve."

"Now?"

"Yes."

Serra raised her arm. Work continued. I went backstage. Marek followed.

"Spoon."

"No."

"You would make a lovely spoon."

"I hope Coln throws you upstairs."

Marek's expression changed. Tiny. I had stepped somewhere. Not terrible. Still.

"Sorry."

He shrugged.

"Don't be. He'd have to catch me."

Then he walked away. Maybe fine. Maybe not. I did not follow. The open rehearsal moved to scenes I was not in. I sat in the green room. Half of it was costumes now. Nessa had won. Or compromised aggressively. Rinna stood over a trunk sorting fabric by a system I could not identify. Pell held the mourning dress up against a local lamp.

"No."

Nessa said, "What?"

"Still wrong."

"Where?"

He pointed at the hem. Nessa crouched. Rinna said, "It's the shoe."

"No," Pell said.

"It was the shoe yesterday."

"Different wrong."

"What different?"

Pell touched the fabric.

"Pulls."

Nessa looked.

"It does."

Rinna said, "Because you shortened it." Pell looked at her. Nessa said, "Not now." Rinna continued sorting. I sat. Nobody asked why. Good. My shoulders hurt. Not badly. The right one had tightened from the hill and rehearsal. My hands were tired. I flexed them. Rinna noticed. Noticed, not cared.

"Your bag's under the stool."

"I know."

"Need stool."

I moved my bag. She took the stool. That was all. I leaned against the wall. Someone onstage forgot a line. Teren supplied it from the house. Someone else argued. A local worker came into the green room looking for a red sash. Nessa said, "No." He said, "Hall sash."

"This is ours."

"Red."

"All red belongs to you?"

"Here, yes."

Rinna threw him a different sash. He left. Pell said, "That was mine." Rinna said, "Not anymore." I closed my eyes. Only for a moment. When I opened them, Orin was sitting beside me. I had not heard him arrive.

"You sleep?"

"No."

"You looked asleep."

"I was resting my eyes."

He nodded.

"Old person phrase."

"You are the old person."

"Exactly."

He held out a small cup. Water. I took it.

"Thank you."

He had another. We drank. From the stage, Marek said something that made the audience laugh. Orin tilted his head.

"He's hunting."

"What?"

"Nothing."

"No, what?"

Orin drank.

"You'll see."

"Is he waiting for ghosts?"

"What?"

"Iven said---"

"I don't care what Iven said."

He stood.

"Where are you going?"

"My scene."

He left. Excellent. I had learned nothing. The house filled further as evening went on. Not full. Maybe sixty at the most. People came and went. A group of apprentices stayed for one scene, laughed at Marek, and left before Orin entered. Mara disappeared. Her father remained. The flower seller from my wrong-fountain mistake appeared near the front and did not recognize me until I came onstage later. Edda sat for exactly one scene. Then left because something in the kitchen required her.

Coln stood at the rear for most of it. He did not laugh. At anything. Possibly principle. Teren called Shopkeeper. Iven appeared beside me.

"You tired?"

"No."

He looked at me.

"Yes."

"Fine."

"Don't make it slow because you're tired."

"I won't."

"Don't make it fast because I said that."

"I hate you."

"Good."

We took places. The audience was larger now than during Sword. Different people. That mattered immediately. I entered correctly. Good. Iven began.

"Master, before you become unreasonable, I have an explanation."

I answered.

"You've had eleven days to improve it."

Nothing. Not one laugh. I had expected something. Not the East Market laugh. Something. Nothing. I continued. Iven said, "You wound me."

"No. Then you would owe me for the floor."

One person laughed. Late. I almost waited for it. Did not. Better. The scene moved. This audience did not care about debt yet. Or me. Fine. Iven's uncle line came.

"Your uncle has become very expensive for a man I have never met."

Two laughs. Small. The children liked that one for some reason. Then Iven changed.

"You're not going to follow me."

Old opening. Danger. I said, "No." The room waited. I did not.

"You're going to come back."

Iven blinked. Not written.

"Why?"

"Because I have your coat."

He looked down. He was wearing a coat. That was luck. Or observation. He grabbed the lapels.

"When did you take my coat?"

"I didn't."

The audience laughed. Iven stared.

"Then how do you have it?"

"I don't. But now you're checking."

Bigger. Iven laughed. I did too. Fuck. Not Sword. Fine. Maybe. He said, "This is my coat."

"Then pay me while you're here."

The children laughed again. Different scene now. Teren did not stop us. We continued. The old almost-standing exchange never happened. Neither did consultation. I noticed. I missed them. That was strange. The scene worked anyway. Not as well as East Market. Different. Near the end, Iven deliberately backed toward the chalked bad board. I saw it. He did not.

"I wouldn't."

He stopped.

"What?"

"Another step and the floor charges interest."

He looked down. Saw the X. The local crew laughed hardest. Of course. Iven moved.

"Even your building is extorting me."

"Not mine."

That got almost nothing. Fine. We finished. No big ending. No callback. Teren said, "Good. Again from uncle." The audience stayed. We went back. Second time was worse. Of course. I tried to reproduce the coat thing. Not exactly. Close enough. Iven did not wear the moment the same way. The laugh was smaller. Then I tried to improve it. Bad. Teren stopped us.

"No."

"I know."

"Good."

Iven said, "Ghost."

"Fuck you."

The front children laughed. Teren pointed at them.

"Don't encourage him."

They laughed more. We reset. Third time, I let the coat go. The scene was fine. Not magical. Fine. Teren moved on. That was all. Backstage, Iven said, "First was better."

"Yes."

"Second bad."

"Yes."

"Third fine."

"Yes."

He looked disappointed.

"What?"

"You agreed too fast."

"I am tired."

"Ah."

He left. I sat on a crate. Davin immediately said, "Need crate." I stood. He took it. Of course. Later, the long iron-cornered box finally moved. Not opened. Moved. Two local workers and Davin carried it through the corridor toward the rear storage room. Coln saw.

"No."

Davin did not stop.

"Not there."

Davin kept moving. Coln followed.

"That room is not included."

Davin stopped. Slowly. He looked at Teren. Teren was in the house. Davin shouted, "Teren." Teren shouted back, "What?"

"Box."

"What about it?"

"Room."

"What room?"

Coln said, "Not included." Teren closed his eyes from twenty yards away. The audience watched. This was apparently part of the entertainment now. Teren walked backstage. Davin waited. Coln waited. The two local workers holding the box waited. One said, "Heavy." Davin said, "Yes." Teren arrived.

"Why does it need that room?"

Davin said, "Dry." Coln said, "No." Teren looked at the box. Then at Coln.

"How much?"

Coln named a number. Teren stared.

"For a room?"

"For use."

"For one box?"

"Room."

Davin said, "Dry." Teren paid. Not happily. The audience applauded. Actual applause. Teren turned toward the house.

"Fuck all of you."

More applause. Even Coln almost smiled. Almost. The box went into the room. Still unopened. Good. The open rehearsal ended without ending. People simply began leaving when Teren stopped calling scenes. Some stayed to talk. Some came backstage despite apparently not being allowed. Nessa chased two children out of the costume area. Marek disappeared. Orin found someone he knew. Iven found food. Serra was still in the house with the yellow-scarf woman. They sat several seats apart at first. Then closer. I did not watch. Much.

I went to get my bag. The apple was still inside. Bruised more. I took it. A bite was missing. I stared. Marek appeared in the doorway chewing.

"You."

"What?"

"My apple."

He looked at the apple.

"Evidence unclear."

"There is a bite."

"Could be old."

"It was whole."

"Roof apples decay quickly."

I threw the apple at him. He caught it.

"Thank you."

"That was not---"

He bit it again. I considered murder. Too tired.

"River House," he said.

"I know."

"You know where?"

"Three streets west."

"Which west?"

I stopped. Marek smiled.

"Come on."

Outside, the air had cooled. People spilled from the hall into the river street, talking about scenes that had not actually been performances. A child passed us saying, "Spoon." Marek pointed at me.

"See?"

"That was Serra."

"You are the spoon."

"I was going to be melted."

"Details."

Serra came out behind us. Alone. She heard.

"Spoon?"

Marek said, "He's famous."

"I hate both of you."

Serra looked tired. More than before. She also looked amused. Both could be true. We started toward River House. Marek ate the rest of my apple. I let him. Mostly because taking it back would require effort. Behind us, the hall remained lit. Davin and local crew were still working. Nessa and Pell were still working. Teren was still inside with Coln. Edda had not left. The day was not over because I was done. That was becoming normal. I shifted my grip on the crutches. My hands hurt.

My shoulders hurt. Tomorrow afternoon there would be a real audience. Not people wandering in and out. Not Teren stopping scenes. Not a rehearsal where a bad line could simply be started again. I should have been worried about that. I was. Marek said something to Serra that I missed. She shoved him toward the gutter. He nearly went in. I laughed. Then we kept walking.

# CHAPTER 150

## THE WORK

River House had six rooms, one bathtub, two washbasins, three chairs that matched, and a woman at the front desk who had already decided she hated actors.

"We are not actors," Marek told her.

She looked at him.

"What are you?"

"Traveling cultural labor."

Serra said, "He's an actor." The woman handed Marek a key.

"Two."

"Two what?"

"Room."

"Which room?"

"Two."

Marek looked at the wooden tag. It said 2.

"Excellent."

I was too tired to enjoy this properly. The common room smelled like beer, wet wool, onions, and whatever had been cooked three hours earlier. Four men played cards beside the hearth. None of them looked up when we entered. A woman near the window was reading a letter. Someone laughed upstairs. The theatre people immediately scattered. Not all toward beds. Orin knew one of the card players. Of course he did. He stopped, said, "You're dead." The man looked up.

"So are you."

They shook hands. Iven asked the desk woman where food was. She pointed at a covered pot. He went there. Serra handed her key to Marek.

"Which room?"

"Three."

"You have three?"

"No. I have three."

"That is what I asked."

She stared at him. He gave the key back. She left. Not upstairs. Front door. Gone. I did not ask. Marek watched the door for a moment. Then he went upstairs. I stood in the middle of the common room with my bag. Nobody told me where I was sleeping. Fine. The desk woman looked at me.

"Name?"

"Greg."

She checked a page.

"Gregory?"

"Yes."

"Room one."

"Who else?"

"Pell."

"Anyone else?"

She checked.

"Maybe."

"What does maybe mean?"

"It means Teren paid for beds, not certainty."

"That is not how beds work."

She looked past me.

"Next."

There was no next. I went upstairs. Room one was at the end of the corridor and had two narrow beds, one window, one chair, and a washstand with a basin that leaned slightly toward the wall. Pell was not there. His bag was. Thread was. A shoe was. One sock hung over the chair. The other did not exist. I took the bed nearest the door. Not because I was selfish. Because the other required moving around the chair. Practical. I sat. Then I did nothing.

For perhaps a minute. Maybe five. My hands rested on my thighs. My shoulders lowered slowly. The room was quiet enough that I could hear someone downstairs arguing about cards. I took off my coat. Boot. Right boot. One. Efficient. Then trousers enough to deal with the wrapping on my left leg. The skin was warm. More irritated than morning. Not damaged. A little red where the wrapping had shifted during the day. I cleaned it. Dried it. Waited. Rewrapped. No drama. No revelation.

I was simply tired enough that tying cloth neatly took two attempts. The first looked wrong. I stared at it. Then almost redid it. No. It was secure. Comfortable. Fine. I left it. That felt more difficult than it should have. Someone knocked.

"Occupied."

The door opened. Marek looked in.

"That isn't what occupied means."

"I am half naked."

He looked down.

"Yes."

"Leave."

"Food."

"I ate."

"When?"

I thought.

"Bread."

"That's not food."

"It is literally food."

"Downstairs."

He left the door open. I threw the washcloth. Missed. It landed in the corridor.

"Fuck."

I had to get up. By the time I came downstairs, Pell had returned. He was carrying the red dress. Or part of it. Nessa followed carrying the rest. They did not appear to be staying at River House so much as colonizing it. Rinna had taken one end of the common table. Fabric covered half of it.

The card players had moved their game six inches and were pretending this had nothing to do with them. Orin was now playing.

"Thought you were dead," the man across from him said.

"Still winning."

"You owe me twelve."

"Dead men don't pay."

"That isn't the rule."

"It is where I come from."

I sat with Iven. He had found stew. Marek had found beer. Iven had both.

"Where?"

He pointed. I got stew. It was mostly potato. Good. I ate. Marek sat opposite me.

"Tomorrow."

I looked up.

"What?"

"Show."

"I know."

"You look worried."

"I am eating."

"You can do both."

"Apparently."

He drank. I said, "How much do we actually do this?"

"Eat?"

"Shows."

He thought.

"Depends."

Everyone in theatre answered everything with depends.

"On what?"

"Town. Money. Weather. Who's sick. Who hates Teren. Who Teren hates. Whether the hall is standing. Whether anyone comes."

Iven said, "Sometimes once."

"Once a day?"

"Once in a town."

Marek said, "Sometimes twice a day for six days." I stopped eating.

"Six?"

"Maybe."

"That is twelve shows."

"Yes."

"The same show?"

"Mostly."

"Mostly?"

Iven said, "Sometimes they pay for another." Marek said, "Sometimes someone dies." Iven looked at him.

"In the play."

"Usually."

I said, "When do you rehearse?" They both looked at me. Iven shrugged.

"When we can."

"That cannot be the system."

Marek leaned back.

"It is a very good system."

"No."

"Sometimes we get a week."

Iven said, "Luxury."

"Sometimes three days."

"Normal."

"Sometimes Teren says, 'You're the priest now.'"

I stared. Marek pointed at me.

"Shopkeeper."

"That was different."

"No."

"I had fourteen lines."

"You had fourteen lines because Meren wasn't there."

"Yes."

"Exactly."

Iven tore bread.

"Once I learned a duke during intermission."

I looked at him.

"During the show?"

"Yes."

"How many lines?"

"Thirty-something."

"That is not possible."

"I was bad."

Marek laughed. Iven said, "Very bad."

"What happened?"

"Second half."

"That is not an answer."

"That is what happened."

Marek leaned forward.

"That's the work."

I waited. He did not turn it into wisdom. Good. Iven said, "If you know the shape, you can fill."

"The shape?"

"Scene."

Marek said, "Who wants what. Who enters. Who leaves. Which line somebody actually needs." Iven said, "Don't invent too much." Marek said, "Unless they deserve it."

"Who is they?"

"Everyone."

I ate stew. This was horrifying. Also--- I understood why nobody had treated Shopkeeper as remarkable. They had not discovered I could act. They had needed a Shopkeeper. I had been nearby. That was less flattering. Better.

"Do you get paid every show?"

"Yes," Iven said.

Marek lifted his beer.

"Which is why tomorrow matters."

"Because money."

"Because money."

Iven raised his cup too.

"Money."

I had water. I raised it.

"Money."

Marek looked offended.

"That is water."

"I know."

"Tomorrow night, not water."

"Why?"

He stared.

"Money."

Iven nodded.

"If both shows go."

Marek said, "Both shows go."

"If nobody dies."

"In the play."

"Preferably."

I smiled. There it was. Work. Not rehearsal. Not learning. Tomorrow afternoon, we did the show and got paid. Then we did it again. Then apparently people drank. Maybe a lot. That seemed reasonable. Across the room, Nessa said, "No." Pell said, "It will hold."

"No."

"It held today."

"Today nobody wore it."

Rinna said, "She wore it."

"For six minutes."

"Still wore."

Nessa pulled the red fabric toward her. A card player lifted his beer before the dress swept through where it had been. Nobody apologized. The front door opened. Teren came in. Everyone noticed. Not immediately. A few seconds. Then Marek lifted his cup.

"Money?"

Teren looked exhausted.

"Yes."

Marek stood. Actually stood.

"Money."

Several people cheered. Not the inn people. Mostly theatre. Teren held up one hand.

"Tomorrow."

Marek sat.

"Cruel."

"Two shows. Afternoon and night. Gate terms are done."

"Good terms?" Orin asked from cards.

"No."

"Bad?"

"Done."

That was apparently enough. Teren crossed to the pot. The desk woman stopped him.

"That costs."

"I paid food."

"You paid rooms."

"I paid food."

"Not here."

Teren stared. Then took out money. She took it. He got stew. Nobody rescued him. I said, "What about Meren?" Teren ate one spoonful before answering.

"No Meren."

"So I do Shopkeeper both?"

"Yes."

"Tomorrow night too."

"Yes."

"Both Sword."

"Yes."

"That is four---"

"Two shows."

"I know, but four roles."

"Two roles twice."

"Yes."

Teren ate. I waited. He looked up.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Good."

Three seconds. He went back to eating. Marek pointed at him.

"See?"

"What?"

"Work."

Teren said without looking up, "If you're explaining work, stop." Marek stopped. For nearly a minute. Then he said, "After tomorrow night---" Teren pointed his spoon. Marek drank. Fine. I finished stew. People kept arriving. Davin came late and ate standing. He had grease on one sleeve.

A local man came with him, said something about a wheel, ate bread, and left again. Serra did not return. Nessa and Pell continued sewing. Rinna disappeared upstairs with two dresses and came back with neither. Orin lost money at cards. He claimed otherwise. Iven fell asleep in his chair. Not metaphorically. His spoon was still in his hand. The desk woman took the bowl away before he could drop it. Apparently she hated actors selectively. I lasted another half hour. Maybe.

Marek began telling a story about a show where a horse entered through the audience. I heard the beginning. Then the horse became two horses. Then I stopped believing him. Then I stopped caring. I went upstairs. Pell came in much later. I woke when the door opened. He moved quietly. Not carefully. There was a difference. He put something on the chair. Undressed. Lay down. I said, "Red dress?" He stopped.

"What?"

"Done?"

"No."

"Morning?"

"No."

"No?"

"No."

"What happens?"

"Blue."

"Oh."

He got into bed.

"Good night."

"Good night."

A moment.

"Pell."

"What?"

"How often do you actually finish costumes before shows?"

Silence.

Then:

"Yes."

"That is not---"

He was already breathing differently. Fine. I slept. Morning arrived because someone pounded on the door.

"Up."

I opened my eyes. Pell was gone. His bed looked as though nobody had slept in it. The pounding came again.

"Greg."

"Teren?"

"Food. Hall in forty."

I sat up.

"Forty?"

Teren had already moved to the next door.

"Up!"

Someone farther down shouted, "Fuck you!" Teren shouted back, "Paid today!" A cheer came through the wall. I laughed. Then stood. My body had opinions. Shoulders stiff. Hands better. Right hip tight. Left leg fine after sleep. I washed. Wrapped. Dressed. The sock on the chair was still there. Not mine. I left it. Downstairs, breakfast was bread, eggs, and chaos. Serra was there. I had no idea when she had returned. She sat with Rinna, drinking something hot. Marek had one eye open. Iven had neither.

Orin was already gone. Nessa was not there. Pell was not there. Davin was not there. Teren stood by the door with a list.

"Eat."

"I am."

"Faster."

"I just sat down."

"Then you have nowhere to go."

He moved on. Serra looked at me.

"You're Shopkeeper twice."

"Yes."

"You know?"

"Yes."

"Meren's not coming."

"I know."

"Good."

She drank. I waited. She did not explain why she was telling me something I knew. Maybe checking. Maybe tired.

"Are you doing Princess the same as last night?"

Her eyes narrowed. I smiled.

"Joke."

"Bad."

"Good."

She almost smiled. Then Rinna said something quietly to her. Serra turned. Conversation over. I ate. At the hall, there was no rehearsal. That was the first thing I noticed. People worked. Benches were set. Lamps checked. Floor swept. Costumes moved. Davin and two local workers brought the long box out of the dry room and carried it toward backstage. I watched. Still closed. Fine. Nessa was in the green room. Red dress across her lap. Still sewing.

"You said blue."

She did not look up.

"Go away."

"Right."

I went away. Teren was onstage.

"Greg."

"Yes."

"Shopkeeper entrance."

I went to the wing.

"Not run. Show me."

I positioned. He looked.

"Crutch."

I moved it.

"Other."

I moved the other.

"Fine."

"What about Sword?"

"Same."

"Spoon?"

He looked at me.

"What?"

"Serra's line."

"Oh. If she says it."

"So keep?"

"If she says it."

"What do I---"

He was gone. That was all the rehearsal I got. Iven passed carrying his debtor coat.

"Have my coat?"

"No."

"Good."

"Are you going to say it?"

"What?"

"The line."

"What line?"

I stared. He smiled. Then left. Fuck him. The hall filled slowly. This time people paid. That changed everything. Not the room. Us. Marek came backstage with two cups. He handed one to Orin.

"After."

Orin sniffed it.

"Now."

"After."

"Coward."

They drank anyway. Nessa slapped the cup out of Marek's hand when he came near the costumes.

"After."

"Everyone is obsessed with after."

"Because before you are useful."

Marek looked at me.

"See?"

I did. The show was not a test. It was not the culmination of rehearsal. It was the thing people had paid for. Everything else existed to get us here. And now we had to do it. Teren appeared backstage.

"Doors closed in five."

Someone said, "Already?"

"Yes."

"Where's Serra?"

"Here," Serra said from behind him.

"Where's Iven?"

"Here."

"Orin?"

"Dead."

"Here," Orin said.

"Nessa?"

"Busy."

"Pell?"

"Busy."

"Davin?"

No answer. Teren said, "Fine." That apparently meant Davin was where he needed to be. He looked at me.

"Greg."

"Yes."

"Don't wait for yesterday."

I frowned.

"That is almost advice."

"Don't get used to it."

He left. The house noise changed. People settling. Talking. Benches scraping. A cough. A child being told to sit. Someone calling to someone across the room. Then the front doors shut. Not silence. Different noise. Contained. Marek rolled his shoulders. Iven adjusted his coat. Serra stood with one hand on the Sword's scabbard. Nobody looked ceremonial. Nobody gave a speech. Nessa still had a needle in her mouth. Pell ran past carrying a shoe. A local worker swore because one lamp smoked. Teren shouted, "Places." People moved. So did I.

My Shopkeeper scene was later. Sword first. I went to the wall opening. Crutches positioned. Hands ready. I could not see the stage. Good. The opening scene began. No stopping. A line came wrong. Nobody stopped. Someone entered early. Nobody stopped. The audience laughed at something I had never thought was funny. Nobody stopped. The show kept going. I listened. My cue was coming. My heart was beating too fast. That was fine. Apparently that was work too. Serra's voice reached me through the wall. Different again. Of course.

I smiled. Then listened.

# CHAPTER 151

## THE SHOW

Then listened. Serra's line came. Not the line I expected. Close enough that I knew where we were. Different enough that I nearly answered the old one. I waited. One beat. Not for laughter. For her. She said, "And if I decide you're more trouble than you're worth?" My cue.

"You already stole me. Complaining now seems dishonest."

A laugh came from somewhere near the middle. Small. I let it go. Serra shifted. Fabric brushed wood.

"You call this stealing?"

"I was on a wall."

"You were unattended."

"I am a legendary weapon, not a pie."

That got more. I had not planned pie. Good. I heard Marek move somewhere beyond the opening. Too early. He was not supposed to enter yet. Serra heard him too.

"Your Majesty," she said.

That was not her line. Marek answered immediately.

"My dear."

He was in. Fine. Apparently the King was here now. The scene was supposed to give Serra another exchange with Sword before he entered. That exchange contained the information that she intended to use me against him. We needed that. I knew we needed that.

I also had no idea how to put it back without announcing that we had missed it. Serra did. She said to Marek, "I was just telling your sword what I intend to do with him." Marek said, "My sword?" There. Fixed. No pause. No panic. The missing information was back. I almost admired it enough to miss my next line. Almost.

"I object to the possessive."

Marek said, "You object to everything."

"Not everything."

"What don't you object to?"

I had nothing. Serra said, "Being stolen."

"I objected immediately."

The audience laughed. Marek crossed closer. I could hear his shoes.

"Give him back."

Serra said, "No." That was supposed to be later. Fine. Marek said, "You cannot simply take a royal weapon."

"I did."

"You cannot keep it."

"I am."

"You see what I endure?" Marek asked me.

"Yes."

I waited half a breath.

"You."

A bigger laugh. Marek made a wounded sound. The room opened. I felt it. Did not chase it. Serra continued. We reached the return threat differently. Not "Perhaps I should return you." Instead she said, "He seems to want you." Marek said, "Naturally." I said, "That is not what I heard." The laugh was smaller. Fine. Serra said, "Would you prefer I melt you?" There it was. Not Marek. Her. Different again. I said, "Into what?" She paused. I knew what she could say. Spoon.

The audience from last night might remember. Some of them were probably here. I waited for her answer. Serra said, "A chamber pot." The room broke. I did too. Not aloud. Almost. Marek said, "That is my sword." Serra said, "Then you may empty him." More laughter. I had no line. None. Three possible answers arrived. All of them wanted the laugh. I discarded them.

"Put me back on the wall."

That was enough. Not huge. Enough. We moved. The scene survived. Later, I missed a cue anyway. Not because I was watching Serra. Because someone backstage dropped something metal and my attention went there. Serra covered without looking toward me.

"Have you nothing to say?"

"Yes."

I spoke the line. Late. The audience never knew. Maybe. Then the scene was over. Serra came through the wing breathing hard. I said, "Chamber pot?" She said, "Spoon was yesterday." Then Nessa grabbed her.

"Stop."

"What?"

"Back."

Serra turned. A seam had opened beneath one arm. Not much. Enough. Nessa shoved a needle through fabric while Serra still wore the dress.

"Don't stab me."

"Then stop breathing."

"That seems excessive."

"Arm."

Serra lifted it. Marek came offstage behind us.

"Chamber pot?"

"Fuck off," Serra said.

"That was excellent."

Nessa said, "Hold this." Marek held fabric. He stopped being King immediately. I moved because someone said, "Move." A local worker passed carrying a lamp. The show continued. I could hear Orin onstage. Different scene. Different problem. He spoke a line. Silence. Then another. A woman answered. Wrong line. I knew because I had heard the scene enough. Orin answered the wrong line as though it were right. She froze. He walked toward her. Not threatening. Giving her something.

"Which is why," he said, "you sent for the physician before the letter arrived."

Her face changed. I could see them through a gap now. She understood.

"Yes," she said. "Before the letter."

Back. The scene found its road again. No one applauded the repair. They did not know it had happened. That was probably the point. I had time before Shopkeeper. Not much. I drank water. A boy from local crew ran past.

"Where's the blue jar?"

Nobody answered. He ran back.

"Blue jar?"

Pell shouted from the green room, "Broken."

"When?"

"Now."

"What do I use?"

"Brown."

"It's supposed to be poison."

"Then poisonous brown."

The boy disappeared. Iven arrived wearing the debtor coat. I looked at it. He saw me look.

"No."

"I didn't say anything."

"Your face."

"Davin says that."

"Davin is right."

"Are we doing coat?"

"No."

"Good."

"Maybe."

"I hate you."

"Good."

Teren appeared between us.

"Shopkeeper. Two minutes."

"Anything changed?" I asked.

"Yes."

"What?"

"Shorten after constable."

"How?"

"Be shorter."

Then he was gone. Iven said, "Excellent direction."

"Shut up."

We waited. My hands were sweating. I wiped one on my trousers. The scene before ours went long. I knew because Iven sighed. Then someone skipped six lines and it became short. Iven looked at me.

"Go."

"That isn't my cue."

"It is now."

He entered. Fuck. I followed. Correctly enough. The audience changed when I stepped out. Not because of me. Because stage light was hotter than backstage and the house became a dark shape beyond it. Faces in the first rows. Bodies farther back. Sound. Someone coughed. A child whispered. Iven turned.

"Master, I can explain."

Not the eleven days line. Fine.

"How much money do you have?"

He stopped.

"That's not an explanation."

"It is the part I care about."

A laugh. Iven put a hand to his chest.

"You reduce friendship to coin."

"We are not friends."

"Then why have you extended me credit?"

"Professional error."

More laughter. Good. Iven paced. Different blocking. I adjusted. He said, "My uncle---"

"No."

"I haven't told you---"

"No."

"You don't even know which uncle."

"None of them."

"My mother's brother is extremely wealthy."

"Then he can afford your debt."

"He is also dead."

"Then he is late."

That landed. Bigger than I expected. I almost smiled. Did not. Iven did. Barely. Then he said, "You are a deeply unpleasant man." There. From rehearsal. I knew "Pay me" worked. The answer sat ready. Too ready. I said it anyway.

"Pay me."

The audience laughed. Good. Not as much as before. Fine. We continued. Iven did not give me the follow line from rehearsal. Instead he said, "I would, but you've taken my purse." I stared. He had a purse. Visible. I could say coat. No.

"You're holding it."

He looked down.

"So I am."

The audience laughed. He tucked it behind his back.

"Now I'm not."

"That is not how theft works."

"How would you know?"

"Because I charge for it."

Nothing. Dead. Bad line. Move. Iven moved.

"Then I will return tomorrow."

"With money."

"With dignity."

"Keep the dignity. It has no resale value."

Better. We found them again. Then the constable did not enter. His cue came. Nothing. Iven looked toward the entrance. I looked too. Bad. The audience saw. Iven said, "Well?" I said, "I was waiting for the law."

"Why?"

"I enjoy disappointment."

A laugh. Still no constable. We needed him because he broke the argument and delivered the notice that moved Iven into the next scene. I did not know the notice. Iven did. He walked toward the entrance.

"Perhaps I should fetch him."

I said, "If you find him, tell him you're under arrest."

"For what?"

I had nothing useful.

"Debt."

"That is not a crime."

"Today is improving."

The constable burst in. Late. Hat sideways.

"Stop!"

Iven turned.

"For debt?"

The constable had no idea what he meant.

"No."

The audience laughed. The constable recovered.

"For disturbing the peace."

I said, "Take him." Iven said, "Him?" The constable pointed at me.

"You."

That was wrong. Very wrong. I looked at him. He looked at me. Iven looked delighted.

"Excellent," he said.

The audience laughed. The constable realized.

"No. Him."

He pointed at Iven. Too late. I said, "Professional error." The audience laughed harder than the first time. Iven put out his hands. The constable delivered the notice. We were back. The scene ended. I got offstage. The constable actor grabbed my arm.

"Sorry."

"Why me?"

"I saw one leg."

"What?"

"I don't know."

Then he ran because he had another entrance. Iven came through laughing.

"You."

"Fuck you."

"You should have been arrested."

"For what?"

"Professional error."

I hated him. I was also laughing. Teren passed.

"Good."

"Which part?"

"Done part."

He kept going. That was apparently my review. The rest of the show happened around me. Not to me. That was different. I watched some. Missed more. Nessa repaired Serra again. Pell changed a hem while the actress wearing it stood on a box.

Davin appeared backstage with a hammer, disappeared beneath the stage, and three minutes later the loose board stopped making noise. I never saw what he did. The poisonous brown jar went onstage. A man drank from it. The audience accepted that brown was poison.

Marek forgot a name and called another character "my loyal friend" until someone supplied it. Orin came offstage furious.

"What?"

I asked.

"They laughed."

"At what?"

He looked offended.

"My death."

From the house came applause. Orin said, "Animals." Then went to change clothes. Serra passed me carrying the Sword.

"Your death was funny."

Orin shouted from the dressing room, "Fuck you." She smiled. The final act tightened. Not because anyone said so. People were tired. Lines moved faster. Entrances came closer. A scene that had dragged in rehearsal suddenly worked because nobody gave it room to drag. Then a chair broke. Marek sat. The chair folded. He vanished. The audience screamed. Then laughed. Marek, from the floor, said, "I have been betrayed." Serra said, "By furniture." He stood without the chair. The scene continued.

A local worker dragged the broken pieces off during the next entrance. No one mentioned it again. Then we were at the end. I knew because everyone backstage began gathering near the wings. Not sentimental. Ready. Final line. Pause. Applause. Real. Louder than open rehearsal. Not enormous. Enough to fill the room. We went out. I stood with crutches. Sword voice belonged nowhere now. Shopkeeper gone. Just me. People clapped. Mara's father shouted, "Roof boy!" Fuck. I bowed anyway. Then we left. The moment ended immediately.

"Water."

"Where's the red dress?"

"Don't sit there."

"Who has my shoe?"

"Move the bench."

"Gate count?"

"Later."

"Where's Teren?"

"Coln."

Of course. I drank water. My shirt stuck to my back. My hands shook slightly from work and heat. Serra sat on the floor while Nessa removed the damaged sleeve. Marek had a scrape on one palm from the chair. Iven was eating bread already. Orin was still offended by his death.

"How long?" I asked.

Iven looked at the wall clock.

"Three hours."

"Until?"

"Doors."

I stared. He tore bread.

"We do it again."

"Yes."

"Same show."

"Hopefully not."

I understood what he meant now. Not different play. Different show. Teren came backstage carrying a small leather purse and several folded slips.

"Pay."

People appeared. Fast. Faster than for notes. Marek first. Of course. Teren handed coins out by name. Not equal piles for everyone. I noticed. Did not ask. Different jobs. Different arrangements. Maybe debts. Maybe advances. Not mine.

"Gregory."

I went over. He put coins in my hand. I looked down. My first payment from the troupe. Not promised. Not theoretical. Money. For the show I had just done. Sword. Shopkeeper. One show. I counted. Teren said, "Don't."

"Why?"

"Because you're blocking everyone."

I moved. Counted elsewhere. Correct. Marek appeared over my shoulder.

"Money."

"Yes."

"Tonight, more money."

"Yes."

"Then beer."

"I am tired."

"Beer."

"I have another show."

"So do I."

"That argues against beer."

"It argues for beer after."

Serra, from the floor, said, "He's new." Marek nodded solemnly.

"True."

I put the coins away. Three hours. Eat. Fix. Drink water. Do it again. Nessa called, "Greg." I looked over. She threw something. I caught it badly against my chest. Thread.

"Pell."

"Where?"

She pointed. I took it. Apparently celebration was later. I went to find Pell.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 152

## THE SECOND SHOW

Pell was under a table. I found his boots first.

"Nessa sent me."

"Condolences."

"What are you doing?"

"Looking for a needle."

"She gave me thread."

"Wonderful. We can start a collection."

I lowered myself enough to see him. He was on one knee beneath the costume table with one arm behind a trunk.

"There are needles on the table."

"Not that needle."

"What needle?"

"The long one."

"They have lengths?"

He looked at me.

"Yes."

"Fine."

I held out the thread. He did not take it.

"Put it there."

"Where?"

"There."

He pointed somewhere behind me. There were four piles of fabric, two boxes, a pair of shoes, three cups, and something that looked like a dead bird but was probably trim.

"Specificity is useful."

"Red."

"Half the room is red."

"The other red."

I put the thread beside a red bundle. Pell crawled farther under the table. I stood. Nessa appeared.

"Did you find him?"

"Yes."

"Did you give him the thread?"

"He refused to physically accept it."

Pell said from beneath the table, "Found it." He emerged holding a needle. Nessa took it from him.

"You had one."

"Not that one."

"That is mine."

"Yes."

"You stole my needle?"

"Borrowed."

"You were looking for the needle you stole from me?"

"I forgot I stole it."

Nessa closed her eyes. I left. Three hours sounded like time until I watched theatre people use it. The broken chair disappeared. Another chair appeared. A local worker sat on it hard three times, declared it acceptable, then marked one leg with chalk anyway.

The poison jar became blue again because somebody found another blue jar in storage. Pell argued that brown had worked. The local boy said brown looked like gravy. Pell said poison could be gravy. Nobody cared. Davin and two local men shifted a bench near the rear doors. I started toward them. Davin saw me.

"No."

"I wasn't---"

"No."

I changed direction. Fine. Iven was asleep on three folded curtains in the green room. Orin was outside smoking with the man from River House. Marek had acquired food. Serra was gone. Again. Nessa worked. Pell worked. Rinna came through carrying a basket of damp stockings, put it down, took two cups of water, and left without the stockings. Five minutes later someone shouted for the stockings. Nobody knew whose they were. I ate because Edda put a bowl in my hands.

"What is it?"

"Food."

"Yes."

"Eat it."

It was beans with bits of pork. Good. I sat on the kitchen threshold because the chairs were occupied by fabric. My first show money was still in my pocket. I touched the purse once to make sure it was there. Then again ten minutes later. Still there. Marek found me.

"Rich man."

"No."

"Paid actor."

"Technically."

"Dangerous."

He sat on the floor and stole a piece of pork from my bowl.

"Buy your own."

"I am saving."

"For what?"

"Beer."

"You were just paid."

"Exactly."

He stole another piece. I moved the bowl.

"After tonight," he said, "we go out."

"Who?"

"Yes."

"That is not a person."

"It can be."

"I am tired."

"So is everyone."

"That does not improve the idea."

"It improves the drinking."

I ate. Marek leaned against the wall. He looked tired too. Actually tired. Not theatrical tired. His eyes were red at the edges. The cut on his jaw had opened slightly during the show.

"Does that hurt?"

"What?"

I pointed. He touched his jaw.

"Oh."

"You forgot?"

"Yes."

"How?"

He shrugged.

"Busy."

Then he closed his eyes. Within perhaps thirty seconds he was asleep sitting against the wall. I finished my food quietly. People did not prepare for the second show. Not in any way I would have recognized as preparation. They repaired damage. They restored objects to approximately where they belonged. They ate. They slept. They argued. They disappeared. They came back. At some point Serra returned carrying a paper packet.

She gave one piece of something fried to Nessa, one to Rinna, kept one, and walked past me.

"Where did you get that?"

"Outside."

"Useful."

"Yes."

She kept walking. I did not ask where outside. Progress. I went to the stage. The house was empty again. Local workers swept between benches. A man adjusted lamp shutters. The chalk mark over the bad board remained, though Davin had stopped the noise. I put my crutches where they belonged for Shopkeeper. Then moved them. Then moved them back. No. I left. I was not rehearsing my crutches.

I found a quiet corner behind the green room and sat on the floor. For perhaps twenty minutes I did nothing. It was excellent. Then Iven sat beside me. He did not speak. Five minutes. Maybe more. I said, "Are you asleep?"

"No."

"You look asleep."

"So do you."

"I am talking."

"Unfortunate."

We sat. Then he said, "Don't do the dead uncle." I looked at him.

"Why?"

"Because you want to."

"I do not."

"You do."

"It worked."

"Yes."

"That is not why."

"It is exactly why."

I disliked him.

"What are you going to say?"

"No idea."

"That is irresponsible."

He smiled without opening his eyes.

"Paid actor."

"Fuck you."

"Later."

Then Teren called him and he got up. I stayed. Doors in one hour. Then forty minutes. Then twenty. The hall changed again. The night audience was louder before they even sat. More groups. More men coming in together. More women dressed for evening rather than errands.

People who had eaten and people who had clearly begun drinking before arriving. Someone in the house sang three lines of a song until another person told him to shut up. Marek heard it backstage.

"Good crowd."

"That sounded terrible."

"Exactly."

Nessa finally abandoned the red dress. Not dramatically. She folded it. Put it in a trunk.

"Blue," she said.

Serra was already wearing blue.

"Excellent decision," Serra said.

Nessa stared at her. Serra left. The long box remained closed in the rear room. I had stopped thinking about it. Mostly. Teren moved through backstage.

"Places."

Again. No speech. No notes. No discussion of the afternoon. Marek had a small cup. I smelled it.

"That is not water."

"No."

"You said after."

"I said beer after."

"What is that?"

"Not beer."

He drank. I looked at Teren. Teren saw.

"Half?"

Marek showed the cup. Teren said, "Fine."

"That is allowed?"

Teren looked at me.

"Are you asking permission?"

"No."

"Good."

He left. Marek handed me the cup. I smelled it again. Sharp.

"No."

"New."

"I have to be a sword."

"Exactly."

I gave it back. Serra passed. She took the cup, drank, handed it to Marek, kept walking. I stared after her. Marek said, "Experienced."

"Apparently."

The doors shut. Second show. Same play. Not the same. I knew that before my first line. The audience laughed earlier. At entrances. At faces. At Marek walking like the King owned the floor. They liked Orin before he spoke. Somebody shouted something I could not make out. Orin answered, "Later." The house laughed. I waited at the wall opening. Serra began. Her Princess was faster tonight. Not happier. Sharper. She cut through Marek's first interruption without giving him space. My cue came. I spoke. Good. Next.

The pie line approached. I could feel it. She gave me almost the same setup. I said, "I am a legendary weapon, not---" Pie. I knew pie. Pie had worked.

"---luggage."

Nothing. Not nothing. One laugh. Fine. Why had I changed it? Because I had been afraid of repeating pie. That was just another way of thinking about pie. Fuck. Serra said, "You complain like luggage." The audience laughed. Of course they did. I said, "Luggage is carried with respect." More. We moved. Marek entered on time. This was somehow more difficult. I had prepared for him being wrong. He was correct. Serra said the actual line. I nearly missed it. Answered. Fine. The melting exchange never happened. No spoon.

No chamber pot. Gone. The scene took another road entirely because Marek said, "You belong to the crown." I said, "Which part?" He stopped.

"What?"

"The crown. Which part owns me?"

"All of it."

"That seems administratively difficult."

Small laugh. Marek said, "I am the administration." Serra made a noise. Not a line. A dismissive breath. The audience laughed harder at that than anything I had said. Marek turned toward her.

"Do you have something to add?"

"No."

Huge laugh. I could hear her smile. I could not see it. We continued. Later I spoke over her. Just once. I knew immediately. Could not take it back. She waited. Then said her line after mine as though I had interrupted her. Which I had. The audience understood the relationship as Sword being rude. Useful. Accidental. Not mine. Offstage, Serra said, "You stepped on me."

"I know."

"Good."

Then she was gone. That was the note. Shopkeeper came faster tonight. Or felt faster. Iven was awake now. Too awake. He entered carrying no purse. No coat either.

"What happened to your coat?"

That was my actual first line. He looked down at himself.

"Sold it."

"To pay me?"

"No."

"Then buy it back."

The audience laughed. Iven said, "You have a narrow understanding of commerce."

"I have a profitable understanding."

Nothing. Bad. Move. He said, "My aunt---"

"Yesterday you had an uncle."

He blinked. That was not in the play. The audience laughed. Iven said, "He died." More. I had walked directly into the dead uncle. He knew it. I knew it. The audience did not. I said, "Convenient."

"He would disagree."

"Then summon him."

"That costs extra."

I almost laughed. Iven had stolen Shopkeeper from me. Fine.

"Everything costs extra."

"There you are."

"What?"

"The man I was warned about."

"By whom?"

"My aunt."

"You just invented her."

Iven paused. Then smiled. The audience saw it.

"She is very new."

The room went. I waited. Not perfectly. Long enough.

Then:

"How much money does she have?"

More laughter. Good. We had found something. Not yesterday. Tonight. The constable entered on time. Correctly. Pointed at Iven. Nobody laughed. He delivered the line. Fine. Apparently competence was less funny. The scene moved toward its end. Then a shout came from the house.

"Arrest the shopkeeper!"

I stopped. Iven looked toward the voice. The constable looked at me. No. Do not. The audience began laughing before any of us spoke. I said to the constable, "Don't." He raised both hands.

"I learned."

Bigger laugh. Iven said, "Professional growth." I said, "Pay me." It landed harder than either previous time. Not because the line was better. Because everything before it had changed. Then we were out. Backstage, Iven grabbed my shoulder.

"Dead uncle."

"You forced it."

"You asked about the coat."

"You weren't wearing one."

"Exactly."

"I hate you."

"Good show."

It was. Not perfect. Not even close. But good. The night crowd gave more and took more. They talked. They shouted. They laughed over lines. Marek played with them until Teren hissed, "Scene," from the wing. Orin ignored a shouted suggestion completely. Serra answered one.

A local worker had to replace a lamp during a scene because it began smoking. The actress nearest it crossed downstage without being told, changing the whole picture while the worker reached behind the curtain. Nobody stopped. The replacement chair survived. Marek looked disappointed. During Orin's death, someone in the audience shouted, "Again!" Orin, lying dead, lifted one finger. The room exploded. Backstage afterward he said, "Animals." But he was smiling. Near the end, fatigue arrived all at once. Not just mine. Everyone. Lines got shorter. People stopped adding.

Marek stopped playing with the audience. Serra's Princess became almost severe. Iven missed a word and did not bother repairing it because nobody needed it. I understood that now. Not every missing thing needed rescue. Only the things holding something else up. The final scene came. Then applause. Louder. Night people. We bowed. Someone shouted for chamber pot. Serra looked at me. I looked at her. She bowed again. Nothing else. Good. Backstage became noise. Real noise. Not work noise. Different. We were still working, but the edge had broken.

Someone opened a bottle before Teren paid anyone. Nessa said, "Away from the costumes." The bottle moved six feet. Apparently sufficient. Teren appeared with the purse.

"Pay."

Again everyone materialized. My second payment felt less strange. Still good. Teren put the coins in my hand.

"Gregory."

"Thank you."

He had already called the next name. I moved before being told. Improvement. Marek appeared.

"Money."

"Yes."

"Twice."

"Yes."

"Beer."

I looked around. Pell was sitting on the floor with his back against a trunk, eyes closed. Nessa had the red dress in her lap again. Rinna was counting something on her fingers with a local woman. Davin was nowhere. Iven was drinking from the bottle.

Orin was arguing with someone from the audience through the backstage door about whether dead men could hear requests. Serra had disappeared. Teren was still paying people. I was exhausted. My shoulders hurt. My hands were tired. My shirt smelled terrible. I had money in my pocket. More money than I had this morning. For two shows. Tomorrow--- I did not know what tomorrow was. That felt important. Marek put an arm around my shoulders. I nearly hit him with a crutch.

"Careful."

"Beer."

"I heard you."

"Then move."

"Where?"

He grinned.

"Outside."

We went. The street beyond the hall was dark except for lamps, windows, and the river reflecting pieces of both. People from the show were still outside talking. A woman called Marek's name. He called hers back. I did not know her. Someone grabbed Orin from behind and nearly got elbowed. Iven came out carrying the bottle. Pell did not. Nessa definitely did not. Teren was still inside. Davin was probably fixing something because Davin was always fixing something. Serra was nowhere I could see. Marek pointed downriver.

"First one."

"What?"

"Drink."

"There are three taverns."

"Yes."

"Which one?"

"Yes."

I laughed. Then followed him. Celebration, apparently, had arrived.

# CHAPTER 153

## THE MONEY

The first tavern was full. Marek opened the door, looked inside, and said, "No."

"You said first one."

"I was wrong."

"That was fast."

"I improve."

Iven walked into my back with the bottle.

"Why are we stopped?"

"Marek has standards."

"Since when?"

"Tonight."

Marek shut the door. A man inside shouted his name before it closed. Marek kept walking.

"You know him?" I asked.

"No."

"He knew you."

"Common problem."

The second tavern had music. Not good music. Still music. A fiddle, a drum, and a woman singing loudly enough that quality had become less important than commitment. The windows were open to the river. Light spilled across the street in yellow blocks. People stood outside with cups because there was nowhere left to sit. Marek stopped.

"Yes."

Iven said, "Too loud."

"Yes."

"That wasn't approval."

Marek went in. We followed. The room smelled like beer, hot bodies, fried onions, river damp, and smoke. Someone had moved two tables against a wall to make space near the musicians. Nobody was dancing exactly. Several people were failing to stand still. A woman near the door saw Marek.

"King!"

He bowed.

"Citizen."

"You owe me money."

He straightened.

"I have never seen you before."

"You borrowed four coppers from me three years ago."

Marek looked at her. Then at me.

"Local history."

She held out her hand. He paid her. Iven laughed so hard he had to lean against the wall. The woman bit one of the coins.

"Interest."

"No."

"Five years."

"You said three."

"Interest."

"That is not how---"

She took another coin from his hand while he argued. Then kissed his cheek.

"Good show."

She disappeared into the room. I stared. Marek wiped his cheek.

"Do not."

"I said nothing."

"Your face."

"Iven says that."

"Iven is right."

Iven was still laughing. We found a table because Orin already had one. Of course. He sat with the man from River House, two women I did not know, and a narrow man with silver rings on three fingers. Four cups and a deck of cards occupied the center. Orin pointed at us.

"Late."

"We left before you," Marek said.

"Yes."

"How?"

Orin shrugged. The man from River House moved his chair enough to make room for Iven. Nobody moved for me. I looked around. A stool stood near the wall. I got it. Marek shouted toward the bar, "Four!" I said, "Three." He looked at me.

"You are here."

"I can buy mine."

He considered.

"Five!"

"That is worse."

A server appeared carrying cups. Not because Marek had shouted. She was already coming. She put one in front of Orin, one in front of the silver-ringed man, and two at another table. Marek watched them go.

"Betrayal."

The server returned.

"What?"

"Four beers."

"Pay."

Marek pointed at me.

"No."

She looked at me. I said, "One."

"Coward," Marek said.

"I am buying one."

"That is how it starts."

The server named a price. I reached into my pocket. For the first time, I spent money I had earned by being a sword and a shopkeeper. The coin looked exactly like every other coin. Good. I gave it to her. She gave me change. Also ordinary. Better. Marek paid for his and Iven's. Orin already had one.

The server looked at the fifth empty place Marek had apparently ordered for. Marek said, "Future." She left. I drank. Beer. Not terrible. Not good. Cold enough. I had expected something. I did not know what. My first troupe money had purchased beer. There should have been a lesson. There was beer. I drank again. Orin's friend said, "Roof." I looked at him.

"No."

He grinned.

"Old man told half the street."

"Excellent."

Marek turned.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Roof?"

"Nothing."

Iven said, "He has another role."

"Fuck you."

Orin said, "Roof?" I drank. The silver-ringed man dealt cards.

"Playing?"

"No."

"Yes," Marek said.

"I said no."

"You don't know the game."

"Exactly."

"Best time."

"No."

The woman beside Orin said, "He's right."

"Which one?"

"Both."

Fine. I watched. For three hands. Then the silver-ringed man dealt me cards anyway. I looked at them.

"What am I doing?"

"Losing," Orin said.

That I understood. The game involved matching something, hiding something else, and lying. Possibly. Everyone lied constantly, including about the rules. I lost two coins. Then won one. Then lost three because Marek told me a rule that did not exist.

"That cannot be allowed."

"It happened."

"You invented it."

"Improvisation."

"No."

Orin said, "Don't use theatre words to cheat." Marek looked offended.

"You cheat."

"Professionally."

"That is worse."

"Yes."

The musicians finished a song. Half the room cheered. The singer drank from someone else's cup. Then started another before the fiddle player was ready. He joined on the second line. Nobody cared. A group from the show recognized Iven. One man pointed.

"Debtor!"

Iven raised his cup. The man shouted, "Pay him!" People around him laughed. Iven pointed at me.

"There."

Several faces turned. I became Shopkeeper for approximately two seconds. A woman near the bar shouted, "Arrest him!" The room laughed. I raised both hands.

"No law."

That got enough. Then they went back to drinking. Good. Marek leaned close.

"You could get free beer from that."

"I have money."

He stared at me.

"That is not the point."

"What is the point?"

"Free beer."

He left the table. Within five minutes he had free beer. I did not know from whom. I kept mine. The room grew louder. Not suddenly. Layer by layer. More people came in after the show. Some had been audience. Some had not. The musicians changed. The drummer left and another man sat down without discussion. The singer vanished. A boy with a wooden flute took her place for two songs. Iven joined a group near the window. Orin kept playing cards. Marek moved everywhere. He knew nobody and everyone.

At one point he was arm-wrestling a dockworker. At another he was telling three women a story with his hands. Then one of the women slapped his shoulder and walked away laughing. Then he was gone. I asked Orin, "Where did Marek go?" Orin looked around.

"No idea."

"You were looking at him."

"I stopped."

Reasonable. I played another hand. Lost. The silver-ringed man said, "You think too long."

"I am learning."

"That is why."

I looked at Orin. He shrugged.

"Sometimes."

I lost again. Fine. I stopped playing. The woman beside Orin had been quiet most of the time. She wore a green scarf around her hair and had a scar through one eyebrow. She said, "Sword." I looked at her.

"Yes?"

"You were better at night."

I waited. She drank. That was apparently the whole statement.

"Thank you."

"Shopkeeper worse."

"Thank you."

Orin laughed. She looked at him.

"You died badly."

Orin stopped laughing.

"I died correctly."

"You fell before the knife touched you."

"It was going to."

"Coward."

Orin turned to me.

"Do you see what I endure?"

I said, "Again." The woman laughed. Orin pointed at me.

"Traitor."

I was enjoying myself. That surprised me enough that I noticed. Then I stopped noticing. Someone dragged the table back two feet because dancing had become real. Nobody asked. The cards moved with it. A cup spilled. The silver-ringed man swore. A woman stepped onto a bench to sing. Not one of the musicians. Just a woman. People joined. I knew none of the words. Marek reappeared beside me.

"Stand."

"No."

"Dance."

"No."

"You have one leg."

"I am aware."

"Excellent excuse."

"For not dancing."

"For dancing badly."

He grabbed my wrist. I did not move. He pulled. Still no.

"Marek."

"Gregory."

"No."

He let go immediately.

"Fine."

Then danced badly beside me. Not mockingly. Just badly. He had both legs and apparently no plan for either. I laughed. A woman joined him. Then another man. Then Iven. Iven was worse. That helped. I stayed on the stool. My shoulders hurt less now that the crutches leaned against the wall. My hands wrapped around the cup. Someone bumped my right foot. Apologized. Someone else stepped on Marek. Did not apologize. The song sped up. Marek nearly fell. He recovered by grabbing Iven. Iven nearly fell. They both shouted.

The room cheered for reasons unrelated to them. I drank. A second beer appeared. I had not ordered it. I looked around. The server pointed toward the bar. The constable actor from the show raised his cup. I raised mine. Free beer. Marek had been right. Terrible. I drank that one too. Slower. The constable actor came over later.

"Sorry again."

"For arresting me?"

"Trying."

"You got it right tonight."

"Boring."

"Yes."

He leaned on the table.

"My brother saw afternoon. Told everyone I arrested the one-legged shopkeeper."

"You did."

"I know."

"He made it sound intentional?"

"Yes."

"Better story."

He nodded. Then someone called him. He left. No name. I realized I still did not know his name. I could ask later. Or not. The theatre had many people I knew by mistakes. That seemed normal now. The front door opened. Teren came in. The room noticed less than I expected. Our table noticed. Orin lifted his cup.

"Money?"

Teren looked at him.

"You already got paid."

"More?"

"No."

Orin lowered the cup. Teren went to the bar. He did not sit with us. He spoke to the tavern keeper. Then a man I did not know joined him. They talked. Not happily. Not angrily. Business. Marek saw.

"Tomorrow."

"What?"

He pointed.

"Booking."

"How do you know?"

"I don't."

"Then why---"

"Could be debt."

"Whose?"

"Yes."

I stopped asking. Teren eventually got a drink. One. He stood at the end of the bar with it. Nobody dragged him into the party. Maybe because he would refuse. Maybe because they knew better. After a while, Rinna came in. Alone.

She looked around, found Orin, said something in his ear, took his drink, finished it, and left. Orin stared after her.

"What was that?"

The green-scarf woman asked.

"Work."

"What work?"

"Not mine."

He dealt. I liked that answer. Davin arrived perhaps an hour later. Grease on both sleeves now. He came through the door, found us, and sat without removing his coat. Marek put a beer in front of him. Davin drank half.

"Box?" I asked.

He looked at me. I regretted it.

"Dry."

"Good."

He drank the rest. Marek said, "Stay."

"No."

"You just arrived."

"Yes."

"Where are you going?"

"Sleep."

"Coward."

Davin stood.

"Wheel at seven."

"What wheel?"

Davin left. Marek looked at me.

"Local history."

"You don't know either."

"No."

Good. No Serra. I noticed because I was not looking for her. That was probably a lie. I saw yellow at the door once and looked. Different woman. Fine. Lyssa came into my head unexpectedly when a couple near the wall began arguing. Not because they resembled us. They did not.

The woman was short and furious. The man kept eating while she spoke. I thought Lyssa would have hated Marek. Then I thought no, she might like him for twenty minutes. Then hate him. Then maybe like him again. I smiled into my cup. Marek saw.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Woman?"

"Yes."

He looked around.

"Which?"

"Not here."

He understood.

"Oh."

That was all. No teasing. Interesting. Then he stole one of my remaining coins. I slapped his hand.

"Fuck you."

"There he is."

I took the coin back. The music changed again. Slower. People paired off. Some left. Some moved closer. Iven was talking to a man by the window with both hands, serious now. Orin's River House friend had disappeared. The green-scarf woman leaned against Orin's shoulder while still beating him at cards. The silver-ringed man had acquired another deck somehow. Teren was gone. I had not seen him leave. Marek vanished again. This time with the woman who had slapped his shoulder earlier. Maybe.

I saw them go toward the back. Could have been anything. Not mine. I bought food. Fried potatoes. Too salty. Perfect. I paid with show money. That felt better than beer. I ate half. Gave the rest to Iven when he returned.

"Why?"

"I can't finish."

He took them. No ceremony.

"Tomorrow," he said.

"What?"

"Leave after noon."

"For Carrow?"

"No."

I waited. He ate.

"Where?"

"North."

"How far?"

"Day."

"Show?"

"Maybe."

"Maybe?"

"Teren's talking."

"Of course."

Iven ate another potato.

"Could be two nights. Could be nothing."

"When will we know?"

"Before we leave."

"That is not enough time."

"For what?"

I had no answer. Packing. Knowing. Preparing. Apparently none required much.

"What about tomorrow morning?"

"Sleep."

"That I can do."

"Then you're ready."

He left with the potatoes. There. Tomorrow. Not rehearsal. Maybe travel. Maybe another town. Maybe another show. I did not know. The uncertainty bothered me less than it should have. Or maybe the beer helped. I stood carefully. Two beers. Not drunk. Different. My head felt warm. My body was still tired beneath it. My hands had stopped hurting because I was not using them. That would change as soon as I picked up the crutches. I did. Yes. Still tired. Marek returned. His hair was worse.

"River House."

"You're leaving?"

"Eventually."

"You look terrible."

"Successful."

"Different word."

"Same profession."

He had lost money. I knew because he checked his pocket, frowned, checked another, then smiled as though this had been expected.

"How much did you spend?"

"No."

"How much?"

"No."

"Do you know?"

He thought.

"No."

I laughed. He pointed at me.

"New man laughs."

"Old man loses money."

"I am twenty-four."

"Ancient."

"Cruel."

We found Iven near the door. Orin refused to leave.

"Winning," he said.

The green-scarf woman said, "Losing."

"Strategically."

We left him. Outside, the river air hit cold. Good. The street had emptied some. Not much. People still moved between taverns. A cart rattled over stones. Somewhere upriver, somebody sang badly without accompaniment. Iven walked ahead. Marek walked beside me for half a block, then stopped to talk to a man sitting on a windowsill. I kept going. He caught up.

"Who was that?" I asked.

"No idea."

"You stopped."

"He knew me."

"Did you know him?"

"Now."

That might have been true. River House appeared after one wrong turn. Marek blamed Iven. Iven had not been with us for the wrong turn. He had gone the correct way. We found him at the front door.

"Idiots."

"Traitor," Marek said.

Inside, the desk woman looked at us.

"No singing."

"We are not singing," Marek said.

"No fighting."

"We are friends."

She looked at me. I said, "Probably."

"No breaking furniture."

Marek looked offended.

"That was the hall."

Her eyes narrowed. We went upstairs. Room one was dark. Pell was asleep. Or unconscious. Hard to tell. I moved quietly. Not carefully. Different. My purse went beneath my folded trousers. Then I took it back out. Counted what remained. Two show payments. Minus beer. Minus cards. Minus food. Still most of it. Good. I put it away. I washed my face. Cleaned up enough. Checked my leg. Fine. Too tired for anything more complicated. Pell spoke from the dark.

"Red."

I froze.

"What?"

"Dress."

"Are you awake?"

"No."

"Is it done?"

"No."

Then he snored. Fine. I lay down. The room moved slightly when I closed my eyes. Not spinning. Considering it. I opened them. Waited. Closed them again. Better. Downstairs, someone laughed. A door shut. Footsteps crossed the hall. Then more footsteps. The troupe had not all come home. Maybe some would not. Tomorrow after noon we might leave north. Maybe for another show. Maybe not. I had no idea what the town was called. That seemed like information I should possess. I could ask in the morning.

I thought about the money beneath my trousers. Not all of it. Most. Enough. I had spent some because I wanted to. Beer. Cards. Potatoes. Stupid things. Mine. I smiled in the dark. Then somebody in the next room began snoring hard enough to shake the wall. I threw a pillow at it. The wall did not care. Pell did not wake. I laughed once. Quietly. Then slept.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# CHAPTER 154

## THE VISITOR

Someone was hammering inside my skull. I opened my eyes. The hammer stopped. A second later it started again. Not my skull. Outside. Somewhere below the window, metal struck metal three times, paused, then struck twice more. Pell was already awake. That offended me.

He sat on the edge of his bed with the red dress across his knees and a needle between his teeth.

"What time is it?"

He took the needle out.

"Morning."

"Useful."

"You asked."

My mouth tasted like old beer and sleep. My shoulders had stiffened overnight. Both hands felt thick when I flexed them. Nothing terrible. Just everything reminding me it had been used yesterday. Pell bent over the dress.

"You came in loud."

"I did not."

"You argued with the wall."

"The wall was snoring."

"That was room two."

"Then room two was snoring through the wall."

Pell considered.

"Fair."

I sat up. The room moved exactly once. Then stopped. Good. Two beers. Apparently two beers had opinions. I drank from the water cup beside the bed. Warm. Excellent.

"Did you finish it?"

Pell looked down at the red dress.

"No."

"You were working on it when I went out."

"Nessa was."

"You were asleep when I came back."

"Yes."

"And now you're working on it."

"Yes."

"When do you stop?"

"When it stops being wrong."

"That sounds dangerous."

He put the needle back between his teeth. I got dressed. My residual limb was warm but normal. The wrapping had shifted slightly overnight. I redid it before standing. No problem. My hands objected to the crutches. They lost. Downstairs, River House had become a collection of consequences. Marek was facedown on a table. Not asleep. I knew because when I entered he lifted one finger.

"Water."

A pitcher sat six inches from his hand. I pushed it closer. He did not move.

"Closer."

"It is touching you."

"Cruel."

I poured a cup and put it beside his head. He turned enough to drink without sitting up.

"Thank you."

"You spent all your money?"

"No."

"How much is left?"

He closed his eyes.

"Do not attack me."

"I asked a question."

"Violence."

Iven sat by the window eating eggs. He looked fine. I disliked him for that.

"You drank more than I did."

"Yes."

"Why are you fine?"

"I am older."

"That should make it worse."

"Experience."

"No."

"Water."

"I drank water."

"More."

I got breakfast. Eggs, bread, something fried, more water. Orin was absent. Serra was absent. Teren was absent. Rinna came through the front door while I ate, carrying a small paper packet and three lengths of cord. She looked as though she had been awake for hours.

"Morning," I said.

She looked at me.

"Is it?"

Then she went upstairs. Marek lifted his head.

"Rinna."

She did not turn.

"Rinna."

Nothing.

"Rinna, I require medical aid."

From upstairs:

"Die quietly."
